An office is the place where an organisation's information is created, recorded, stored and moved. Every business, school, hospital and government body has one, because somebody has to receive the letter, keep the file, write the report and pay the bill. This unit explains how that work is managed and what rules make it orderly. You will meet the meaning and importance of office management, how an office should be laid out, how a piece of work travels through the office as a *procedure*, and the four everyday documents of an office — the noting, the draft, the report and the order. Then you will learn how papers are kept after the work is over: filing, indexing and the safe disposal of old records.

## Chapter summary

- An **office** is where information is received, recorded, arranged and supplied; **office management** is planning, organising, directing, coordinating and controlling that work efficiently and economically.
- The **areas** of office management are personnel, layout and environment, machines and equipment, records, forms and stationery, communication, and routine financial work.
- **Office layout** arranges space for straight-line flow, minimum movement, light, space, flexibility, supervision and safety. **Open** layout is cheap and easy to supervise but noisy and public; **closed** layout is private and quiet but costly; most offices use a **mixed** plan.
- An **office procedure** is the fixed sequence for one kind of work: receipt, sorting, recording, action, noting and drafting, approval, dispatch, follow-up. It must be simple, economical, flexible, written and reviewed.
- A **noting** is the internal record of facts, rules, views and a proposal, written for the deciding officer. A **draft** is the outgoing letter, prepared in final form, with the seven standard parts and one subject only.
- A **report** states terms of reference, method, findings, conclusions and practical recommendations. An **office order** instructs staff; a **toc order** is the day-book entry by which every paper handled is traceable.
- **Filing** keeps documents safe and traceable. It must be simple, prompt, economical, flexible, safe, accessible and compact.
- Filing is done by **method** (horizontal, vertical, lateral, suspension) and by **classification** (alphabetical, numerical, alphanumerical, chronological, subject, geographical, decimal, colour). The choice must fit the query the office must answer.
- Filing may be **centralised** (one record room, cheap, easy to control, slower for distant departments) or **decentralised** (fast locally, duplicated cost); most offices use both.
- **Indexing** tells where a record is kept and is what makes numerical filing usable. Card, visible, strip, loose-leaf and computer indexes are the common forms.
- **Records management** fixes the retention period for each class of record and provides for safe retention, transfer, conversion or destruction, with fire, water and carelessness as the real enemies.

chapters.question_answers:
## Choosing a layout

**Problem.** A municipal office has 12 clerks in one hall and 3 officers who handle land-revenue records. The clerks complain of noise; the officers complain that confidential files are read over their shoulders. Rent is limited. Which layout do you advise?

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Identify the conflicting needs. Clerks: many people, routine repetitive work, need supervision and quick paper movement, noise is tolerable. Officers: few people, confidential and varied work, need quiet and privacy.
Step 2 — Match layout to need. Routine mass work suits an **open plan**; confidential individual work suits a **closed cabin**.
Step 3 — Combine within the budget. Keep the 12 clerks in the **open hall** (cheap, well supervised) and give the 3 officers **screened cubicles along one wall**, not full rooms. This is a **mixed layout**.
Step 4 — Add the principles: the record room is placed next to the officers' cubicles, the public counter next to the entrance, and the photocopier at the far end away from both.
**Answer.** A mixed layout — open hall for the clerks, screened cubicles for the confidential work.

## Which classification?

**Problem.** A district survey office files by the name of the landowner. As the district is subdivided, several owners now have identical names, and clerks frequently pull the wrong file. The office also needs to answer questions such as "how many plots of arable land in ward 4 were registered last year?", which the present system cannot answer at all. Suggest a better classification and say why.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Diagnose. Alphabetical filing by a **non-unique key** (a name shared by many people) causes collisions. It also carries no geographic or subject information, so a ward-wise query cannot be answered.
Step 2 — Choose a rule that gives every plot a unique key and groups related plots. A **numerical** file number based on the *plot number* with a **geographical** prefix for the ward is unique by construction: ward 4, plot 218, file number 4/218.
Step 3 — Add the link back to the name. Keep an **index** from owner name to file number, updated whenever land is transferred.
Step 4 — Check the objectives: simplicity (a clerk can use it), prompt location (the number is unique), economy (no extra cabinets), flexibility (new wards get a new prefix), safety and easy cross-reference (a sale touches two plots; the file notes both).
**Answer.** Replace alphabetical filing with a geographical-plus-numerical system (ward number / plot number), retaining a name index.

## How long is each record kept?

**Problem.** A village municipality is clearing its record room and has to decide what to do with each of the following. Advise the office, giving a reason in each case. (a) The cash book and the annual financial statements for the last 12 years. (b) Paid vouchers and bills for the last 8 years that have already been audited. (c) Correspondence about a street-light repair completed five years ago. (d) Land ownership and plot maps of the whole municipality. (e) A tender file for a road contract that was completed last month but carries a two-year defect liability period.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Apply the rule: the retention period follows **legal and audit need**, not the age of the paper.
Step 2 — (a) Cash books and annual statements are permanent records of accountability — **retain permanently**.
Step 3 — (b) Vouchers supporting audited accounts are usually kept five to ten years; at eight years and already audited, they may be **transferred to the record room and disposed of under a written disposal order** once the period fixed by the prescribed authority has run.
Step 4 — (c) Routine correspondence is kept two to five years — **due for disposal** after making sure no dispute or claim is pending.
Step 5 — (d) Title and property documents are **permanent**; they must never be destroyed.
Step 6 — (e) The contract file must remain until the defect liability period expires, because a claim can still arise — **retain for at least two more years**.

**Answer.** (a) permanent, (b) dispose after the fixed period and a written order, (c) dispose, (d) permanent, (e) retain until the liability period ends.
**What it means.** Two rules decide every case: keep what the law and the audit require, and destroy nothing that forms part of an audited account without the written permission of the prescribed authority.

chapters.summary:
- A **financial institution** collects money from savers and lends or invests it for borrowers, matching different maturities and carrying risk. It is either **banking** (central bank, commercial banks, development banks, finance companies, microfinance institutions) or **non-banking** (insurance, provident fund, CIT, mutual funds, cooperatives).
- A **bank** accepts deposits, lends, and provides payment services, and it **creates credit** when it lends. Its income is the spread between deposit and lending rates plus fees.
- A **central bank** is the apex institution. **Nepal Rastra Bank** was established on 26 April 1956 A.D. (2013 B.S.).
- The central bank **issues currency, acts as banker to the government and to the banks, is the lender of last resort, makes monetary policy, manages foreign exchange, supervises the banks and financial institutions, runs the clearing house** and promotes the financial sector.
- A **commercial bank's** primary functions are accepting deposits (savings, current, fixed, recurring), advancing loans (cash credit, overdraft, demand loan, term loan, bill discounting) and credit creation. Its agency and general utility functions include collection and payment, safe custody, drafts and pay orders, cards, mobile banking, remittance and foreign exchange.
- **Development banks** give medium and long-term project finance; **finance companies** do hire purchase, lease, housing and consumer credit; **microfinance institutions** lend small amounts to groups of poor households.
- **Insurance** is a contract under which the insurer pays on a stated event in return for a premium. It works by **pooling risk**. Life insurance covers human life; non-life covers fire, marine, motor, health, accident, crop and livestock. **Beema Samiti** is the regulator.
- A **financial cooperative** is member-owned and lends to its members; **banking instruments** are the cheque, draft, pay order, traveller's cheque, letter of credit, debit card, credit card and mobile/internet banking.
- A **cheque** may be open (bearer), order or **crossed**; crossing means it can only be credited to an account and is the ordinary safety device.
- **Remittance** is money sent home by migrant workers; it is one of Nepal's largest sources of foreign exchange. Formal channels are safer and legal; *hundi* is illegal.
- The **money market** trades funds and securities of up to one year (treasury bills, call money); the **capital market** trades long-term securities (shares, debentures, bonds) on NEPSE under SEBON; the **commodity market** trades goods such as gold, silver and agricultural produce.

chapters.question_answers:
## How much money can a bank create?

**Problem.** A commercial bank receives a new deposit of Rs. 50,000. The cash reserve ratio fixed by Nepal Rastra Bank is 10 per cent, and the bank lends out everything it is allowed to. Find (a) the amount of the first loan, (b) the total deposits the banking system can create from this deposit, and (c) the credit multiplier.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — The bank must keep 10 % of Rs. 50,000 as reserve: $0.10 \times 50{,}000 = Rs.\ 5{,}000$.
Step 2 — It may lend the rest: $50{,}000 - 5{,}000 = Rs.\ 45{,}000$. That is the first loan, and once it is spent and re-deposited it becomes a new deposit.
Step 3 — The same process repeats with each new deposit, so the total deposits are the original deposit times the multiplier.
Step 4 — Credit multiplier $= \frac{1}{\text{cash reserve ratio}} = \frac{1}{0.10} = 10$.
Step 5 — Total deposits $= 50{,}000 \times 10 = Rs.\ 5{,}00{,}000$.

**Answer.** First loan Rs. 45,000; total deposits Rs. 5,00,000; multiplier 10.
**What it means.** One rupee of new reserve supports ten rupees of deposits. If NRB raised the reserve ratio to 12.5 per cent, the same Rs. 50,000 would support only Rs. 4,00,000 — which is exactly how a central bank squeezes credit out of the system.

## Is there an insurable interest?

**Problem.** Decide, giving a reason, whether each of the following can take out a valid insurance policy: (a) a shopkeeper insuring his own stock against fire; (b) a man insuring his neighbour's house against fire; (c) a bank insuring the building it has lent money against; (d) a trader insuring a consignment of goods he has already sold and delivered.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — State the test. Insurance requires an **insurable interest**: the person must gain by the safety of the thing insured and lose by its destruction.
Step 2 — Apply the test to each.
(a) The shopkeeper owns the stock, so he loses if it burns — **valid**.
(b) The neighbour loses nothing if the house burns — **not valid**; this would be a wager, not insurance.
(c) The bank has lent money on the building, so its security is at risk — **valid**, to the extent of its interest.
(d) The goods are already sold and delivered; the trader loses nothing — **not valid**.

**Answer.** (a) valid, (b) invalid, (c) valid, (d) invalid.
**What it means.** Insurance restores a loss, it never creates a profit. That is why the insured can never recover more than the actual loss — the principle of indemnity.

## Which market, and how much does the family get?

**Problem.** (a) A commercial bank has Rs. 2 crore of surplus cash that it can lend for seven days. In which market will it lend? (b) A hydro company needs Rs. 5 crore for ten years to build a plant. From which market will it raise the money? (c) A migrant worker in Qatar sends Rs. 1,20,000 home. The bank charges a service fee of Rs. 500 and the exchange rate is Rs. 160 to one riyal. How many riyals did he send?

**Solution.**
Step 1 — (a) Seven days is under one year, so this is a **money market** transaction — an inter-bank (call money) loan.
Step 2 — (b) Ten years is over one year, so the company raises it from the **capital market** — shares, debentures or a long-term loan.
Step 3 — (c) The amount the family receives plus the fee is what was sent in rupees: $1{,}20{,}000 + 500 = Rs.\ 1{,}20{,}500$.
Step 4 — Convert at the given rate: $1{,}20{,}500 \div 160 = 753.125$ riyals.

**Answer.** (a) money market; (b) capital market; (c) 753.125 riyals.
**What it means.** Maturity decides the market; and every remittance has a price — the service fee and the exchange rate together decide what actually reaches the family.

Step 2 — (b) Ten years is over one year, so the company raises it from the **capital market** — shares, debentures or a long-term loan.
Step 3 — (c) The amount the family receives plus the fee is what was sent in rupees: $1{,}20{,}000 + 500 = Rs.\ 1{,}20{,}500$.
Step 4 — Convert at the given rate: $1{,}20{,}500 \div 160 = 753.125$ riyals.

**Answer.** (a) money market; (b) capital market; (c) 753.125 riyals.
**What it means.** Maturity decides the market; and every remittance has a price — the service fee and the exchange rate together decide what actually reaches the family.

A government cannot run on goodwill. This unit explains where revenue comes from, what a tax is and what makes a good tax, how taxes are classified, and then two things every office worker in Nepal must know in practice — the **Permanent Account Number (PAN)** and **Value Added Tax (VAT)**.

## Chapter summary

- **Revenue** is the income a government raises for public expenditure. It is **tax revenue** (compulsory, no direct return) or **non-tax revenue** (fees, fines, royalties, dividends, interest, rent, grants). In Nepal more than 85 % of revenue comes from taxes.

- Adam Smith's **canons**: equality (ability to pay), certainty, convenience and economy; modern writers add simplicity, flexibility, elasticity and neutrality.
- **Objectives of taxation**: revenue, redistribution of income, control of inflation, protection of domestic industry, discouragement of harmful consumption, encouragement of saving and investment, and balanced regional development.
- **Direct tax** is borne by the person on whom it is legally imposed and cannot be shifted (income tax, house and land tax, capital gains tax). **Indirect tax** is shifted to the final consumer (VAT, excise, customs).
- **PAN** is a unique **nine-digit**, permanent number issued by the **Inland Revenue Department**. It is compulsory for industry, trade, business, profession and employment. It is a **personal PAN** for an individual and a **business PAN** for a firm or company, and it must be quoted in bank transactions and in bills.
- **VAT** is an indirect tax on the value added at each stage of production and distribution. In Nepal it has applied from **1 Mangsir 2054 B.S.**, under the **VAT Act, 2052** and **VAT Rules, 2053**, at a single rate of **13 per cent**.

chapters.question_answers:
## The VAT chain, step by step

**Problem.** A producer makes goods worth Rs. 1,00,000 and sells them to a wholesaler for Rs. 1,00,000 plus VAT. The wholesaler sells the same goods to a retailer for Rs. 1,20,000 plus VAT, and the retailer sells them to the final consumer for Rs. 1,30,000 plus VAT. The rate of VAT is 13 per cent. Find the VAT each of the three dealers deposits and the total VAT the government receives. Show that this equals the VAT on the final sale price.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Write down each dealer's sale and purchase and compute output and input tax.
Step 2 — **Producer:** output tax $= 13\% \times 1{,}00{,}000 = Rs.\ 13{,}000$; input tax $= 0$; tax deposited $= 13{,}000 - 0 = Rs.\ 13{,}000$.
Step 3 — **Wholesaler:** sale Rs. 1,20,000; output tax $= 13\% \times 1{,}20{,}000 = Rs.\ 15{,}600$; input tax $= Rs.\ 13{,}000$; tax deposited $= 15{,}600 - 13{,}000 = Rs.\ 2{,}600$.
Step 4 — **Retailer:** sale Rs. 1,30,000; output tax $= 13\% \times 1{,}30{,}000 = Rs.\ 16{,}900$; input tax $= Rs.\ 15{,}600$; tax deposited $= 16{,}900 - 15{,}600 = Rs.\ 1{,}300$.
Step 5 — Total deposited $= 13{,}000 + 2{,}600 + 1{,}300 = Rs.\ 16{,}900$.
Step 6 — Check: $13\% \times 1{,}30{,}000 = Rs.\ 16{,}900$. Equal.

| Stage | Sale price (Rs.) | Value added (Rs.) | Output tax (Rs.) | Input tax (Rs.) | Tax deposited (Rs.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Producer | 1,00,000 | 1,00,000 | 13,000 | — | 13,000 |
| Wholesaler | 1,20,000 | 20,000 | 15,600 | 13,000 | 2,600 |
| Retailer | 1,30,000 | 10,000 | 16,900 | 15,600 | 1,300 |
| **Total** | | **1,30,000** | | | **16,900** |

**Answer.** Producer Rs. 13,000, wholesaler Rs. 2,600, retailer Rs. 1,300; total Rs. 16,900, which is exactly 13 % of the final price of Rs. 1,30,000.
**What it means.** The final consumer bears the whole tax, but no dealer bears more than 13 % of the value he himself added. The tax is collected in instalments along the chain, which is why VAT is difficult to evade.

## Direct tax on a salary

**Problem.** An employee's annual salary is Rs. 6,00,000. The tax-free threshold is Rs. 5,00,000 and the amount above it is taxed at 10 per cent. Find the tax payable and state whether the tax is direct or indirect, with a reason.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Taxable income = salary − threshold $= 6{,}00{,}000 - 5{,}00{,}000 = Rs.\ 1{,}00{,}000$.
Step 2 — Tax $= 10\% \times 1{,}00{,}000 = Rs.\ 10{,}000$.
Step 3 — Classify. The employee who earns the salary is the person who pays the tax and he cannot pass the burden to anybody else.

**Answer.** Rs. 10,000; **direct tax**, because it is imposed on, and borne by, the same person.

## Tax and non-tax revenue

**Problem.** A municipality expects the following receipts in a year: house and land tax Rs. 40,00,000; business tax Rs. 15,00,000; building-permit fees Rs. 8,00,000; fines for illegal construction Rs. 2,00,000; dividend from a municipal enterprise Rs. 5,00,000; and a grant from the provincial government Rs. 30,00,000. Find the total revenue, the tax revenue and the non-tax revenue, and the share of tax revenue.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Tax revenue $= 40{,}00{,}000 + 15{,}00{,}000 = Rs.\ 55{,}00{,}000$.
Step 2 — Non-tax revenue $= 8{,}00{,}000 + 2{,}00{,}000 + 5{,}00{,}000 + 30{,}00{,}000 = Rs.\ 45{,}00{,}000$.
Step 3 — Total revenue $= 55{,}00{,}000 + 45{,}00{,}000 = Rs.\ 1{,}00{,}00{,}000$.
Step 4 — Share of tax revenue $= \frac{55{,}00{,}000}{1{,}00{,}00{,}000} \times 100 = 55\%$.

**Answer.** Total Rs. 1,00,00,000; tax Rs. 55,00,000; non-tax Rs. 45,00,000; tax share 55 %.
**What it means.** A local body that raises only 55 % of its money from its own taxes depends heavily on money from above — which is exactly why local governments are pressed to widen their own tax base.

chapters.summary:
- **Accounting** identifies, measures, records, classifies, summarises and communicates economic information. The **accounting cycle** runs: record in the journal, post to the ledger, take a trial balance, adjust and rectify, prepare the final accounts, communicate.
- **Financial accounting** records transactions with outsiders and reports profit or loss and financial position; **cost accounting** finds the cost per unit; **management accounting** supplies whatever information managers need. **Book-keeping** is only the recording stage; **accountancy** is the whole body of knowledge.
- The **accounting equation** is $Assets = Liabilities + Capital$; every transaction keeps it true, which is what double entry means.
- **Rules of debit and credit**: assets and expenses increase on the debit side; liabilities, capital and income increase on the credit side.
- **Objectives of financial accounting**: systematic record, profit or loss, financial position, control, evidence for tax and audit, communication. Its users are internal (owners, management, employees) and external (banks, creditors, government, investors, auditors, public).
- An **accounting standard** is a written rule on how to recognise, measure, present and disclose transactions; it makes statements **comparable, consistent and reliable**.
- In Nepal standards are issued by **ICAN** through its **Accounting Standards Board**: **NFRS** for listed and large entities, **NFRS for SMEs** for smaller ones, and the older **NAS** for the rest.
- A **chart of accounts** is the numbered list of all account heads, arranged in the five groups — assets, liabilities, capital, income and expenses. It gives every head one name and one code.
- A Nepali **government office** uses the uniform chart of accounts prescribed by the Financial Comptroller General Office, so that the accounts of every office can be added up.

## Chapter summary

- **Financial accounting** records transactions with outsiders and reports profit or loss and financial position; **cost accounting** finds the cost per unit; **management accounting** supplies whatever information managers need. **Book-keeping** is only the recording stage; **accountancy** is the whole body of knowledge.
- The **accounting equation** is $Assets = Liabilities + Capital$; every transaction keeps it true, which is what double entry means.
- **Rules of debit and credit**: assets and expenses increase on the debit side; liabilities, capital and income increase on the credit side.
- **Objectives of financial accounting**: systematic record, profit or loss, financial position, control, evidence for tax and audit, communication. Its users are internal (owners, management, employees) and external (banks, creditors, government, investors, auditors, public).
- An **accounting standard** is a written rule on how to recognise, measure, present and disclose transactions; it makes statements **comparable, consistent and reliable**.
- In Nepal standards are issued by **ICAN** through its **Accounting Standards Board**: **NFRS** for listed and large entities, **NFRS for SMEs** for smaller ones, and the older **NAS** for the rest.
- A **chart of accounts** is the numbered list of all account heads, arranged in the five groups — assets, liabilities, capital, income and expenses. It gives every head one name and one code.

chapters.question_answers:
## Does the equation still balance?

**Problem.** A trader starts a business with Rs. 5,00,000 of his own money. He takes a bank loan of Rs. 2,00,000. He buys furniture for Rs. 1,50,000 in cash and goods for resale for Rs. 3,00,000 on credit. Show the accounting equation after each transaction.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Cash Rs. 5,00,000 = Capital Rs. 5,00,000: $5{,}00{,}000 = 0 + 5{,}00{,}000$.
Step 2 — Add loan: cash becomes $5{,}00{,}000 + 2{,}00{,}000 = Rs.\ 7{,}00{,}000$; liabilities Rs. 2,00,000. $7{,}00{,}000 = 2{,}00{,}000 + 5{,}00{,}000$. ✔
Step 3 — Buy furniture for cash: cash $= 7{,}00{,}000 - 1{,}50{,}000 = Rs.\ 5{,}50{,}000$; furniture Rs. 1,50{,}000. Total assets $= 5{,}50{,}000 + 1{,}50{,}000 = Rs.\ 7{,}00{,}000$. $7{,}00{,}000 = 2{,}00{,}000 + 5{,}00{,}000$. ✔
Step 4 — Buy goods on credit: stock Rs. 3,00,000, creditors Rs. 3,00,000. Total assets $= 5{,}50{,}000 + 1{,}50{,}000 + 3{,}00{,}000 = Rs.\ 10{,}00{,}000$; right side $= (2{,}00{,}000 + 3{,}00{,}000) + 5{,}00{,}000 = Rs.\ 10{,}00{,}000$. Balanced.

**Answer.** After all four transactions: assets Rs. 10,00,000, liabilities Rs. 5,00,000, capital Rs. 5,00,000. The equation holds after every single transaction.

## Give the head and the code

**Problem.** Name the main group and suggest a suitable code for each of the following, using the scheme in the figure: (a) cash in hand, (b) a loan taken from Rastriya Banijya Bank, (c) salary paid to staff, (d) commission received, (e) goods bought for resale, (f) amount owed to a supplier.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Decide, in each case, whether the item is something the business owns (asset), owes (liability), the owner's claim (capital), money coming in (income) or money going out (expense).
Step 2 — (a) cash in hand — the business owns it — **asset, 1000**.
Step 3 — (b) bank loan — the business owes it — **liability, 2100**.
Step 4 — (c) salary paid — an expense of running the business — **expense, 5100**.
Step 5 — (d) commission received — income — **income, 4100**.
Step 6 — (e) goods bought for resale — these are stock, which the business owns — **asset (stock), 1300**; and at the moment of purchase the same transaction is a **purchase, expense group 5000** when the periodic system is used.
Step 7 — (f) amount owed to a supplier — **liability, 2000 (creditors)**.

**Answer.** (a) asset 1000, (b) liability 2100, (c) expense 5100, (d) income 4100, (e) stock 1300 / purchase 5000, (f) liability 2000.
**What it means.** The five groups are decided by asking one question: does the item make the business richer (asset or income) or poorer (liability, capital withdrawal or expense)? The code simply files the answer.

## Journal entry to the ledger head

**Problem.** A firm bought office furniture for Rs. 60,000, paying Rs. 20,000 in cash and agreeing to pay the balance next month. Which accounts are affected and which is debited and which is credited?

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Identify the accounts: furniture (asset), cash (asset), creditor (liability).
Step 2 — Furniture increases: an asset increasing is **debited** → Furniture A/c Dr. Rs. 60,000.
Step 3 — Cash decreases: an asset decreasing is **credited** → Cash A/c Cr. Rs. 20,000.
Step 4 — Creditors increase: a liability increasing is **credited** → Creditor A/c Cr. Rs. 40,000.
Step 5 — Check the equation: assets rise by $60{,}000 - 20{,}000 = 40{,}000$, liabilities rise by Rs. 40,000. Balanced.

**Answer.**
Furniture A/c Dr. 60,000
To Cash A/c 20,000
To Creditor A/c 40,000
(Being furniture purchased for cash and on credit.)

chapters.name: Bank Reconciliation Statement (बैंक हिसाब मिलान)
topics: Bank reconciliation statement: meaning, need and causes of difference
Effect of transactions on the cash book and on the passbook
Preparing a bank reconciliation statement from the cash book balance
Preparing a bank reconciliation statement from the passbook balance
Adjusted cash book method and treatment of bank charges, interest and dishonoured cheques
chapters.summary:
- A **bank reconciliation statement** explains, on a given date, the difference between the bank column of the **cash book** and the **passbook**, and makes the two agree.
- The cash book is the trader's record, written when a cheque is issued or received; the passbook is the bank's record, written when the cheque actually reaches the bank. A **debit** balance in the cash book is a **credit** balance in the passbook.
- Its **need**: to check accuracy, to find the true bank balance, to detect dishonoured cheques and unauthorised charges, to prepare the balance sheet, to prevent fraud and to satisfy the auditor.
- **Causes of difference**: cheques issued but not presented; cheques deposited but not collected; items recorded by the bank only (bank charges, interest, collection of dividends, direct deposits, standing instructions, dishonoured cheques); and errors in either book.
- Working from the **cash book** balance: **add** cheques issued but not presented, interest and dividends collected by the bank, direct deposits and wrong credits by the bank; **less** cheques deposited but not collected, bank charges and interest on overdraft, dishonoured cheques, standing instructions and wrong debits by the bank.
- Working from the **passbook** balance reverses every item. Where either balance is an **overdraft**, reason out each item instead of using the list.

## Topics to cover

- Bank reconciliation statement: meaning, need and causes of difference
- Effect of transactions on the cash book and on the passbook
- Preparing a bank reconciliation statement from the cash book balance
- Preparing a bank reconciliation statement from the passbook balance
- Adjusted cash book method and treatment of bank charges, interest and dishonoured cheques
- Adjusted cash book method

A trader keeps a **cash book** with a bank column. The bank keeps its own record of the same account, and sends the trader a **passbook** or a bank statement. In theory the two balances should be identical, because they are two records of one account. In practice they hardly ever are, and the reason is almost never a mistake — it is **time**. A cheque written today may reach the bank five days later. This unit explains why the two balances differ, how to write the **bank reconciliation statement** that explains the difference, and how to adjust the cash book when the bank has done something the trader has not yet recorded.

## Chapter summary

- A **bank reconciliation statement** explains, on a given date, the difference between the bank column of the **cash book** and the **passbook**, and makes the two agree.
- The cash book is the trader's record, written when a cheque is issued or received; the passbook is the bank's record, written when the cheque actually reaches the bank. A **debit** balance in the cash book is a **credit** balance in the passbook.
- Its **need**: to check accuracy, to find the true bank balance, to detect dishonoured cheques and unauthorised charges, to prepare the balance sheet, to prevent fraud and to satisfy the auditor.
- **Causes of difference**: cheques issued but not presented; cheques deposited but not collected; items recorded by the bank only (bank charges, interest, collection of dividends, direct deposits, standing instructions, dishonoured cheques); and errors in either book.
- Working from the **cash book** balance: **add** cheques issued but not presented, interest and dividends collected by the bank, direct deposits and wrong credits by the bank; **less** cheques deposited but not collected, bank charges and interest on overdraft, dishonoured cheques, standing instructions and wrong debits by the bank.
- Working from the **passbook** balance reverses every item. Where either balance is an **overdraft**, reason out each item instead of using the list.
- In the **adjusted cash book method**, items appearing only in the passbook are first entered in the cash book to find an adjusted balance; then the reconciliation is drawn using only the timing differences — cheques issued but not presented (add) and cheques deposited but not collected (less) — and any uncorrected error.

chapters.question_answers:
## From the cash book balance

**Problem.** From the following particulars of a trader as on 30 Chaitra, prepare a bank reconciliation statement.

i. Cash book showed a bank balance of Rs. 50,000 (debit).
ii. A cheque of Rs. 12,000 was issued but not presented for payment.
iii. A cheque of Rs. 8,000 was deposited but not collected by the bank.
iv. Bank charges of Rs. 1,500 were debited only in the passbook.
v. Interest on investment of Rs. 6,000 was collected by the bank and appears only in the passbook.
vi. A customer directly deposited Rs. 9,000 into the bank, not recorded in the cash book.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Start with the cash book balance: Rs. 50,000.
Step 2 — Cheque issued but not presented (ii): the trader has already reduced his book, the bank has not, so the bank's balance is higher → **add Rs. 12,000**.
Step 3 — Interest collected by the bank (v): this increases the bank balance and is missing from the cash book → **add Rs. 6,000**.
Step 4 — Customer's direct deposit (vi): same reasoning → **add Rs. 9,000**.
Step 5 — Cheque deposited but not collected (iii): the trader has already increased his book, the bank has not → **less Rs. 8,000**.
Step 6 — Bank charges (iv): the bank has reduced the balance, the trader does not know → **less Rs. 1,500**.
Step 7 — Total the two sides.

| Particulars | Amount (Rs.) | Amount (Rs.) |
|---|---|---|
| Balance as per cash book | | 50,000 |
| Add: cheque issued but not presented | 12,000 | |
| Add: interest on investment collected by the bank | 6,000 | |
| Add: amount deposited directly by a customer | 9,000 | 27,000 |
| | | 77,000 |
| Less: cheque deposited but not collected | 8,000 | |
| Less: bank charges debited by the bank | 1,500 | 9,500 |
| **Balance as per passbook** | | **67,500** |

**Answer.** Balance as per passbook Rs. 67,500.

## From the passbook balance

**Problem.** On 31 Ashad the passbook of a firm showed a credit balance of Rs. 40,000. Prepare a bank reconciliation statement from the following.
i. Cheques issued but not presented for payment: Rs. 15,000.
ii. Cheques deposited but not collected: Rs. 7,000.
iii. Bank charges not entered in the cash book: Rs. 500.
iv. Interest allowed by the bank: Rs. 2,500.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Start with the passbook balance Rs. 40,000.
Step 2 — Cheques deposited but not collected (ii): the trader has already added them in his book, the bank has not credited them, so the **cash book balance is higher** by Rs. 7,000 → add.
Step 3 — Bank charges (iii): the bank has reduced the passbook, the trader's book still shows the higher figure → the cash book balance is higher by Rs. 500 → add.
Step 4 — Cheques issued but not presented (i): the trader has reduced his book, the bank has not → the **cash book balance is lower** by Rs. 15,000 → less.
Step 5 — Interest allowed (iv): the bank has added it, the trader has not → the cash book balance is lower by Rs. 2,500 → less.
Step 6 — Total.

| Particulars | Amount (Rs.) | Amount (Rs.) |
|---|---|---|
| Balance as per passbook | | 40,000 |
| Add: cheques deposited but not collected | 7,000 | |
| Add: bank charges not entered in the cash book | 500 | 7,500 |
| | | 47,500 |
| Less: cheques issued but not presented | 15,000 | |
| Less: interest allowed by the bank | 2,500 | 17,500 |
| **Balance as per cash book** | | **30,000** |

**Answer.** Balance as per cash book Rs. 30,000 (debit).

## Adjusted cash book and a short statement

**Problem.** The cash book of Sita Traders showed a bank balance of Rs. 36,000 on 31 Chaitra. On comparing it with the passbook the following were found.
i. Bank charges Rs. 400 and interest on overdraft Rs. 1,100 had been debited by the bank only.
ii. A customer had deposited Rs. 5,000 directly into the bank.
iii. A cheque of Rs. 3,000 deposited earlier had been dishonoured.
iv. Cheques of Rs. 14,000 issued were not presented for payment; cheques of Rs. 6,000 deposited were not yet collected.
Prepare the adjusted cash book and the bank reconciliation statement.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Identify the items that appear only in the passbook: (i), (ii) and (iii). These adjust the cash book.
Step 2 — Identify the items that are timing differences: (iv). These stay in the reconciliation.

*Adjusted cash book (bank column)*

| Particulars | Amount (Rs.) | Particulars | Amount (Rs.) |
|---|---|---|---|
| To Balance b/d | 36,000 | By Bank charges | 400 |
| To Customer's direct deposit | 5,000 | By Interest on overdraft | 1,100 |
| | | By Cheque dishonoured | 3,000 |
| | | By Balance c/d (adjusted) | 36,500 |
| **Total** | **41,000** | **Total** | **41,000** |

Step 3 — Adjusted cash book balance $= 41{,}000 - 4{,}500 = Rs.\ 36{,}500$.
Step 4 — Prepare the reconciliation from Rs. 36,500.

*Bank reconciliation statement as on 31 Chaitra*

| Particulars | Amount (Rs.) | Amount (Rs.) |
|---|---|---|
| Balance as per adjusted cash book | | 36,500 |
| Add: cheques issued but not presented | | 14,000 |
| | | 50,500 |
| Less: cheques deposited but not collected | | 6,000 |
| **Balance as per passbook** | | **44,500** |

**Answer.** Adjusted cash book balance Rs. 36,500; balance as per passbook Rs. 44,500.
**What it means.** Only the two timing items now separate the books. Every genuine difference — the charges, the interest, the direct deposit and the dishonoured cheque — has been brought into the trader's own record, so the cash book now shows what the bank balance really is.

chapters.name: Accounting Errors (लेखात्मक गल्तीहरू)
topics: Types of errors: errors of principle, omission, commission, compensating errors
Detection of errors through the trial balance
Rectification of errors before and after the trial balance
Suspense account (उज्राती खाता): meaning, preparation and use
chapters.summary:
- An **accounting error** is a mistake in recording, posting, casting, carrying forward or summarising a transaction, or in applying an accounting principle.
- Its causes are carelessness, ignorance of principle, wrong classification, wrong side, omission, compensating mistakes, faulty arithmetic and the wrong account of the same class.
- **Types**: errors of **principle** (capital expenditure treated as revenue or the reverse); errors of **omission** (complete or partial); errors of **commission** (wrong amount, wrong account, wrong side, wrong casting or balancing); and **compensating** errors.
- The **trial balance** tests only that total debits equal total credits. It detects **one-sided** errors — casting errors, wrong side, wrong amount posted once, partial omission, a balance carried forward wrongly.
- It **cannot** detect errors of principle, complete omission, compensating errors, a wrong account of the same class, or the same transaction entered twice in both accounts. A trial balance proves arithmetical accuracy, not correctness.
- **Rectification before the trial balance** is by an ordinary journal entry putting the amounts where they belong. An error of principle is corrected by reversing the wrong entry and passing the correct one.
- **Rectification after the trial balance** is by a journal entry in which the other side of a **one-sided** error goes to the suspense account; two-sided errors are corrected exactly as before.
- A **suspense account** is a temporary account holding the difference in the trial balance. The short side of the trial balance is the side on which the suspense account is entered. It must be cleared to nil; until then a credit balance appears on the liabilities side and a debit balance on the assets side of the balance sheet.

## Topics to cover

- Accounting errors: meaning and causes
- Types of errors: errors of principle, omission, commission, compensating errors
- Detection of errors through the trial balance
- Rectification of errors before and after the trial balance
- Suspense account (उज्राती खाता): meaning, preparation and use
- Types of errors
- Rectification of errors
- Suspense account

Nobody keeps a perfect set of books. A figure is copied wrongly, a posting is made to the wrong side, a capital expense is treated as a revenue expense, or a whole transaction is left out. Some of these mistakes make the trial balance disagree and shout for attention; others are silent and can survive for years. This unit classifies errors, shows which of them the **trial balance** can catch, explains how each one is corrected — before the trial balance and after it — and introduces the **suspense account**, the temporary account that holds the difference until the mistake is found.

## Chapter summary

- An **accounting error** is a mistake in recording, posting, casting, carrying forward or summarising a transaction, or in applying an accounting principle.
- Its causes are carelessness, ignorance of principle, wrong classification, wrong side, omission, compensating mistakes, faulty arithmetic and the wrong account of the same class.
- **Types**: errors of **principle** (capital expenditure treated as revenue or the reverse); errors of **omission** (complete or partial); errors of **commission** (wrong amount, wrong account, wrong side, wrong casting or balancing); and **compensating** errors.
- The **trial balance** tests only that total debits equal total credits. It detects **one-sided** errors — casting errors, wrong side, wrong amount posted once, partial omission, a balance carried forward wrongly.
- It **cannot** detect errors of principle, complete omission, compensating errors, a wrong account of the same class, or the same transaction entered twice in both accounts. A trial balance proves arithmetical accuracy, not correctness.
- **Rectification before the trial balance** is by an ordinary journal entry putting the amounts where they belong. An error of principle is corrected by reversing the wrong entry and passing the correct one.
- **Rectification after the trial balance** is by a journal entry in which the other side of a **one-sided** error goes to the suspense account; two-sided errors are corrected exactly as before.
- A **suspense account** is a temporary account holding the difference in the trial balance. The short side of the trial balance is the side on which the suspense account is entered. It must be cleared to nil; until then a credit balance appears on the liabilities side and a debit balance on the assets side of the balance sheet.

chapters.question_answers:
## Errors before the trial balance

**Problem.** The following errors were found before the trial balance was prepared. Pass the rectifying entries.
i. Salary of Rs. 20,000 paid was wrongly debited to the rent account.
ii. A sale of goods of Rs. 15,000 to Mohan was debited to Sohan's account.
iii. Purchase of furniture of Rs. 40,000 was debited to the purchases account.
iv. A cash sale of Rs. 5,000 was completely omitted from the books.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — (i) Two accounts, both expense accounts: salary should have been debited and rent should not have been. *Salary A/c Dr. 20,000; To Rent A/c 20,000.*
Step 2 — (ii) Two debtors, same class: Mohan's account should have been debited. *Mohan A/c Dr. 15,000; To Sohan A/c 15,000.*
Step 3 — (iii) This is an error of **principle** — a capital expenditure treated as revenue. *Furniture A/c Dr. 40,000; To Purchases A/c 40,000.*
Step 4 — (iv) A complete omission: nothing at all was written. *Cash A/c Dr. 5,000; To Sales A/c 5,000.*
Step 5 — State the effect on the trial balance: (i) and (ii) are two-sided errors — the trial balance agreed and still agrees. (iii) is a two-sided error of principle — the trial balance agreed; but profit is understated by Rs. 40,000 and furniture is understated. (iv) is a complete omission — the trial balance agreed, and it still agrees after rectification.

**Answer.** The four entries above. No suspense account is needed because the trial balance has not yet been prepared.

## One-sided errors after the trial balance

**Problem.** After preparing the trial balance, the following errors were discovered. Pass the rectifying entries and show the suspense account.
i. The purchases book was undercast by Rs. 5,000.
ii. Sales of Rs. 8,000 to Kamal were posted to Kamal's account as Rs. 800.
iii. A cash purchase of Rs. 3,000 was posted to the debit of the purchase account as Rs. 300 while the cash account was correctly posted.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — (i) The purchases book was undercast: the debit side of the ledger is short by Rs. 5,000. The trial balance was short on the debit side, so the difference sits in the credit of the suspense account. *Purchases A/c Dr. 5,000; To Suspense A/c 5,000.*
Step 2 — (ii) Kamal's account was debited Rs. 800 instead of Rs. 8,000, so the debit is short by Rs. 7,200. *Kamal A/c Dr. 7,200; To Suspense A/c 7,200.*
Step 3 — (iii) The purchase account was debited with Rs. 300 instead of Rs. 3,000 — short by Rs. 2,700 on the debit side. *Purchases A/c Dr. 2,700; To Suspense A/c 2,700.*
Step 4 — Total the suspense account: three credits of Rs. 5,000, Rs. 7,200 and Rs. 2,700 = Rs. 14,900. This is exactly the difference that the trial balance showed.

*Suspense account*

| Date | Particulars | Rs. | Date | Particulars | Rs. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | To Balance b/d (if any) | — | | By Purchases A/c (undercast) | 5,000 |
| | | | | By Kamal A/c (short posting) | 7,200 |
| | | | | By Purchases A/c (short posting) | 2,700 |
| | **Total** | **14,900** | | **Total** | **14,900** |

**Answer.** The debit side of the trial balance was short by Rs. 14,900, which was sitting in the credit of the suspense account. The three entries above clear it.

## Which errors make the trial balance disagree?

**Problem.** State, with a reason, whether the trial balance will agree in each of the following cases, and name the kind of error.
(a) A credit sale of Rs. 20,000 to Gita was not entered anywhere.
(b) The purchases returns book was overcast by Rs. 2,000.
(c) A purchase from Bimal of Rs. 6,000 was posted to his account as Rs. 6,600.
(d) Wages paid for the erection of a machine of Rs. 15,000 were debited to the wages account.
(e) A payment of Rs. 4,000 to a creditor was posted to the creditor's account twice on the debit side while cash was posted once.
(f) The carriage inward account was undercast by Rs. 3,000 and the carriage outward account was undercast by Rs. 3,000.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — (a) Nothing was written on either side, so both sides of the trial balance keep the same totals. **Agrees** — complete omission.
Step 2 — (b) The returns book total is used for postings on one side only, so one side becomes short by Rs. 2,000. **Does not agree** — one-sided casting error; suspense account needed.
Step 3 — (c) The journal and the debit to purchases are right; only the creditor's account is wrong, by Rs. 600 on the credit side. **Does not agree** — one-sided error; suspense account needed.
Step 4 — (d) The entry is complete and balanced; only the head is wrong. **Agrees** — error of principle; but profit and the asset figure are both wrong.
Step 5 — (e) The creditor's account has been debited Rs. 8,000 while cash was credited Rs. 4,000, so one side is short by Rs. 4,000. **Does not agree** — one-sided error; suspense account needed.
Step 6 — (f) Both errors are Rs. 3,000 on the same side (debit), so they add up: the debit side is short by Rs. 6,000. **Does not agree** — two one-sided errors, not a compensating pair.

**Answer.** Agrees: (a) and (d). Does not agree: (b) Rs. 2,000, (c) Rs. 600, (e) Rs. 4,000, (f) Rs. 6,000.
**What it means.** The test is not the size of the error but **how many sides of the trial balance it disturbs**. If it disturbs one side only, the trial balance will not agree and a suspense account is opened.

(f) The carriage inward account was undercast by Rs. 3,000 and the carriage outward account was undercast by Rs. 3,000.

Step 1 — (a) Nothing was written on either side, so both sides of the trial balance keep the same totals. **Agrees** — complete omission.
Step 2 — (b) The returns book total is used for postings on one side only, so one side becomes short by Rs. 2,000. **Does not agree** — one-sided casting error; suspense account needed.
Step 3 — (c) The journal and the debit to purchases are right; only the creditor's account is wrong, by Rs. 600 on the credit side. **Does not agree** — one-sided error; suspense account needed.
Step 4 — (d) The entry is complete and balanced; only the head is wrong. **Agrees** — error of principle; but profit and the asset figure are both wrong.
Step 5 — (e) The creditor's account has been debited Rs. 8,000 while cash was credited Rs. 4,000, so one side is short by Rs. 4,000. **Does not agree** — one-sided error; suspense account needed.
Step 6 — (f) Both errors are Rs. 3,000 on the same side (debit), so they add up: the debit side is short by Rs. 6,000. **Does not agree** — two one-sided errors, not a compensating pair.

**Answer.** Agrees: (a) and (d). Does not agree: (b) Rs. 2,000, (c) Rs. 600, (e) Rs. 4,000, (f) Rs. 6,000.
**What it means.** The test is not the size of the error but **how many sides of the trial balance it disturbs**. If it disturbs one side only, the trial balance will not agree and a suspense account is opened.

- **Final accounts** are prepared at the end of the year from the trial balance, after adjustments, to show the profit or loss of the period and the financial position on the closing date. They are also called the financial statements.
- Their **objectives** are to find gross profit, to find net profit, to show the financial position, to allow comparison, to provide the basis for tax and audit, and to supply the owner with information for decisions.
- The **trading account** deals with goods: opening stock, purchases and direct expenses on the debit side; sales and closing stock on the credit side; the balance is the gross profit.
- $Gross\ profit = Sales - Cost\ of\ goods\ sold$ and $Cost\ of\ goods\ sold = Opening\ stock + Purchases + Direct\ expenses - Closing\ stock$.
- The **profit and loss account** starts with the gross profit and adds other incomes and deducts indirect expenses; the balance is the net profit.
- The **balance sheet** is a statement, not an account, of assets, liabilities and capital on the closing date: $Assets = Liabilities + Capital$.
- An **adjustment** brings in an item that is earned or incurred but not yet recorded. **Every adjustment has two effects** — one in the trading or profit and loss account and one in the balance sheet.
- The treatment of the common adjustments: closing stock (credit trading, asset), outstanding expense (add to expense, liability), prepaid expense (less from expense, asset), accrued income (add to income, asset), income in advance (less from income, liability), depreciation (debit profit and loss, deduct from asset), interest on capital (debit profit and loss, add to capital), interest on drawings (credit profit and loss, deduct from capital), goods taken by the owner (credit purchases, deduct from capital), provision for doubtful debts (debit profit and loss, deduct from debtors), manager's commission (debit profit and loss, liability).
- **Steps**: complete the trial balance; prepare the trading account; prepare the profit and loss account; carry the net profit to capital and deduct drawings; prepare the balance sheet; check that the two sides agree.
- **Accounting notes** explain the policies used, break down large figures, disclose contingent liabilities and events after the balance sheet date, and reconcile the statements with the accounts. The statements are incomplete without them.

chapters.question_answers:
## Full final accounts from a trial balance

**Problem.** The following is the trial balance of Surya Traders as on 31 Ashad 2082.

| Particulars | Debit (Rs.) | Credit (Rs.) |
|---|---|---|
| Opening stock | 40,000 | |
| Purchases | 2,00,000 | |
| Carriage inward | 10,000 | |
| Wages | 30,000 | |
| Salaries | 25,000 | |
| Rent | 15,000 | |
| Furniture | 60,000 | |
| Debtors | 45,000 | |
| Bank | 35,000 | |
| Cash | 5,000 | |
| Capital | | 1,20,000 |
| Sales | | 2,90,000 |
| Creditors | | 35,000 |
| Commission received | | 20,000 |
| **Total** | **4,65,000** | **4,65,000** |

Additional information: (i) closing stock Rs. 55,000; (ii) outstanding salary Rs. 5,000; (iii) prepaid rent Rs. 3,000; (iv) depreciation on furniture 10 per cent.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — *Trading account.* Debit: opening stock, purchases, carriage inward, wages, and gross profit c/d. Credit: sales and closing stock.
Cost of goods sold $= 40{,}000 + 2{,}00{,}000 + 10{,}000 + 30{,}000 - 55{,}000 = Rs.\ 2{,}25{,}000$; gross profit $= 2{,}90{,}000 - 2{,}25{,}000 = Rs.\ 65{,}000$.

*Trading account for the year ended 31 Ashad 2082*

| Particulars | Rs. | Particulars | Rs. |
|---|---|---|---|
| To Opening stock | 40,000 | By Sales | 2,90,000 |
| To Purchases | 2,00,000 | By Closing stock | 55,000 |
| To Carriage inward | 10,000 | | |
| To Wages | 30,000 | | |
| To Gross profit c/d | 65,000 | | |
| **Total** | **3,45,000** | **Total** | **3,45,000** |

Step 2 — *Profit and loss account.* Salary becomes $25{,}000 + 5{,}000 = Rs.\ 30{,}000$; rent becomes $15{,}000 - 3{,}000 = Rs.\ 12{,}000$; depreciation $= 10\% \times 60{,}000 = Rs.\ 6{,}000$.

*Profit and loss account for the year ended 31 Ashad 2082*

| Particulars | Rs. | Particulars | Rs. |
|---|---|---|---|
| To Salaries | 25,000 | By Gross profit b/d | 65,000 |
| To Add: outstanding salary | 5,000 | By Commission received | 20,000 |
| | 30,000 | | |
| To Rent | 15,000 | | |
| To Less: prepaid rent | 3,000 | | |
| | 12,000 | | |
| To Depreciation on furniture | 6,000 | | |
| To Net profit (transferred to capital) | 37,000 | | |
| **Total** | **85,000** | **Total** | **85,000** |

Step 3 — *Balance sheet.* Capital $= 1{,}20{,}000 + 37{,}000 = Rs.\ 1{,}57{,}000$; furniture $= 60{,}000 - 6{,}000 = Rs.\ 54{,}000$.

*Balance sheet as on 31 Ashad 2082*

| Liabilities | Rs. | Assets | Rs. |
|---|---|---|---|
| Capital | 1,20,000 | Furniture | 60,000 |
| Add: Net profit | 37,000 | Less: Depreciation | 6,000 |
| | 1,57,000 | | 54,000 |
| Creditors | 35,000 | Closing stock | 55,000 |
| Outstanding salary | 5,000 | Debtors | 45,000 |
| | | Bank | 35,000 |
| | | Cash | 5,000 |
| | | Prepaid rent | 3,000 |
| **Total** | **1,97,000** | **Total** | **1,97,000** |

**Answer.** Gross profit Rs. 65,000; net profit Rs. 37,000; balance sheet total Rs. 1,97,000.

## Find the missing figures

**Problem.** From the following, compute the gross profit, the net profit and the closing capital.
Opening stock Rs. 30,000; purchases Rs. 1,80,000; carriage inward Rs. 8,000; wages Rs. 22,000; closing stock Rs. 40,000; sales Rs. 2,60,000; office salary Rs. 20,000; rent Rs. 10,000; advertisement Rs. 6,000; commission received Rs. 12,000; opening capital Rs. 90,000; drawings Rs. 15,000.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Cost of goods sold $= 30{,}000 + 1{,}80{,}000 + 8{,}000 + 22{,}000 - 40{,}000 = Rs.\ 2{,}00{,}000$.
Step 2 — Gross profit $= 2{,}60{,}000 - 2{,}00{,}000 = Rs.\ 60{,}000$.
Step 3 — Total indirect expenses $= 20{,}000 + 10{,}000 + 6{,}000 = Rs.\ 36{,}000$.
Step 4 — Net profit $= 60{,}000 + 12{,}000 - 36{,}000 = Rs.\ 36{,}000$.
Step 5 — Closing capital $= 90{,}000 + 36{,}000 - 15{,}000 = Rs.\ 1{,}11{,}000$.

**Answer.** Gross profit Rs. 60,000; net profit Rs. 36,000; closing capital Rs. 1,11,000.

## The two effects of each adjustment

**Problem.** State the two effects of each of the following adjustments: (a) closing stock Rs. 25,000; (b) outstanding wages Rs. 4,000; (c) insurance prepaid Rs. 2,000; (d) depreciation on machinery Rs. 9,000; (e) goods worth Rs. 3,000 taken by the proprietor for personal use.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — (a) Credited in the trading account (credit side) and shown as a current asset in the balance sheet.
Step 2 — (b) Added to wages on the debit side of the trading account and shown as a current liability in the balance sheet.
Step 3 — (c) Deducted from insurance on the debit side of the profit and loss account and shown as a current asset (prepaid insurance) in the balance sheet.
Step 4 — (d) Debited to the profit and loss account and deducted from machinery in the balance sheet.
Step 5 — (e) Credited to the purchases account (which reduces the cost of goods sold) and deducted from capital as drawings in the balance sheet.

**Answer.** As above. Notice that in each case one effect is in a revenue statement and the other in the balance sheet.
**What it means.** An adjustment is never a single entry. If only one effect is written, the profit will be right and the balance sheet wrong, or the reverse — and the balance sheet will not tally.

chapters.summary:
- **Government accounting** is the system by which a government records, classifies, summarises and reports its revenue, expenditure and financial position, in order to be accountable to the legislature and the people. In Nepal it is governed by the **Financial Procedures and Fiscal Responsibility Act, 2076** and its Rules, 2077, and operated by the **Financial Comptroller General Office**.
- Its **bases** are: the legal basis, the **cash basis**, the **double-entry system**, the **fund basis**, **uniformity of forms and chart of accounts**, **budget classification**, the **two levels of accounting**, the **banking arrangement**, and **external audit**.
- **Commercial and government accounting** both use double entry and documentary evidence, but they differ in **objective** (profit against accountability), **basis** (accrual against cash), **ownership**, the **standing of the budget** (plan against law), **funds**, the **statements** prepared, **performance measurement** and **audit**.
- Nepal has **three tiers** — federal, provincial and local — each with its own consolidated fund, budget and audit, linked by the divisible fund and the grant system.
- **Central level accounting** records the transactions of the centre at the FCGO; **operating level accounting** records a district or local office's transactions in the office itself, through the bank cash book, reported monthly by the statement of expenditure.
- The **chart of accounts** is the uniform coded list of revenue, expenditure, fund and asset heads, following the budget classification (for example 21111 remuneration, 22111 uniform, 22311 travelling expenses). It makes a payment checkable in advance and the national accounts addable.
- Government **formats** (the म.ले.प.फा. series) are prescribed centrally: the vouchers (निकासा, आम्दानी, गोश्वारा), the **bank cash book (No. 209)**, the ledgers, the advance register, the statement of expenditure and the revenue statement.
- The **areas** of government accounting are revenue, expenditure, store (jinsi), fund, deposit and retention, loan and grant, and asset and liability accounting.
- The **consolidated fund** is the government's main account: all revenue is deposited into it and nothing may be withdrawn except under an appropriation made by law. The **single account fund** is the one bank account an office keeps for all its receipts and payments, recorded in the bank cash book.

## Topics to cover

- Government accounting (सरकारी लेखाप्रणाली): introduction and features

- Accounting of the federal, provincial and local levels

A shopkeeper's accounts answer to the owner. A government office's accounts answer to the **people who pay the taxes** — which is why government accounting is built differently. Every rupee must be traceable from the budget passed by Parliament to the bill paid in a village office, and every office must use the same forms, the same codes and the same rules, or the national accounts cannot be added up. This unit explains what government accounting is, the bases on which Nepal's system rests, how it differs from commercial accounting, how the three tiers of government and the two levels of office keep their accounts, and the two words every student must be able to define — the **consolidated fund** and the **single account fund**.

chapters.question_answers:
## Consolidated fund and single account fund

**Problem.** State, with a reason, which of the following is a matter of the **consolidated fund** and which of the **single account fund**.
(a) A district office maintains one bank account at Rastriya Banijya Bank and pays every bill from it.
(b) Parliament passes the Appropriation Act authorising the government to spend Rs. 1,700 billion.
(c) A municipality deposits the house tax it collects into its main account at the Nepal Bank.
(d) The Treasury and Comptroller Office releases a month's budget to a district office, which is credited to its operating account.
(e) No payment may be made from the government's main account for a purpose for which no appropriation was passed.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Ask whether the point is about **authority to spend from the main fund** (consolidated fund) or about **how an office keeps its operating bank account** (single account fund).
Step 2 — (a) One operating bank account for all transactions → **single account fund**.
Step 3 — (b) The authority to spend, given by the legislature → **consolidated fund**.
Step 4 — (c) Revenue deposited into the main fund of the local level → **consolidated fund**.
Step 5 — (d) Budget released into the operating account of the office → **single account fund** arrangement.
Step 6 — (e) The rule that nothing may be spent without an appropriation → **consolidated fund**.

**Answer.** (a) and (d) single account fund; (b), (c) and (e) consolidated fund.

## Similarities and differences

**Problem.** A bank asks a newly appointed accountant of a district office why the office's accounts do not show the office's "profit". Explain, giving four differences between commercial accounting and government accounting.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — The objective is different. A business exists to earn profit for its owners; a government office exists to deliver services under an approved budget. There is no profit to measure, so there is no profit and loss account.
Step 2 — The basis is different. A commercial firm generally follows the accrual basis; the government follows the cash basis, recording a receipt when money is received and a payment when money is paid.
Step 3 — The drive is different. A business is guided by a budget but may depart from it; a government office may not spend one rupee outside its budget head, because the budget is a law and not a plan.
Step 4 — The accountability is different. The owners of a business may read its accounts if they wish; the accounts of a government office are audited by the Office of the Auditor General and laid before Parliament and the public.

**Answer.** The four differences are objective (accountability, not profit), basis (cash, not accrual), the standing of the budget (law, not plan) and accountability (public audit, not private audit).

## Choosing the budget head

**Problem.** A district office has to record the following payments. Choose the most suitable budget head from the chart of accounts and give its code: (a) the monthly salary of a section officer; (b) a new computer for the account section; (c) a steel almirah for the record room; (d) the travelling allowance of a staff member sent to a training in Pokhara; (e) the purchase of paper, ink and registers.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Decide first whether the payment is **recurrent** (running the office) or **capital** (acquiring an asset). Salaries, allowances, travel and stationery are recurrent; a computer and an almirah are capital.
Step 2 — (a) Salary of staff is remuneration → **21111, Remuneration**.

self_checks.question: Consolidated fund and single account fund
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** State, with a reason, which of the following is a matter of the **consolidated fund** and which of the **single account fund**.
(a) A district office maintains one bank account at Rastriya Banijya Bank and pays every bill from it.
(b) Parliament passes the Appropriation Act authorising the government to spend Rs. 1,700 billion.
(c) A municipality deposits the house tax it collects into its main account at the Nepal Bank.
(d) The Treasury and Comptroller Office releases a month's budget to a district office, which is credited to its operating account.
(e) No payment may be made from the government's main account for a purpose for which no appropriation was passed.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Ask whether the point is about **authority to spend from the main fund** (consolidated fund) or about **how an office keeps its operating bank account** (single account fund).
Step 2 — (a) One operating bank account for all transactions → **single account fund**.
Step 3 — (b) The authority to spend, given by the legislature → **consolidated fund**.
Step 4 — (c) Revenue deposited into the main fund of the local level → **consolidated fund**.
Step 5 — (d) Budget released into the operating account of the office → **single account fund** arrangement.
Step 6 — (e) The rule that nothing may be spent without an appropriation → **consolidated fund**.

**Answer.** (a) and (d) single account fund; (b), (c) and (e) consolidated fund.

self_checks.question: Similarities and differences
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** A bank asks a newly appointed accountant of a district office why the office's accounts do not show the office's "profit". Explain, giving four differences between commercial accounting and government accounting.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — The objective is different. A business exists to earn profit for its owners; a government office exists to deliver services under an approved budget. There is no profit to measure, so there is no profit and loss account.
Step 2 — The basis is different. A commercial firm generally follows the accrual basis; the government follows the cash basis, recording a receipt when money is received and a payment when money is paid.
Step 3 — The drive is different. A business is guided by a budget but may depart from it; a government office may not spend one rupee outside its budget head, because the budget is a law and not a plan.
Step 4 — The accountability is different. The owners of a business may read its accounts if they wish; the accounts of a government office are audited by the Office of the Auditor General and laid before Parliament and the public.

**Answer.** The four differences are objective (accountability, not profit), basis (cash, not accrual), the standing of the budget (law, not plan) and accountability (public audit, not private audit).

chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- Revenue accounting: introduction and objectives
- Revenue accounting codes (सङ्केतहरू)
- Formats used in revenue accounting
- Banking arrangement of revenue accounting
- Reporting arrangement of revenue accounting
- Preparation of the revenue statement (फाँटबारी)
- Revenue accounting codes

A government office collects money as well as spends it. It receives tax, fees for a passport, examination fees, rent from government property, income from the sale of old goods. Every rupee of it must be entered against the right head, deposited into the consolidated fund through a bank on the same day as it is collected, and reported upwards. **Revenue accounting** is that side of government accounting. This unit covers what it is, the codes that name each revenue head, the formats used, the banking arrangement (why a government office may not keep cash), and how the monthly revenue statement is prepared.

## Chapter summary

- **Revenue accounting** records the collection of government revenue, its deposit into the consolidated fund through the bank, and its reporting to the Treasury and Comptroller Office and the FCGO.
- Its **objectives** are to record every rupee with evidence, to deposit the whole collection into the consolidated fund, to compare collection with the estimate, to detect leakage, to supply the annual financial statement and to keep the account public.
- **Revenue must be deposited the same day.** A government office may not hold its collection as cash and may not spend out of it; expenditure requires a separate appropriation.
- Every revenue head carries a **code** in the uniform chart of accounts: **11000** is the tax group (for example **11111** income tax on sole proprietorships and individuals); **13000, 14000 and 15000** are the non-tax groups (for example **14224** examination fee, **14227** passport fee, **14251** company registration fee, **14221** judicial fee, **14151** rent of government property, **14311** judicial fine).

- Under the **banking arrangement** each office has one designated bank account, deposits revenue the same day, never pays an expense from it, reconciles the bank every month, and is watched by the Treasury and Comptroller Office.
- **Reporting** is daily (bank cash book), monthly (the revenue statement with the bank reconciliation), quarterly (review against the estimate) and annual (consolidation into the government's financial statement and audit by the Auditor General).
- The **revenue statement (फाँटबारी)** shows head by head the revenue collected, the amount deposited into the consolidated fund and the cash still in hand, and must satisfy **revenue collected = amount deposited + cash in hand**.

chapters.question_answers:
## Prepare the revenue statement

**Problem.** During the month of Mangsir a District Education Office collected the following revenue. Prepare the revenue statement and show the amount to be deposited into the consolidated fund. It had no opening cash balance.

| Head | Description | Amount collected (Rs.) |
|---|---|---|
| 14223 | Income from the education sector | 4,42,600 |
| 14224 | Examination fee | 1,75,500 |
| 14227 | Passport fee | 60,000 |
| 14151 | Rent of government property | 2,38,800 |

Of the examination fee, Rs. 35,100 had not yet been deposited into the bank at the end of the month.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Add the collection: $4{,}42{,}600 + 1{,}75{,}500 + 60{,}000 + 2{,}38{,}800 = Rs.\ 9{,}16{,}900$.
Step 2 — The undeposited amount is Rs. 35,100, so the deposit made in the month is $9{,}16{,}900 - 35{,}100 = Rs.\ 8{,}81{,}800$.
Step 3 — Check: collected = deposited + cash in hand → $9{,}16{,}900 = 8{,}81{,}800 + 35{,}100$. ✔
Step 4 — Write the statement head by head.

*Revenue statement for the month of Mangsir*

| Head code | Description | Revenue collected (Rs.) | Deposited into the consolidated fund (Rs.) | Cash in hand (Rs.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 14151 | Rent of government property and other income | 2,38,800 | 2,38,800 | — |
| 14223 | Income from the education sector | 4,42,600 | 4,42,600 | — |
| 14224 | Examination fee | 1,75,500 | 1,40,400 | 35,100 |
| 14227 | Passport fee | 60,000 | 60,000 | — |
| | **Total** | **9,16,900** | **8,81,800** | **35,100** |

**Answer.** Total revenue collected Rs. 9,16,900; to be deposited Rs. 8,81,800 in the month; Rs. 35,100 still to be deposited on the first working day of the next month.
**What it means.** The last column is the whole purpose of the statement. A revenue statement with a cash-in-hand figure that is not explained is the first thing an auditor looks at.

## Which head and which code?

**Problem.** Choose the correct revenue code for each of the following: (a) a fee charged to a private company for drawing water from a government spring; (b) the fee paid by a company when it is registered; (c) the rent received for a government building let to a bank; (d) a fine imposed by a court; (e) the fee paid by a candidate sitting an examination.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — (a) Private use of a water source → **14216 निजी धाराबापतको शुल्क**.
Step 2 — (b) Registration of a company → **14251 कम्पनी रजिस्ट्रेसन दस्तुर**.
Step 3 — (c) Rent of government property → **14151 सरकारी सम्पत्तिको बहाल तथा अन्य आय**.
Step 4 — (d) A court fine → **14311 न्यायिक दण्ड**.
Step 5 — (e) An examination fee → **14224 परीक्षा शुल्क**.

**Answer.** (a) 14216, (b) 14251, (c) 14151, (d) 14311, (e) 14224.
**What it means.** Every one of these is non-tax revenue — money the government earns from a service, a property or a penalty, not a compulsory contribution. That is why none of them falls under the 11000 tax group.

## Revenue and the consolidated fund

**Problem.** An office collects Rs. 2,00,000 of revenue in a month. Its electricity bill for the month is Rs. 18,000. The head clerk proposes to pay the bill out of the money collected, "so that the office does not have to ask for a release". Say whether this is allowed, and what should be done instead.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — State the rule. All revenue must be deposited into the **consolidated fund**; money may be spent only under an **appropriation made by law**, through a payment order and a budget release.
Step 2 — Applying the rule, the proposal is **not allowed**. Paying an expense out of collected revenue would create expenditure outside the budget, and the Auditor General would report it as an irregular payment.
Step 3 — What should be done: deposit the whole Rs. 2,00,000 into the government account the same day, record it in the bank cash book and the revenue statement, and pay the electricity bill in the normal way — by issuing a payment order against the budget head for electricity, and entering the payment in the bank cash book when the release is received.

**Answer.** Not allowed. Deposit the revenue in full and pay the bill through the appropriation and the bank cash book.
**What it means.** The separation of revenue and expenditure is the whole foundation of legislative control. Once an office may spend what it collects, the budget has stopped being a law.

chapters.name: Accounting of Government Expenditure (सरकारी खर्चको लेखा)
topics: Expenditure and appropriation accounting (खर्च अर्थात् विनियोजन लेखा): introduction
Formats used in expenditure accounting and reporting
Payment order and its types; advance payment and clearance
Bank cash book (A.G.F. No. 209) and its preparation
Statement of expenditure and its preparation
Budget release, budget transfer and re-appropriation
Payment order, advance payment and clearance
chapters.summary:
- **Expenditure (appropriation) accounting** records what an office spends against its approved budget head, the advances it gives and recovers, the deductions it holds and its bank balance.
- An expenditure is **regular** only when it is within the approved head, for the approved purpose, supported by evidence, sanctioned by the authorised officer, actually incurred and recorded in the prescribed formats.
- The key terms are **appropriation** (what the legislature voted), **release** (what has been made available) and **expenditure** (what has been spent). $Available\ balance = Appropriation - Expenditure - Uncleared\ advances$.
- **Expenditure codes** follow the uniform chart of accounts: the organisational classification says who spends; the economic classification says what, with **2** for recurrent (21111 remuneration, 22111 uniform, 22311 office materials, 22612 fuel, 22711 miscellaneous) and **3** for capital (31111 machinery, 31121 furniture, 31131 vehicles).
- The **formats** are the payment order, the vouchers (गोश्वारा, निकासा, आम्दानी, धरौटी), the advance register, the **bank cash book (No. 209)**, the head-wise ledger, the **statement of expenditure** and the deposit and retention ledgers.
- A **payment order** authorises the Treasury and Comptroller Office to pay. A payment is either **final** or an **advance**; an advance is a recoverable debt, cleared on the bill, and an uncleared advance is deducted from the available balance.
- The **bank cash book (A.G.F. No. 209)** shows the date, voucher number, particulars, debit (receipts), credit (payments) and the running balance. Budget release, revenue and refunds are debits; expenditure, advances and payments over of deductions are credits.
- The **statement of expenditure** reports, head by head, the annual appropriation, the cumulative and monthly expenditure, the uncleared advance and the available balance. It is the document on which further releases are made.
- **Budget release** makes money available; **budget transfer** moves budget between offices; **re-appropriation** moves savings between heads of the same office. None of them increases the total the legislature voted, and protected heads may not be raided.
- **Journal vouchers** in government accounting always name the budget head, follow the double-entry form with a narration, carry the evidence, and are signed by the authorised officer. The **गोश्वारा भौचर** records a transfer where no money moves.

chapters.question_answers:
## Advance payment and clearance — journal vouchers

**Problem.** Pass the journal vouchers for the following transactions of a District Education Office.
(a) A payment order of Rs. 60,000 was issued against budget head 31111 for the purchase of a computer.
(b) An advance of Rs. 80,000 was given to Section Officer Mr. Rana against budget head 31121 for the purchase of furniture for the office.
(c) Mr. Rana cleared his furniture advance by submitting a bill of Rs. 95,000 for furniture purchased out of his own arrangement.
(d) Provident fund of Rs. 30,000 and income tax of Rs. 5,000 deducted from the salary of Shrawan were deposited into the concerned office.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — (a) The government has incurred capital expenditure and the DTCO will pay. Debit the expenditure head, credit the DTCO.
*31111 Machinery and equipment (computer) A/c Dr. 60,000*
*To DTCO A/c 60,000*
(Being a payment order issued for the purchase of a computer.)
Step 2 — (b) An advance is not an expense; it is a debt recoverable from the officer.
*Furniture advance (Mr. Rana) A/c Dr. 80,000*
*To DTCO A/c 80,000*
(Being an advance issued for the purchase of furniture.)
Step 3 — (c) The advance is cleared, the asset is recognised at the full bill value, and the excess is a further charge on the same head.
*31121 Furniture and fixtures A/c Dr. 95,000*
*To Furniture advance (Mr. Rana) A/c 80,000*
*To DTCO A/c 15,000*
(Being the furniture advance cleared on a bill of Rs. 95,000, the excess of Rs. 15,000 being payable.)
Step 4 — (d) The deductions were never the office's money; they were held on behalf of others and are now paid over.
*Provident fund payable A/c Dr. 30,000*
*Income tax payable A/c Dr. 5,000*
*To Bank A/c 35,000*
(Being the amount deducted from salary deposited into the concerned office.)

**Answer.** The four vouchers above.
**What it means.** An advance and an expenditure are different things. Booking an advance as an expenditure inflates the year's spending and hides a recoverable debt — and it is exactly the kind of thing the Auditor General looks for at the year end.

## Bank cash book for the month of Shrawan

**Problem.** The following transactions took place in the bank account of a District Coordination Unit during the month of Shrawan. There was no opening balance. Prepare the bank cash book (A.G.F. No. 209).
i. 2082/04/03 — Budget release received from the Treasury and Comptroller Office Rs. 5,00,000.
ii. 2082/04/08 — Payment order issued against 22311 office materials for Rs. 80,000.
iii. 2082/04/14 — Advance of Rs. 50,000 given to a section officer against 31121 for furniture.
iv. 2082/04/25 — Salary payment order issued for the month of Shrawan, total salary Rs. 2,00,000, after deducting provident fund Rs. 30,000 and income tax Rs. 5,000.
v. 2082/04/26 — The provident fund and income tax deducted were deposited into the concerned office.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — The budget release is money received: **debit Rs. 5,00,000**; balance Rs. 5,00,000.
Step 2 — The office materials payment is money paid: **credit Rs. 80,000**; balance Rs. 4,20,000.
Step 3 — The advance is money paid (and recoverable): **credit Rs. 50,000**; balance Rs. 3,70,000.
Step 4 — The salary: the full salary is Rs. 2,00,000, of which Rs. 30,000 + Rs. 5,000 = Rs. 35,000 is deducted and only the **net Rs. 1,65,000** is paid out. **Credit Rs. 1,65,000**; balance Rs. 2,05,000.
Step 5 — The deductions, when deposited, leave the office's account: **credit Rs. 35,000**; balance Rs. 1,70,000.
Step 6 — Total both sides and carry the closing balance.

*Bank cash book (म.ले.प.फा.नं. २०९) — month of Shrawan, 2082*

| Date | Voucher no. | Particulars | Debit (Rs.) | Credit (Rs.) | Balance (Rs.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 04/03 | 1 | Budget release received from the DTCO | 5,00,000 | | 5,00,000 |
| 04/08 | 2 | Payment order — 22311 office materials | | 80,000 | 4,20,000 |
| 04/14 | 3 | Advance to section officer — 31121 furniture | | 50,000 | 3,70,000 |
