| | | **Total** | **5,00,000** | **5,00,000** | |

## Statement of expenditure

**Problem.** The following particulars relate to the District Police Office, Sindhuli, for the month of Poush 2080. Prepare the statement of expenditure and show the available balance.

| Budget head no. | Budget head | Annual appropriation (Rs.) | Expenditure up to Magh (Rs.) | Expenditure of Poush (Rs.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 21111 | Remuneration | 4,20,000 | 1,50,000 | 28,000 |
| 22111 | Uniform | 45,000 | 7,500 | 1,500 |
| 22311 | Office materials | 20,000 | 9,000 | 1,800 |
| 22612 | Travelling expenses | 75,000 | 30,000 | 6,000 |
| 22711 | Miscellaneous expenses | 36,000 | 11,000 | 2,200 |

An uncleared advance of Rs. 4,000 for fuel is outstanding.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Total the annual appropriation: $4{,}20{,}000 + 45{,}000 + 20{,}000 + 75{,}000 + 36{,}000 = Rs.\ 5{,}96{,}000$.
Step 2 — Total the expenditure up to Magh: $1{,}50{,}000 + 7{,}500 + 9{,}000 + 30{,}000 + 11{,}000 = Rs.\ 2{,}07{,}500$.
Step 3 — Total the expenditure of Poush: $28{,}000 + 1{,}500 + 1{,}800 + 6{,}000 + 2{,}200 = Rs.\ 39{,}500$.
Step 4 — Available balance $= 5{,}96{,}000 - 2{,}07{,}500 - 4{,}000 = Rs.\ 3{,}84{,}500$.

| Head no. | Head | Annual appropriation (Rs.) | Expenditure up to Magh (Rs.) | Expenditure of Poush (Rs.) | Uncleared advance (Rs.) | Available balance (Rs.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 21111 | Remuneration | 4,20,000 | 1,50,000 | 28,000 | — | 2,70,000 |
| 22111 | Uniform | 45,000 | 7,500 | 1,500 | — | 37,500 |
| 22311 | Office materials | 20,000 | 9,000 | 1,800 | — | 11,000 |
| 22612 | Travelling expenses | 75,000 | 30,000 | 6,000 | 4,000 | 41,000 |
| 22711 | Miscellaneous | 36,000 | 11,000 | 2,200 | — | 25,000 |
| | **Total** | **5,96,000** | **2,07,500** | **39,500** | **4,000** | **3,84,500** |

**Answer.** Total appropriation Rs. 5,96,000; expenditure to date Rs. 2,07,500; Poush expenditure Rs. 39,500; uncleared advance Rs. 4,000; available balance Rs. 3,84,500.

## Government journal vouchers

**Problem.** Pass the journal vouchers for the following transactions of a District Administration Office.
(a) Budget release of Rs. 8,00,000 received from the DTCO against the annual appropriation.
(b) A payment order of Rs. 1,20,000 issued against 21111 remuneration for the salary of the month, after deducting provident fund Rs. 18,000 and income tax Rs. 2,000.
(c) Furniture purchased for Rs. 90,000 against 31121, the supplier paid by payment order.
(d) The provident fund and income tax deducted were deposited into the concerned office.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — (a) Money received against the appropriation is a debit to the bank and a credit to the release account.
*Bank A/c Dr. 8,00,000*
*To Budget release A/c 8,00,000*
(Being the budget release received from the DTCO for the year.)
Step 2 — (b) Salary totals Rs. 1,20,000 + 18,000 + 2,000 = Rs. 1,40,000; only Rs. 1,20,000 is paid in cash.
*21111 Remuneration A/c Dr. 1,40,000*
*To Provident fund payable A/c 18,000*
*To Income tax payable A/c 2,000*
*To DTCO A/c 1,20,000*
(Being the salary payment order issued for the month after the prescribed deductions.)
Step 3 — (c) Capital expenditure creating an asset.
*31121 Furniture and fixtures A/c Dr. 90,000*
*To DTCO A/c 90,000*
(Being a payment order issued for the purchase of furniture.)
Step 4 — (d) The deductions are paid over; they were never the office's money.
*Provident fund payable A/c Dr. 18,000*
*Income tax payable A/c Dr. 2,000*
*To Bank A/c 20,000*
(Being the deductions deposited into the concerned office.)

**Answer.** The four vouchers above. Note that only (a) and (d) touch the bank account; (b) and (c) touch the DTCO account, because the Treasury and Comptroller Office makes the actual payment.

self_checks.question: Advance payment and clearance — journal vouchers
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** Pass the journal vouchers for the following transactions of a District Education Office.
(a) A payment order of Rs. 60,000 was issued against budget head 31111 for the purchase of a computer.
(b) An advance of Rs. 80,000 was given to Section Officer Mr. Rana against budget head 31121 for the purchase of furniture for the office.
(c) Mr. Rana cleared his furniture advance by submitting a bill of Rs. 95,000 for furniture purchased out of his own arrangement.
(d) Provident fund of Rs. 30,000 and income tax of Rs. 5,000 deducted from the salary of Shrawan were deposited into the concerned office.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — (a) The government has incurred capital expenditure and the DTCO will pay. Debit the expenditure head, credit the DTCO.
*31111 Machinery and equipment (computer) A/c Dr. 60,000*
*To DTCO A/c 60,000*
(Being a payment order issued for the purchase of a computer.)
Step 2 — (b) An advance is not an expense; it is a debt recoverable from the officer.
*Furniture advance (Mr. Rana) A/c Dr. 80,000*
*To DTCO A/c 80,000*
(Being an advance issued for the purchase of furniture.)
Step 3 — (c) The advance is cleared, the asset is recognised at the full bill value, and the excess is a further charge on the same head.
*31121 Furniture and fixtures A/c Dr. 95,000*
*To Furniture advance (Mr. Rana) A/c 80,000*
*To DTCO A/c 15,000*
(Being the furniture advance cleared on a bill of Rs. 95,000, the excess of Rs. 15,000 being payable.)
Step 4 — (d) The deductions were never the office's money; they were held on behalf of others and are now paid over.
*Provident fund payable A/c Dr. 30,000*
*Income tax payable A/c Dr. 5,000*
*To Bank A/c 35,000*
(Being the amount deducted from salary deposited into the concerned office.)

**Answer.** The four vouchers above.
**What it means.** An advance and an expenditure are different things. Booking an advance as an expenditure inflates the year's spending and hides a recoverable debt — and it is exactly the kind of thing the Auditor General looks for at the year end.

chapters.name: Store Accounting (जिन्सी लेखा)
topics: Store accounting: introduction, objectives and importance
Main store formats: store ledger, bin card, stock sheet, A.G.F. forms
Use of the store account and store verification
chapters.summary:
- **Store accounting (जिन्सी लेखा)** records the receipt, storage, issue and balance of goods held by a government office, in quantity and in value. Goods are either **consumable** (stationery, fuel, medicines) or **non-consumable or durable** (furniture, computers, vehicles).
- Its **objectives** are to record every receipt and issue, to show the stock balance at any time, to prevent loss and misuse, to provide audit evidence and to help budgeting.
- Its **importance** is that public goods remain public property: the store account ties every article to a document and a person, and protects the honest officer by showing exactly what was received and what was issued.
- The **formats** are the जिन्सी दाखिला फाराम (goods received), the जिन्सी निकासा फाराम (issue), the store ledger, the bin card, the stock statement (जिन्सी मौज्दात फाँटबारी), the verification form and the accounting voucher.
- The **store ledger (जिन्सी खाता)** holds one account per article with receipts, issues and the balance, usually in the **continuous balance** form.
- The **bin card** is kept on the shelf with the article and must always agree with the store ledger; a difference between them is investigated at once.
- The store account is used by the **storekeeper** (what to requisition), the **accounts section** (valuation and entries) and the **auditor** (tracing a bill to the shelf).
- **Store verification** is a physical count, usually annual, by a store inspection committee of at least two officers, one unconnected with the store. Differences are explained — an excess brought into account, a shortage recovered or written off, and unserviceable goods written off and disposed of with the prescribed approval.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- Store accounting: introduction, objectives and importance
- Formats used in store accounting
- Main store formats: store ledger, bin card, stock sheet, A.G.F. forms
- Use of the store account and store verification
- Main store formats

A government office does not spend all its money on salaries and services. It also buys **goods** — furniture, computers, stationery, uniforms, spare parts, medicines, fuel — and those goods have to be looked after. Somebody must know how many chairs were received, how many were issued to which room, how many are in the store today, and where the tenth one went. That record is the **store account (जिन्सी लेखा)**. This unit explains what store accounting is and why it matters, the formats it uses, the main store formats, and how the store is verified.

## Chapter summary

- **Store accounting (जिन्सी लेखा)** records the receipt, storage, issue and balance of goods held by a government office, in quantity and in value. Goods are either **consumable** (stationery, fuel, medicines) or **non-consumable or durable** (furniture, computers, vehicles).
- Its **objectives** are to record every receipt and issue, to show the stock balance at any time, to prevent loss and misuse, to provide audit evidence and to help budgeting.
- Its **importance** is that public goods remain public property: the store account ties every article to a document and a person, and protects the honest officer by showing exactly what was received and what was issued.
- The **formats** are the जिन्सी दाखिला फाराम (goods received), the जिन्सी निकासा फाराम (issue), the store ledger, the bin card, the stock statement (जिन्सी मौज्दात फाँटबारी), the verification form and the accounting voucher.
- The **store ledger (जिन्सी खाता)** holds one account per article with receipts, issues and the balance, usually in the **continuous balance** form.
- The **bin card** is kept on the shelf with the article and must always agree with the store ledger; a difference between them is investigated at once.
- The store account is used by the **storekeeper** (what to requisition), the **accounts section** (valuation and entries) and the **auditor** (tracing a bill to the shelf).
- **Store verification** is a physical count, usually annual, by a store inspection committee of at least two officers, one unconnected with the store. Differences are explained — an excess brought into account, a shortage recovered or written off, and unserviceable goods written off and disposed of with the prescribed approval.

## Study route

Close the book and explain the key ideas in your own words.

Attempt a worked example before revealing its solution.

Complete the chapter practice, correct mistakes, then mark the chapter revised.
chapters.question_answers:
## Store ledger entries

**Problem.** The store of a District Education Office holds steel almirahs under head 31121. During Baisakh the following took place. Baisakh 1 — 50 almirahs received from Nepal Trading at Rs. 6,000 each against a bill of Rs. 3,00,000. Baisakh 5 — 10 issued to the accounts section. Baisakh 12 — 25 received from Nepal Trading. Baisakh 20 — 15 issued to the school supervision section. Complete the store ledger and state the balance.
Show also the value of the closing stock.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Enter each receipt in the receipt column and each issue in the issue column, and carry the balance after every entry.

| Date | Particulars | Receipt (no.) | Issue (no.) | Balance (no.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baisakh 1 | Received from Nepal Trading | 50 | | 50 |
| Baisakh 5 | Issued to the account section | | 10 | 40 |
| Baisakh 12 | Received from Nepal Trading | 25 | | 65 |
| Baisakh 20 | Issued to the school supervision section | | 15 | 50 |

Step 2 — Rate: Rs. 6,000 each (from the Baisakh 1 bill).
Step 3 — Closing stock $= 50 \times 6{,}000 = Rs.\ 3{,}00{,}000$.
Step 4 — Check against the documents: total received $= 50 + 25 = 75$; total issued $= 10 + 15 = 25$; balance $= 75 - 25 = 50$. ✔

**Answer.** Closing balance 50 almirahs, valued at Rs. 3,00,000; total received 75, total issued 25.
**What it means.** The bin card on the almirah shelf must show exactly the same three numbers — 75 in, 25 out, 50 in hand. If it does not, either a receipt or an issue went unrecorded, and that is the beginning of a shortage.

## Is this an irregularity?

**Problem.** A storekeeper has 12 reams of paper in the store. A clerk asks for 2 reams for the account section and says he will "sign the register tomorrow". The storekeeper hands over the paper. Two months later the store ledger shows a shortage of 2 reams. Decide whether the storekeeper acted correctly, and what he should have done.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — State the rule. No article may be issued from a government store without a written requisition and a signed **जिन्सी निकासा फाराम**.
Step 2 — What actually happened. The paper left the store without any document, so nothing in the records explains where it went. The store ledger and the bin card still show 12 reams while the shelf holds 10.
Step 3 — The consequence. The shortage of 2 reams is unexplained; if the clerk denies taking the paper, the storekeeper must make it good, because he is answerable for the goods in his charge.
Step 4 — What should have been done: insist on the requisition, fill the जिन्सी निकासा फाराम, obtain the receiving officer's signature, enter the issue in the store ledger and the bin card, and only then hand over the paper.

**Answer.** The storekeeper acted irregularly. He must have a written requisition and a signed issue form before any article leaves the store.
**What it means.** Every rule in store accounting exists to answer one question: who has the goods, and where is the paper that says so?

## Bin card against store ledger

**Problem.** At the annual verification of the store of a District Office, the bin card on the shelf of electric fans shows a balance of 14, while the store ledger shows 15. The committee counts 13 fans on the shelves. Explain what has happened and what the committee should do.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Compare the three figures. Count 13; bin card 14; store ledger 15. So at least one issue of 1 fan and probably another have gone unrecorded, or a fan has been removed without a document.
Step 2 — Check the issue forms against the ledger for the year. If an issue form for 1 fan exists which was not entered in the bin card, the bin card is wrong and must be corrected on the spot.
Step 3 — Trace the remaining difference. A shortage of 1 fan is still unexplained. The committee asks the storekeeper for an explanation and inspects the sections that received fans, because a fan may have been taken to a room without an issue form.
Step 4 — Record the result in the जिन्सी जाँच फाराम, with the reasons; the shortage of 1 fan is reported to the head of office, who will either recover its value from the person responsible or write it off with the approval of the prescribed authority.
Step 5 — Correct the records so that the store ledger, the bin card and the physical count all read 13.

**Answer.** The bin card is corrected to 13, the missing issue form is traced, and the unexplained shortage of 1 fan is reported for recovery or write-off with approval.
**What it means.** A bin card that has not been written up is worse than no bin card at all, because it looks like a record while it is not one. Every issue is entered on both the ledger and the card, on the same day.

Step 4 — Record the result in the जिन्सी जाँच फाराम, with the reasons; the shortage of 1 fan is reported to the head of office, who will either recover its value from the person responsible or write it off with the approval of the prescribed authority.
Step 5 — Correct the records so that the store ledger, the bin card and the physical count all read 13.

**Answer.** The bin card is corrected to 13, the missing issue form is traced, and the unexplained shortage of 1 fan is reported for recovery or write-off with approval.
**What it means.** A bin card that has not been written up is worse than no bin card at all, because it looks like a record while it is not one. Every issue is entered on both the ledger and the card, on the same day.

chapters.question_answers:
## Retention withheld and released

**Problem.** A contractor's running bill for a road contract is Rs. 4,00,000. The office withholds retention at 5 per cent. Show the journal voucher (a) when the bill is passed and the retention is deducted, and (b) when the retention is released after the defect liability period, and (c) when the retention is forfeited because the contractor failed to remedy a defect costing Rs. 12,000.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Retention $= 5\% \times 4{,}00{,}000 = Rs.\ 20{,}000$; the contractor is paid $4{,}00{,}000 - 20{,}000 = Rs.\ 3{,}80{,}000$.
Step 2 — (a) The whole bill is expenditure; part of it is paid and part is held.
*Road construction expenditure A/c Dr. 4,00,000*
*To Contractors' retention A/c 20,000*
*To Bank / DTCO A/c 3,80,000*
(Being the running bill of the contractor passed, retention of 5 per cent withheld and the balance paid.)
Step 3 — (b) No defect appeared, so the money is the contractor's and is paid to him.
*Contractors' retention A/c Dr. 20,000*
*To Bank A/c 20,000*
(Being the retention money released to the contractor on the expiry of the defect liability period.)
Step 4 — (c) A defect costing Rs. 12,000 was not remedied; the office will get the work done at the contractor's cost and the balance is forfeited to the government.
*Contractors' retention A/c Dr. 20,000*
*To Repair and maintenance expenditure A/c 12,000*
*To Miscellaneous revenue A/c 8,000*
(Being the retention money adjusted against the cost of remedying the defect and the balance forfeited to government revenue.)

**Answer.** Retention Rs. 20,000 in each case; the net paid on the bill Rs. 3,80,000; on forfeiture Rs. 12,000 is set against the repair expenditure and Rs. 8,000 becomes revenue.
**What it means.** Until the retention is released or forfeited, it is a **liability**, not revenue. An office that treats retention as income overstates its revenue for the year and will be short when the contractor is finally paid.

## Personal retention

**Problem.** The salary bill of a section is Rs. 2,20,000. The office deducts provident fund Rs. 20,000 and income tax Rs. 2,000 and pays the net. A week later it deposits the deductions into the concerned office. Show the journal vouchers and state what kind of retention each deduction is.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — The whole salary is expenditure; only the net leaves the bank.
*Remuneration expenditure A/c Dr. 2,20,000*
*To Provident fund payable (personal retention) A/c 20,000*
*To Income tax payable (personal retention) A/c 2,000*
*To Bank / DTCO A/c 1,98,000*
(Being the salary of the month passed after the prescribed deductions.)
Step 2 — The deductions belong to the employees and to the tax authority, so the office merely holds and then pays them over.
*Provident fund payable A/c Dr. 20,000*
*Income tax payable A/c Dr. 2,000*
*To Bank A/c 22,000*
(Being the amount deducted from salary deposited into the concerned office.)

**Answer.** Both deductions are **personal retention** — money held on behalf of a person. Net paid Rs. 1,98,000; Rs. 22,000 deposited a week later.
**What it means.** The office was never entitled to that Rs. 22,000. It is the employee's money in the provident fund account and the state's money in the tax account, and the office is only a custodian.

## Distributing the divisible fund

**Problem.** The divisible fund for a year is Rs. 1,20,000 crore. The recommended shares are 30 per cent to the provinces and 25 per cent to the local levels, the remainder staying with the federation. A province receives its share according to a formula in which population has a weight of 50 per cent, area 25 per cent and development 25 per cent. Province A has 20 per cent of the national population, 15 per cent of the area and ranks as a less developed province with a development indicator of 30 per cent. Compute (a) the total provincial share, (b) the total local share and (c) Province A's entitlement as a percentage of the provincial share.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Provincial share $= 30\% 	imes 1{,}20{,}000 = Rs.\ 36{,}000$ crore.
Step 2 — Local share $= 25\% 	imes 1{,}20{,}000 = Rs.\ 30{,}000$ crore.
Step 3 — Province A's weighted index $= (50\% 	imes 20\%) + (25\% 	imes 15\%) + (25\% 	imes 30\%) = 10\% + 3.75\% + 7.5\%$.
Step 4 — Weighted index $= 21.25$ per cent of the total weight, which after normalising across all provinces gives its share of the provincial pool.

**Answer.** (a) Rs. 36,000 crore to the provinces, (b) Rs. 30,000 crore to the local levels, (c) Province A's weighted entitlement works out to an index of 21.25 per cent before normalisation.
**What it means.** The formula is the political heart of federal revenue sharing: give population the largest weight and a big province gains; raise the weight on area and development and a remote, backward province gains. That is why the weights are recommended by an independent commission rather than fixed by the government of the day.

chapters.name: Internal Control and Auditing (आन्तरिक नियन्त्रण र लेखा परीक्षण)
topics: Internal control: introduction, need and use
Government audit in Nepal and the Office of the Auditor General
chapters.summary:
- **Internal control** is the whole system of policies, procedures, records and checks by which an organisation keeps its work accurate, efficient, lawful and honest and protects its assets. It is a system, not a person.
- Its **objectives** are to safeguard assets, to keep the records accurate and complete, to secure efficiency, to ensure compliance with the law, to prevent and detect fraud and error, and to make an audit possible.
- Its **elements** are segregation of duties, authorisation, documentation, physical control, reconciliation, supervision and review, rotation of duties and compulsory leave, internal audit, and comparison with the budget.
- An **audit** is an independent examination of the books and records, carried out so that the auditor may express an opinion on whether the financial statements show a true and fair view.
- The **importance of audit** is confidence for owners and lenders, deterrence and detection of fraud, compliance with the law, advice on internal control, protection of the honest employee, and accountability of the executive to the legislature.
- **Types of audit**: internal and external; continuous, interim and final; complete, partial and special; and by object — financial (regularity), performance, management and propriety.
- An **internal audit** is done by the organisation's own employees, continuously, reporting to the management, mainly to test the internal control system; its independence is limited.
- A **final audit** is done after the year end, by an independent external auditor, and ends in a statutory report with an opinion on the accounts.
- In Nepal government audit is carried out by the **Office of the Auditor General**, a constitutional body whose independence is protected by the manner of the Auditor General's appointment and removal. It audits the federation, the provinces, the local levels, the constitutional bodies, the courts, government corporations and foreign aid, and it audits stores and assets as well as money.
- Government audits are of four kinds — **regularity, performance, special and propriety** — and the report goes to the President and then to Parliament, where the **Public Accounts Committee** examines it and decides what action follows. Observations are settled by producing the asset, the money or the authority, or by recovery.

This unit explains what internal control is and what it must contain, what an audit is and what kinds there are, the difference between an internal audit and a final audit, and how government audit works in Nepal through the Office of the Auditor General.

chapters.question_answers:
## Is internal control adequate?

**Problem.** In a small office, Mr. A receives cash from customers, writes the receipt, enters it in the cash book, and also prepares the monthly bank reconciliation. State what weaknesses exist and suggest the minimum changes possible with only two other staff members (Mr. B and Ms. C).

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Identify the duties that must not be in one pair of hands. Receipt of cash, writing the receipt, recording it, banking it and reconciling the bank.
Step 2 — The danger of the present arrangement. Mr. A could receive cash, not issue a receipt, not enter it and not deposit it, and then prepare a bank reconciliation that hides the shortage. No other person would ever see the difference.
Step 3 — Redistribute with two staff. Let **Mr. B** write the receipt and hold the receipt book, while Mr. A receives the cash and enters the cash book; let **Ms. C** take the daily collection to the bank and keep the deposit slips; and let the **bank reconciliation be prepared by Ms. C** — or, better, by the owner or the senior officer — from the passbook, not from Mr. A's cash book.
Step 4 — Add the cheap controls. Pre-numbered receipt books accounted for leaf by leaf; daily deposit of the collection; surprise counting of cash by the senior officer; and monthly comparison of the receipt-book counterfoils with the cash book.
Step 5 — State the result. No single person can now both misappropriate money and conceal it, so the internal control is adequate for a small office.

**Answer.** Separate the receipt custody, the recording and the bank reconciliation among Mr. A, Mr. B and Ms. C; make the deposit daily; and have the senior officer make surprise checks and compare the counterfoils.
**What it means.** Good internal control in a small office is not expensive equipment. It is the rule that no one person touches a transaction from beginning to end.

## Which audit, and why?

**Problem.** Say what kind of audit is required in each case: (a) the annual audit of a public limited company by a chartered accountant; (b) a check by the organisation's own staff that the store ledger agrees with the bin card each month; (c) an examination by the Office of the Auditor General of whether a road built for Rs. 10 crore produced the traffic benefits claimed for it; (d) an examination, ordered from outside, of the purchase of land by a municipality at a price much above the market rate.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — (a) It is done after the year end, by an independent outsider, for the owners — **final (statutory) external audit**.
Step 2 — (b) It is done by the organisation's own staff, continuously, and it tests a control — **internal audit** (as part of internal control).
Step 3 — (c) The question is not whether the accounts are right but whether value was obtained — **performance (value-for-money) audit**.
Step 4 — (d) A particular transaction is under investigation on a specific order, and propriety as well as regularity is in question — **special audit**, with a propriety angle.

**Answer.** (a) final external audit, (b) internal audit, (c) performance audit, (d) special audit.
**What it means.** The type of audit follows from two questions: **who** is asking, and **what** they want to know. Where the question is "are the accounts true?", it is a financial audit; where it is "was the money well spent?", it is a performance audit.

## Settling an audit observation

**Problem.** An audit of a district office finds that Rs. 40,000 was paid for office furniture but no furniture was entered in the store ledger, and that Rs. 15,000 of revenue collected in Ashad was deposited only in Bhadra. Advise the office on how each observation should be settled.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Furniture Rs. 40,000, paid but not in the store ledger. The auditor cannot see that the government got anything for the money, so this is a **serious** observation. The office must produce the goods, enter them in the store ledger and the bin card with the purchase voucher and the जिन्सी दाखिला फाराम, and report the correction; if the goods cannot be produced, the amount becomes **recoverable** from the officer who passed the bill.
Step 2 — Revenue of Rs. 15,000 deposited late. Money was held outside the consolidated fund for about two months, contrary to the rule that revenue is deposited the same day. The office must explain the delay with evidence (for example, that the bank was closed and the office was in a remote area), produce the deposit slip, and record the reason; if the delay is unexplained, it is a **regularity** observation requiring explanation and, if there is any loss of interest, recovery.
Step 3 — Record the settlement. Both observations are answered in writing to the Office of the Auditor General, with the evidence attached; the store ledger is corrected; and the file is kept so that the same observation is not raised again next year.

**Answer.** The furniture observation is settled by bringing the goods into the store records, failing which the amount is recovered; the late deposit is settled by a written explanation with evidence and, if unexplained, by recovery.
**What it means.** An audit observation is not closed by an argument. It is closed by producing the asset, the money or the authority — and every Nepali government office carries a list of the observations still unsettled against it.

self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** An audit of a district office finds that Rs. 40,000 was paid for office furniture but no furniture was entered in the store ledger, and that Rs. 15,000 of revenue collected in Ashad was deposited only in Bhadra. Advise the office on how each observation should be settled.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — Furniture Rs. 40,000, paid but not in the store ledger. The auditor cannot see that the government got anything for the money, so this is a **serious** observation. The office must produce the goods, enter them in the store ledger and the bin card with the purchase voucher and the जिन्सी दाखिला फाराम, and report the correction; if the goods cannot be produced, the amount becomes **recoverable** from the officer who passed the bill.
Step 2 — Revenue of Rs. 15,000 deposited late. Money was held outside the consolidated fund for about two months, contrary to the rule that revenue is deposited the same day. The office must explain the delay with evidence (for example, that the bank was closed and the office was in a remote area), produce the deposit slip, and record the reason; if the delay is unexplained, it is a **regularity** observation requiring explanation and, if there is any loss of interest, recovery.
Step 3 — Record the settlement. Both observations are answered in writing to the Office of the Auditor General, with the evidence attached; the store ledger is corrected; and the file is kept so that the same observation is not raised again next year.

**Answer.** The furniture observation is settled by bringing the goods into the store records, failing which the amount is recovered; the late deposit is settled by a written explanation with evidence and, if unexplained, by recovery.
**What it means.** An audit observation is not closed by an argument. It is closed by producing the asset, the money or the authority — and every Nepali government office carries a list of the observations still unsettled against it.

chapters.summary:
- Government accounting is a chain of accountability, and each link is an institution: the **Ministry of Finance**, the **National Planning Commission**, the **Financial Comptroller General Office**, the **Treasury and Comptroller Offices**, the spending offices, the **Office of the Auditor General**, the **Public Accounts Committee** and **Nepal Rastra Bank**.
- The **Ministry of Finance** prepares the budget and the annual financial statement, frames revenue and fiscal policy, manages the consolidated fund and the contingency fund, arranges loans and grants, controls public expenditure and lays the FCGO's annual report before the legislature.
- The **Financial Comptroller General Office** releases the budget, keeps the central accounts, supervises the Treasury and Comptroller Offices, consolidates the accounts, maintains the chart of accounts and the formats and runs the computerised systems. It is the accountant of the whole government.
- The **National Planning Commission** prepares the periodic plan, sets priorities and sectoral ceilings, appraises large projects and provides the resource envelope for the budget.
- The **Treasury and Comptroller Offices** (DTCO at district level, PTCO at provincial level) receive the release, make payments on the offices' payment orders, keep the operating level accounts, control expenditure against the release, operate the single account fund and report to the FCGO.
- The **Office of the Auditor General** audits the accounts of the federation, the provinces, the local levels, the constitutional bodies, the courts, government corporations and foreign aid, and reports to the President and thence to Parliament.
- The **Public Accounts Committee** examines the audit report, calls the officials concerned to explain, directs recovery or correction and reports to the House. It is what turns an observation into an action.
- **Nepal Rastra Bank** is the banker to the government: it keeps the government's accounts, receives revenue, makes payments through the Treasury offices and manages government borrowing.
- Under the **banking arrangement**, each office keeps one designated account under the single account fund; the release is credited to it; payments are made by cheque or electronic transfer on a payment order from the Treasury and Comptroller Office; revenue is deposited and never spent; the bank cash book is written daily and reconciled monthly; the account may not be overdrawn and no private accounts are allowed. The arrangement makes the government's cash position knowable, keeps expenditure inside the budget and makes reconciliation possible.

chapters.question_answers:
## Which agency?

**Problem.** Name the agency responsible in each case, and say in one line what the agency is doing. (a) Preparing the annual budget of the Government of Nepal. (b) Releasing the quarterly budget to a district office. (c) Paying the salary of a district office's staff. (d) Auditing the accounts of a municipality. (e) Asking the Secretary of a ministry why a contract was given at an unusually high price, on the basis of the audit report. (f) Keeping the bank account of the government and issuing treasury bills.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — (a) The budget is prepared by the **Ministry of Finance**, using the plan and the ceilings set by the National Planning Commission.
Step 2 — (b) The release is made by the **Financial Comptroller General Office**, through the Treasury and Comptroller Office.
Step 3 — (c) The payment is made by the **Treasury and Comptroller Office** (the DTCO) on the office's payment order — not by the spending office itself.
Step 4 — (d) The audit is by the **Office of the Auditor General**, which audits the local levels as well as the federation and the provinces.
Step 5 — (e) The **Public Accounts Committee** of the legislature examines the audit report and calls the official to explain.
Step 6 — (f) **Nepal Rastra Bank**, which is the banker to the government and manages government borrowing.

**Answer.** (a) Ministry of Finance, (b) FCGO, (c) DTCO, (d) Office of the Auditor General, (e) Public Accounts Committee, (f) Nepal Rastra Bank.
**What it means.** Every agency in the chain exists to make it impossible for one office to both spend public money and be the only witness to how it was spent.

## The banking arrangement in practice

**Problem.** A newly appointed accountant of a district office proposes to open a separate account in a nearby commercial bank for a project fund, "so that the project money is separate and easy to use". Advise him.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — State the rule. A government office may open its account only in the bank named by the FCGO, and under the single account fund it keeps **one** account for its transactions.
Step 2 — Applying the rule, the proposal is **not allowed**. Opening a private account would take government money outside the treasury single account, make the government's cash position unknown, and allow expenditure to escape the release and the budget.
Step 3 — The legitimate need — to see the project's money separately — is met **inside** the system, in two ways: by opening a separate **budget head** for the project with its own code and its own ledger account, and by marking the project fund separately in the office's accounts and monthly statements.
Step 4 — What he should do: apply to the FCGO through the Treasury and Comptroller Office for a separate bank account if the rules permit it, or simply use a distinct budget head and a distinct ledger account within the existing account.

**Answer.** Not allowed as proposed. Use a separate budget head and ledger account within the office's existing government account.
**What it means.** Separation of money for accounting purposes is done with **heads and ledgers**, not with private bank accounts. The single bank account is precisely what makes the government's cash position knowable.

## Functions of the FCGO

**Problem.** A district office has submitted its monthly statement of expenditure and its bank reconciliation to the Treasury and Comptroller Office. State four things the Financial Comptroller General Office will do with that information, and explain why the district office cannot simply keep the figures to itself.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — The DTCO consolidates the district's statement with those of the other offices in its area and forwards it to the FCGO.
Step 2 — The **FCGO records it in the central accounts**, so that the national account of expenditure under each budget head includes the district's figures.
Step 3 — The **FCGO compares expenditure with the release** and sanctions further releases for the coming months; an office spending faster than expected is asked why, and one that is not spending at all may lose part of its allocation.
Step 4 — The **FCGO consolidates all the offices' figures into the government's annual financial statement**, which is audited by the Office of the Auditor General and laid before Parliament.
Step 5 — The **FCGO supervises the office's accounting** — it checks that the prescribed formats, codes and rules were used, and it maintains the chart of accounts and the formats that the district office works with.
Step 6 — Why the office cannot keep the figures to itself: the district office's money is not its own but the government's, voted by Parliament for the whole country; until the district's figures are consolidated the national accounts are incomplete, further releases cannot be justified, and the legislature cannot see how its money was spent.

**Answer.** Consolidation and central accounting; comparison of expenditure with release and the sanction of further releases; consolidation into the annual financial statement for audit and Parliament; and supervision of the prescribed formats, codes and systems.
**What it means.** Operating level accounting in the office is only half the system. The figures have to travel upwards, or the nation's accounts would be a sum of fragments and the legislature would be voting money blind.

chapters.summary:
- A **computer** accepts data, processes it by stored instructions, stores it and outputs it; its parts are the input unit, the processing unit, memory, the output unit and storage.
- **Information technology** is the whole set of hardware, software, networks, data, people and procedures by which information is collected, stored, processed and communicated.
- **Office packages** are the application software of an office: the word processor (letters and reports), the spreadsheet (salary sheets, budgets, registers), the presentation package (slides), the database (large structured records), the accounting package (double-entry accounts) and e-mail.
- In a **spreadsheet**, a formula refers to other cells and the results update automatically when a figure changes — which is why it is the office tool for repeated calculations.
- The **internet** is a worldwide network of computers using common rules. An office uses it for communication, information, government services, banking, publishing, cloud working and electronic procurement, and must guard against fraud, phishing, viruses and leakage.
- A computer is used in an office for correspondence, electronic filing, accounts, payroll, stores, budgeting, bank work, communication, data analysis and security.
- The **advantages** of information technology are speed, accuracy, storage and retrieval, automatic posting, instant reporting, communication, less paper, better control and consistency. The **disadvantages** are cost, dependence, data loss, fraud and hacking, training, unemployment, health, garbage in garbage out, loss of the paper trail and obsolescence.
- In **business accounting**, the computer records the transaction once, posts it automatically, keeps the ledgers and trial balance always current, and produces the final accounts and reports for any period. It needs controls: passwords and user rights, daily backup, the audit trail, and printed signed copies. Software used in Nepal includes **Tally, Swastik, Easy Account, Quick Book**; in banks, **Pumori, Finacle, FlexCube, Globus**.
- In **government accounting** Nepal uses **BMIS** (budget preparation, release and transfer in the Ministry of Finance), **LMBIS** (line ministry budget formulation and implementation; PLMBIS in the provinces), **FMIS** (integrated national financial reporting, FCGO), **TSA** (the single account through which the budget is released and spent, operated by the Treasury and Comptroller Offices), **CGAS** (activity-based accounting linked to LMBIS, under the FCGO) and **SUTRA** (the integrated system for local levels), besides PAMS, PMIS, E-GP, ITS and RAS.
- These systems make the government's finances visible and its controls automatic, and they are integrated, so a figure entered at one end is seen at the other.

chapters.question_answers:
## Word or Excel?

**Problem.** Say which office package should be used for each job, and why: (a) typing an office order for the signature of the head of office; (b) preparing the salary sheet of 45 staff for the month; (c) preparing a stock register in which the balance must update whenever goods are received or issued; (d) preparing the slides for a training session; (e) recording the daily transactions of a business and producing the profit and loss account at the end of the year.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — (a) A letter or order is text, to be formatted and printed → **word processor (Word)**.
Step 2 — (b) A salary sheet is a calculation repeated over many rows, with totals and deductions → **spreadsheet (Excel)**, because the formulae update themselves when a figure changes.
Step 3 — (c) A stock register with an updating balance is a calculation over a list → **spreadsheet** again (or a small **database**, if the register is large and has to be queried).
Step 4 — (d) Slides for a presentation → **presentation package (PowerPoint)**.
Step 5 — (e) Recording transactions and producing the final accounts requires double entry, a ledger and reports → an **accounting package (Tally, Swastik, Easy Account)**, not a spreadsheet.

**Answer.** (a) Word, (b) Excel, (c) Excel or a database package, (d) PowerPoint, (e) an accounting package.
**What it means.** Choose the tool by the nature of the job: text by a word processor, calculation by a spreadsheet, double-entry accounting by an accounting package. Using a spreadsheet where an accounting package belongs is how businesses end up with a balance sheet that does not tally.

## Advantages and disadvantages weighed

**Problem.** A small district office with five staff has to decide whether to computerise its accounts. Two staff have computer training and one does not. Advise the office.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — List what the office would gain. Speed and accuracy in the salary and the store registers; automatic totalling and reporting; the monthly statement of expenditure produced from the ledger; less paper and less filing space; and better control through passwords and an audit trail.
Step 2 — List what it would cost. A computer, a printer, a licensed accounting package, a backup drive and, above all, the training of the staff who have none.
Step 3 — Identify the real risks. The volume of work in a five-person office is modest, so the gain is smaller than in a large commercial office; if the one trained clerk leaves, the system may stop; and if no backup is taken, a single failure loses the year's accounts.
Step 4 — Decide. Computerise in stages: first the salary and the store register (the two jobs that repeat most), with a written backup routine and one more member of staff trained; keep a printed copy of every statement signed and filed; and move the accounts to an accounting package only when the volume justifies it and two staff can operate it.

**Answer.** Computerise by stages, train a second operator, take a daily backup and keep printed signed copies.
**What it means.** Information technology is not automatically an improvement. It is an improvement **if** the volume of work justifies it, the staff can run it and the controls — training, backup and audit trail — are in place.

## Which government system?

**Problem.** Name the system used in each case: (a) a ministry preparing its budget proposal and sending it to the Ministry of Finance; (b) the Ministry of Finance preparing the budget and releasing money; (c) the Financial Comptroller General Office consolidating the national financial report; (d) a district office receiving a budget release and making payments from a single account; (e) a rural municipality preparing its budget and keeping its accounts.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — (a) A line ministry's budget formulation and implementation → **LMBIS** (in the provinces, PLMBIS).
Step 2 — (b) Budget preparation, release and transfer at the Ministry of Finance → **BMIS**.
Step 3 — (c) The integrated national financial reporting system run by the FCGO → **FMIS**; the activity-based accounting linked with LMBIS is **CGAS**.
Step 4 — (d) The single account through which the budget is released and spent, operated by the Treasury and Comptroller Office → **TSA** (Treasury Single Account).
Step 5 — (e) The integrated system for the local levels — budget, execution, accounting and reporting → **SUTRA**.

**Answer.** (a) LMBIS, (b) BMIS, (c) FMIS (with CGAS), (d) TSA, (e) SUTRA.
**What it means.** Each system covers one link of the same chain: the ministry plans, the Ministry of Finance budgets and releases, the FCGO consolidates, the district pays through the single account, and the local level runs its own treasury. They are integrated, so a figure entered at one end is visible at the other.

Step 3 — Identify the real risks. The volume of work in a five-person office is modest, so the gain is smaller than in a large commercial office; if the one trained clerk leaves, the system may stop; and if no backup is taken, a single failure loses the year's accounts.
Step 4 — Decide. Computerise in stages: first the salary and the store register (the two jobs that repeat most), with a written backup routine and one more member of staff trained; keep a printed copy of every statement signed and filed; and move the accounts to an accounting package only when the volume justifies it and two staff can operate it.

**Answer.** Computerise by stages, train a second operator, take a daily backup and keep printed signed copies.
**What it means.** Information technology is not automatically an improvement. It is an improvement **if** the volume of work justifies it, the staff can run it and the controls — training, backup and audit trail — are in place.

self_checks.question: Which government system?
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** Name the system used in each case: (a) a ministry preparing its budget proposal and sending it to the Ministry of Finance; (b) the Ministry of Finance preparing the budget and releasing money; (c) the Financial Comptroller General Office consolidating the national financial report; (d) a district office receiving a budget release and making payments from a single account; (e) a rural municipality preparing its budget and keeping its accounts.

**Solution.**
Step 1 — (a) A line ministry's budget formulation and implementation → **LMBIS** (in the provinces, PLMBIS).
Step 2 — (b) Budget preparation, release and transfer at the Ministry of Finance → **BMIS**.
Step 3 — (c) The integrated national financial reporting system run by the FCGO → **FMIS**; the activity-based accounting linked with LMBIS is **CGAS**.
Step 4 — (d) The single account through which the budget is released and spent, operated by the Treasury and Comptroller Office → **TSA** (Treasury Single Account).
Step 5 — (e) The integrated system for the local levels — budget, execution, accounting and reporting → **SUTRA**.

**Answer.** (a) LMBIS, (b) BMIS, (c) FMIS (with CGAS), (d) TSA, (e) SUTRA.
**What it means.** Each system covers one link of the same chain: the ministry plans, the Ministry of Finance budgets and releases, the FCGO consolidates, the district pays through the single account, and the local level runs its own treasury. They are integrated, so a figure entered at one end is visible at the other.

- Cell [8]: prokaryotic and eukaryotic cell; cell wall; cell membrane; mitochondria; plastids; endoplasmic reticulum; golgi apparatus; lysosomes; ribosomes; nucleus; chromosomes; cilia and flagella; cell inclusions

names the molecules of life and says what each one does. Then it takes the cell

chapters.question_answers:
## Worked example 1.1 — counting peptide bonds

**Problem.** (a) A polypeptide contains 150 amino acid residues in a single
unbranched chain. How many peptide bonds does it contain, and how many water
molecules were released when it was made? (b) Glycine has relative molecular
mass 75 and alanine 89. Find the relative molecular mass of the dipeptide
glycylalanine.

**Solution.**

(a) Each peptide bond joins two neighbouring residues, so a chain of $n$
residues has $n - 1$ bonds:

$$ \text{peptide bonds} = 150 - 1 = 149 $$

One water molecule is lost per bond formed, so 149 molecules of water were
released.

(b) Condensation removes one water molecule (RMM 18):

$$ 75 + 89 - 18 = 146 $$

The dipeptide has a relative molecular mass of **146**.

## Worked example 1.2 — using Chargaff's rule

**Problem.** A sample of double-stranded DNA contains 22 % adenine. Calculate the
percentage of each of the other three bases, and find the ratio
$\dfrac{A+T}{G+C}$.

**Solution.** Chargaff's rule for double-stranded DNA is $A = T$ and $G = C$.

Since $A = 22\ \%$, thymine $T = 22\ \%$, so $A + T = 44\ \%$.

The four bases must total 100 %, so $G + C = 100 - 44 = 56\ \%$, and because
$G = C$,

$$ G = C = \frac{56}{2} = 28\ \% $$

Hence $A = T = 22\ \%$, $G = C = 28\ \%$, and

$$ \frac{A+T}{G+C} = \frac{44}{56} = 0.79 $$

## Worked example 1.3 — magnification

**Problem.** (a) A microscope has a 10× eyepiece and a 45× objective. What is the
total magnification? (b) On a photomicrograph taken at ×600, a chloroplast
measures 2.7 mm. Find its actual length in micrometres.

**Solution.**

(a) Magnifications multiply:

$$ M = 10 \times 45 = 450\times $$

(b) Magnification $= \dfrac{\text{image size}}{\text{actual size}}$, so

$$ \text{actual size} = \frac{2.7\ \text{mm}}{600} = 0.0045\ \text{mm} $$

Since $1\ \text{mm} = 1000\ \mu\text{m}$, the chloroplast is
$0.0045 \times 1000 = 4.5\ \mu\text{m}$ long — a normal value.

## Worked example 1.4 — why cells stay small

**Problem.** Treat two cells as cubes of side 10 μm and 30 μm. Calculate the
surface area, volume and surface-area-to-volume ratio of each, and comment.

**Solution.** For a cube of side $a$, surface area $= 6a^{2}$ and volume $= a^{3}$,
so the ratio is

$$ \frac{S}{V} = \frac{6a^{2}}{a^{3}} = \frac{6}{a} $$

For $a = 10\ \mu\text{m}$: $S = 600\ \mu\text{m}^{2}$,
$V = 1000\ \mu\text{m}^{3}$, $S/V = 0.6\ \mu\text{m}^{-1}$.

For $a = 30\ \mu\text{m}$: $S = 5400\ \mu\text{m}^{2}$,
$V = 27\,000\ \mu\text{m}^{3}$, $S/V = 0.2\ \mu\text{m}^{-1}$.

Trebling the side divides the ratio by three. Materials enter through the
surface but are used by the whole volume, so a large cell cannot supply its
interior fast enough by diffusion. That is why cells stay small, and why cells
that must absorb a lot — root hairs, intestinal cells — throw out extensions to
raise the surface area instead of growing bigger.

## Worked example 1.5 — counting chromosomes through division

**Problem.** The onion *Allium cepa* has $2n = 16$. For a root-tip cell,
state (a) the number of chromosomes and of chromatids at mitotic metaphase,
(b) the number of chromosomes moving to each pole at mitotic anaphase, and
(c) the number of bivalents at metaphase I and the chromosome number of each cell
at the end of meiosis in an anther.

**Solution.**

(a) DNA has replicated in S phase, so there are still **16 chromosomes**, but
each has 2 chromatids:

$$ 16 \times 2 = 32\ \text{chromatids} $$

(b) At anaphase each centromere splits, so all 32 chromatids become separate
chromosomes and half go to each pole:

$$ \frac{32}{2} = 16\ \text{chromosomes to each pole} $$

— which is why each daughter cell is again $2n = 16$.

(c) A bivalent is a pair of homologues, so

$$ \text{bivalents} = \frac{16}{2} = 8 $$

Meiosis halves the number, so each of the four microspores has
$n = 8$ chromosomes.

chapters.name: Floral Diversity
topics: Introduction [1]: three domains of life; binomial nomenclature; five-kingdom classification; flora status of Nepal
Angiosperm [16]: morphology; taxonomic hierarchy; artificial, natural and phylogenetic systems; Brassicaceae; Fabaceae; Solanaceae; Liliaceae
chapters.summary:
- **Three domains** — Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya — were proposed by Woese (1977)
  from 16S rRNA sequences. Archaea and Bacteria are prokaryotic; only Archaea have
  branched, ether-linked membrane lipids.
- **Binomial nomenclature** (Linnaeus, *Species Plantarum*, 1753) gives every
  species a two-word Latin name: capitalised genus, lower-case species epithet,
  italicised in print, underlined separately in handwriting, governed by the ICN
  and the principle of priority.
- **Whittaker's five kingdoms** (1969) — Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae,
  Animalia — separate organisms by cell type, body organisation and **mode of
  nutrition**. Viruses fall outside the scheme entirely.
- **Nepal** holds over **3 %** of the world's known plants on **0.1 %** of its
  land: about 6,500 angiosperms, 28 gymnosperms, 534 pteridophytes, 1,150
  bryophytes, 771 lichens, with about 300 endemic flowering plants.
- **Fungi** are achlorophyllous absorptive heterotrophs with chitin walls,
  glycogen reserve and a mycelium of coenocytic or septate hyphae. Sexual
  reproduction runs plasmogamy → karyogamy → meiosis, with a **dikaryotic** stage
  in the higher classes. Four classes: Phycomycetes (zygospore), Ascomycetes
  (8 ascospores in an ascus), Basidiomycetes (4 basidiospores on a basidium),
  Deuteromycetes (sexual stage unknown).
- **Lichens** are fungus + alga: the mycobiont gives the body and absorbs water,
  the photobiont gives the food. Crustose, foliose and fruticose growth forms;
  reproduction chiefly by **soredia** and **isidia**. They are pioneers of rock
  succession, indicators of SO₂ pollution and the source of litmus.
- **Algae** are thalloid autotrophs with unicellular sex organs and no embryo.
  Fritsch's classes are recognised by pigment and reserve food: green (starch),
  brown (laminarin, fucoxanthin), red (floridean starch, phycoerythrin, **no
  flagella**). Sexual reproduction advances through isogamy → anisogamy → oogamy.
- **Bryophytes** are the amphibians of the plant kingdom: **gametophyte dominant**,
  no vascular tissue, rhizoids instead of roots, jacketed antheridia and
  archegonia, water needed for fertilisation, and a dependent sporophyte of foot,
  seta and capsule.
- **Pteridophytes** are **vascular cryptogams**: **sporophyte dominant** with true
  root, stem and leaf, xylem of tracheids, sporangia in sori with an annulus and
  indusium, and a small independent prothallus. Heterospory (*Selaginella*,
  *Marsilea*, *Salvinia*) is the evolutionary step towards the seed.
- **Gymnosperms** bear **naked seeds** on open megasporophylls in cones, lack
  vessels (except Gnetales), are wind-pollinated directly on to the micropyle,
  form **haploid endosperm before fertilisation**, show polyembryony, and never
  form fruit.
- **Angiosperms** enclose the ovule in an ovary, undergo **double fertilisation**
  and form fruit; they divide into monocots (one cotyledon, fibrous roots,
  parallel venation, scattered closed bundles, trimerous flowers) and dicots.
- The **taxonomic hierarchy** is Kingdom → Division → Class → Order → Family →
  Genus → Species; only the species is a natural unit.
- Classification systems are **artificial** (Linnaeus, a few characters),
  **natural** (Bentham and Hooker, *Genera Plantarum* 1862–83, many characters,
  gymnosperms wrongly placed between dicots and monocots) and **phylogenetic**
  (Engler and Prantl, and today APG, based on descent).
- The four families reduce to four formulae: **Brassicaceae K2+2 C4 A2+4 G(2)**,
  **Fabaceae K(5) C1+2+(2) A(9)+1 G1**, **Solanaceae K(5) C(5) A5 G(2)**,
  **Liliaceae P3+3 A3+3 G(3)**.

Nepal occupies about one tenth of one per cent of the land surface of the Earth,

chapters.question_answers:
## Worked example 2.1 — Nepal's flora in proportion

Nepal's land area is 147,181 km²; the world's land area is about
148,940,000 km². Nepal has about 6,500 flowering plants; the world has about
250,000. Show that Nepal's flora is disproportionately rich, and express that
disproportion as a single number.

**Share of land area**

(147,181 ÷ 148,940,000) × 100 = 0.0988 % ≈ **0.1 %**

**Share of flowering plants**

(6,500 ÷ 250,000) × 100 = **2.6 %**

**The disproportion** is the ratio of these two shares:

2.6 ÷ 0.0988 ≈ **26**

So a square kilometre of Nepal carries, on average, about **26 times** as many
species of flowering plant as an average square kilometre of the Earth's land
surface. This single figure is the quantitative statement of "Nepal is a
biodiversity hotspot", and the cause is the altitudinal range: climbing 1,000 m
is climatically equivalent to travelling roughly 1,000 km towards the pole, so a
single Nepali hillside stacks many climates one above another.

## Worked example 2.2 — Ploidy through the life cycle

A moss has a haploid chromosome number of n = 14. State the chromosome number of
(i) a spore, (ii) the protonema, (iii) a leaf cell of the green plant,
(iv) an antherozoid, (v) the egg, (vi) the zygote, (vii) a cell of the seta,
(viii) a spore mother cell, and (ix) the spores it produces. Then find how many
spores 10 spore mother cells yield.

**Method.** Draw one line through the cycle and mark the only two events that
change ploidy: **fertilisation doubles** it, **meiosis halves** it. Everything
between those two events has the same number.

Fertilisation happens when egg meets antherozoid; meiosis happens in the spore
mother cells inside the capsule. So *everything from the spore up to the
gametes* is haploid, and *everything from the zygote to the spore mother cell*
is diploid.

| Stage | Ploidy | Chromosome number |
|---|---|---|
| (i) spore | n | 14 |
| (ii) protonema | n | 14 |
| (iii) leaf cell of the gametophyte | n | 14 |
| (iv) antherozoid | n | 14 |
| (v) egg | n | 14 |
| (vi) zygote | 2n | 28 |
| (vii) seta (part of the sporophyte) | 2n | 28 |
| (viii) spore mother cell | 2n | 28 |
| (ix) spores produced from it | n | 14 |

**Spore count.** Meiosis of one spore mother cell gives four spores, so

10 × 4 = **40 spores**.

Note the trap in (vii): the seta *looks* like part of the moss plant and is
attached to it, but it belongs to the sporophyte and is therefore diploid. The
same logic answers every ploidy question in this unit — including the fern, where
the answers come out the other way round because the *sporophyte* is the big
plant there.

## Worked example 2.3 — Using a dichotomous key

A key is a branching set of paired statements (**couplets**); at each couplet you
choose the half that fits your specimen and follow the number at its end. Use the
key below to identify four specimens: **A** a small green plant, 2 cm tall, with
no roots and a stalked capsule; **B** a plant with an underground rhizome and
coiled young leaves bearing brown patches beneath the mature ones; **C** a tree
with needle leaves in threes and a woody cone; **D** a herb with yellow
four-petalled flowers and a long pod.

```
1a. Vascular tissue absent; no true roots ................................... 2
1b. Vascular tissue present; true roots present ............................. 3
2a. Plant a flat thallus .......................................... Liverwort
2b. Plant a leafy axis with a stalked capsule .......................... Moss
3a. Seeds absent; reproduction by spores ............................... Fern
3b. Seeds present ........................................................... 4
4a. Seeds naked on a cone scale; leaves needle-like ............... Gymnosperm
4b. Seeds enclosed in a fruit; flowers present .................... Angiosperm
```

**A.** No roots, so take 1a, then 2. It has a leafy axis and a stalked capsule, so
2b → **moss** (a bryophyte such as *Funaria*). The stalked capsule is the
sporophyte.

**B.** It has roots and vascular tissue, so 1b → 3. There are no seeds; the brown
patches are **sori** of sporangia, so 3a → **fern** (a pteridophyte such as
*Dryopteris*). Circinate vernation confirms it.

**C.** 1b → 3, seeds present → 4, needles and a woody cone → 4a → **gymnosperm**
(*Pinus roxburghii*, since the needles are in threes).

**D.** 1b → 3 → 4; flowers and a fruit are present → 4b → **angiosperm**. Four
petals and a long pod make it a crucifer — *Brassica campestris*.

The two points to notice are that a key uses only **contrasting, easily observed**
characters, and that each couplet must be **mutually exclusive and exhaustive**,
so that exactly one path is possible for any specimen.

## Worked example 2.4 — Writing a floral formula from a description

"The flower is subtended by a bract. It is bisexual and can be divided into two
equal halves in one plane only. There are five united sepals, five free petals of
which one is large and posterior, two are lateral and two are fused below, ten
stamens of which nine are joined by their filaments and one is free, and a single
carpel whose ovary lies above the other whorls." Write the floral formula, name
the family and predict the fruit.

**Step 1 — decode each phrase into a symbol.**

| Phrase in the description | Meaning | Symbol |
|---|---|---|
| subtended by a bract | bracteate | Br |
| divisible into two equal halves in one plane only | zygomorphic | % (or state in words) |
| five united sepals | gamosepalous calyx of 5 | K(5) |
| one posterior + two lateral + two fused | papilionaceous corolla | C1+2+(2) |
| nine joined, one free | diadelphous androecium of 10 | A(9)+1 |
| single carpel | monocarpellary gynoecium | G1 |
| ovary above the other whorls | hypogynous, superior ovary | underline G |

**Step 2 — assemble.** Brackets mean united, a plus sign separates whorls or
groups, and a bar under the G means the ovary is superior:

**Bisexual, zygomorphic — K(5) C1+2+(2) A(9)+1 G1**

**Step 3 — identify.** A zygomorphic papilionaceous corolla with a diadelphous
(9)+1 androecium and a monocarpellary superior ovary is diagnostic of
**Fabaceae** (Papilionoideae) — for example *Pisum sativum*.

**Step 4 — predict the fruit.** A single carpel with marginal placentation
dehiscing along both sutures gives a **legume** (pod), and the seeds will be
non-endospermic with food stored in the two fleshy cotyledons.

Work the same three steps backwards to answer the commoner version of this
question: "given the formula K(5) C(5) A5 G(2), describe the flower" — five
united sepals, five united petals, five epipetalous stamens, a bicarpellary
syncarpous superior ovary, actinomorphic and bisexual, so **Solanaceae**, and the
fruit is a berry or a capsule.

self_checks.question: Worked example 2.1 — Nepal's flora in proportion
self_checks.answer:
Nepal's land area is 147,181 km²; the world's land area is about
148,940,000 km². Nepal has about 6,500 flowering plants; the world has about
250,000. Show that Nepal's flora is disproportionately rich, and express that
disproportion as a single number.

**Share of land area**

(147,181 ÷ 148,940,000) × 100 = 0.0988 % ≈ **0.1 %**

**Share of flowering plants**

(6,500 ÷ 250,000) × 100 = **2.6 %**

**The disproportion** is the ratio of these two shares:

2.6 ÷ 0.0988 ≈ **26**

So a square kilometre of Nepal carries, on average, about **26 times** as many
species of flowering plant as an average square kilometre of the Earth's land
surface. This single figure is the quantitative statement of "Nepal is a
biodiversity hotspot", and the cause is the altitudinal range: climbing 1,000 m
is climatically equivalent to travelling roughly 1,000 km towards the pole, so a
single Nepali hillside stacks many climates one above another.

topics: The growth of a bacterial population
chapters.summary:
- Monera contains all prokaryotes: no nuclear envelope, no membrane-bound
  organelles, 70S ribosomes, a single naked circular DNA, and a peptidoglycan
  wall (absent in *Mycoplasma*, non-peptidoglycan in Archaebacteria).
- Bacterial shapes are coccus, bacillus, vibrio and spiral; the prefixes diplo-,
  strepto-, staphylo-, tetrad and sarcina name the arrangements.
- Gram-positive walls have thick peptidoglycan and teichoic acid and stain
  violet; Gram-negative walls have thin peptidoglycan plus an outer
  lipopolysaccharide membrane and stain pink.
- Reproduction is binary fission (amitosis); endospores are for survival, not
  reproduction; DNA is exchanged by transformation, conjugation and transduction.
- Population growth is geometric: $N = N_0 \times 2^{n}$ with $n = t/g$.
- A virus is a nucleoprotein particle — one kind of nucleic acid in a capsid of
  capsomeres — that is inert outside its host and multiplies only inside it,
  by the lytic or the lysogenic cycle.
- T4 bacteriophage: icosahedral head of dsDNA, collar, contractile sheath, hollow
  core, base plate, tail fibres. TMV: helical rod 300 × 18 nm, 2130 capsomeres,
  ssRNA.
- Microbial biotechnology uses restriction enzymes, ligase, plasmid vectors and
  *E. coli* hosts to make insulin, vaccines, Bt crops, biofertilisers, biogas and
  bioremediation agents — with biosafety and biopiracy as the chief concerns.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- Monera [3]
- Virus [1]
- Impacts of biotechnology in microbiology [1]
- Monera
- Virus
- Impacts of biotechnology in microbiology
- General characters
- Shape and arrangement
- Structure of a bacterial cell
- Nutrition
- Reproduction
- The growth of a bacterial population
- Classification of Monera
- Economic importance of bacteria
- Living and non-living characters
- Structure
- Multiplication — the lytic cycle

Microbiology is the study of organisms too small to see with the naked eye. Two
groups dominate this unit: the **bacteria** of kingdom Monera, which are true
cells but have no nucleus, and the **viruses**, which are not cells at all. They
matter out of all proportion to their size — they fix the nitrogen in a lentil
field in Bara, set curd in a Kathmandu kitchen, rot the jute in a Jhapa retting
pit, and cause cholera, typhoid and COVID-19. The unit ends with what happens
when we deliberately re-engineer them: biotechnology.

## Chapter summary

- Monera contains all prokaryotes: no nuclear envelope, no membrane-bound
  organelles, 70S ribosomes, a single naked circular DNA, and a peptidoglycan
  wall (absent in *Mycoplasma*, non-peptidoglycan in Archaebacteria).
- Bacterial shapes are coccus, bacillus, vibrio and spiral; the prefixes diplo-,
  strepto-, staphylo-, tetrad and sarcina name the arrangements.
- Gram-positive walls have thick peptidoglycan and teichoic acid and stain
  violet; Gram-negative walls have thin peptidoglycan plus an outer
  lipopolysaccharide membrane and stain pink.
- Reproduction is binary fission (amitosis); endospores are for survival, not
  reproduction; DNA is exchanged by transformation, conjugation and transduction.
- Population growth is geometric: $N = N_0 \times 2^{n}$ with $n = t/g$.
- A virus is a nucleoprotein particle — one kind of nucleic acid in a capsid of
  capsomeres — that is inert outside its host and multiplies only inside it,
  by the lytic or the lysogenic cycle.
- T4 bacteriophage: icosahedral head of dsDNA, collar, contractile sheath, hollow
  core, base plate, tail fibres. TMV: helical rod 300 × 18 nm, 2130 capsomeres,
  ssRNA.
- Microbial biotechnology uses restriction enzymes, ligase, plasmid vectors and

  bioremediation agents — with biosafety and biopiracy as the chief concerns.

chapters.question_answers:
## Worked example 3.1

**Problem.** A culture starts with $1 \times 10^{3}$ cells of *Escherichia coli*
whose generation time is 20 minutes. How many cells are present after 3 hours of
exponential growth?

**Solution.** Time available $t = 3 \times 60 = 180$ minutes, so

$$ n = \frac{t}{g} = \frac{180}{20} = 9 \ \text{generations} $$

$$ N = N_0 \times 2^{n} = 1\times10^{3} \times 2^{9} = 1\times10^{3} \times 512 = 5.12 \times 10^{5}\ \text{cells} $$

## Worked example 3.2

**Problem.** A bacterial population rises from $5 \times 10^{3}$ to
$3.2 \times 10^{5}$ cells in 2 hours. Find the number of generations and the
generation time.

**Solution.** The growth factor is

$$ \frac{N}{N_0} = \frac{3.2\times10^{5}}{5\times10^{3}} = 64 = 2^{6} $$

so $n = 6$ generations. Then

$$ g = \frac{t}{n} = \frac{120\ \text{min}}{6} = 20\ \text{minutes} $$

## Worked example 3.3

**Problem.** A milk sample is diluted $10^{-5}$ times. $0.1\ \text{mL}$ of the
dilution is spread on nutrient agar and gives 148 colonies. Calculate the number
of colony-forming units (CFU) per millilitre of the original milk.

**Solution.** Each colony arose from one cell, so

$$ \text{CFU mL}^{-1} = \frac{\text{colonies}}{\text{volume plated} \times \text{dilution}}
 = \frac{148}{0.1 \times 10^{-5}} $$

$$ = 148 \times 10^{6} = 1.48 \times 10^{8}\ \text{CFU mL}^{-1} $$

The milk is heavily contaminated: the acceptable limit for pasteurised milk is
about $10^{5}\ \text{CFU mL}^{-1}$.

## Worked example 3.4

**Problem.** One T4 phage infects a single *E. coli* cell. Each lytic cycle takes
25 minutes and has a **burst size** of 200. Assuming every released phage at once
finds a fresh host, how many free phages exist after 75 minutes?

**Solution.** In 75 minutes there are $75/25 = 3$ complete cycles. Each phage
becomes 200, so

$$ N = 200^{3} = 8 \times 10^{6}\ \text{phages} $$

from a single starting particle — which is why a phage-infected culture clears
within an hour.

chapters.name: Ecology
topics: Food chain, food web and trophic levels
Energy flow and the ten per cent law
chapters.summary:
- An ecosystem (Tansley, 1935) has abiotic components (climatic, edaphic,
  inorganic, organic) and biotic components (producers, consumers, decomposers).
- Food chains are grazing or detritus type; crossing chains form a food web,
  which gives the ecosystem stability.
- Energy flow is **unidirectional**: about 1 % of incident light is fixed, and
  only ~10 % passes from each trophic level to the next (Lindeman's ten per cent
  law). Matter, in contrast, moves in cycles.
- $\text{NPP} = \text{GPP} - R$; standing crop is a mass, productivity is a rate.
- Pyramids of number and of biomass may be inverted; the **pyramid of energy is
  always upright**.
- Population density $D = N/A$; unlimited growth is exponential,
  $N_t = N_0 e^{rt}$ (J-shaped); limited growth is logistic,
  $dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K$ (S-shaped), levelling at the carrying capacity $K$.
- Nitrogen cycle: fixation → ammonification → nitrification (*Nitrosomonas*,
  then *Nitrobacter*) → assimilation → denitrification (*Pseudomonas
  denitrificans*).
- Carbon cycle: photosynthesis takes CO₂ in; respiration, decomposition and
  combustion of fossil fuels put it back.
- Succession runs pioneer → seral stages → climax; hydrosere begins in water,
  xerosere on bare rock, and both end in the same mesic forest.
- Hydrophytes have aerenchyma, thin cuticle and reduced roots; xerophytes have
  deep roots, thick cuticle, sunken stomata and often CAM.
- Ecological imbalance in Nepal shows as Chure degradation, invasive *Mikania*
  and *Eichhornia*, retreating glaciers and glacial lake outburst floods; the
  answers are afforestation, community forestry, soil conservation, pollution
  control and law.

## Topics to cover

- Ecosystem ecology [7]
- Ecological Adaptation [2]

- Ecosystem ecology
- Ecological adaptation
- Ecological imbalances
- Components of an ecosystem

- Biogeochemical cycles
- Ecological succession
- Hydrophytes — plants of water
- Xerophytes — plants of dry places

- Causes

Ecology is the study of the relationship between organisms and their

every monsoon, why *Mikania* is choking the sal forest. The unit works outward

chapters.question_answers:
## Worked example 4.1

**Problem.** The producers of a grassland fix $20{,}000\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1}$.
Using the ten per cent law, find the energy available to the herbivores, to the
carnivores and to the top carnivores, and the total energy lost as heat between
the producer and the top-carnivore levels.

**Solution.** Each level receives one tenth of the previous one:

$$ E_2 = 0.10 \times 20{,}000 = 2000\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1} $$
$$ E_3 = 0.10 \times 2000 = 200\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1} $$
$$ E_4 = 0.10 \times 200 = 20\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1} $$

Energy lost as heat is the difference between what enters a level and what leaves
it:

$$ \text{loss} = (20{,}000-2000) + (2000-200) + (200-20) = 18{,}000 + 1800 + 180 $$

$$ = 19{,}980\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1} $$

That is 99.9 % of the producers' energy — the tiger lives on the last 0.1 %.

## Worked example 4.2

**Problem.** In one year a hectare of sal forest fixes a gross primary production
of $12{,}000\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}$ and uses $7500\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}$ in its own
respiration. Calculate the net primary productivity and express it as a
percentage of GPP.

**Solution.**

$$ \text{NPP} = \text{GPP} - R = 12{,}000 - 7500 = 4500\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1} $$

$$ \frac{\text{NPP}}{\text{GPP}} \times 100 = \frac{4500}{12{,}000} \times 100 = 37.5\ \% $$

Only 37.5 % of what the forest fixes is available to every animal and decomposer
in it; a forest spends more on respiration than a crop field does because it
carries a large mass of non-photosynthetic wood.

## Worked example 4.3

**Problem.** A student lays 20 quadrats, each $1\ \text{m}^{2}$, in a Shivapuri
grassland. *Imperata cylindrica* occurs in 15 of them, and 240 shoots are counted
altogether. Calculate its density, frequency and abundance.

**Solution.**

$$ \text{Density} = \frac{\text{total individuals}}{\text{total quadrats studied}}
= \frac{240}{20} = 12\ \text{shoots m}^{-2} $$

$$ \text{Frequency} = \frac{15}{20} \times 100 = 75\ \% $$

$$ \text{Abundance} = \frac{\text{total individuals}}{\text{quadrats of occurrence}}
= \frac{240}{15} = 16\ \text{shoots per occupied quadrat} $$

## Worked example 4.4

**Problem.** A protected population of 1000 chital deer grows exponentially with
$r = 0.20\ \text{yr}^{-1}$. What will the population be after 5 years?
Take $e = 2.718$.

**Solution.**

$$ N_t = N_0\,e^{rt} = 1000 \times e^{0.20 \times 5} = 1000 \times e^{1} $$

$$ = 1000 \times 2.718 = 2718\ \text{deer} $$

The population has nearly trebled in five years — which is why a fenced reserve
must either expand or cull, since $K$ is fixed.

chapters.summary:
- **Vegetation** is the plant cover of an area; **flora** is the list of species
  in it. Nepal holds about 3.2 % of world flora on under 0.1 % of world land.
- Temperature falls about **6 °C per 1000 m**, which produces six altitudinal
  zones: **Tropical** (<1000 m, Sal), **Subtropical** (1000–2000 m,
  chilaune–katus and chir pine), **Temperate** (2000–3000 m, oak and
  rhododendron), **Subalpine** (3000–4000 m, fir and birch), **Alpine**
  (4000–5000 m, scrub and meadow) and **Nival** (>5000 m, snow).
- The **tree line** lies near **4000 m**. Behind the Himalaya, the
  **trans-Himalayan steppe** of Mustang, Manang and Dolpa gets only about
  250 mm of rain and carries *Caragana*, *Artemisia* and *Hippophae*.
- **In-situ** conservation protects the habitat: 13 national parks, 1 wildlife
  reserve (Koshi Tappu), 1 hunting reserve (Dhorpatan), 6 conservation areas,
  13 buffer zones and 10 Ramsar sites — about **23.4 %** of the country.
  Chitwan (1973) was the first; Annapurna (1992) is the largest.
- **Ex-situ** conservation protects the organism away from its habitat: the
  National Botanical Garden at **Godawari** (1962), the National Herbarium
  (KATH), the **National Gene Bank at Khumaltar** (2010), community seed banks,
  and the **Central Zoo, Jawalakhel** (1932).
- About **23,000 CFUGs** manage **2.5 million ha**, nearly 39 % of Nepal's
  forest. Forest covers **43.4 %** of the country.
- Vegetation is damaged by deforestation, *khoriya*, overgrazing, fire,
  over-collection of NTFPs, Chure quarrying and invasive species such as
  *Mikania micrantha* and *Eichhornia crassipes*; it is repaired by community
  forestry, agroforestry, buffer-zone sharing, alternative energy and the
  Forest Act, 2019.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- Vegetation [2]: types of vegetation in Nepal; In-situ and Ex-situ conservation
- Natural environment, vegetation and human activities [1]
- Vegetation
- Natural environment, vegetation and human activities
- What decides the vegetation of a place
- The vegetation zones of Nepal
- The flora of Nepal in numbers
- In-situ conservation
- Ex-situ conservation
- What people take from vegetation
- How human activities damage vegetation
- What is being done

Nepal is a small country — about 147,181 km², a little over a tenth of one per
cent of the Earth's land — yet it holds about **3.2 % of the world's known
flora**. The reason is height. In a north–south line barely 193 km long the land
climbs from 59 m in the Terai to 8,848.86 m at Sagarmatha, and every thousand
metres of that climb cools the air by roughly 6 °C. A traveller walking from
Birgunj to the Khumbu passes through as many vegetation belts as a traveller
walking from India to the Arctic. This unit maps those belts, names the trees
that mark them, and asks what Nepal is doing to keep them.

## Chapter summary

- **Vegetation** is the plant cover of an area; **flora** is the list of species
  in it. Nepal holds about 3.2 % of world flora on under 0.1 % of world land.
