chapters.question_answers:
## Worked example

**Problem.** Fill in with *should*, *ought to* or *must*: "Someone picked my pocket." — "You ____ immediately inform the police."

**Solution.** A strong, urgent duty → **must**.

## Worked example

**Problem.** Say whether the modal shows advice, moral obligation or compulsion: "You must abide by traffic rules while driving."

**Solution.** It is a rule with a penalty → **compulsion**.

## Worked example

**Problem.** Fill in a/an/the: "Would you like to be ____ actor in the future?"

**Solution.** *Actor* starts with a vowel sound → **an**.

## Worked example

**Problem.** "I saw a boy in the street. ____ boy was crying." Which article?

**Solution.** Second mention, specific → **The**.

## Model email

**To:** sambridhi@example.com
**Subject:** Sorry — I can't come to the wedding

Dear Sambridhi,

Thank you very much for the invitation to your brother Naman's wedding. I was really looking forward to celebrating with you and your family.

Unfortunately, an urgent family matter has come up, and I have to travel to Pokhara on the day of the wedding. I am very sorry that I cannot be there. I know how much this day means to you.

Please give Naman and his wife my warmest congratulations and best wishes for a happy married life. I will call you as soon as I return, and I would love to see the wedding photographs.

With love,
Niti

## Model article

**Internet and Cyber Security: Protecting Our Digital Lives**

The internet has become as important as electricity. From online classes to digital wallets, technology has made life faster and easier for millions of Nepalis.

Students search for study materials, shopkeepers receive payments by QR codes, and families in Nepal talk to relatives abroad on video calls. Government services such as passport and licence applications are also moving online.

However, the same internet can be abused. Criminals send fake messages to steal bank details, hackers break into accounts, and some people spread rumours or bully others on social media. Many young users share personal information without thinking of the risks.

Therefore, data privacy is essential. Users should create strong passwords, use two-factor authentication, update their software, avoid unknown links and keep personal details private. Parents and teachers should teach children safe online habits, and the government should enforce cybercrime laws.

In short, the internet is a powerful tool, but we must use it carefully. A safe digital world needs careful users as well as strong laws.

- Devices in the poem: rhyming couplets, repetition, simile, metaphor, light imagery, symbolism.

## Worked example

**Problem.** Change into the passive: "The police catch a lot of criminals in a city."

**Solution.** Object *a lot of criminals* → subject; simple present → *are caught*; the agent *the police* may be dropped. *A lot of criminals are caught in a city.*

## Worked example

**Problem.** Change into the passive: "Someone has stolen my bicycle."

**Solution.** Present perfect → *has been stolen*. *My bicycle has been stolen.* (The agent *someone* is unknown, so it is omitted.)

## Worked example

**Problem.** Change into the passive: "They were repairing the road."

**Solution.** Past continuous → *was being repaired*. *The road was being repaired.*

## Worked example

**Problem.** Rewrite using *being*: "Nobody likes people laughing at them."

**Solution.** *Nobody likes being laughed at.*

## Worked example

**Problem.** Change into active: "The prize was given to Maya by the principal."

**Solution.** *The principal gave the prize to Maya.*

## Model essay

**My Hobbies and My Future**

A hobby is an activity we enjoy in our free time. My hobbies are reading and drawing, and I believe they will influence my career.

Reading is my first hobby. I read story books, newspapers and science magazines. It has improved my vocabulary and my writing and has made me curious about the world. If I become a teacher or a journalist, these skills will help me explain things clearly.

My second hobby is drawing. I draw buildings, trees and houses in my village. Drawing has taught me patience, careful observation and the use of shapes and proportion. If I become an engineer or an architect, I will use these skills to design buildings that are useful and beautiful.

My hobbies also help me relax after hard study, so I do my school work with a fresh mind. A relaxed person works better in any job.

In conclusion, hobbies are not a waste of time. Mine have shown me what I enjoy, and I would like to choose a career in which I can use them.

**Experience:** At least two years of teaching experience at secondary level.

**Other:** Good command of spoken and written English; computer skills.

**How to apply:** Send a written application with copies of your citizenship, academic certificates and experience letters and two passport-size photographs to the school office.

**Deadline:** 15 Ashwin 2082 (5 pm). Only shortlisted candidates will be called for an interview.

Phone: 061-000000 — Headteacher

## Worked example

**Problem.** Fill in: "The alarm (go) while Trishna (sleep)."

**Solution.** The alarm is the short action; sleeping is the long one. *The alarm went while Trishna was sleeping.*

## Worked example

**Problem.** Fill in: "When we (wake), we (see) the sun shining brightly."

**Solution.** Two actions one after another → simple past. *When we woke, we saw the sun shining brightly.*

## Worked example

**Problem.** Make a sentence: *Kamal / fall off / while / play on the verandah.*

**Solution.** *Kamal fell off while he was playing on the verandah.*

## Worked example

**Problem.** Complete: "Ram ____ (buy) the ticket before he went to the cinema."

**Solution.** The buying came first → *had bought*.

## Worked example

**Problem.** Complete the story: "A young woman entered a shop. She (put) food in a bag and (wait) until no one was looking. When the shopkeeper (check) the goods, she (give) him a thousand-rupee note."

**Solution.** *She put food in a bag and waited until no one was looking. When the shopkeeper checked the goods, she gave him a thousand-rupee note.* (a sequence of completed actions → simple past)

## Model paragraphs

Nepal's journey from the Panchayat system to multiparty democracy was long and full of struggle. On 1 Poush 2017 BS, King Mahendra dismissed the elected government of Prime Minister B. P. Koirala, dissolved parliament, arrested the leaders and banned political parties. In 2019 BS a new constitution established the party-less Panchayat system, in which the king held the real power.

Opposition to the system continued. In 2036 BS student protests spread across the country, and King Birendra announced a national referendum. On 20 Baisakh 2037 BS the people were asked to choose between the reformed Panchayat system and a multiparty system, and a narrow majority voted to keep the reformed Panchayat. Dissatisfaction remained, however. In Falgun 2046 BS the Nepali Congress and the left parties started the People's Movement (Jana Andolan), and thousands of people went to the streets. After weeks of protest and many deaths, King Birendra lifted the ban on political parties in Chaitra 2046 BS. In this way, the party-less system ended and multiparty democracy returned to Nepal.

## Model essay

**Why We Must Study History**

Some people say that history is only a list of dead kings and old dates. I disagree. I believe that studying history is essential.

First, history teaches us lessons. By learning how people succeeded or failed in the past, we can avoid repeating their mistakes. The story of the Rana regime and the movements that ended it, for example, shows why freedom and equal rights matter.

Second, history gives us an identity. When we know who built Hanuman Dhoka or how Nepal became one country, we understand and respect our culture and we take pride in it. A person who does not know the past is like a tree without roots.

Third, history improves our thinking. It teaches us to compare evidence, to ask why things happened and to judge fairly.

It is true that some students find history boring when it is taught only by memorising dates. However, this is a problem of method, not of the subject. Visits to museums, old temples and stories make history live.

In conclusion, history is not a waste of time. It guides the present and helps to build a wiser future.

## Model story

**The Bat, the Birds and the Beasts**

Once upon a time there was a great quarrel between the birds and the beasts. Neither side would give way, so both gathered their armies and prepared for a terrible war.

When the armies were ready, the bat was asked to join the birds. He refused and said, "I am a beast. I have fur and teeth." Later the beasts asked him to join them. "I am a bird," he said, "because I have wings and fly." In this way the bat kept out of the fight and waited to see who would win.

Before the battle began, however, wise leaders on both sides spoke to each other, and peace was made. There was great rejoicing, and the birds and beasts began to celebrate together.

The bat, seeing that both sides were happy, wished to join the celebration. But the birds remembered that he had refused to fight with them, and the beasts remembered that he had refused to join them. Both turned against him and threatened to tear him to pieces. The frightened bat flew away and hid in a dark cave. Since that day he has come out only at night.

**Moral:** A person who is false to both sides will be trusted by neither.

Nepal's journey from the Panchayat system to multiparty democracy was long and full of struggle. On 1 Poush 2017 BS, King Mahendra dismissed the elected government of Prime Minister B. P. Koirala, dissolved parliament, arrested the leaders and banned political parties. In 2019 BS a new constitution established the party-less Panchayat system, in which the king held the real power.

Opposition to the system continued. In 2036 BS student protests spread across the country, and King Birendra announced a national referendum. On 20 Baisakh 2037 BS the people were asked to choose between the reformed Panchayat system and a multiparty system, and a narrow majority voted to keep the reformed Panchayat. Dissatisfaction remained, however. In Falgun 2046 BS the Nepali Congress and the left parties started the People's Movement (Jana Andolan), and thousands of people went to the streets. After weeks of protest and many deaths, King Birendra lifted the ban on political parties in Chaitra 2046 BS. In this way, the party-less system ended and multiparty democracy returned to Nepal.

## Worked example 10.1 — choosing the tense

**Problem.** Complete: "It ______ (rain) all night, and the roads ______ (flood)."

**Solution.** "All night" shows duration, so *has been raining*. The flooded roads are a present result, so *have flooded* (or *are flooded*). Answer: *It has been raining all night, and the roads have flooded.*

## Worked example 10.2 — active to passive

**Problem.** Change into the passive: "Who might have stolen your bicycle?"

**Solution.** The tense frame is *might have + V3*. Passive: *might have been + V3*. The question word *who* becomes *by whom*. Answer: *By whom might your bicycle have been stolen?*

## Worked example 11.1 — to negative and back

**Problem.** (a) Change to negative: "Ram visits me often." (b) Change to affirmative: "There is not anyone in the locality living in luxury."

**Solution.** (a) *Visits* needs *does*. *Often* becomes *rarely* or *not often*. Answer: *Ram does not visit me often* (or *Ram rarely visits me*). (b) *Not any one* ↔ *someone*. Answer: *There is someone in the locality living in luxury.*

## Worked example 11.2 — choose the verb

**Problem.** "Either the sculpture or the paintings ______ (was / were) in the museum today."

**Solution.** With *either … or*, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, *paintings* (plural). Answer: *were*.

The first text is a factual article on the **Kathmandu–Terai/Madhesh Fast Track**, one of Nepal's biggest development projects. The second is a famous poem by William Wordsworth, "Composed upon Westminster Bridge", in which a great city looks as peaceful as a field. ## Worked example 12.1 — choose the form

**Problem.** Fill in: "Tennis practice starts at 10 and we plan to play for two hours. By 12 o'clock we ______ (practise) for two hours."

**Solution.** The sentence looks at a future deadline (12 o'clock) and describes the length of an activity up to that point, so the answer is *will have practised* (or *will have been practising*).

## Worked example 12.2 — will or going to?

**Problem.** (a) "Look at those clouds. It ______ rain." (b) "The phone is ringing. I ______ answer it."

**Solution.** (a) There is **present evidence** (clouds), so *is going to rain*. (b) A **sudden decision** made at the moment, so *will answer*.

Spring weather (cuckoo, nightingale, chestnut showers, girls in sprig-muslin) is liked; winter weather (shepherd, brown beeches, overflowing streams, rooks going home) is shunned. - A travelogue is personal, in the past tense; a brochure uses headings and bullets to persuade.

## Worked example 14.1 — find the tag

**Problem.** Add a question tag: "Your phone didn't break down."

**Solution.** The statement is negative, so the tag is positive. The verb *break* has no auxiliary, so we use *do* in the past: *did*. The pronoun for *phone* is *it*. Answer: *Your phone didn't break down, did it?*

## Worked example 14.2 — a tricky one

**Problem.** Add a tag: "I think he's busy."

**Solution.** The tag goes with the clause *he's busy* (*he is busy*), so it is *isn't he?* Answer: *I think he's busy, isn't he?*

**Problem.** Add a question tag: "Your phone didn't break down."

**Solution.** The statement is negative, so the tag is positive. The verb *break* has no auxiliary, so we use *do* in the past: *did*. The pronoun for *phone* is *it*. Answer: *Your phone didn't break down, did it?*

self_checks.answer:

**Solution.** The tag goes with the clause *he's busy* (*he is busy*), so it is *isn't he?* Answer: *I think he's busy, isn't he?*

## Worked example 15.1 — joining sentences

**Problem.** Join: "The boy committed a cybercrime. The judge sent him to jail."

**Solution.** The repeated noun is *the boy* (a person; in the second sentence it is the object *him*). Write: *The judge sent the boy who committed a cybercrime to jail.* (Here *who* is the subject of *committed*, so it is **who**, not **whom**.)

## Worked example 15.2 — choose the pronoun

**Problem.** "I want to help those children ______ economic condition is very poor."

**Solution.** The condition *belongs to* the children, so we need **whose**: *… children whose economic condition is very poor.*

## Worked example 15.3 — choose the preposition

**Problem.** "The bus leaves ______ 9:15 pm ______ Friday."

**Solution.** A clock time takes **at**; a day takes **on**. Answer: *at 9:15 pm on Friday.*

- A linnet's song and the sight of one small crying boy melt the Giant's heart; he
  lifts the boy into the tree, breaks down the wall and gives the garden to the

- The boy disappears. Years later he returns with nail-prints in his hands and
  feet, calls them "the wounds of Love", and takes the dying Giant to Paradise.

"The Selfish Giant" is a literary fairy tale by the Irish writer Oscar Wilde,
first published in his 1888 collection *The Happy Prince and Other Tales*. On the
surface it is a simple story for children: a giant shuts children out of his
garden and winter never leaves it. Underneath, it is a carefully built parable
about selfishness, repentance and love, with a clear Christian allegory in its
closing pages. It opens the Grade 11 course because it teaches you to read a
short, easy text on two levels at once — the story, and what the story stands for.

## Chapter summary

- Oscar Wilde (1854–1900), Irish, leader of Aestheticism; "The Selfish Giant"
  comes from *The Happy Prince and Other Tales* (1888).
- A Giant returns after seven years with the Cornish ogre, drives the children
  out of his garden, walls it and posts TRESPASSERS WILL BE PROSECUTED.
- Spring, Summer and Autumn never come; Snow, Frost, North Wind and Hail settle
  in — the Giant's selfishness becomes his own punishment.
- A linnet's song and the sight of one small crying boy melt the Giant's heart; he
  lifts the boy into the tree, breaks down the wall and gives the garden to the
  children.
- The boy disappears. Years later he returns with nail-prints in his hands and
  feet, calls them "the wounds of Love", and takes the dying Giant to Paradise.
- Themes: selfishness punishes itself; love and repentance restore life; the value
  of childhood innocence; walls and exclusion; Christian sacrifice and salvation.
- Devices: personification of the seasons, pathetic fallacy, symbolism of the wall
  and garden, situational irony, Christian allegory, biblical diction at the close.
- Structure: four movements, third-person omniscient narration, with the real
  climax followed by a long coda covering many years.

chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** The Giant came home after seven years and found the village children
playing in his garden. He believed that "my own garden is my own garden" and
would allow nobody but himself to enjoy it, so he built a high wall and put up a
notice-board warning that trespassers would be prosecuted.

**2.** The Snow and the Frost stayed all year, and they invited the North Wind
and then the Hail. They were pleased because Spring had forgotten the garden,
which left them free to live there permanently and spoil it — the Snow covering
the grass, the Frost silvering the trees, the Hail breaking the roof slates.

**3.** One morning he heard a linnet singing and looked out to see the children
sitting in the blossoming trees, having crept in through a hole in the wall. In
one corner a tiny boy was crying because he could not reach the branches. That
sight made the Giant's heart melt and he said, "How selfish I have been!"

**4.** He did not run because his eyes were so full of tears that he simply did
not see the Giant coming. On the symbolic level, his staying suggests that
innocent love does not fear, and it is this one child who remains who becomes the
means of the Giant's change and salvation.

**5.** He meant that winter is not death but a pause: the flowers are only
resting under the ground and will come back. It shows how much he has changed —
the man who once complained that Spring was late can now wait patiently, because
he has learned that love, like spring, returns.

**6.** There were the prints of two nails on his palms and two on his little feet
— the marks of the Crucifixion. When the Giant angrily demanded who had dared to
wound him, the child answered, "Nay! but these are the wounds of Love,"
identifying himself as Christ, who was wounded out of love for humankind.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** On the surface Wilde tells a simple tale, but its details point steadily
towards Christian teaching. The garden stands for the human soul; the high wall
with its legal notice stands for selfishness and pride; and the endless winter
stands for a life from which love has been shut out. The turning point is caused
by the weakest character in the story, a child too small to climb a tree — an
echo of the Gospel idea that the least are the greatest. When the child returns
at the end, the allegory becomes explicit: he bears the prints of two nails on
his hands and two on his feet, and when the Giant demands the name of the person
who wounded him, he answers that "these are the wounds of Love". This is Christ
crucified, and his wounds are voluntary. His final words make the exchange plain:
because the Giant once let him play in his garden, he will now take the Giant to
his own garden, "which is Paradise". The Giant's death is therefore not a
punishment but a reward, and the white blossom that covers his body is the colour
of forgiveness and innocence. Read this way, the story is about repentance,
grace and salvation, not merely about learning to share.

**2.** At the start the Giant is selfish, ignorant and lonely. He has spent seven
years with the Cornish ogre and has nothing left to say; his only moral idea is
the possessive sentence "my own garden is my own garden". He drives the children
out, walls the garden, threatens the law, and Wilde ends the paragraph with a
blunt verdict: "He was a very selfish Giant." His punishment is automatic —
the garden freezes — yet he is too dull to see the cause, and sits at the window
wondering why Spring is late. The change is brought about by two small things, a
linnet's song and the sight of one crying boy who cannot reach the branches. Pity
does what argument could not. He admits his fault, lifts the boy into the tree,
takes an axe to his own wall, and gives the garden to the children for ever. In
old age he is a different man: gentle, patient, no longer hating winter, and
valuing the children above his flowers. The love he receives from the child —
first a kiss, and finally the promise of Paradise — completes a change that began
in pity and ended in humility, for he kneels before the child at the last.

**3.** Wilde makes the garden a picture of the Giant's inner life, so that the
reader can *see* his moral state. While the children are welcome, all four
seasons work: blossom in spring, fruit in autumn, birds in the trees. The moment
he builds the wall, the garden is cut off from the ordinary year and locked into a
single season. Nature is personified to make the judgement clear — the birds "did
not care to sing" where there were no children, the trees "forgot to blossom", and
Autumn refuses fruit with the words, "He is too selfish." Snow, Frost, the North
Wind and the Hail move in as guests, so that the Giant's chosen isolation is
staffed by cold, noise and damage. This is **pathetic fallacy**: the weather
carries the feeling. When the children creep back, blossom returns tree by tree,
and the one corner that stays frozen marks the one part of the Giant not yet
reached by love. At the end the garden goes beyond nature altogether: in
midwinter a single tree stands in white blossom with golden branches and silver
fruit — no longer a report on the Giant's heart but a promise of Paradise.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) The Selfish Giant says it, speaking to himself in the presence of the
children he has just frightened away from his garden, immediately after returning
from seven years with the Cornish ogre. (b) He at once builds a high wall all
round the garden and puts up a notice-board reading TRESPASSERS WILL BE
PROSECUTED. (c) The repetition of "my own" in a single short sentence shows a
mind that can think only in terms of ownership. He is not cruel so much as
narrow: he has a legal right and never asks what using it will cost the children.

and says that because the Giant once let him play in his garden he shall today
come to the child's garden, which is Paradise. That afternoon the children find
the Giant lying dead under the tree, covered all over with white blossoms.

self_checks.question: Model answers — short questions
self_checks.answer:
**1.** The Giant came home after seven years and found the village children
playing in his garden. He believed that "my own garden is my own garden" and
would allow nobody but himself to enjoy it, so he built a high wall and put up a
notice-board warning that trespassers would be prosecuted.

**2.** The Snow and the Frost stayed all year, and they invited the North Wind
and then the Hail. They were pleased because Spring had forgotten the garden,
which left them free to live there permanently and spoil it — the Snow covering
the grass, the Frost silvering the trees, the Hail breaking the roof slates.

**3.** One morning he heard a linnet singing and looked out to see the children
sitting in the blossoming trees, having crept in through a hole in the wall. In
one corner a tiny boy was crying because he could not reach the branches. That
sight made the Giant's heart melt and he said, "How selfish I have been!"

**4.** He did not run because his eyes were so full of tears that he simply did
not see the Giant coming. On the symbolic level, his staying suggests that
innocent love does not fear, and it is this one child who remains who becomes the
means of the Giant's change and salvation.

**5.** He meant that winter is not death but a pause: the flowers are only
resting under the ground and will come back. It shows how much he has changed —
the man who once complained that Spring was late can now wait patiently, because
he has learned that love, like spring, returns.

**6.** There were the prints of two nails on his palms and two on his little feet
— the marks of the Crucifixion. When the Giant angrily demanded who had dared to
wound him, the child answered, "Nay! but these are the wounds of Love,"
identifying himself as Christ, who was wounded out of love for humankind.

self_checks.question: Model answers — long questions
self_checks.answer:
**1.** On the surface Wilde tells a simple tale, but its details point steadily
towards Christian teaching. The garden stands for the human soul; the high wall
with its legal notice stands for selfishness and pride; and the endless winter
stands for a life from which love has been shut out. The turning point is caused
by the weakest character in the story, a child too small to climb a tree — an
echo of the Gospel idea that the least are the greatest. When the child returns
at the end, the allegory becomes explicit: he bears the prints of two nails on
his hands and two on his feet, and when the Giant demands the name of the person
who wounded him, he answers that "these are the wounds of Love". This is Christ
crucified, and his wounds are voluntary. His final words make the exchange plain:
because the Giant once let him play in his garden, he will now take the Giant to
his own garden, "which is Paradise". The Giant's death is therefore not a
punishment but a reward, and the white blossom that covers his body is the colour
of forgiveness and innocence. Read this way, the story is about repentance,
grace and salvation, not merely about learning to share.

**2.** At the start the Giant is selfish, ignorant and lonely. He has spent seven
years with the Cornish ogre and has nothing left to say; his only moral idea is
the possessive sentence "my own garden is my own garden". He drives the children
out, walls the garden, threatens the law, and Wilde ends the paragraph with a
blunt verdict: "He was a very selfish Giant." His punishment is automatic —
the garden freezes — yet he is too dull to see the cause, and sits at the window
wondering why Spring is late. The change is brought about by two small things, a
linnet's song and the sight of one crying boy who cannot reach the branches. Pity
does what argument could not. He admits his fault, lifts the boy into the tree,
takes an axe to his own wall, and gives the garden to the children for ever. In
old age he is a different man: gentle, patient, no longer hating winter, and
valuing the children above his flowers. The love he receives from the child —
first a kiss, and finally the promise of Paradise — completes a change that began
in pity and ended in humility, for he kneels before the child at the last.

**3.** Wilde makes the garden a picture of the Giant's inner life, so that the
reader can *see* his moral state. While the children are welcome, all four
seasons work: blossom in spring, fruit in autumn, birds in the trees. The moment
he builds the wall, the garden is cut off from the ordinary year and locked into a
single season. Nature is personified to make the judgement clear — the birds "did
not care to sing" where there were no children, the trees "forgot to blossom", and
Autumn refuses fruit with the words, "He is too selfish." Snow, Frost, the North
Wind and the Hail move in as guests, so that the Giant's chosen isolation is
staffed by cold, noise and damage. This is **pathetic fallacy**: the weather
carries the feeling. When the children creep back, blossom returns tree by tree,
and the one corner that stays frozen marks the one part of the Giant not yet
reached by love. At the end the garden goes beyond nature altogether: in
midwinter a single tree stands in white blossom with golden branches and silver
fruit — no longer a report on the Giant's heart but a promise of Paradise.

## Topics to cover

- About the author
- The story
- Characters
- Themes
- Setting, structure and point of view
- Literary devices
- Glossary

"The Oval Portrait" is one of the shortest stories Edgar Allan Poe ever wrote —
under a thousand words — and one of the most tightly built. A wounded traveller
takes shelter in an abandoned castle, notices a portrait of a young woman that
seems frighteningly alive, and reads the terrible explanation in a book beside
his bed. It is on the syllabus because it shows, in a very small space, how a
Gothic writer creates atmosphere, how a frame narrative works, and how a whole
argument about art and life can be made in a single closing sentence.

## Chapter summary

- A wounded narrator and his valet Pedro shelter in an abandoned château in the
  Apennines and take a small turret room hung with paintings.
- Moving the candelabrum at midnight reveals an oval portrait of a young girl whose

- A book on the pillow explains it: a painter married a beautiful girl who hated

- Absorbed in his work, he did not see her fading; the colours he laid on the canvas
  were drawn from her cheeks.

chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** The narrator was desperately wounded and could not spend a night in the open
air. His valet Pedro therefore broke into an abandoned château in the Apennines so
that his master could rest, and they settled in a small room in a remote turret.

**2.** At midnight the narrator was displeased with the position of the tall
candelabrum and reached out to move it so that its light fell better on his book.
The candles then lit a niche that had been hidden in shadow by a bed-post, and the
portrait appeared in vivid light.

**3.** It was not the skill of the painting nor the beauty of the face, and he did
not mistake it for a living woman. What appalled him was its "absolute
life-likeliness of expression" — the picture seemed to be alive, and that impression
first startled, then confused and finally overcame him.

**4.** She hated Art because it was her rival. The painter already had a bride in
his Art, and the palette and brushes took him away from her, so that she was
deprived of her husband's company and even of his face. When he wished to paint her,
she therefore heard it as terrible news.

**5.** "Incipient delirium" means a fever-madness that is just beginning. Poe
mentions it so that the reader cannot be certain whether the portrait is truly
uncanny or whether the narrator's sick imagination is at work. This uncertainty
deepens the fear and makes the narrator unreliable.

**6.** The painter believes he has captured life on canvas, and in that instant he
has — but the life came out of his wife. He shouts his triumph over a woman who has
just died, and the picture is "Life itself" only because she is no longer alive.
Success and disaster arrive in the same moment.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** Poe builds the story on a single idea: that a work of art may be paid for
with a human life, and he presents it literally rather than as a figure of speech.
The painter already has "a bride in his Art" before he marries; the living wife is
therefore a second wife from the beginning, and she knows it, for she hates only
the Art which is her rival and dreads the palette and brushes that steal her
husband from her. When she begins to sit in the dark turret, the exchange starts.
The narrator of the book tells us that the painter "would not see" that the light
withered her, and would not see that the tints he spread on the canvas were "drawn
from the cheeks of her who sate beside him". Week by week the portrait gains
exactly what the model loses, so that the perfection of the one requires the
extinction of the other. The two curves meet at the final brush-stroke: the moment
the picture becomes "Life itself" is the moment she stops living. Poe's original
title, "Life in Death", states the theme directly. The conclusion is not that art
is evil but that an art which stops looking at the human being in front of it has
already killed something.

**2.** Poe said that a short story should aim at one single effect, and here that
effect is dread. He gets it first from the setting. Everything is Gothic: an
abandoned château among the Apennines, "commingled gloom and grandeur", a remote
turret, heavy shutters closed against the night, black velvet bed-curtains,
tattered antique decorations, and candlelight as the only illumination. He even
names Mrs Radcliffe, so the reader recognises the tradition. He then makes light
itself the instrument of terror: a single small movement of the candelabrum takes a
picture out of the darkness, as though the room had been concealing it. The frame
narrative does the rest. We meet a narrator who is wounded and half-delirious, so
we cannot fully trust him; inside his story sits an old book, and inside the book
sits the painter's tale in archaic, legendary language. Each layer makes the horror
older and less escapable. Most importantly, Poe does not come back out. The story
ends on the book's last words, "She was dead!", with no return to the turret and no
comforting comment from the narrator, leaving the reader shut inside the innermost
box.

**3.** The painter is presented in four words — "passionate, studious, austere" and
already wedded to his Art — and every later detail develops them. He is celebrated,
"of high renown", and he genuinely loves his wife: those who saw the portrait spoke
of it as proof both of his power and of his deep love for the woman he painted so
well. Yet he is also "wild, and moody", a man who becomes lost in reveries. As the
work advances he shuts everyone out of the turret, works day and night, and barely
lifts his eyes from the canvas even to look at the living face he is copying. Poe
twice uses the same phrase, that he "would not see" — that the ghastly overhead
light was destroying her health, and that his colours were being taken from her
cheeks. The repetition is bitterly ironic in a man whose art is seeing. Is he
guilty? Not of murder: there is no violence, no intention, and he is appalled at
the end. But he is guilty of a moral blindness that amounts to neglect. He had
weeks in which any ordinary husband would have noticed, and he chose the canvas
over the woman every single day. His cry of triumph over her corpse is his
punishment as well as his achievement.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) They are the opening words of the entry in the small volume found on the
narrator's pillow — the account of the oval portrait — and they describe the young
woman in the picture, the painter's bride. (b) The wounded narrator is reading them
at midnight, in a turret room of an abandoned château in the Apennines, after the
candelabrum's light has accidentally revealed the portrait and frightened him.
(c) The line shows her as she was before the painting began — beautiful, laughing,
"frolicsome as the young fawn" — which makes the rest of the account unbearable, for
that living gaiety is exactly what the weeks in the dark turret slowly take away
from her. (d) The formal, old-fashioned phrasing, with its inverted construction and
its "And evil was the hour" a line later, shows that the inner tale is told in the
voice of an old book rather than of a modern person. That legendary voice makes the
events feel distant and fated, which increases their power.

**2.** (a) The painter says it in the innermost story, at the instant he lays the
last brush-stroke on the mouth and the last tint on the eye of his wife's portrait,
after many weeks of work in the shut turret. (b) He means that he has succeeded
completely: the painted face is no longer a mere likeness but seems to possess life
of its own, and for one moment he stands entranced before what he has made.
(c) He grows pale, trembling and aghast, turns round to look at his beloved, and
finds that she is dead. (d) It is the climax because the two lines of the story meet
here. The life the painter has been transferring to the canvas is his wife's life,
so the completion of the portrait is necessarily the end of her. The sentence is the
story's supreme irony and also its theme in five words, and Poe ends the whole
narrative two lines later without another word of comment.

chapters.summary:
- Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910), Russian realist and moral thinker; "God Sees the Truth,
  but Waits" (1872) takes its title from a Russian proverb.
- Aksionov, a merchant of Vladimir, ignores his wife's warning dream and travels to
  the Nizhny fair; a fellow merchant is murdered at the inn.
- A blood-stained knife is found in Aksionov's bag; he is flogged and sent to Siberia
  for twenty-six years, charged with a murder he did not commit.
- His wife's question, "was it not you who did it?", ends his hope of human help; he
  stops petitioning and turns to prayer.
- In prison he becomes "Grandfather" and "The Saint"; Makar Semyonich, the real
  murderer, arrives and gives himself away.
- Aksionov refuses to betray Makar's escape tunnel to the Governor, and later forgives
  him — "God will forgive you! Maybe I am a hundred times worse than you."
- Makar confesses, but Aksionov dies before the release order arrives.
- Themes: injustice; forgiveness as release; faith and patience; suspicion; revenge
  refused. Devices: foreshadowing, dramatic and situational irony, symbolism,
  understatement, extreme plainness of style.

## Topics to cover

- About the author

Leo Tolstoy's "God Sees the Truth, but Waits" (1872) tells of a merchant who is
convicted of a murder he did not commit and spends twenty-six years in a Siberian
prison. It is a story about injustice, but far more about what a man does with
injustice once he has stopped expecting help from the world. The title is an old
Russian proverb, and the story is Tolstoy's argument that truth and forgiveness may
arrive very late — and still be worth waiting for.

## Chapter summary

- Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910), Russian realist and moral thinker; "God Sees the Truth,
  but Waits" (1872) takes its title from a Russian proverb.
- Aksionov, a merchant of Vladimir, ignores his wife's warning dream and travels to
  the Nizhny fair; a fellow merchant is murdered at the inn.
- A blood-stained knife is found in Aksionov's bag; he is flogged and sent to Siberia
  for twenty-six years, charged with a murder he did not commit.
- His wife's question, "was it not you who did it?", ends his hope of human help; he
  stops petitioning and turns to prayer.
- In prison he becomes "Grandfather" and "The Saint"; Makar Semyonich, the real
  murderer, arrives and gives himself away.
- Aksionov refuses to betray Makar's escape tunnel to the Governor, and later forgives
  him — "God will forgive you! Maybe I am a hundred times worse than you."
- Makar confesses, but Aksionov dies before the release order arrives.

chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** She dreamt that he returned from the town and that when he took off his cap
his hair had turned completely grey, and she begged him not to start that day.
Aksionov laughed at her fear, joked that she was afraid he would go on a spree at
the fair, called the dream a lucky sign and drove away.

**2.** The police-officer found a blood-stained knife in Aksionov's bag. Added to
this were the facts that Aksionov had slept in the room next to the murdered
merchant, that the house was locked from inside, and that he had left the inn before
dawn. His pale face and broken voice were taken as further proof.

**3.** Because his own wife asked him whether he had really committed the murder.
Once the person closest to him doubted him, he decided that only God could know the
truth and that it was to God alone he should appeal. He gave up all hope of help
from men and simply prayed.

**4.** He laughed at the idea that anyone could have hidden a knife in the bag under
a sleeping man's head without waking him — a detail only the murderer could know. He
also exclaimed how wonderful it was that they should meet, and asked how Aksionov
had grown so old, but refused to explain his surprise.

**5.** Telling the truth would have had Makar flogged almost to death, and Aksionov

builds the whole plot so that we can measure its cost. Aksionov has lost twenty-six
years, his business, his wife and his children to a crime he did not commit, and he
knows exactly who is responsible. When the escape tunnel is discovered, he is given
a perfect revenge: a lawful authority asks him a direct question, and one honest
sentence would have had Makar flogged nearly to death, with nobody able to blame the
informer. He refuses, saying only, "It is not God's will that I should tell." The
second and greater act comes that night. Makar kneels, beats his head on the floor
and begs pardon, and Aksionov at first answers bitterly that he has nowhere left to
go. Then he hears the man sobbing, weeps himself, and says, "God will forgive you!
Maybe I am a hundred times worse than you." Tolstoy records the result in one plain
sentence: his heart grew light and the longing for home left him. Forgiveness is
therefore shown as something that frees the victim, not the offender. It changes
Makar too — he confesses although he has been forgiven — but its first effect is on
Aksionov, who no longer needs the freedom he had wanted for twenty-six years.

marriage. He is confident to the point of carelessness, laughing at his wife's dream
and promising her presents from the fair. The arrest destroys this man. Frightened
and unable to explain the knife, he stammers and trembles, and his very innocence
makes him look guilty. The second stage is despair. His wife's question — "was it
not you who did it?" — hurts him more than the flogging, and after it he stops

chapters.name: The Wish - Roald Dahl
topics: Setting, structure and point of view
chapters.summary:
- Roald Dahl (1916–1990), British, born in Wales of Norwegian parents, RAF pilot,
  author of macabre adult stories and famous children's books; "The Wish" is from
  *Someone Like You* (1953).
- A small boy alone in the hall picks off a scab, examines the new skin, and then
  studies the large red, black and yellow carpet.
- He invents a game: black is poisonous snakes, red is red-hot coals, yellow is
  safe; the prize for crossing is a puppy for his birthday the next day.
- As he crosses, the imagined danger becomes real to him — the snakes seem to stir
  and watch — and he begins to show the physical signs of real fear.
- A wide band of black forces an enormous stretch; he loses his balance, whirls his
  arms and puts his hand down on black. He screams.
- The story ends outside in the sunshine with his mother searching for him, and
  explains nothing.
- Themes: imagination and its dangers; self-imposed rules and play; loneliness and
  absent adults; desire (the puppy); the blurred line between imagined and real.
- Devices: symbolism and colour symbolism, tactile imagery, personification,
  suspense, foreshadowing, irony, free indirect style, and a deliberately
  ambiguous ending.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- About the author
- The story
- Characters
- Themes
- Setting, structure and point of view
- Literary devices
- Glossary

Roald Dahl's "The Wish" is barely a thousand words long and almost nothing happens
in it. A small boy, alone in the hall of his house, invents a game on the patterned
carpet: the black parts are snakes, the red parts are burning coals, and only the
yellow is safe. Within a page the game has stopped being a game. The story is on
the syllabus because it shows how suspense is built out of ordinary materials, and
how an ending can frighten a reader most by refusing to say what happened.

## Chapter summary

- Roald Dahl (1916–1990), British, born in Wales of Norwegian parents, RAF pilot,
  author of macabre adult stories and famous children's books; "The Wish" is from
  *Someone Like You* (1953).
- A small boy alone in the hall picks off a scab, examines the new skin, and then
  studies the large red, black and yellow carpet.
- He invents a game: black is poisonous snakes, red is red-hot coals, yellow is
  safe; the prize for crossing is a puppy for his birthday the next day.
- As he crosses, the imagined danger becomes real to him — the snakes seem to stir
  and watch — and he begins to show the physical signs of real fear.
- A wide band of black forces an enormous stretch; he loses his balance, whirls his
  arms and puts his hand down on black. He screams.
- The story ends outside in the sunshine with his mother searching for him, and
  explains nothing.
- Themes: imagination and its dangers; self-imposed rules and play; loneliness and
  absent adults; desire (the puppy); the blurred line between imagined and real.
- Devices: symbolism and colour symbolism, tactile imagery, personification,
  suspense, foreshadowing, irony, free indirect style, and a deliberately
  ambiguous ending.

## Study route

Read the topics and identify unfamiliar terms.

Close the book and explain the key ideas in your own words.

Attempt a worked example before revealing its solution.

Complete the chapter practice, correct mistakes, then mark the chapter revised.
chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** He is sitting alone at the foot of the stairs, carefully picking the scab off
his knee and examining the clean pink skin underneath. It shows that he is solitary,
patient and closely interested in small, slightly unpleasant things — exactly the
kind of attention he will soon turn on the carpet.

**2.** The black parts of the carpet are poisonous snakes, the red parts are red-hot
lumps of coal, and only the yellow parts are safe. If he touches black he will be
bitten and die; if he touches red he will be burnt. He must cross the whole carpet
stepping on yellow alone.

**3.** He has decided that if he crosses the carpet without a single mistake, he will
be given a puppy for his birthday, which falls the very next day. The smallness of
this reward, set against the death he has imagined for himself, is one of the
story's quiet ironies.

**4.** Dahl stops describing what the boy pretends and starts describing what he
sees: the snakes appear to stir, raise their heads and watch him, and the red looks
genuinely hot. At the same time the boy's body reacts — his breathing quickens and
he feels dizzy and frightened — which shows that he now believes in the danger.

**5.** A wide band of black lies across his route, and the nearest yellow patch on
the far side is further away than a normal step. He can only reach it by an enormous
stretch, with one foot behind and his weight hanging over the black, which leaves
him no way to recover if he wobbles.

**6.** Because the sudden distance is more frightening than any description of what
happened. After a whole story spent inside the boy's mind, the reader is pushed
outside into warm daylight, where an ordinary mother is looking for a child she
cannot find. Dahl explains nothing, and the silence does the work.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** Dahl builds tension out of materials that are completely harmless, which is
why the effect is so striking. First he establishes the rules, and makes them
absolute: black means snakes and death before teatime, red means burning, yellow
alone is safe. Because the reader accepts the rules, every later step can be
measured against them. Second, he arranges the physical difficulty in a rising
order. The early steps are simple; then the yellow patches narrow, so the boy must
balance on tiptoe and on one foot; and finally a wide band of black demands a
stretch no child of his size can make. The reader can see the crisis approaching
several paragraphs before it arrives, which is the classic source of suspense.
Third, he moves from pretence to perception. At first the boy decides that the black
is snakes; soon he sees them stir and lift their heads to watch him. Fourth, he
reports the boy's body — the quickened breathing, the dizziness, the arms whirling
like a windmill — so that the fear is felt physically rather than described. Last,
he controls the speed of the prose, slowing to almost nothing for the great stretch,
then delivering the fall, the scream and the closing sentence in a few lines.

**2.** Almost nothing happens in this story except inside one child's head, and Dahl
arranges everything else to make that inner life visible. The boy is alone: no adult
appears until the last sentence, no other child is mentioned, and the house is
silent. That solitude is the condition for the whole game. It is also the reason
nobody interrupts him — an older brother or a mother in the hall would have laughed
and the danger would have collapsed. Into this emptiness the boy pours an
extraordinary imaginative energy. He takes an ordinary domestic pattern and turns it
into a landscape with laws, punishments and a prize; he populates it with adders and
cobras "thick like tree-trunks"; and he then submits to his own invention so
completely that he suffers real, physical fear. Dahl shows how close such
imagination lies to the ordinary details of childhood: the story opens with the boy
absorbed in the scab on his own knee, a small private world of exactly the same kind.
The longing behind the game is childish and touching — a puppy for tomorrow's
birthday — and the punishment he invents is death. The story therefore ends by
asking whether imagination this strong is a gift or a danger, and Dahl leaves it
genuinely unclear, which is his answer.

**3.** The ending is abrupt and deliberately incomplete. The boy's hand comes down on
black, he screams, Dahl gives a single short paragraph of snakes, and then the story
leaves the house altogether for one last sentence, in which his mother is outside in
the sunshine, searching for him. Everything a conventional ending would supply is
missing: no rescue, no explanation, no return to the hall. Two readings remain
possible, and the text supports both. In the natural reading, the boy has frightened
himself into a panic, has fallen, fainted or run and hidden, and his mother simply
cannot find him for the moment; the snakes were never there. In the uncanny reading,
the game has somehow become true, and the last sentence quietly tells us that the
boy is gone. Dahl refuses to decide. He also changes the viewpoint at the same
moment, pulling back from the child's mind — where we have been for the entire story
— to a cool outside view in ordinary daylight. The contrast between that warm,
normal world and the terror we have just shared is what makes the ending memorable.
The horror is handed to the reader to complete, which is always more frightening
than being told.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) The phrase describes the black patches of the large carpet in the hall of
the boy's house, which he has decided are poisonous snakes. It comes to us through
the narrator, but in the boy's own words and imagination. (b) He is sitting alone at
the bottom of the staircase, having just picked the scab off his knee, and is looking
across the carpet that stretches from the stairs to the front door. (c) He has made
the rule that if he touches a black patch he will be bitten and will die before
teatime, while red means burning coals and yellow alone is safe ground; if he crosses
untouched, he will get a puppy for his birthday the next day. (d) The detail is
specific and physical — named species, and a comparison to the thickness of
tree-trunks — so the reader can see the snakes too. Having accepted them once, we
accept them again when they begin to stir and watch him, and the fear of the final
stretch becomes ours as well as his.

**2.** (a) It is the last line of the story, standing alone after the boy has fallen
and screamed. (b) He has attempted an enormous stretch over a wide band of black,
failed to bring his weight across, whirled his arms to save his balance and put his
hand down flat on the black. He screams, and Dahl gives one brief paragraph of the
snakes. (c) Because after an entire story spent inside the child's mind, the sudden
move outside to warm sunshine and an ordinary parent creates a shock of distance. The
reader is separated from the boy at exactly the moment he most needs company, and
nothing is explained. (d) Either the boy has simply panicked, fallen or hidden, and
his mother will find him in a moment — the snakes having been imaginary all along; or
the game has become real and the boy has been lost for good. Dahl provides no
evidence for either, and that refusal is the source of the ending's power.

the game has become real and the boy has been lost for good. Dahl provides no
evidence for either, and that refusal is the source of the ending's power.

## Topics to cover

Chinua Achebe's "Civil Peace" is set in Nigeria in the first weeks after the
Nigerian Civil War of 1967–70. Its hero, Jonathan Iwegbu, has lost a son, a job and
almost everything he owned, and still insists that he is an extraordinarily lucky
man. The story is on the syllabus because it shows, in very few pages, what
ordinary people do after a war ends — and how little the word "peace" may actually
mean to them.

## Chapter summary

- Chinua Achebe (1930–2013), Nigerian, author of *Things Fall Apart*; "Civil Peace"
  comes from *Girls at War and Other Stories* (1972) and is set just after the
  Nigerian Civil War of 1967–70.
- Jonathan Iwegbu counts five "inestimable blessings" — his own head, his wife
  Maria's and those of three of his four children — and repeats "Nothing puzzles
  God."
- His buried bicycle survives the war; as a taxi it earns him a hundred and fifteen
  pounds in two weeks, which takes the family back to Enugu.
- Their small zinc house still stands among ruins; the whole family works — mangoes,
  akara, a palm-wine bar — since the coal mine will not reopen.
- At the treasury he receives a twenty-pound ex-gratia award, which the crowd calls
  "egg-rasher".
- That night thieves knock; nobody answers the family's cries for help, and the
  leader mockingly calls for the police himself, saying "This time na Civil Peace."
- Jonathan hands over the whole twenty pounds; by morning the family is back at
  work, and he says again that nothing puzzles God.
- Themes: peace in name only, survival and work, loss, faith or fatalism, and the
  collapse of law and community; devices include irony, the repeated refrain, the
  bicycle as symbol, Pidgin English and a circular structure.

chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** They are five heads that survived the war: his own, his wife Maria's, and
those of three of his four children. The fourth child died. He counts survival
itself as wealth, which shows both his gratitude and how much the war destroyed.

**2.** The bicycle is the machine that restarts his life: used as a taxi between the
camps and the military cemetery, it earns him a hundred and fifteen pounds in two
weeks. He saved it during the war by paying two pounds to an officer who wanted to
commandeer it, and then burying it in the ground until the fighting was over.

**3.** Everyone works. Jonathan rides his bicycle as a taxi and later opens a bar
selling palm-wine in his house; Maria makes and sells akara balls; and the children
pick mangoes and sell them to soldiers' wives. His old job at the coal mine no
longer exists.

**4.** It is the crowd's pronunciation of "ex-gratia award", a payment of twenty
pounds made by the treasury to anyone who handed in the now worthless Biafran
currency. Jonathan queues for his and receives it, and it is exactly this money the
thieves demand that night.

**5.** Nothing happens. They call for neighbours, police and soldiers, and no one
answers. The leader of the thieves then shouts for the police himself, in mockery,
to prove to Jonathan that there is no help anywhere in the neighbourhood.

**6.** He refuses to be upset. He tells the sympathising neighbours not to trouble
themselves, saying that the money came to him from nowhere only a few days before,
so that losing it means nothing to him; and he repeats "Nothing puzzles God." He and
his family are already back at work.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** The title is ironic from beginning to end. It comes from the thief himself,
who tells Jonathan through the locked door that the civil war is finished and that
this time it is "Civil Peace" — meaning that nobody need be killed provided the
money is handed out. Achebe's point is that for ordinary Nigerians the end of the
fighting brought a change of name rather than a change of condition. In the official
version, peace has returned: the treasury is paying awards, offices are open, the
government has won. In Jonathan's version, a man is robbed in the treasury queue,
armed men knock at his door at night, and when his family screams for the police,
the neighbours, and the soldiers, no one in the entire quarter answers. The thief
even shouts for the police himself to prove the point. The irony is deepened by
Jonathan's own language: he calls himself "extraordinarily lucky" when he has lost a
child, a job and nearly all his property, and he describes the survival of five
heads as inestimable blessings. In a genuine peace, none of this would be luck. The
title therefore does exactly what a good title should: it states the official word
for the situation and leaves the reader to discover what the word conceals.

**2.** Jonathan Iwegbu is a small man with an extraordinary capacity to begin again.
Achebe shows him almost entirely through action. He bribes an officer to keep his
bicycle and then buries it; he digs it up and has it earning money within days; he
repairs a ruined house with wire and cardboard; he abandons the coal mine as soon as
he sees the job will not return; he sets his wife and children to work; and when
armed thieves come, he gives up everything rather than risk a life. His faith is of
the same practical kind — "Nothing puzzles God" is less a doctrine than a refusal to
be paralysed by what he cannot control. Much of this is admirable: his energy,
independence and refusal of self-pity are exactly the qualities that rebuild a
country, and Achebe clearly respects them. But the story also leaves room for doubt.
Jonathan counts a dead son inside an arithmetic of blessings; he asks nobody for
justice; he loses his award to criminals and by morning has decided that it does not
matter. Endurance of that completeness may also be a kind of surrender, since a
society in which everybody shrugs will never demand anything better. Achebe does not
decide for us, and the best answers hold both views together.

**3.** Achebe's post-war Nigeria is drawn in a handful of exact details, and every
one of them tells us something. Physically, the country is broken: houses lie in
rubble, and Jonathan's flimsy zinc house survives when stronger ones did not, so
that survival looks arbitrary rather than deserved. Economically, it is in
collapse: the coal mine cannot say when it will reopen, the Biafran currency is
waste paper, and the government's answer is a flat twenty-pound award for everyone.
Whole families therefore live on tiny trades — mangoes, fried akara, palm-wine, a
bicycle taxi that earns its money carrying people to and from a military cemetery.
Socially, the most disturbing fact is the silence. The old protections have gone: no
police come, no soldiers come, and the neighbours who will arrive at dawn to
sympathise do not open a door at night. Violence has simply moved from the
battlefield into the street, and its new practitioners are polite, organised and
confident that nobody will stop them. Against all this Achebe sets the stubborn
industry of one family. The picture that results is neither hopeless nor
comfortable: people survive, but they survive alone, and the peace that has been
declared protects nobody.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) The words are Jonathan Iwegbu's, and they are first heard at the very
beginning of the story, when he is counting the five "inestimable blessings" he has
brought out of the civil war — his own head, his wife Maria's, and those of three of
his four children. (b) He means that God's ways cannot be understood or questioned,
so that whatever happens, good or bad, has to be accepted without complaint. (c) The
same line closes the story, on the morning after the thieves have taken his entire
twenty-pound award, when the neighbours come to sympathise. Placing it at both ends
makes the story circular and shows that nothing has shaken him. (d) It reveals a man
whose religion is entirely practical. He does not use it to explain the world but to
avoid being destroyed by it; it is what allows him to stop grieving and start
working again, and it is also, less comfortably, what allows him to demand nothing
from anyone.

**2.** (a) They are spoken by the leader of the group of thieves, calling through the
door to Jonathan Iwegbu at night. (b) The thieves have knocked and asked politely
for the owner of the house; the family has screamed for neighbours, police and
soldiers, and nobody has come — the leader has just mocked them by shouting for the
police himself. He is now demanding a hundred pounds and assuring Jonathan that
nobody need be hurt. (c) Achebe writes the thieves' speech in Nigerian Pidgin
English because it is the real language of the street in that place and time. It
makes the man immediately believable, and its casual, almost friendly tone against
such a threat is far more frightening than shouting would be. (d) The irony is
complete: the word "peace" is spoken by an armed robber, and what he means by it is
only that he will not kill anyone if he is paid. It gives the story its title and
states its theme — that the end of the war brought ordinary people a new name for
their danger rather than safety from it.

chapters.summary:
- Guy de Maupassant (1850–1893), French Realist and Naturalist, pupil of Flaubert,
  author of about three hundred stories including "Boule de Suif" and "The
  Necklace"; he died in an asylum at forty-two.
- Two young Breton soldiers, Luc Le Ganidec and Jean Kerderen, walk every Sunday
  from their barracks at Courbevoie, over the bridge at Bezons, to a spot near the
  wood of Champioux that reminds them of home.
- Their ritual is fixed: the pause on the bridge, the cheap provisions, the hidden
  bricks, the fire, the sausage, the silence on the grass.
- A dairymaid begins to speak to them, gives them milk "to remind them of home",
  accepts their two sous' worth of sweets, and joins their Sunday meal.
- Luc secretly takes leave twice in one week; on the next Sunday the girl kisses him
  in front of Jean, and the two go off into the wood together.
- Jean is stunned and silent; the girl walks past him with a careless nod, and
  Maupassant notes simply that she did not offer him any milk that day.
- On the walk home they stop on the bridge as always; Jean leans further and
  further over the railing and falls into the Seine. Boatmen recover the body.
- Luc reports an accident, and the story ends with the narrator's line, "If he had
  only known."
- Themes: homesickness and exile, fragile friendship, jealousy and exclusion, the
  pain that cannot be put into words, and an ending deliberately left ambiguous.

Guy de Maupassant's "Two Little Soldiers" follows two homesick young Breton
conscripts who spend every Sunday in the same spot outside Paris. A dairymaid
begins to share their meal; one of them wins her; and the other walks home and goes
over the bridge. The story is on the syllabus because it shows how much a writer can
say about jealousy and loneliness while appearing to say almost nothing at all.

chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** Because the place at the edge of the wood of Champioux reminds them of
Brittany. The trees recall the forest of Kermarivan, a large stone recalls the dolmen
of Locneuven, and the fields look like Plounivon. Being homesick conscripts, they
feel happy nowhere else.

**2.** They buy a piece of sausage, a few cents' worth of bread and a quart of wine
in Bezons and carry it wrapped in their handkerchiefs. At their usual corner they
take two bricks out of a hedge, light a fire of dry branches and roast the sausage on
the points of their knives, then lie on the grass side by side.

**3.** Seeing that they always sit in the same spot, she speaks to them and teases
them gently; then, returning with her pail full, she offers them milk, saying it
will remind them of home. She has guessed exactly what they are missing, and both
soldiers are moved.

**4.** He obtains leave on a Tuesday and does not come back until ten at night, and
then borrows ten sous from a comrade and takes leave again on the Friday. On Sunday
he seems strange and disturbed. Jean notices all this, suspects something, but cannot
guess that Luc has been meeting the dairymaid.

**5.** Because it is the moment Jean's exclusion becomes complete. The milk had been
the sign that the girl treated the two friends alike and understood their
homesickness; withholding it, with only a careless nod, tells him wordlessly that he
is now outside. Maupassant replaces any description of Jean's despair with this one
small omission.

**6.** On the walk home they stop on the bridge at Bezons as they always do. Jean
leans further and further over the railing, as if hypnotised by the water, and falls
into the Seine; boatmen recover his body the same day. Luc, weeping, reports it at
the barracks as an accident, and the story ends with the line "If he had only known."

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** Everything the two soldiers value in the story is a substitute for Brittany.
They are conscripts from a fishing and farming country, shut up in a barracks at
Courbevoie, and their one pleasure is a walk to a wood that resembles the forest of
Kermarivan. On the way they stop on the bridge to watch white sails that recall
their fishing boats; they halt at a stone because it is like the dolmen of
Locneuven; Jean says every week that the fields are just like Plounivon; and the
dairymaid's milk is welcome mainly because, as she says, it will remind them of
home. Maupassant sums up their condition in a single simile — the slow sorrow of a
captive animal that remembers its freedom. Their friendship grows directly out of
this exile. They are not friends because they are alike in character; they are
friends because they come from the same country and want the same thing at the same
moments, which is why they can walk for an hour without speaking. Such a friendship
looks solid and is in fact very fragile: it has no words in it, no agreements, no
way of handling a disagreement. When Luc begins to want something of his own, the
whole structure falls, and Jean, who has nothing else in the world, falls with it.

**2.** The ending is shocking but not sudden, because almost every element of it has
already been planted. The bridge at Bezons is introduced in the third paragraph, and
we are told that the soldiers *always* stop there for several minutes, bending over
the railing to watch the Seine. The reader therefore accepts the final pause on the
bridge as ordinary, which is precisely why it is dangerous. Maupassant also
establishes the men's total silence: they walk for long stretches without a word,
and their faces never betray anything, so that when Jean is destroyed we are warned
that nothing will be said about it. The last Sunday is then written as a systematic
reversal of the habits we have learned — neither of them is hungry, the girl does
not glance at Jean, there is no milk, and the walk home is conducted with the empty
bottle. Small physical details do the rest: Jean's inability to stand, the "wall of
leaves" through which the lovers vanish, the sun and the lowing cow indifferent
behind them. By the time Jean leans over the railing "as though he had seen
something in the stream which hypnotized him", the reader has all the material
needed, and the fall takes one sentence.

**3.** Maupassant deliberately refuses to decide, and a good answer holds both
readings. The case for suicide is strong. Jean has just been shown, in public, that
he has lost both his friend and the girl; he is described as dazed, heart-broken,
too weak to stand, wanting to run away and never see anyone again; he is a boy with
no words for his feelings and nobody to tell them to; and he leans over the railing
"further and further", as if hypnotised, at the very moment when he has nothing
left. The narrator's closing line, "If he had only known", strongly implies that Luc
might have prevented it had he understood — which suits a suicide better than a
slip. On the other side, nothing is stated. The text says that Jean's head carried
the rest of his body away, which is the language of an accident; Luc, the only
witness, reports it as one; and the two of them had leant over that railing every
Sunday for months without harm. It is also true to the characters that Jean, who
cannot even speak his grief, might not be capable of forming an intention. The
ambiguity is the point: Maupassant shows a death that arises naturally out of
despair without ever accusing anyone of anything.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) The words are spoken by Jean Kerderen to his friend Luc Le Ganidec, and
Luc agrees with him. (b) They are on the narrow path across the plain between the
village of Bezons and the little wood of Champioux, with wheat and oat fields on
either side, on their usual Sunday walk from the barracks at Courbevoie. (c) He says
it every single week because the whole outing is a ritual of remembering: the two
Breton boys come to this place precisely because it resembles their home, and
repeating the sentence is part of the pleasure. (d) It tells us that their real lives
are elsewhere. They are conscripts far from Brittany, poor, homesick and inarticulate,
and they survive by finding substitutes — a wood like Kermarivan, a stone like the
dolmen of Locneuven, sails like their fishing boats. Their friendship rests entirely
on this shared longing.

**2.** (a) It is the last sentence of the story, standing alone after Luc's broken
report at the barracks. (b) "He" is Luc Le Ganidec, and what he did not know was the
state of his friend's mind — that by winning the dairymaid in secret and then kissing
her in front of Jean, he had taken away the only thing Jean had. (c) On the walk home
the two had stopped on the bridge at Bezons as they always did; Jean leant further
and further over the railing, as though hypnotised by the water, and fell into the
Seine, where he drowned; boatmen recovered his body the same day. (d) Because it says
the least possible and implies the most. It hints that the death could have been
prevented, and therefore that it may not have been an accident, without ever stating
it; it makes Luc a second victim, condemned to a lifetime of not understanding; and
it leaves the reader to supply the grief that no character in the story is able to
express.

self_checks.answer:
**1.** Everything the two soldiers value in the story is a substitute for Brittany.
They are conscripts from a fishing and farming country, shut up in a barracks at
Courbevoie, and their one pleasure is a walk to a wood that resembles the forest of
Kermarivan. On the way they stop on the bridge to watch white sails that recall
their fishing boats; they halt at a stone because it is like the dolmen of
Locneuven; Jean says every week that the fields are just like Plounivon; and the
dairymaid's milk is welcome mainly because, as she says, it will remind them of
home. Maupassant sums up their condition in a single simile — the slow sorrow of a
captive animal that remembers its freedom. Their friendship grows directly out of
this exile. They are not friends because they are alike in character; they are
friends because they come from the same country and want the same thing at the same
moments, which is why they can walk for an hour without speaking. Such a friendship
looks solid and is in fact very fragile: it has no words in it, no agreements, no
way of handling a disagreement. When Luc begins to want something of his own, the
whole structure falls, and Jean, who has nothing else in the world, falls with it.

**2.** The ending is shocking but not sudden, because almost every element of it has
already been planted. The bridge at Bezons is introduced in the third paragraph, and
we are told that the soldiers *always* stop there for several minutes, bending over
the railing to watch the Seine. The reader therefore accepts the final pause on the
bridge as ordinary, which is precisely why it is dangerous. Maupassant also
establishes the men's total silence: they walk for long stretches without a word,
and their faces never betray anything, so that when Jean is destroyed we are warned
that nothing will be said about it. The last Sunday is then written as a systematic
reversal of the habits we have learned — neither of them is hungry, the girl does
not glance at Jean, there is no milk, and the walk home is conducted with the empty
bottle. Small physical details do the rest: Jean's inability to stand, the "wall of
leaves" through which the lovers vanish, the sun and the lowing cow indifferent
behind them. By the time Jean leans over the railing "as though he had seen
something in the stream which hypnotized him", the reader has all the material
needed, and the fall takes one sentence.

**3.** Maupassant deliberately refuses to decide, and a good answer holds both
readings. The case for suicide is strong. Jean has just been shown, in public, that
he has lost both his friend and the girl; he is described as dazed, heart-broken,
too weak to stand, wanting to run away and never see anyone again; he is a boy with
no words for his feelings and nobody to tell them to; and he leans over the railing
"further and further", as if hypnotised, at the very moment when he has nothing
left. The narrator's closing line, "If he had only known", strongly implies that Luc
might have prevented it had he understood — which suits a suicide better than a
slip. On the other side, nothing is stated. The text says that Jean's head carried
the rest of his body away, which is the language of an accident; Luc, the only
witness, reports it as one; and the two of them had leant over that railing every
Sunday for months without harm. It is also true to the characters that Jean, who
cannot even speak his grief, might not be capable of forming an intention. The
ambiguity is the point: Maupassant shows a death that arises naturally out of
despair without ever accusing anyone of anything.

self_checks.question: Model answers — reference to the context
self_checks.answer:
**1.** (a) The words are spoken by Jean Kerderen to his friend Luc Le Ganidec, and
Luc agrees with him. (b) They are on the narrow path across the plain between the
village of Bezons and the little wood of Champioux, with wheat and oat fields on
either side, on their usual Sunday walk from the barracks at Courbevoie. (c) He says
it every single week because the whole outing is a ritual of remembering: the two
Breton boys come to this place precisely because it resembles their home, and
repeating the sentence is part of the pleasure. (d) It tells us that their real lives
are elsewhere. They are conscripts far from Brittany, poor, homesick and inarticulate,
and they survive by finding substitutes — a wood like Kermarivan, a stone like the
dolmen of Locneuven, sails like their fishing boats. Their friendship rests entirely
on this shared longing.

**2.** (a) It is the last sentence of the story, standing alone after Luc's broken
report at the barracks. (b) "He" is Luc Le Ganidec, and what he did not know was the
state of his friend's mind — that by winning the dairymaid in secret and then kissing

and further over the railing, as though hypnotised by the water, and fell into the

the least possible and implies the most. It hints that the death could have been
prevented, and therefore that it may not have been an accident, without ever stating

R. K. Narayan's "An Astrologer's Day" takes one evening in the working life of a
street fortune-teller who knows nothing whatever about the stars. A single customer
arrives, and by the end of the story we discover why this particular fraud is able
to tell this particular man the exact truth about his past. The story is on the
syllabus as a model of compact plotting: every detail in the opening page turns out,
by the last page, to have been necessary.

  shows the astrologer the man's face and he tries to call the bet off.
- He then tells Guru Nayak, accurately, that he was stabbed, pushed into a well and
