chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** It consists of a dozen cowrie shells, a square piece of cloth covered with
mystic charts, a notebook and palmyra writing, together with the sacred ash and
vermilion on his forehead and a saffron turban. None of it has any use except
display: it makes him look like a holy man with occult knowledge, and so it draws
customers to his mat.

**2.** He relies on shrewd guesswork rather than the stars. He lets the customer talk
for about ten minutes first, watches him closely, and then gives advice based on what
Narayan calls a working analysis of mankind's troubles — marriage, money and the
tangles of human ties. Since his answers are flattering and sensible, the customers
go away satisfied.

**3.** Guru Nayak challenges him to say something worth hearing. They agree that if
the astrologer answers his questions correctly he will be paid a rupee, and that if
he is proved wrong he must pay back double. Guru Nayak grips his wrist to hold him
to the terms.

**4.** Because the flame of the match lights the stranger's face, and the astrologer
recognises the man he stabbed and threw into a well years before in his own village.
He realises he is sitting in front of someone who has come to kill him, and he wants
to get away before he is recognised in turn.

**5.** He tells him that the man he has been hunting was crushed under a lorry four
months ago in a far-off town, and warns him to go home at once and never travel
southward again, promising that he will then live to be a hundred. The advice is a
lie, and its purpose is to keep Guru Nayak permanently away from the town where his
attacker actually lives.

**6.** Because he has discovered that Guru Nayak is alive. For years he had believed
he had killed a man in his village and had been living with the fear and guilt of
it — indeed it was why he ran away, changed his life and became an astrologer.
Meeting his victim alive removes that burden at a stroke, and he goes to bed calm
enough to yawn.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** Irony is not one feature of this story; it is the whole design. The largest
example is situational. The astrologer is an admitted fraud who, as Narayan tells us
on the first page, knows nothing whatever about the stars — and yet the reading he
gives Guru Nayak is entirely accurate, down to the knife, the well and the man's own
name. He can be accurate for one reason only: he is the criminal. A second irony
follows immediately. Guru Nayak has spent years searching for the man who tried to
kill him, and he pays that very man twelve and a half annas to be told that his
enemy is dead; the victim finances his own deception, and goes away pleased. A third
is quieter but sharper: the astrologer, who once tried to murder this man, is
genuinely annoyed at being cheated of a few small coins by him. There is dramatic
irony too, since in the closing scene the reader knows the truth while Guru Nayak
never will, and will keep away from the south for the rest of his life on the
strength of a lie. Finally there is the irony that the lie does real good: it saves
the astrologer's life, prevents a murder, and buys jaggery and coconut for a child.
Narayan never points any of this out. He lets the facts sit side by side, which is
what makes the ending so satisfying.

**2.** The astrologer is a poor man living by his wits, and Narayan draws him without
either admiration or contempt. Professionally he is a fake, and he knows it. The
sacred ash, the vermilion, the saffron turban, the cowrie shells and the charts are
described frankly as equipment, chosen because they attract customers as a lotus
attracts bees. Yet he is not stupid or lazy: he is genuinely skilled at reading
people, he listens before he speaks, and his understanding that most human unhappiness
comes down to marriage, money and family quarrels is not a bad working philosophy.
Morally he is a mixture. He tried to kill a man in a drunken quarrel over gambling
and ran away instead of facing the consequences; he lies to Guru Nayak for his own
safety; he is sharp enough, at the end of a terrifying evening, to count his money
and complain. But he is also a husband and father supporting a family on a few annas
a day, and his relief at learning that he is not a murderer is completely sincere.
What finally defines him is competence under pressure. In the space of a few minutes
he recognises his enemy, sees that confession means death, and constructs a story
that disposes of the danger for ever. He is an ordinary man with an extraordinary
secret, which is Narayan's usual subject.

**3.** Narayan plays fair with the reader. Every fact needed for the ending is
supplied early, but none of it is emphasised. In the opening pages we are told
plainly that the astrologer has no knowledge of the stars, which is what makes the
later accuracy of his reading significant rather than magical. We are also told,
almost in passing, that he had never intended to take up this work, that he would
otherwise have lived and died a farmer, and that he left his village abruptly
without telling anybody — three sentences that mean nothing on a first reading and
everything on a second. The setting is arranged with equal care: the park has no
municipal lighting, the sellers work by flares and lanterns, and faces are visible
only in flashes, so that a man may sit there for years unrecognised. Narayan then
uses one struck match, lit for a cheroot, to break that protection at precisely the
right moment. The astrologer's reaction is shown but not explained — he suddenly
wants the wager cancelled, he is uneasy, he tries to leave — which creates suspense
without cheating. Even the wager itself is necessary, since Guru Nayak's grip on his
wrist traps him into speaking. When the truth finally comes out in the conversation
with his wife, the reader does not feel tricked but enlightened, because the clues
were all in plain sight.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) The astrologer, who sits under a tamarind tree on Town Hall Road and
earns his living telling fortunes, although he has no knowledge at all of astrology.
(b) It means that instead of studying the stars he has studied people, and has
learned that nearly every trouble a customer brings him concerns a marriage, a
question of money, or a quarrel within a family. (c) He uses it as a system. He lets
the client speak for about ten minutes, observes him closely, and then produces
answers that fit one of those three categories, delivered with confidence and a
little flattery, so that the customer leaves satisfied and pays. (d) It is essential
preparation for the ending. Because Narayan has established that the man is a fraud
with no occult powers whatever, his astonishingly exact reading of Guru Nayak cannot
be explained as magic. The reader is therefore forced to look for a natural
explanation, and finds it in the confession at home.

**2.** (a) The astrologer says it to his last customer of the evening, Guru Nayak,
just before the man pays him and leaves. (b) He has told him, correctly, that he was
once stabbed, thrown into a well and left for dead, and has named him; then he has
told him a lie — that the man he has been hunting for years died four months ago,
crushed under a lorry in a distant town. (c) Because Guru Nayak has said openly that
he means to kill his attacker with his own hands, and the attacker is the astrologer
himself. Sending the man home for good, with a solemn warning never to come south
again, is the only way to make sure they never meet a second time. (d) The irony is
double. The advice is entirely false as prophecy and yet entirely true as
prediction: if Guru Nayak stays away he really will live longer, because the man he
wants to kill is the man giving him the advice. And the warning is paid for by the
person it is designed to deceive, who walks away grateful to his own would-be
murderer.

chapters.name: Corona Says - Vishnu S. Rai
topics: Movement 1 — The virus admits it is hated
Movement 2 — The virus turns the accusation round
Movement 3 — The virus as a teacher of equality
Movement 4 — The earth breathes, and the warning
chapters.summary:
The poem is a **dramatic monologue**: one speaker talks, and we understand the
silent listener only from what the speaker says. The speaker is the coronavirus.
The listener is the whole human race. The poem moves through four clear stages,
which are best studied one at a time.

### Movement 1 — The virus admits it is hated

The virus begins by acknowledging what human beings feel about it. It knows that
people hate it, fear it and want it dead, and that they call it a killer. It does
not argue with this. It accepts, calmly, that it has caused death and that the
world is frightened of it. This quiet, reasonable opening is important: the
speaker sounds not like a monster but like someone willing to discuss the charge.

### Movement 2 — The virus turns the accusation round

Having accepted the charge, the virus asks who the greater killer really is. It
reminds human beings of what they have done to the earth long before any virus
arrived: forests cut down, rivers and air poisoned, other living creatures
hunted, caged and killed for pleasure or profit, and wars in which human beings
destroyed their own kind in millions. The point the virus makes is one of
proportion. Whatever harm a virus has done in a few months, humankind has done
far more, for far longer, and on purpose. A virus kills because that is its
nature; people destroy while knowing exactly what they are doing.

### Movement 3 — The virus as a teacher of equality

The virus then describes its own most uncomfortable quality: it makes no
distinctions. It does not ask whether a body is rich or poor, powerful or
powerless, of one religion or another, of one colour or another, from a rich
country or a poor one. Money, weapons, armies and titles are of no use against
it. In a world organised around exactly such differences, this is presented as a
kind of grim lesson: the virus has shown human beings the equality they preach
but never practise.

### Movement 4 — The earth breathes, and the warning

Finally the virus points to what happened while human beings stayed shut in their
houses. Factories and vehicles stopped; the air cleared; rivers ran cleaner; birds
and animals were heard and seen in places from which people had driven them away.
The planet, in other words, recovered a little the moment human activity paused —
which quietly proves the virus's case about who the real destroyer is. The poem
closes on a conditional note rather than a triumphant one: the virus will pass,
as such things do, but whether human beings have actually learnt anything is left
as an open question addressed to the reader.

"Corona Says" is a short poem written by the Nepali writer Vishnu S. Rai during
the COVID-19 pandemic of 2020. Its trick is simple and powerful: the virus itself
is given a voice. Instead of a human complaining about a disease, a disease
complains about human beings. By the end of the poem the reader is no longer sure
which of the two is the real infection of the earth.

## Model answers — short questions

**1.** The speaker is the coronavirus itself, given a human voice by the poet. It
addresses the whole human race — the repeated "you" of the poem. The poet himself
never speaks directly; his opinion reaches us only through what the virus says.

**2.** The virus accuses human beings of cutting down forests, poisoning rivers
and the air, hunting, caging and killing other creatures, and destroying millions
of their own kind in wars. Its point is that all this damage was deliberate,
long-lasting and far greater than the harm a virus can do.

**3.** The virus does not ask whether the body it enters is rich or poor, of
which country, colour, caste or religion, or how powerful its owner is. Wealth,
weapons and rank give no protection. In a world divided by exactly these
differences, the virus treats everybody the same, and so becomes an equaliser.

**4.** During the lockdown the air became clear, the rivers ran cleaner, and
birds and wild animals reappeared in places from which people had driven them.
The earth recovered as soon as human activity stopped, which supports the virus's
claim that human beings, not viruses, are the planet's real problem.

**5.** Free verse has no fixed metre or rhyme, so the poem sounds like ordinary
speech rather than a song. That plain, calm, conversational voice makes the
virus's accusation sound reasonable, and keeps the reader's attention on the
terrible content instead of on pretty sound patterns.

**6.** A dramatic monologue is a poem in which an invented speaker, who is not
the poet, talks at length to a silent listener whose presence we infer from the
speech. In "Corona Says" the invented speaker is the virus, the silent listener
is humankind, and we learn what humankind feels ("you hate me") only from the
virus's words.

**7.** The irony is that a deadly disease takes the moral high ground and lectures
human beings about killing. The accused becomes the accuser, and the creature we
call a killer proves that we kill more. The gap between our view of ourselves as
civilised and the evidence the virus produces is the poem's irony.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** The poem begins where the reader already stands: the virus is the killer,
human beings are its victims, and the speaker openly admits that it is hated and
wished dead. Having accepted that charge, it immediately reverses it. It asks who
has done more killing, and answers with a list of human acts — forests cut down,
rivers and air poisoned, animals hunted and caged, wars in which millions of
human beings destroyed one another. The comparison is one of scale and of
intention: a virus spreads because that is its nature, while people destroy
knowing exactly what they do. The reversal is then confirmed by evidence from the
lockdown. When human activity stopped, the sky cleared, the water cleaned itself
and animals returned to the streets — so the planet was healthier without us than
with us. By the end, the word "virus" has changed owners: the true infection of
the earth is humankind, and the disease is merely a symptom. Because the
accusation comes from the enemy's own mouth and not from the poet's, the reader
cannot dismiss it as preaching, and has to sit with the discomfort.

**2.** Satire attacks human folly and wrongdoing by holding it up to ridicule,
and that is precisely what this poem does. Its satirical method is to give the
speech to the coronavirus, so that human behaviour is described from outside by
somebody with no reason to flatter us. The targets are exact. First, our
hypocrisy: we call the virus a murderer while conducting wars and slaughtering
other species. Second, our arrogance: we believed money, technology, armies and
borders had made us masters of the earth, and an organism too small to see
undid that belief in weeks. Third, our inequality: we announce that all human
beings are equal and then organise the world by wealth, colour, religion and
nationality, and it takes a disease — which asks none of those questions — to
treat us all alike. Fourth, our carelessness towards nature, proved by how
quickly the earth improved without us. The tone is not shrill; the virus is calm,
patient and almost polite, and this restraint sharpens the attack. The poem ends
not with a punishment but with a question about whether we have learnt anything,
which is satire's real aim: not to wound but to correct.

**3.** The poem is written in free verse: the lines are short, of unequal length,
and there is no metre and no rhyme scheme at all. This is a deliberate choice. A
regular pattern would have made the virus sound like a chant or a hymn, whereas
free verse makes it sound like a person speaking quietly and reasonably to
someone across a table, which is far more unsettling. The vocabulary matches the
form: ordinary, unornamented words, so that the frightening content — felled
forests, poisoned water, war dead — is allowed to do the work without help from
grand poetic language. Structurally the poem is an argument rather than a story:
the charge is accepted, a counter-charge is made, evidence is produced, and the
conclusion is handed to the reader. Two devices hold everything together.
**Personification** frames the whole poem, since without a speaking virus there
is no poem at all. **Apostrophe** — the insistent "you" — keeps the reader inside
the poem as the accused rather than outside it as an observer. Enjambment lets
the short lines run on so the voice never falls into singsong, and the stacked
clauses of accusation give the passage the rhythm of a charge-sheet being read
out in court. Form, language and meaning are therefore inseparable: a poem about
stripping away human pretence is itself stripped of poetic decoration.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) The speaker is the coronavirus, which the poet has personified and
allowed to address humankind throughout the poem.
(b) It describes the virus's complete **indifference to human distinctions**. It
infects anyone, and wealth, power, caste, colour, nationality and religion give
no protection. This is why the poem presents it as the one true equaliser.
(c) The comment is a bitter one about human hypocrisy. Human society claims that
all people are equal, yet it is organised by exactly the differences the virus
ignores. It has taken a disease to give human beings the equality their own
declarations promise but their behaviour denies. The lines therefore work as
satire: the virus is not boasting, it is exposing us.

**2.** (a) The passage describes the COVID-19 lockdown of 2020, when factories,
vehicles and daily movement stopped almost everywhere in the world.
(b) The speaker mentions these changes as **evidence** in its argument. Having
claimed that human beings, not viruses, are the earth's real destroyers, it
points to what happened the moment human activity paused: the proof of the claim
is that the planet immediately began to recover.
(c) The passage suggests that the relationship has become one-sided and harmful —
nature does not need human beings, but suffers from them, and is able to heal
itself quickly if the pressure is lifted. It carries one hopeful implication: the
damage is not yet beyond repair. Whether people will choose to reduce that
pressure after the pandemic is the open question on which the poem ends.

chapters.name: A Red, Red Rose - Robert Burns
chapters.summary:
### Stanza 1 — Two similes

> O my Luve's like a red, red rose,
> That's newly sprung in June;
> O my Luve's like the melodie
> That's sweetly play'd in tune.

The speaker compares his beloved to two things. First to a rose — not any rose,
but a **red** one that has **just** opened in June, so the comparison carries
colour, freshness, perfection and the height of summer. Then to a **melody**
sweetly played in tune. The first comparison appeals to the eye, the second to
the ear; the first is a thing of nature, the second a thing of art. Together they
say that the beloved is both beautiful to look at and harmonious to live with.

### Stanza 2 — The first vow

> As fair art thou, my bonnie lass,
> So deep in luve am I;
> And I will luve thee still, my dear,
> Till a' the seas gang dry.

Now the speaker moves from description to promise. The construction is careful:
*as* beautiful as you are, *so* deeply am I in love — his love is measured by her
beauty. He then swears to go on loving her until all the seas dry up, which is to
say for ever, since the seas will not dry up.

### Stanza 3 — The vow made larger

> Till a' the seas gang dry, my dear,
> And the rocks melt wi' the sun;
> And I will luve thee still, my dear,
> While the sands o' life shall run.

The stanza opens by repeating the last line of stanza two, so the two stanzas
lock together like links in a chain — a device taken straight from folk song. The
impossible condition is then raised higher: not only until the seas dry, but until
the very rocks melt in the heat of the sun. The last line quietly changes the
measure from the life of the earth to the life of a man: he will love her while
"the sands o' life shall run", that is, as long as the sand keeps falling through
the hourglass of his own life.

### Stanza 4 — The farewell

> And fare-thee-weel, my only Luve!
> And fare-thee-weel, a while!
> And I will come again, my Luve,
> Tho' 'twere ten thousand mile!

Only in the final stanza do we learn that the lovers are about to be separated.
The whole poem has in fact been a parting speech. The speaker says goodbye twice,
then softens it at once with "a while" — this is not an ending but an interval —
and promises to return even if ten thousand miles lie between them. The poem
closes on movement towards the beloved rather than away from her, which is why it
feels joyful and not sad.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- About the poet
- Summary
- Themes
- Form, structure and rhyme
- Poetic devices
- Glossary
- Stanza 1 — Two similes
- Stanza 2 — The first vow
- Stanza 3 — The vow made larger
- Stanza 4 — The farewell

"A Red, Red Rose" is probably the best-known love song in the English language,
and it is barely sixteen lines long. Robert Burns took two old Scottish folk
songs, reshaped them, and produced a lyric that says only one thing — I love you
and I will not stop — but says it with such music that it has been sung for more
than two hundred years. This unit looks at how so plain a statement is made so
memorable.

## Chapter summary

### Stanza 1 — Two similes

> O my Luve's like a red, red rose,
> That's newly sprung in June;
> O my Luve's like the melodie
> That's sweetly play'd in tune.

The speaker compares his beloved to two things. First to a rose — not any rose,
but a **red** one that has **just** opened in June, so the comparison carries
colour, freshness, perfection and the height of summer. Then to a **melody**
sweetly played in tune. The first comparison appeals to the eye, the second to
the ear; the first is a thing of nature, the second a thing of art. Together they
say that the beloved is both beautiful to look at and harmonious to live with.

### Stanza 2 — The first vow

> As fair art thou, my bonnie lass,
> So deep in luve am I;
> And I will luve thee still, my dear,
> Till a' the seas gang dry.

Now the speaker moves from description to promise. The construction is careful:
*as* beautiful as you are, *so* deeply am I in love — his love is measured by her
beauty. He then swears to go on loving her until all the seas dry up, which is to
say for ever, since the seas will not dry up.

### Stanza 3 — The vow made larger

> Till a' the seas gang dry, my dear,
> And the rocks melt wi' the sun;
> And I will luve thee still, my dear,
> While the sands o' life shall run.

The stanza opens by repeating the last line of stanza two, so the two stanzas
lock together like links in a chain — a device taken straight from folk song. The
impossible condition is then raised higher: not only until the seas dry, but until
the very rocks melt in the heat of the sun. The last line quietly changes the
measure from the life of the earth to the life of a man: he will love her while
"the sands o' life shall run", that is, as long as the sand keeps falling through
the hourglass of his own life.

### Stanza 4 — The farewell

> And fare-thee-weel, my only Luve!
> And fare-thee-weel, a while!
> And I will come again, my Luve,
> Tho' 'twere ten thousand mile!

Only in the final stanza do we learn that the lovers are about to be separated.
The whole poem has in fact been a parting speech. The speaker says goodbye twice,
then softens it at once with "a while" — this is not an ending but an interval —
and promises to return even if ten thousand miles lie between them. The poem
closes on movement towards the beloved rather than away from her, which is why it
feels joyful and not sad.

## Study route

Read the topics and identify unfamiliar terms.

Close the book and explain the key ideas in your own words.

Attempt a worked example before revealing its solution.

Complete the chapter practice, correct mistakes, then mark the chapter revised.
chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** He compares her to a red rose that has just opened in June, and to a
melody sweetly played in tune. The first is an image for the eye and suggests
colour, freshness and perfection; the second is an image for the ear and suggests
harmony and sweetness. Together they praise both how she looks and how she makes
him feel.

**2.** He says he will love her till all the seas run dry, till the rocks melt in
the sun, and for as long as the sands of his own life keep running. Since none of
the first two can happen, the vow means "for ever", measured against the age of
the earth and then against his own lifetime.

**3.** It refers to the sand falling through an hourglass, and so means the time a
person has left to live. It brings the huge, geological exaggerations of the
earlier lines back to a human scale, and quietly admits that the speaker himself
is mortal even while his love claims to be endless.

**4.** The whole poem turns out to be a parting speech: the lovers are about to be
separated. The farewell explains why the speaker has been swearing constancy, and
because he says goodbye only "a while" and promises to return "tho' 'twere ten
thousand mile", the poem ends looking forward to reunion rather than to loss.

**5.** The rhyme scheme is **ABCB** in each of the four stanzas — only the second
and fourth lines rhyme (June/tune, I/dry, sun/run, while/mile). The stanza form is
the **ballad stanza**, or common metre: a quatrain of alternating four-beat and
three-beat lines.

**6.** The metre alternates iambic tetrameter and iambic trimeter. The line scans
as four iambs: "O **my** | Luve's **like** | a **red**, | red **rose**" —
da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM. The repeated "red" pulls an extra stress into the
third foot, which is a deliberate variation.

**7.** Scots was the everyday speech of the Ayrshire country people Burns lived
and worked among. Using it keeps the poem close to real speech and to oral folk
song, gives it a distinct music ("gang", "bonnie", "a'"), and asserts the dignity
of ordinary Scottish life at a time when poets were expected to write polished
English.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** Hyperbole — deliberate exaggeration — is the engine of the poem's second
half. The speaker promises to love "till a' the seas gang dry", until "the rocks
melt wi' the sun", and to return even if "ten thousand mile" separate them. Taken
literally these are absurd; nobody expects oceans to evaporate. But the poem is a
song, not a contract, and the exaggeration is doing emotional work rather than
factual work. Each image is drawn from the most permanent things the speaker can
think of — the sea, the rock, the sun — so that love is measured against the
largest and most unchanging objects in the world, and still claims to outlast
them. The exaggerations also **escalate**: the seas drying is followed by
something even less likely, rocks melting, and the chain link between the stanzas
makes the vow sound sworn twice. What saves the poem from sounding foolish is the
plainness of everything around the hyperbole: simple Scots words, a folk-song
rhythm, and the very human admission of "the sands o' life", which reminds us that
the speaker will die. The exaggeration therefore strengthens the poem. It does not
ask us to believe the seas will dry; it asks us to feel how much a young man in
love needs to say that they might.

**2.** Burns chooses the ballad stanza — four quatrains of alternating iambic
tetrameter and trimeter, rhyming ABCB — and every feature of it serves the
meaning. The metre is the *da-DUM* of ordinary English and Scots speech, so the
declaration sounds spoken rather than composed. The short three-beat lines leave a
silent fourth beat at the end of each, the natural gap for a singer's tune, which
is why the poem has been sung for two centuries. Rhyming only the second and
fourth lines leaves the long lines free to run on, giving the movement of easy
speech while the returning rhyme still rounds each stanza off. Repetition works at
three levels: inside the line ("red, red"), inside the stanza ("fare-thee-weel …
fare-thee-weel"), and between stanzas, where the last line of stanza 2 becomes the
first line of stanza 3 — the chain link of oral ballad, which makes the promise
sound repeated and therefore binding. Small departures from the metre carry
meaning too: the double stress on "red, red rose" presses the colour on us, and
the extra light syllable in stanza 3's short lines keeps the song from becoming
mechanical. The structure moves from description (stanza 1) to vow (stanzas 2–3)
to farewell (stanza 4), so the form delivers the surprise of the ending. Simple
feeling is given a simple, perfect shape.

**3.** The subject of the poem looks like love, but almost every line is really
about duration. Stanza 1 already contains time: the rose is "newly sprung in
June", caught at the exact moment of perfection — and any reader knows that a June
rose has a fortnight to live. The praise therefore carries its own shadow. The
middle stanzas answer that shadow by measuring love against the biggest clocks the
speaker knows: the seas will have to dry and the rocks melt before his love
changes. These are geological spans, far beyond a human life, and they are
invoked precisely because they are beyond it. Then stanza 3 turns the measure
inward — he will love "while the sands o' life shall run", an hourglass image that
brings us from the age of the earth back to one man's mortality, honestly admitted.
The last stanza changes the unit again, from time to distance and back: the parting
is only "a while", and the ten thousand miles will be crossed. The poem's real
argument, then, is that love is the one human thing willing to stand up against
time, even though the lover knows perfectly well that the rose fades and the sand
runs out. Its confidence is moving because it is not ignorant.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) **Simile** — the comparisons are made openly with the word "like",
first to a rose and then to a melody.
(b) June is the height of the Scottish summer and "newly sprung" means the flower
has only just opened. The beloved is therefore compared not to a rose in general
but to a rose at the single moment of its greatest freshness, colour and
perfection. The detail also hints, without saying so, at how briefly such
perfection lasts — which is why the rest of the poem is so concerned with
lastingness.
(c) The rose is seen; the melody is heard. The second simile moves the praise from
sight to sound, and from nature to art. A tune "sweetly play'd in tune" suggests
harmony, order and rightness, so the beloved is not only beautiful to look at but
pleasing to be with. Between them the two similes praise her whole effect on the
speaker.

**2.** (a) It reveals, for the first time, that the lovers are about to be
**separated**: the speaker is leaving, and the entire poem has been a parting
speech rather than a general praise of love.
(b) Hyperbole: "ten thousand mile", a deliberately enormous distance. Repetition:
"fare-thee-weel" is repeated in consecutive lines (and "my Luve" twice in the
stanza), giving the insistence of a song.
(c) Because the farewell is immediately limited and then cancelled. "A while" turns
the goodbye into a short interval, and the last two lines promise return in spite
of any distance. The stanza therefore ends on the idea of coming back, not of
going away, and the final movement of the poem is towards the beloved.

**2.** Burns chooses the ballad stanza — four quatrains of alternating iambic
tetrameter and trimeter, rhyming ABCB — and every feature of it serves the
meaning. The metre is the *da-DUM* of ordinary English and Scots speech, so the
declaration sounds spoken rather than composed. The short three-beat lines leave a
silent fourth beat at the end of each, the natural gap for a singer's tune, which
is why the poem has been sung for two centuries. Rhyming only the second and
fourth lines leaves the long lines free to run on, giving the movement of easy
speech while the returning rhyme still rounds each stanza off. Repetition works at
three levels: inside the line ("red, red"), inside the stanza ("fare-thee-weel …
fare-thee-weel"), and between stanzas, where the last line of stanza 2 becomes the
first line of stanza 3 — the chain link of oral ballad, which makes the promise
sound repeated and therefore binding. Small departures from the metre carry
meaning too: the double stress on "red, red rose" presses the colour on us, and
the extra light syllable in stanza 3's short lines keeps the song from becoming
mechanical. The structure moves from description (stanza 1) to vow (stanzas 2–3)
to farewell (stanza 4), so the form delivers the surprise of the ending. Simple
feeling is given a simple, perfect shape.

**3.** The subject of the poem looks like love, but almost every line is really
about duration. Stanza 1 already contains time: the rose is "newly sprung in
June", caught at the exact moment of perfection — and any reader knows that a June
rose has a fortnight to live. The praise therefore carries its own shadow. The
middle stanzas answer that shadow by measuring love against the biggest clocks the
speaker knows: the seas will have to dry and the rocks melt before his love
changes. These are geological spans, far beyond a human life, and they are
invoked precisely because they are beyond it. Then stanza 3 turns the measure
inward — he will love "while the sands o' life shall run", an hourglass image that
brings us from the age of the earth back to one man's mortality, honestly admitted.
The last stanza changes the unit again, from time to distance and back: the parting
is only "a while", and the ten thousand miles will be crossed. The poem's real
argument, then, is that love is the one human thing willing to stand up against
time, even though the lover knows perfectly well that the rose fades and the sand
runs out. Its confidence is moving because it is not ignorant.

self_checks.question: Model answers — reference to the context
self_checks.answer:
**1.** (a) **Simile** — the comparisons are made openly with the word "like",
first to a rose and then to a melody.
(b) June is the height of the Scottish summer and "newly sprung" means the flower
has only just opened. The beloved is therefore compared not to a rose in general
but to a rose at the single moment of its greatest freshness, colour and
perfection. The detail also hints, without saying so, at how briefly such
perfection lasts — which is why the rest of the poem is so concerned with
lastingness.
(c) The rose is seen; the melody is heard. The second simile moves the praise from
sight to sound, and from nature to art. A tune "sweetly play'd in tune" suggests
harmony, order and rightness, so the beloved is not only beautiful to look at but
pleasing to be with. Between them the two similes praise her whole effect on the
speaker.

**2.** (a) It reveals, for the first time, that the lovers are about to be
**separated**: the speaker is leaving, and the entire poem has been a parting
speech rather than a general praise of love.
(b) Hyperbole: "ten thousand mile", a deliberately enormous distance. Repetition:
"fare-thee-weel" is repeated in consecutive lines (and "my Luve" twice in the
stanza), giving the insistence of a song.
(c) Because the farewell is immediately limited and then cancelled. "A while" turns
the goodbye into a short interval, and the last two lines promise return in spite
of any distance. The stanza therefore ends on the idea of coming back, not of
going away, and the final movement of the poem is towards the beloved.

chapters.name: All the World's a Stage - William Shakespeare
topics: Ages one to three: infant, schoolboy, lover
Ages four and five: soldier and justice
Ages six and seven: pantaloon and second childishness
chapters.summary:
*As You Like It* is set largely in the Forest of Arden, where a banished duke and
his followers live in exile. Just before this speech, Duke Senior remarks that the
world is a wide theatre full of sadder scenes than their own. Jaques — the
melancholy lord of the play, a man who enjoys being gloomy — picks up the image
and expands it into the speech we study.

### The governing metaphor

Jaques begins by declaring that the whole world is a stage and that all men and
women are merely players on it. Each person enters at birth and leaves at death —
"They have their exits and their entrances" — and in between plays many parts.
He then fixes the number of parts at seven, and the rest of the speech is the
list.

### Ages one to three: infant, schoolboy, lover

The **infant** comes first, "Mewling and puking in the nurse's arms": crying and
being sick, completely helpless, not yet even able to hold itself.

Next the **schoolboy**, with his satchel and "shining morning face", creeping
"like snail / Unwillingly to school". The face is washed and bright, but the boy
is dragging his feet; Shakespeare catches in one line something every student
recognises.

Third the **lover**, "Sighing like furnace", writing a sad ballad in praise of his
mistress's eyebrow. The detail is comic: a grown man breathing out hot sighs and
composing poetry about one small feature of a girl's face. Love at this stage is
mostly performance.

### Ages four and five: soldier and justice

The **soldier** is full of strange oaths and "bearded like the pard" (the
leopard). He is touchy about his honour, quick to quarrel, and hunts "the bubble
reputation / Even in the cannon's mouth" — he will risk death at the mouth of a
gun for a fame that is as light and as short-lived as a bubble.

Then the **justice**, a judge. He has grown a "fair round belly" lined with good
capon — bribes, in the shape of dinners, are implied. His eyes are stern, his
beard trimmed in the correct official fashion, and he is full of "wise saws and
modern instances": old proverbs and fashionable examples, borrowed wisdom
delivered as though it were his own. He has reached the top, and Jaques quietly
tells us it is mostly an act.

### Ages six and seven: pantaloon and second childishness

The sixth age "shifts / Into the lean and slippered pantaloon" — the thin,
slippered old man of Italian comedy, spectacles on his nose and a money-pouch at
his side. The body has begun to shrink: the stockings he carefully saved from his
youth are now "a world too wide / For his shrunk shank", and the deep manly voice
has turned back to a childish treble that pipes and whistles when he speaks.

The last age, which "ends this strange eventful history", is "second
childishness and mere oblivion" — a return to the helplessness of the infant, and
then forgetfulness of everything. The speech closes with one of the most famous
lines Shakespeare wrote: "Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything."
*Sans* is French for "without". Everything the man gathered in seven ages is
taken away again.

## Topics to cover

- About the poet
- Summary
- Themes
- Form, structure and rhyme

- Ages one to three: infant, schoolboy, lover

"All the World's a Stage" is not a separate poem at all. It is twenty-eight lines
of a play — a speech given to a character called Jaques in Shakespeare's comedy
*As You Like It*, Act II, Scene vii. In it a bitter, watchful man compares human
life to a play in seven acts and takes us from a crying baby to a toothless old
man in a single breath. It is the most quoted description of a human lifetime in
English.

chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** The lines are spoken by **Jaques**, the melancholy lord, in Shakespeare's
comedy *As You Like It*, **Act II, Scene vii**. He speaks them in the Forest of
Arden, to the banished Duke Senior and his followers, taking up an image the Duke
has just used.

**2.** Infant, schoolboy, lover, soldier, justice (judge), pantaloon (the lean
slippered old man), and second childishness or oblivion.

**3.** It is a metaphor for fame won in battle. A bubble is bright and round and
attractive, but weightless and certain to burst in a moment. The soldier will face
the mouth of a cannon for something that empty, which is Shakespeare's comment on
military glory.

**4.** He is described with his satchel and "shining morning face", "creeping like
snail / Unwillingly to school". The washed, bright face shows he has been
carefully prepared by others, while the snail simile shows that he has no wish to
go. The gap between the two is the comedy of the second age.

**5.** Because the very old man returns to the condition of the infant he once
was. He cannot feed or look after himself, his voice has climbed back to a child's
high treble, and finally memory and the senses go. Life is therefore shown as a
circle rather than a straight line.

**6.** Blank verse is unrhymed **iambic pentameter**: lines of five iambic feet
(ten syllables, a *da-DUM* beat five times over) with no rhyme at the line-ends.
It is the standard verse form of Elizabethan drama because it is the closest verse
form to natural English speech.

**7.** "Sans" means "without", and it is repeated four times in one short line.
Each repetition removes something more — teeth, eyes, taste, and then
"everything". The rhythm of the line therefore imitates the process it describes:
loss after loss, until nothing at all is left.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** Jaques presents seven pictures in time order. The **infant** is helpless,
"Mewling and puking in the nurse's arms". The **schoolboy**, with satchel and
shining morning face, creeps "like snail / Unwillingly to school". The **lover**
sighs "like furnace" and writes a sad ballad to his mistress's eyebrow. The
**soldier**, bearded like the leopard and quick to quarrel, chases "the bubble
reputation" even at the cannon's mouth. The **justice**, with a fair round belly
lined with capon and a formally cut beard, hands out borrowed wisdom in the form
of "wise saws and modern instances". The sixth age is the **pantaloon**, thin and
slippered, spectacles on nose, his youthful stockings now "a world too wide / For
his shrunk shank" and his voice piping like a child's. The seventh is **second
childishness and mere oblivion**, "Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans
everything". Each picture is chosen for one reason: to show the person acting a
part supplied by his age rather than living a life he has chosen. The ages also
form an arc, rising to the judge at the top of the world and then falling; and
because the last age returns to the helplessness of the first, the arc closes into
a circle. The argument, built entirely out of pictures, is that a human life is
short, borrowed and repetitive.

**2.** The speech is built on a single comparison carried through to the end,
which is what an extended metaphor means. The world becomes a stage, men and
women become "merely players", birth and death become "entrances" and "exits", and
a lifetime becomes a play in seven acts. Once the metaphor is set, every detail
follows from it: each age arrives with a costume (satchel, beard, spectacles,
slippers), a voice (mewling, sighing, swearing, piping) and a set of lines (the
ballad, the oaths, the proverbs). The metaphor does real work, because it lets
Jaques suggest that our behaviour is not personal but scripted — the soldier
quarrels because soldiers quarrel, the judge pronounces because judges pronounce.
There is truth in this. We do take on roles, and much of what we call personality
is behaviour expected of our age, our job and our place in society. But the
metaphor is not the whole truth, and Shakespeare knows it. Actors can put the
costume off; human beings cannot. More importantly, a script cannot explain the
scene that follows immediately in the play, where the starving old servant Adam
is carried in and fed with real kindness. That act is not in anybody's part. The
metaphor is brilliant and partial at the same time, which is why the play gives it
to a character rather than stating it as truth.

**3.** The speech is written in **blank verse** — unrhymed iambic pentameter, five
*da-DUM* feet to a line, as in "And **one** man **in** his **time** plays **ma**-ny
**parts**". Shakespeare uses the pattern loosely: many lines carry an extra
unstressed syllable at the end (a feminine ending, such as "merely players"),
strong pauses cut lines in half, and the sense constantly runs over the line-break
in enjambment. These freedoms matter, because they make verse sound like a man
thinking aloud. Rhyme would have been fatal here; it would have turned a bitter
observation into a jingle, and would have given each age a neat, satisfying close
that the argument does not want. Instead the lines push forward without rest, one
age spilling into the next, exactly as time does. The context matters just as
much. These are not Shakespeare's opinions but **Jaques's**, and Jaques is the
play's professional pessimist, a man who, as another character says, enjoys his
own sadness. He speaks in the Forest of Arden, in a scene where Duke Senior has
just made the same comparison more gently. Within thirty lines the play answers
him: old Adam is brought in, weak and hungry, and is treated with tenderness — so
the audience sees that the seventh age need not be "mere oblivion" after all.
Recognising the speaker keeps us from mistaking a character's mood for the play's
conclusion.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) The speaker is **Jaques**, the melancholy lord in *As You Like It*
(Act II, Scene vii). He is speaking in the Forest of Arden to the banished Duke
Senior and the other exiled lords, taking up a comparison the Duke has just made.
(b) The figure of speech is **metaphor**, and because it is carried through the
whole speech it is an **extended metaphor**. The world is called a stage and human
beings are called actors, without "like" or "as". The comparison suggests that
people do not simply live their lives but perform parts written for them by their
age and situation.
(c) "Exits" and "entrances" are stage directions: the moments an actor leaves and
comes on. Here they stand for **death and birth**. Calling them stage directions
makes them routine and impersonal — actors come and go all evening — which is
exactly the cool, detached view of human life that Jaques wants to press on his
listeners.

**2.** (a) The **seventh and last age**, extreme old age, which Jaques calls
"second childishness and mere oblivion".
(b) Because a lifetime is full of incident — seven different parts, each with its
own costume, ambitions and follies — yet it is "strange" in that all this activity
leads only back to the helplessness it began in. Calling it a "history" also keeps
the theatre metaphor alive, since a history was a kind of play.
(c) The last line lists four losses in a single breath, using the French word
"sans" ("without") four times. The repetition (anaphora) makes the line sound like
a series of subtractions, and the movement from three concrete losses — teeth,
eyes, taste — to the sweeping "sans everything" empties the life out completely.
There is no consolation offered and no rhyme to soften it; the play's most famous
line is a line of pure absence.

chapters.name: Who are you, little i? - E. E. Cummings
topics: Lines 1–4 — the question and the child at the window
Lines 5–8 — the sunset and the child's thought
chapters.summary:
The poem is a single unbroken stanza of eight lines and a single sentence. It
divides naturally into two halves.

### Lines 1–4 — the question and the child at the window

The poem opens with a question — "who are you,little i" — addressed to a small
child who is, we soon realise, the speaker himself at the age of five or six. The
age is given in brackets, as though it were a quiet aside. The child is
"peering" — looking hard and with concentration — out of a high window. The word
"high" tells us two things at once: the window is upstairs, and the child is
small. He is not playing; he is watching something, and the sentence carries us
over the line-break to find out what.

### Lines 5–8 — the sunset and the child's thought

What he is watching is "the gold / of november sunset". November is late autumn,
the year's own evening, and the sunset is the day's ending; the one colour named
is gold, which makes the ending rich rather than sad. The last three lines, again
placed in brackets, give us the child's own feeling: that **if** the day has to
turn into night, then this is a beautiful way for it to happen. Nothing more is
said. The poem has no full stop; it closes with a bracket and leaves the child at
the window.

The force of the poem lies in what it does not spell out. An old poet is asking
his childhood self a question, and the child's answer — the acceptance of a
beautiful ending — turns out to be the answer the adult needs about his own life.

This poem is eight short lines long, contains one sentence, and has not a single
capital letter in it. An adult looks back at himself as a child of five or six,
standing at a high window watching a November sunset. The child thinks that if
the day must end, this is a lovely way for it to go — and the grown man, much
closer to his own ending, finds that the child was right.

## Model answers — short questions

**1.** "little i" is the poet's own self as a child of five or six, remembered
many years later. The questioner is the grown poet. The poem is therefore a
conversation between one person's two selves, which is why the same small "i"
serves for both.

**2.** He is "peering" — looking hard and with concentration — out of a high
window, watching the gold of a November sunset. He is alone, still, and completely
absorbed in what he sees.

**3.** November is late autumn in the northern hemisphere, the last month before
winter, so the year itself is ending. Putting the day's ending inside the year's
ending doubles the idea of things drawing to a close, and prepares us for the
poem's real subject, the end of a life.

**4.** To make the self small and humble. A capital "I" would put the speaker at
the centre of the poem; the lower-case "i" matches the size of a five-year-old
child at a high window and keeps him in proportion to the enormous sunset he is
watching. It is one of Cummings's trademark devices, not an error.

**5.** Lines 1–4 rhyme **A B A B** ("i" with "high", "old" with "gold"); lines 5–8
rhyme **C D E D** ("day" with "way", while "sunset" and "night" do not rhyme with
anything). Apart from this the poem is free verse.

**6.** The brackets turn the last three lines into a private, inner voice — the
child's own feeling, thought rather than spoken. We seem to overhear it instead of
being told it, which makes the poem's large statement about death sound gentle and
unforced.

**7.** Because a full stop would close the moment. Cummings ends on a bracket
instead, leaving the child still standing at the window and the light still going.
The thought is left open, so the reader carries it on rather than filing it away.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** The sunset is the centre of the poem and its main symbol. On the surface it
is simply what the child can see: the gold of the sky at the end of a November
afternoon, watched from an upstairs window. But every detail is chosen to make it
mean more. It is a **sunset**, the oldest image in poetry for the close of a life.
It is in **November**, so the year is in its own late afternoon, with winter next.
The only colour named is **gold**, which turns the fading light into something
precious rather than something lost. And it is watched through a **window**,
which frames it like a picture and keeps the small watcher separate from the vast
sky. The child's response makes the symbolism explicit: if day *has* to become
night, this is a beautiful way for it to happen. The word "has to" admits that the
ending is not optional. What the child offers is not denial but acceptance — the
recognition that an ending can be beautiful. Read back through the grown poet who
asks the opening question, the sunset therefore becomes his own. A man near the
end of his life asks his childhood self what to think about endings, and is given
a gold sky as the answer.

**2.** Cummings trained as a painter, and he treats the printed page as a surface
to be designed. In this poem every unusual mark does a job. The **lower-case "i"**
refuses the tall capital of the adult ego and makes the speaker small — the exact
size of a five-year-old, and the right size to stand under a whole sky. The
**missing spaces** after the comma, semicolon and colon ("you,little",
"window;at", "feeling:that") press the words together, so the eye has to slow down
and pick them apart; the effect is of speech hurrying, and of a child's attention
that does not pause where grammar says it should. The **brackets** around the
second line and the last three create a second, quieter voice inside the poem, so
the child's feeling is overheard rather than announced — which is why so large a
thought about death can be carried by so small a poem. The **line-break** at "some
high / window" leaves the word "high" hanging at the edge of the line, raised
above the noun it describes. Keeping **"november"** in lower case levels every
word, so no part of the picture shouts. Finally, the **absent full stop** refuses
to close the moment. Take away these choices, print the poem in ordinary
sentences, and nothing survives but a pleasant memory of a sunset. The typography
is not a style laid over the meaning; it is how the meaning exists.

**3.** The poem presents childhood as a state of clear seeing rather than of
ignorance. The child does nothing remarkable — he stands at a window and looks —
but his looking is total, which is what "peering" conveys. He is not told about
the sunset and does not describe it to anyone; he simply receives it, and out of
that receiving comes a thought that most adults never manage: that if an ending
must come, it can come beautifully. Cummings gives the child no argument and no
consolation, only acceptance, and that is precisely the point. The relation
between the two selves is the poem's structure. The adult asks; the child, sixty
years back and without knowing he is answering, replies. The question "who are
you" holds the two apart — the man cannot simply step back into the boy — while
the single unbroken sentence and the single small "i" hold them together. The
grown poet, writing in his sixties and nearer his own night than his morning,
goes back to his earliest self not for nostalgia but for instruction. That is the
poem's quiet reversal: the small, lower-case, five-year-old "i" turns out to be
the wiser of the two.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) The question is asked by the grown poet, E. E. Cummings, and he
addresses his own self as a small child — the "little i" he once was. The poem is
a conversation between two selves of the same person.
(b) Because of **enjambment**. The sentence runs on to "window" in the next line,
so "high" is left hanging at the line's edge with nothing after it. The word is
physically raised above the noun it belongs to, and the reader has to climb to the
window just as the small child had to.
(c) It suggests that the self is not simple. The adult can see the child clearly,
yet has to ask who he is, as though looking at a stranger; and at the same time
the poem is one sentence in one voice, with the same small "i" used throughout. We
are both continuous with the children we were and separated from them, and the
poem holds both truths without resolving them.

**2.** (a) He is looking through a high window at the gold of a November sunset —
the last light of a late-autumn day.
(b) The sunset is a symbol for the end of a life, and November, the last month
before winter, doubles the idea of things closing. The child's feeling — that if
the ending must come, it may come beautifully — is therefore a quiet acceptance of
death, arrived at innocently by someone far too young to know what he has said.

acceptance becomes the answer he is looking for.

overhear the child's private thought instead of being lectured, and the poem's
largest idea therefore arrives in its smallest, softest form. The bracket that
closes the poem also takes the place of a full stop, so the moment is never quite
shut.

chapters.name: The Gift in Wartime - Tran Mong Tu
topics: Movement 2 — what he gives in return
Movement 3 — the last exchange and the bitter peace
chapters.summary:
The poem is a **dramatic monologue** in free verse, spoken by a young widow
standing at the grave of the soldier she loved. It is arranged as a series of
short stanzas built on one repeated pattern: *I offer you this* — *you give me
that*. The poem therefore reads like a list of accounts being settled, and it
moves in three stages.

### Movement 1 — what she offers

She begins with the gifts of the living. She brings roses and lays them on the
newly dug grave, and she offers the wedding ring that bound her to him. These
are the ordinary objects of love and marriage, and she is giving them to someone
who can no longer receive anything. To them she adds herself: her youth, her
beauty, her love, and all the years of her life that she will now spend alone.
The tone in this movement is tender and formal, like a ritual being performed
properly.

### Movement 2 — what he gives in return

The pattern then turns over, and the same courteous verb is used for gifts of a
very different kind. What the soldier gives her is what war gives: the smell of
blood from his uniform, his body brought back from the field, the medals and
official honours that are handed to the families of the dead, and the loneliness
she must now carry. Every "gift" in this list is an injury dressed in polite
language. The speaker never raises her voice — she simply goes on using the word
"gift", and lets the reader hear how wrong it sounds.

### Movement 3 — the last exchange and the bitter peace

In the closing movement the exchange is completed and the speaker reaches her
hardest thought. The dead man is at rest; he has finished with the war, and the
earth holds him quietly. She is the one still alive, and being alive is now the
harder condition: she must go on counting the days, wearing her grief, and
living out a marriage that has nothing left in it but memory. The poem ends
without comfort and without anger. The last gift the war has given her is the
rest of her life.

## Topics to cover

- About the poet
- Summary
- Themes
- Form, structure and rhyme
- Poetic devices

- Movement 1 — what she offers
- Movement 2 — what he gives in return
- Movement 3 — the last exchange and the bitter peace

A woman stands at a soldier's grave and does what people do at graves: she brings
gifts. Then she sets out, item by item, what she has given him and what he has
given her in return. The word "gift" is used for both lists, and the whole force
of the poem lies in that one word being made to cover roses on one side and blood
on the other.

chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** The speaker is a young Vietnamese widow standing at the grave of the
soldier she loved. She addresses him directly as "you", although he is dead and
cannot answer. The poem is therefore a one-sided conversation, which is part of
its sadness.

**2.** She offers roses, which she lays on his newly dug grave, and her wedding
ring. Beyond these objects she offers herself — her youth, her beauty, her love,
and all the years of the life she must now live without him.

**3.** She receives the things war hands out: the smell of blood from his
uniform, his dead body returned from the field, the medals and official honours
given to the families of the dead, and a lifetime of loneliness and mourning.

**4.** Because a "gift" is something freely given that the receiver wants, and
nothing in the second list is wanted by anybody. Calling blood, a corpse and a
medal "gifts" uses the language of love and celebration for the products of
killing, and the mismatch is the poem's protest against war.

**5.** The roses stand for love, beauty and mourning, and — because cut flowers
die quickly — for how briefly the couple's happiness lasted. The wedding ring is a
circle, a symbol of a bond meant to have no end, and it is now being handed over
to a grave.

**6.** The tone is quiet, formal and controlled — tender at first, then bitterly
ironic, and finally flat and resigned. The speaker never shouts and never accuses
anyone by name. That restraint is deliberate: an angry poem could be argued with,
while this calm listing of facts cannot.

**7.** There is **no rhyme scheme**: the poem is free verse. Two reasons should be
given. First, free verse suits a speaking, grieving voice better than a fixed
pattern would. Second, the poem is a **translation** from Vietnamese, and the
sound-patterns of the original cannot cross into English; what survives is the
structure and the imagery.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** Irony means a gap between what is said and what is actually the case, and
this poem is built on one enormous example of it. The word "gift" belongs to
weddings, birthdays and festivals; it implies choice, affection and pleasure. Tran
Mong Tu takes that word and makes it carry the entire traffic of a war. On one
side of the exchange it behaves normally: roses for a grave, a wedding ring, a
young woman's love. On the other side the same word is attached to the smell of
blood on a uniform, a body brought home from the field, and a medal handed to a
widow in place of her husband. Nothing in that second list was chosen, wanted or
given out of love, yet the speaker keeps her courteous vocabulary throughout. The
effect is far stronger than protest would be. If she called the war murderous, a
reader could agree or disagree; because she calls its products "gifts", the reader
has to do the arithmetic and arrive at the anger themselves. A second irony closes
the poem: the medals, which the state offers as honour and compensation, are shown
to be worth nothing beside the life that bought them. The poem never says so
directly. It simply places them in the same list as the blood.

**2.** The poem quietly reverses the usual view that the dead soldier is war's
chief victim. He has suffered and died, but his suffering is finished; the earth
holds him and he is at rest. The woman at the graveside is the one with a future,
and the poem shows exactly what that future contains. She has already given away
everything that made her happy — her youth, her beauty, her wedding ring, her
love — and received in exchange the smell of blood, a corpse, a decoration and an
unending routine of mourning. Her marriage continues, but on one side only: she
goes on bringing presents to a man who cannot receive them. The final movement
makes the reversal explicit by weighing her survival against his rest and finding
survival heavier. This is why the poem is spoken by a woman and set at a grave
rather than on a battlefield. Battlefield poems count the dead; this poem counts
what the dead leave behind, and finds that the real casualty list — widows,
mothers, children — is far longer than the official one and is never published.
The soldier's war ended on a particular day. Hers has no end in the poem at all.

**3.** The poem is written in free verse: short lines, no metre, no rhyme, and a
translation's plain English vocabulary. Into that loose form the poet puts a very
tight structure. Each stanza sets one of her gifts against one of his, using the
same repeated grammatical shape — *I offer you …*, *you give me …*. This
**anaphora** does three things. It gives the poem the steady rhythm of a ritual,
which suits a grave-side. It forces the reader to compare the two columns, since
they arrive in identical packaging. And it builds an expectation that the final
movement can break, when the last thing left to weigh turns out to be her own
survival. The tone is the poem's other great instrument. It begins tender and
formal, as a widow performing the proper ceremonies; it passes through irony as
the second list accumulates; and it settles into a flat, exhausted acceptance at
the end. At no point does it rise. The restraint is a deliberate strategy:
understatement leaves the reader to supply the outrage, and an outrage the reader
has produced is far harder to dismiss than one delivered from the page.
Structure, then, imposes a neat order on the poem, and that neatness is itself
meaningful — it is the desperate tidiness of someone holding herself together at a
funeral.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) The speaker is a young Vietnamese widow, and she is standing at the
freshly made grave of the soldier she loved, during the Vietnam War.
(b) The **roses** stand for love, beauty and mourning; because cut flowers wither
within days, they also stand for how short her happiness was. The **wedding ring**
is a circle with no beginning and no end, the symbol of a bond that was supposed to
last a lifetime — and she is now returning it to the earth.
(c) Because giving is all she has left of the marriage. Ceremony is how human
beings hold on to the dead: bringing flowers, keeping anniversaries, speaking
aloud at a grave. Her gifts are an act of continuing love, and at the same time the
poem shows their futility, since nothing she offers can be received. The
one-sidedness of the exchange is exactly what makes the passage painful.

**2.** (a) The giver is her dead husband — but behind him, and really, the giver
is the **war** itself, which the poem treats as a person arriving with presents.
(b) The governing figure is **irony**. A gift is something freely given that the
receiver wants; nothing here is wanted by anyone. By keeping the polite word
"gift" for blood, a corpse and a medal, the speaker makes the reader feel the
distance between the language and the reality. The passage also uses
**juxtaposition** — the wedding ring of the previous stanza set beside the smell of
blood — and strong **sensory imagery**, since smell is the most physical and
inescapable of the senses.
(c) It reduces them to nothing. Medals are placed in the same list as the corpse
and the blood, as though they were one more thing the war handed over, and no line
is spent praising them. The implication is that official honour is a cheap
substitute offered by the state in place of a life, and that it does not balance
the account by even a little.

**3.** The poem is written in free verse: short lines, no metre, no rhyme, and a
translation's plain English vocabulary. Into that loose form the poet puts a very
tight structure. Each stanza sets one of her gifts against one of his, using the
same repeated grammatical shape — *I offer you …*, *you give me …*. This
**anaphora** does three things. It gives the poem the steady rhythm of a ritual,
which suits a grave-side. It forces the reader to compare the two columns, since
they arrive in identical packaging. And it builds an expectation that the final
movement can break, when the last thing left to weigh turns out to be her own
survival. The tone is the poem's other great instrument. It begins tender and
formal, as a widow performing the proper ceremonies; it passes through irony as
the second list accumulates; and it settles into a flat, exhausted acceptance at
the end. At no point does it rise. The restraint is a deliberate strategy:
understatement leaves the reader to supply the outrage, and an outrage the reader
has produced is far harder to dismiss than one delivered from the page.
Structure, then, imposes a neat order on the poem, and that neatness is itself
meaningful — it is the desperate tidiness of someone holding herself together at a
funeral.

self_checks.question: Model answers — reference to the context
self_checks.answer:
**1.** (a) The speaker is a young Vietnamese widow, and she is standing at the
freshly made grave of the soldier she loved, during the Vietnam War.
(b) The **roses** stand for love, beauty and mourning; because cut flowers wither
within days, they also stand for how short her happiness was. The **wedding ring**
is a circle with no beginning and no end, the symbol of a bond that was supposed to
last a lifetime — and she is now returning it to the earth.
(c) Because giving is all she has left of the marriage. Ceremony is how human
beings hold on to the dead: bringing flowers, keeping anniversaries, speaking
aloud at a grave. Her gifts are an act of continuing love, and at the same time the
poem shows their futility, since nothing she offers can be received. The
one-sidedness of the exchange is exactly what makes the passage painful.

**2.** (a) The giver is her dead husband — but behind him, and really, the giver
is the **war** itself, which the poem treats as a person arriving with presents.
(b) The governing figure is **irony**. A gift is something freely given that the
receiver wants; nothing here is wanted by anyone. By keeping the polite word
"gift" for blood, a corpse and a medal, the speaker makes the reader feel the
distance between the language and the reality. The passage also uses
**juxtaposition** — the wedding ring of the previous stanza set beside the smell of
blood — and strong **sensory imagery**, since smell is the most physical and
inescapable of the senses.
(c) It reduces them to nothing. Medals are placed in the same list as the corpse
and the blood, as though they were one more thing the war handed over, and no line
is spent praising them. The implication is that official honour is a cheap
substitute offered by the state in place of a life, and that it does not balance
the account by even a little.

chapters.name: Sharing Tradition - Frank LaPena
chapters.summary:
### What makes a person "traditional"

LaPena begins with a question rather than a definition. Who counts as a
traditional person? Not, he argues, whoever knows the most facts about the old
ways, and certainly not whoever owns the most old objects. A traditional person is
someone who **lives** the tradition: who takes part in the ceremonies, keeps the
obligations, behaves in the way the community expects, and accepts the discipline
that goes with all this. Tradition, in his account, is something you do, not
something you have.

### How tradition is learnt

It is learnt from the elders, and it is learnt slowly. The old people do not hand
over information in lessons; they teach by example, by letting a young person be
present, by giving small tasks, and by telling stories whose meaning may not be
clear for years. Much of what matters is passed on **orally** — in songs, names,
prayers and accounts of what happened long ago — and much of it is learnt through
the body, by dancing and by doing, rather than through the head.

This also means that knowledge is **earned**. A learner has to show patience,
respect and steadiness before more is given. Some knowledge is sacred and is not
given to everybody at all; certain songs and names belong to particular families
or to particular ceremonial roles. To LaPena, this is not secrecy for its own
sake. It is the recognition that some things are powerful and can be damaged by
careless handling.

### Ceremony, art and the world

Ceremony is the heart of the essay. Dances and songs are not entertainment and
not performances put on for an audience; they are work that has to be done, and
their purpose is to keep the relationship between the people and the natural
world in good order — to renew the world, to give thanks, to mark the seasons and
the passages of a life.

This changes what "art" means. The traditional artist does not make objects to be
admired in a gallery or sold to collectors. Regalia, baskets, feathers, paint and
song are made for use, and they carry obligations: how they are made, who may make
them, what may be done with them afterwards. An object taken out of that setting,
put behind glass and labelled, is no longer the thing it was. It has become
information about a tradition rather than a part of one.

LaPena is direct about what follows. When outsiders — anthropologists, collectors,
tourists, businesses — take songs, designs and ceremonies out of their community
and use them for study, decoration or profit, they are not preserving a culture.
They are removing the living part and keeping the shell.

### Tradition is not frozen

A common misunderstanding, he says, is that a tradition must stay exactly as it
was or it is not "authentic". Living traditions have always changed: new materials
are used, new songs are received, practices are adapted to the circumstances of
each generation. What has to stay constant is not the outward detail but the
relationship — the respect, the purpose and the connection to the ancestors and to
the land. A tradition that cannot change is already a museum piece.

### Sharing as responsibility

The essay closes on the idea in its title. Because tradition exists only in its
practice, each generation holds it in trust rather than owning it. Receiving
knowledge from the elders therefore creates a debt, and the debt is paid forward,
not back: the receiver is obliged to live the tradition properly and to give it to
those who come after. Sharing, in LaPena's sense, is not the same as making
everything public. It means teaching the right things to the right people at the
right time, which is the only way a tradition can survive.

Frank LaPena was a Native American artist, dancer and teacher, and this essay is
his attempt to explain something outsiders almost always get wrong: what a
tradition actually is. It is not a set of old objects or a list of customs
recorded in a book. It is a living relationship between people, their ancestors
and the land, and it survives only for as long as somebody keeps doing it — and
passing it on.
