chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** A traditional person is one who **lives** the tradition: who takes part in
the ceremonies, keeps the obligations that go with them, accepts the discipline of
the community and behaves accordingly. Knowing many facts about the old ways, or
owning old objects, does not make anyone traditional.

**2.** It is passed on by the elders, orally and by example — through songs,
names, prayers, stories and, above all, through taking part in ceremonies and
dances. The learner is present, watches, is given small tasks, and slowly grows
into the knowledge instead of being taught it in lessons.

**3.** Because some knowledge is sacred and powerful, and careless handling can
damage both the knowledge and the person. A learner has to show patience, respect
and steadiness before more is given; certain songs, names and roles belong to
particular families and are not given out generally. Earning it is part of
learning to treat it properly.

**4.** The traditional artist makes things for **use** — regalia, baskets, songs,
paint for a ceremony — under obligations about how they are made and what may be
done with them. A gallery artist makes objects to be looked at, judged and sold.
The first kind of art has a job to do in the life of a community; the second is
complete when it is admired.

**5.** Because its meaning lay in its use. Once it is taken out of the ceremony,
put behind glass and labelled, it is cut off from the people, the purpose and the
relationships that made it what it was. It looks the same, but it has become
information about a tradition rather than a living part of one.

**6.** No. He says that living traditions have always changed — new materials, new
songs, new circumstances in every generation — and that a tradition which cannot
change has already become a museum piece. What must stay constant is not the
outward detail but the relationship behind it: the respect, the purpose and the
connection to ancestors and land.

**7.** It means passing the tradition on: teaching the right things to the right
people at the right time, so that the practice continues into the next
generation. It does **not** mean making everything public. Because each generation
holds the tradition in trust rather than owning it, sharing is a duty owed to the
ancestors who gave it and to the children who have not yet received it.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** LaPena's thesis is that tradition is a **living practice** rather than a
body of information or a collection of objects, that it belongs to a community
rather than to an individual, and that anyone who receives it takes on the
responsibility of living it properly and handing it on. He builds this in five
moves. First he redefines the key term: instead of asking what tradition is, he
asks who counts as a traditional person, and answers that it is the one who takes
part, keeps the obligations and accepts the discipline — so tradition shifts from
*things known* to *things done*. Second, he shows how the knowledge travels: from
elders, orally, slowly, through participation and the body, so that it cannot be
detached from the people who carry it. Third, he applies the same test to art:
regalia, songs and baskets are made for use in ceremony, which gives him his
strongest evidence, because an object removed from its use looks identical and is
not the same thing. Fourth, he disposes of the obvious objection — that a real
tradition must be unchanging — by pointing out that living things change, and that
what must be constant is the relationship, not the detail. Finally he draws the
conclusion the reader has already reached: since a tradition exists only while it
is practised, keeping it alive is a duty owed backwards to the ancestors and
forwards to the children.

**2.** In LaPena's account the three are not separable. Ceremony is the centre of
community life: dances and songs are not entertainment but work that has to be
done, to give thanks, to mark the seasons and the stages of a life, and to keep
the relationship between the people and the natural world in good repair. Art
exists to serve that work. Regalia, feathers, baskets, paint and song are made for
use, and they come with obligations — who may make them, how, and what may be done
with them afterwards. There is no separate category of "the artist" standing apart
from the community and expressing a private vision; the maker is a member with a
job. This is exactly why LaPena objects to collection and display. A ceremonial
object in a museum has been cut away from the people who used it, the occasion it
was used for, and the obligations that surrounded it; what remains behind the
glass is the shape of the thing without the thing itself. Worse, the removal is
presented as preservation, when in fact it takes the living part away and keeps
the shell. The same objection covers songs recorded by researchers, designs
borrowed by businesses, and ceremonies watched as tourist spectacle. His position
is consistent rather than merely protective: if meaning lies in practice, then
anything taken out of practice has lost its meaning, however carefully it is
stored.

**3.** LaPena writes a reflective personal essay in the first person, and his
authority is that of a participant rather than a researcher — he has danced, not
merely studied. That position governs everything else. The tone is calm, patient
and explanatory; he sets out to make an outsider understand rather than to accuse,
and the restraint is persuasive, because a reader who would argue with a protest
will often accept an explanation. His central technique is **redefinition**: he
takes familiar words — tradition, art, authentic, sharing — and quietly replaces
the reader's everyday meaning with his own, so that the argument is largely won at
the level of vocabulary before any conclusion is stated. He keeps the essay
readable by attaching ideas to concrete things: dances, songs, regalia, baskets,
the behaviour of the old people. The pronouns "we" and "our" mark him as a member
of the community, turning parts of the essay into testimony. Key words —
*tradition*, *respect*, *responsibility*, *share* — are repeated until they carry
the weight of the argument, much as repetition in a ceremony gathers force.
Finally, his criticism of collectors, researchers and commercial users is made by
**understatement**: he describes what a tradition is and lets the reader work out
what removing it must do. The essay ends on the idea its title began with,
closing a circle — which is also the shape of the tradition it describes.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) It implies that tradition is a **living practice** — something done
rather than something known or possessed. A tradition exists in ceremonies
performed, songs sung, obligations kept and discipline accepted, not in facts
stored or objects owned.
(b) It matters because every later claim in the essay rests on it. If tradition
lives only in practice, then knowledge cannot be separated from the people who
carry it, ceremonial art cannot be separated from its use, and a recorded or
collected version of a tradition is necessarily a dead one. The definition is the
foundation of the whole argument.
(c) It makes each person a **custodian** rather than an owner. Because the
tradition exists only while it is practised, the individual who has received it
must go on living it properly and must pass it on to those who come after. The
responsibility runs in two directions: to the ancestors who handed it down and to
the children who have not yet received it.

**2.** (a) Because the meaning of such an object lay in its **use**. It was made
for a ceremony, under obligations about who could make it and what could be done
with it. Behind glass it is separated from the people, the occasion and the
relationships that gave it meaning, so what survives is the shape of the thing
without the thing itself.
(b) The implied criticism is of anthropologists, collectors, tourists and
businesses who take songs, designs and objects out of living communities for
study, decoration or profit, and then describe what they are doing as preserving a
culture. LaPena's logic makes this impossible: they remove the living part and
keep the shell. He makes the charge by understatement rather than accusation,
which gives it more force.
(c) By continuing to practise it. Traditions are kept alive by elders teaching,
young people taking part, ceremonies being performed, and knowledge being earned
and then passed on at the right time to the right people. Traditions may change
their outward details in every generation, and should; what must be preserved is
the relationship of respect between the community, its ancestors and the natural
world.

chapters.name: How to Live Before You Die - Steve Jobs
topics: The first story: connecting the dots
The second story: love and loss
chapters.summary:
- "How to Live Before You Die" is Steve Jobs's commencement address to Stanford
  University, delivered on 12 June 2005 by a speaker who never graduated from
  college himself.
- It has a **tripartite structure**: three autobiographical stories, announced in
  advance, each ending in a rule for living.
- **Story one, connecting the dots:** adopted at birth, Jobs drops out of Reed
  College, sits in on a calligraphy class with no practical use, and ten years
  later builds that typography into the Macintosh. Lesson — trust that the dots
  will connect, because you can only join them looking backward.
- **Story two, love and loss:** he builds Apple from a garage, is publicly fired
  at thirty, and finds that his love of the work has survived. NeXT, Pixar and a
  return to Apple follow. Lesson — find what you love, and don't settle.
- **Story three, death:** a wrong diagnosis of incurable pancreatic cancer, one
  day lived under sentence, then a curable tumour and successful surgery. Lesson
  — remembering that you will die clears away pride, fear and other people's
  expectations.
- The three lessons form one argument: your time is limited, so do work you love
  and live a life that is genuinely your own.
- Its power comes from **personal narrative** rather than advice, from plain
  concrete diction, from antithesis and paradox, and from direct address at the
  points where the lesson lands.
- It closes on four borrowed words from the back cover of the last *Whole Earth
  Catalog*: **"Stay Hungry. Stay Foolish."**

This is not an essay written at a desk. It is a speech, delivered out loud to
several thousand people on a summer afternoon, by a man who had been told a year
earlier that he had a few months to live. Steve Jobs told the graduating class of
Stanford University three stories from his own life — no statistics, no advice
list, no famous quotations except one on a book cover — and left them with four
words. The speech has since been watched tens of millions of times, and the
reason it works is worth studying as carefully as the message itself.

## Model answers — short questions

**1.** His biological mother was a young unmarried graduate student who decided to
give him up for adoption, insisting that he be adopted by college graduates. The
lawyer and his wife who were to take him changed their minds at the last moment
because they wanted a girl, so a couple on the waiting list were telephoned in the
middle of the night and asked whether they wanted "an unexpected baby boy." They
said, "Of course." Because the adoptive mother had never finished college and the
father had never finished high school, his biological mother refused to sign the
papers, and relented only when they promised the boy would one day go to college.

**2.** He means that the usefulness of an experience is almost never visible at
the time, and becomes clear only years afterwards when it turns out to have fed
into something else. His own calligraphy class had no apparent purpose when he
took it and became essential a decade later. Since you cannot know in advance
which experiences will matter, you cannot plan a life logically forward; you can
only follow curiosity and trust that the pieces will fit.

**3.** He was fired from Apple, the company he had founded. Apple had grown in ten
years into a two-billion-dollar company with over four thousand employees and had
just released the Macintosh. The executive Jobs had recruited to run the company
with him came to disagree with him about the future, they had a falling out, and
the Board of Directors sided with the other man. Jobs was dismissed publicly, and
found that the focus of his entire adult life had gone.

**4.** "Don't settle" means: do not accept second-best work, or a job you merely
tolerate, simply because looking for the right one is difficult or slow. Jobs
compares the search to a search for love — you will recognise the right thing when
you find it — and insists that until you find it you should keep looking rather
than making do. Settling, in his view, guarantees that you will never do great
work, since great work only comes from loving what you do.

**5.** He is admitting that his advice cannot be proved. Since you cannot see
ahead, following curiosity instead of a plan requires an act of faith in
*something* — instinct, fate, the divine order, karma. Jobs deliberately offers a
list rather than a single name, so that listeners of any religion or none can
accept the point. What matters to him is not which belief you hold but that you
have enough confidence in your own path to act on it before its value is proved.

**6.** He means that the shortness of life makes borrowed living wasteful. Most
people spend their days meeting other people's expectations, following inherited
opinions, and fearing disapproval — but the time so spent is subtracted from the
only life they will ever have. Since the span is fixed and unknown, Jobs argues,
the only rational course is to follow your own heart and intuition rather than
somebody else's plan for you.

**7.** They were the farewell words on the back cover of the final issue of *The
Whole Earth Catalog*, and Jobs adopts them as his own wish for the graduates. To
"stay hungry" is to remain unsatisfied — to keep wanting to learn and to make,
instead of resting on what you have already achieved. To "stay foolish" is to keep
the courage to attempt what sensible, experienced people would dismiss, and to
risk looking ridiculous. Together they describe a life of continuing curiosity and
continuing nerve.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** The third story moves from an idea to an experience. As a boy of seventeen
Jobs read that a person who lives each day as though it were his last will one day
be right, and for thirty-three years he used it as a daily test in the mirror. He
then describes the morning a scan showed a tumour on his pancreas, the doctors'
verdict of three to six months, and the instruction to "get his affairs in order"
— which he translates as saying goodbye to his children. The reversal comes that
evening, when a biopsy shows a rare curable form of the disease.

Out of this he makes his claim. Death is the destination everyone shares, and it
is a good thing rather than a cruelty, because it is "Life's change agent": it
clears out the old to make room for the new. The graduates in front of him are the
new, and in time they will be cleared away in their turn. The practical value of
remembering this is that "all external expectations, all pride, all fear of
embarrassment or failure" fall away in the face of death, leaving only what is
genuinely important, and that a person who expects to die has nothing left to
lose — "You are already naked."

The claim is defensible if it is read as being about *usefulness* rather than
comfort. Death gives a life its shape and its urgency; without a limit there would
be no reason to choose one thing over another, and no renewal between generations.
It is also true that fear of embarrassment loses most of its force when measured
against mortality. Against this, one may object that Jobs speaks as a man who
survived: for those who lose a parent or a child, death is not a well-designed
mechanism but a bereavement, and telling the grieving that death is an invention of
life would be an insult. A fair conclusion is that the line is true as a rule for
living and false as a consolation — it is excellent advice about how to spend a
life, and no help at all in losing one.

**2.** Jobs' claim is that work will fill a large part of anyone's life, that the
only way to be truly satisfied is to do what you believe is great work, and that
the only way to do great work is to love what you do. If you have not found it, he
says, keep looking and don't settle; you will know it when you find it, as with
any matter of the heart.

The speech supports the claim with evidence rather than assertion. The calligraphy
class was chosen purely because Jobs found it fascinating, with no prospect of
use, and it produced the one feature that distinguished the Macintosh. More
importantly, love of the work is what survived his sacking: "I had been rejected,
but I was still in love." Because that remained, the five years that followed
became the most creative of his life. The argument is therefore that love of work
is not a pleasant extra but the load-bearing part of a career — the thing that
keeps a person going when reputation, money and position have all been taken away.

There is much to agree with here. Great work demands years of unrewarded effort,
and only genuine interest will sustain attention through the boring middle of any
difficult task; a person who dislikes the work will do the minimum, which is
exactly what excellence is not. One may still qualify the claim in two ways.
First, love often *follows* competence rather than preceding it: many people grow
to love a subject only after becoming good at it, so "keep looking" may sometimes
be worse advice than "stay longer." Second, the freedom to hold out for beloved
work is not evenly distributed — a student supporting a family cannot simply
refuse to settle, and Jobs, speaking at Stanford, addressed the most fortunate
audience in the country. The honest position is that Jobs is right about what
produces great work, but that his advice assumes a freedom of choice not everyone
has; for most people the practical version is to find what can be loved within
the work available.

**3.** Jobs uses the **personal narrative** or autobiographical style: instead of
arguing a thesis, he tells three true stories from his own life and lets each one
end in a rule. The speech is informal, conversational and plainly worded, is
organised in a **tripartite structure** announced in advance, and moves steadily
from private experience to direct second-person instruction.

The technique is effective for several reasons. It establishes the speaker's
right to advise: a man who slept on friends' floors, returned bottles for their
deposits, was publicly sacked at thirty and was told he had months to live is not
lecturing the graduates from above. It disarms resistance, since a young audience
that would reject a sermon will listen to a story. It makes abstractions concrete
— resilience is not defined but shown, in a garage, a board meeting and a hospital
room. It builds trust by admitting weakness: the second sentence of the speech
concedes that he never graduated from college, and the second story admits public
failure and apology. And the pattern itself does work, because after the first
story the audience can predict the shape and so listens for the meaning.

The language reinforces all this. Jobs prefers short sentences and concrete
nouns — Coke bottles, a brick, an endoscope, a country road — and keeps his
biggest ideas in the plainest words: "You are already naked." He uses antithesis
to make a lesson portable ("looking forward… looking backward"), paradox to
startle ("Death is very likely the single best invention of Life"), anaphora to
drive the closing instructions home, and a single four-word motto to carry the
whole speech away with the listener. The result is a speech that persuades by
testimony rather than by argument, and is remembered because it was felt before it
was analysed.

**4.** Jobs' company campaigned under the slogan **"Think different"**, and the
speech is that slogan turned into autobiography. Thinking differently clearly can
produce success: every one of Jobs' achievements began with a refusal of the
ordinary view. Staying at Reed as a drop-in rather than a student, believing that
a calligraphy class belonged inside a computer, and building a company in a garage
were all unconventional choices, and the last two reshaped an entire industry.
Independent thinking finds the openings that conventional thinking has already
searched and abandoned; it is also the only way to do something no one has done
before, and therefore the only way to be first.

The difficulties are serious and the speech does not hide them. Different thinking
looks like foolishness while it is happening — nobody at Reed could have told Jobs
his lettering class was valuable. It attracts opposition: Jobs was outvoted by his
own board and dismissed from his own company. It carries real risk of failure, and
of public failure, which is why he speaks of apologising to David Packard and Bob
Noyce and of wanting to run away. It costs security, since the unconventional
route rarely has a salary attached, and it demands that a person hold a belief for
years without evidence, which is exactly why Jobs says you have to trust "your
gut, destiny, life, karma, whatever."

A **visionary** is someone who sees clearly what does not yet exist but could, and
then works to bring it about. The difference from a fortune teller is the
difference between making and predicting. A fortune teller claims knowledge of a
future that is fixed and outside his control, offers no reasoning that can be
checked, and does nothing to bring the future about; his predictions are unfalsifiable
and cost him nothing. A visionary makes no claim to know the future — Jobs insists
the dots cannot be connected looking forward — but forms a judgement about what
people will need, stakes his time, money and reputation on it, and builds the thing
that makes the prediction true. The Macintosh did not come true; it was made true,
by ten years of work. Vision is therefore accountable and laborious where
fortune-telling is neither.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) The baby boy was Steve Jobs himself, newly born in San Francisco in
1955 to an unmarried graduate student who had decided to give him up for adoption.
(b) It is the adoption agency's telephone call in the middle of the night, asking
whether the couple will take the child. Put plainly, it asks whether they will
accept a baby they had not been expecting and become his parents — a question
about a whole life, asked in six ordinary words. The bluntness of the phrasing,
"do you want him", is what gives the line its force: a human being is being
offered like an unclaimed parcel.
(c) 'They' refers to Paul and Clara Jobs, the working-class couple on the
adoption waiting list who became his parents and who later spent their entire
savings on his college fees.
(d) He begins here for three reasons. First, it answers the question he has just
asked — why he dropped out — because the promise his parents made, that he would
one day go to college, is what sent him to an expensive one in the first place.
Second, it is the earliest possible example of his thesis: his whole life turned
on a stranger's late-night decision that could not have been foreseen, which is
precisely what "you can't connect the dots looking forward" means. Third, it wins
the audience. A speaker who opens by telling several thousand graduates that he
was an unwanted baby has made himself human before he makes any demand on them.

**2.** (a) It was a large American publication created by Stewart Brand in Menlo
Park, California, in the late 1960s — a catalogue of tools, books and ideas for
people who wanted to build and learn things for themselves. Jobs calls it "one of
the bibles of my generation." It was produced with typewriters, scissors and
Polaroid cameras, long before personal computers or desktop publishing existed.
(b) Because its purpose was the same: it gathered in one place, for anyone who
opened it, the information and tools needed to do almost anything — "sort of like
Google in paperback form, 35 years before Google came along." The comparison is a
bridge between two generations. His listeners of 2005 have never seen the
*Catalog*, but they use a search engine every day, so the analogy tells them
instantly what it was and why it mattered.
(c) Partly because the words are better than any he could invent: four syllables a
side, balanced, memorable, and open enough to mean something to every listener.
But the choice also demonstrates his argument. He has spent the speech urging the
graduates to follow their own voice, and he ends by showing what that looks like
in practice — you take what you love from wherever you find it, acknowledge where
it came from, and carry it forward to the next generation. Ending on a farewell
message from a publication that had "run its course" also fits the third story
exactly: the old is cleared away, and what was good in it is passed to the new.
Finally, by repeating the words as his wish for the graduates, he turns a printed
sign-off into a personal blessing.

chapters.name: What I Require from Life - J.B.S. Haldane
topics: A peaceful age and a heroic age
The summing up, and the requirements of death
chapters.summary:
- "What I Require from Life" (1940) is a short first-person essay by the
  geneticist J.B.S. Haldane, first published in the British communist newspaper
  the *Daily Worker*.
- Haldane begins by refusing utopia: he will accept the universe as it is and ask
  only for what is possible.
- He contrasts the **peaceful age** into which he was born with the **heroic
  age** that began in 1914, and resolves to make the best of the time he
  actually lives in.
- Assuming food, water, clothes and shelter, he requires four things: **work with
  a decent wage, freedom (especially of speech), health, and friendship between
  equals.** For himself alone he adds **adventure** — which he distinguishes
  sharply from a mere thrill.
- He separates **desire** from **demand**: a car, books, a bath, a garden are
  pleasant, and he is content without them.
- Because most people lack what he regards as essential, he requires **socialism**
  for his society: work for all, workers' control of industry, health for all,
  and an end to class and sex subjection. "Freedom should begin in the workshop."
- He deliberately omits **peace and security** from his own list as unobtainable
  while fascism lives, admits that his appetite for adventure is a symptom of his
  age, and demands **security rather than adventure for others**.
- His summing-up: for himself, **food, warmth, work, liberty, health and
  friendship**; for his society, **socialism**. He closes by naming Socrates'
  death — for his convictions, with his work done, and laughing — as the most
  enviable he knows.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- About the author
- The context of the essay
- The essay, step by step
- The argument
- Themes
- Style and technique
- Glossary
- The opening premise
- A peaceful age and a heroic age
- The four requirements for himself
- Adventure: the personal extra
- Desires that are not demands
- What he requires for others
- What is deliberately missing
- The summing up, and the requirements of death

Most people, asked what they want from life, produce a wish-list. Haldane does
something harder and much more interesting: he draws a line between what he
*requires*, what he merely *desires*, and what it would be silly to ask for at
all — and then, having settled his own account, he turns round and asks the same
question on behalf of everybody else. The result is a very short essay that
manages to be a personal confession, a definition of happiness and a political
argument at the same time.

Close the book and explain the key ideas in your own words.

Attempt a worked example before revealing its solution.

Complete the chapter practice, correct mistakes, then mark the chapter revised.

## Model answers — short questions

**1.** A **peaceful age** is one in which ordinary safety can be assumed, so that
a person may reasonably plan a quiet life; Haldane was born into such an age in
1892 and expected to live in it. A **heroic age** is one of wars, revolutions and
upheavals, in which nothing can be assumed and everyone must improvise. Haldane
says that since 1914 he has been living in a heroic age and sees no prospect of
surviving into another peaceful one, so he must make the best of the time he has.

**2.** Because he already has far more freedom than most people and can see
exactly where it stops. He would like to say and write in public what he believes
about Lord Blank's newspapers, Mr Dash's pills and Sir John Asterisk's beer — all
of which, he says, are poisonous — and the law of libel prevents him. He wants
freedom of speech not to indulge himself but to expose things that harm the
public, and the invented names show him reporting the problem while still trapped
by it.

**3.** Work, together with a decent wage for it; freedom, especially freedom of
speech; health; and friendship — specifically the friendship of equals who can
criticize one another. Haldane treats food, water, clothes and shelter as already
assumed, and lists adventure separately as a requirement of his own rather than a
general human need.

**4.** A **requirement** or demand is something without which a human life is
genuinely damaged: work, freedom, health, friendship. A **desire** is something
that would be pleasant but whose absence can be borne. Haldane illustrates the
difference from his own life — he would like a room of his own with books, a
motor-car, a daily bath, a garden or a river nearby, but he has not got them,
"and I bear up quite happily." The distinction matters because it stops the essay
becoming a wish-list and keeps his political demands modest and defensible.

**5.** Because he does not trust his own taste for adventure. He admits that peace
and security are rightful aims and that his own desire for violent adventure is
"probably merely an adaptation to the age in which I live" — a habit forced on
him by living through wars, not a virtue. Calling himself "a child of my age, and
all the worse for being one," he refuses to impose his own restlessness on
everybody else, and asks for others the settled safety he has never had.

**6.** Because he defines friendship as the society of equals who can criticize
one another freely. Where one person must obey another's orders without criticism
before or after, criticism in both directions becomes impossible, and so does
honesty; what remains is a relation of rank, not friendship. For the same reason
he finds friendship with people much richer or poorer than himself very difficult.
This is why his private definition of friendship leads directly to his public
demand for equality.

**7.** For three reasons. First, they supply ready definitions he does not need to
argue for: Aristotle gives him happiness as "unimpeded activity" and Socrates
gives him a model of a good death. Second, they give the essay an authority older
and wider than any political party, so that his demands look like ordinary human
sense rather than communist doctrine. Third, they show that his question is not a
modern or political one at all but the oldest question in philosophy — what does
a human being need in order to live well?

**8.** On three grounds. Socrates died for his convictions when he could easily
have saved himself by betraying them; he died at about seventy, still in full
possession of his faculties and having completed all the work he could reasonably
hope to do; and he died laughing, since his last words were a joke. Haldane does
not expect all three conditions, which are very rarely met together, but says that
if he can achieve even two he will have done well — and that his friends may
lament him provided they do not pity him.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** Haldane calls himself a socialist three separate times in the essay, and
each time he gives a different reason, so that the three together amount to a
complete case.

He is a socialist, first, **because of unemployment**. He wants to see every
healthy man and woman at work, and he observes that unemployment, at least in
times of depression, is an essential feature of capitalism rather than an accident
of it. Since work is the first of his four human requirements, a system that
regularly denies it to millions fails at the first hurdle.

He is a socialist, second, **because he wants industry controlled by the
workers**. He controls his own conditions of work to a considerable extent and
knows how much that is worth; most work is dull, unhealthy and exhausting, and he
believes this need not be so and will not be so after a few generations of
democracy in industry. His evidence that work can be pleasant is disarmingly
simple: when people have time and money to spare, two of their favourite
occupations are hunting and gardening — the work of our paleolithic and neolithic
ancestors. Hence his slogan, "Freedom should begin in the workshop."

He is a socialist, third, **because he wants others to enjoy the advantages he
enjoys himself**. He is exceptionally lucky, he says, but cannot be completely
happy while his fellows are unhappy. So he also wants health for all, on the
scale that human biology demands and modern technique can supply, and the end of
class subjection and sex subjection — because equality is the condition of
fraternity, and because the main barriers between classes and the main reasons for
the subjection of women are economic.

The method of the argument is as important as its content. Haldane does not begin
from Marxist theory and deduce a way of living; he begins with the ordinary things
that make his own life good, notices that other people are denied them, and asks
what is preventing them. He is also candid about the limits of what he expects:
socialism will not confer these advantages in an instant, and he will die happy if
he merely lives to see the workers in power through most of Europe. A critical
reader will note that he assumes, rather than demonstrates, that the causes of
inequality are wholly economic, and that his confidence rests on what he saw in
Russia and Spain — evidence a modern reader will weigh far more sceptically than
he did in 1940.

**2.** **Socialism** is a political and economic system in which the means of
production — land, factories, machines, mines, transport — are owned and
controlled in common, either by the workers themselves or by the state on behalf
of the whole community, and in which what is produced is distributed according to
need or contribution rather than according to ownership. **Capitalism** is a
system in which those same means of production are privately owned, in which
goods and labour are bought and sold in a market, and in which the owner of
capital keeps the profit generated by the work of employees.

The differences may be set out under four heads. **Ownership:** private under
capitalism, common or public under socialism. **Purpose of production:** profit
for the owner under capitalism, satisfaction of need under socialism.
**Distribution:** by market outcome and inheritance under capitalism, which
produces wide inequalities of wealth, against planned or need-based distribution
under socialism, which aims at rough equality. **Control of work:** decisions are
taken by owners and managers under capitalism, whereas socialism in Haldane's
version means that workers control their own conditions of work.

Each system is defended by serious arguments. Capitalism's supporters point to
competition as a spur to innovation, to the efficiency of prices in matching
supply to demand, and to the freedom of individuals to start enterprises and keep
what they earn. Socialism's supporters point to unemployment, insecurity, unsafe
and degrading work, and the concentration of wealth in few hands. Haldane's own
complaint is a good illustration of the socialist case: he discovers new
biological facts that nobody applies, because although the community would
benefit, no individual would make a profit from the application. Most modern
states are in fact mixed economies — private enterprise alongside public
education, public health services and regulation — and Nepal's own constitution
describes the country as oriented towards socialism while permitting private
business.

**3.** **Subject.** The essay's subject is stated in its title: what a human being
genuinely requires in order to live well. Haldane treats it in two halves — what
he requires for himself, and what he requires for the society he lives in — and
adds a short postscript on what he would require of his own death.

**Purpose.** The purpose is double, and the doubleness is the point. On the
surface the essay is a piece of self-examination; underneath it is a work of
political persuasion written for the readers of a communist newspaper in 1940. By
making the political conclusion grow out of the personal confession, Haldane
persuades without appearing to argue.

**Point of view.** It is written wholly in the **first person**. The pronoun "I"
begins most paragraphs, and the authority of the essay rests on the reader's
belief that the speaker is honest. Haldane earns that belief by admitting
uncomfortable things: that he is exceptionally lucky, that his love of adventure
is a defect of his age, that socialism will not deliver quickly.

**Mode of writing.** It is **expository and argumentative**, organised as a
series of lists rather than as a narrative — premise, four requirements, one
personal extra, a class of non-demands, the public transposition of the same
items, two deliberate omissions, a summing-up, a postscript. This list structure
is what makes so short an essay so easy to remember.

**Language.** Plain, brief, concrete and unadorned. A professional scientist
writing for working readers, Haldane uses almost no technical vocabulary and
almost no ornament. His sentences are short and often end in a small shock
("Freedom should begin in the workshop"; "And he died laughing"). He is fond of
understatement, of homely evidence such as hunting and gardening, and of a dry
humour — the invented names Lord Blank, Mr Dash and Sir John Asterisk let him
attack real firms while obeying the law of libel, and demonstrate the censorship
he is complaining about in the very act of complaining. The tone throughout is
conversational, self-critical and completely without self-pity.

**4.** *(A personal answer; what follows is a model.)* Taking Haldane's own
method, I would separate what I require from what I merely desire.

I require, first, **education and work that uses it**. Like Haldane I do not want
easy work; I want work that is hard but interesting and whose results I can see.
For a Nepali student that means finishing my studies and then finding employment
in which my training is actually used — which is why the migration of so many
young people to the Gulf and Malaysia for work far below their training seems to
me the central problem of my generation.

I require **health, and the means of keeping it**: clean drinking water, food
that is enough and safe, and a health post within reach that is staffed and
stocked. Haldane says he wants only to be fit for work and enjoyment in the
intervals between illnesses, and that modest standard seems to me the right one.

I require **freedom** — to say what I think, to read what I choose, to worship or
not, and to disagree with those in authority without fear. And I require
**friendship of the kind Haldane describes**: friends who will criticize me and
whom I can criticize, which means friends who treat me as an equal.

Beyond these I require two things Haldane was too honest to ask for: **peace and
security**, which in my country means a stable government, roads that survive the
monsoon, and the confidence that an earthquake will not destroy my school again.

The things I desire but do not demand are ordinary: a room of my own, a good
internet connection, a motorcycle, the chance to travel. I would enjoy them; I can
live well without them. Finally, I share Haldane's last requirement — that I
should not be satisfied while the people around me lack what I regard as
essential, since a comfortable life in an unjust society is not a satisfying one.

**5.** *(A model free-writing answer.)*

**My dream house.** My dream house would not be a mansion. It would stand on the
lower slope of a hill above a village, facing east, so that the first sun of the
morning came through the windows and the ridge behind kept the worst of the wind
off in winter.

It would be built of stone and timber in the local manner, but on a modern frame,
because I have seen what an earthquake does to a house built without one. There
would be two storeys: a large kitchen and one common room below, where the family
eats and visitors sit, and three bedrooms above. Every room would have a window
large enough to read by, since nothing makes a house feel poorer than darkness.

dream but a kind of exile.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) It comes at the end of the paragraph in which Haldane adds
**adventure** to his four general human needs as a requirement of his own. He has
just explained that, because his life is useful, it would be wrong to risk it for
the sake of risk — by mountaineering or motor racing — and that the adventures he
permits himself are experiments on his own body as a physiologist and
participation in wars and revolutions of which he approves.
(b) He is distinguishing **adventure** from **thrill**. A thrill is a momentary
rush of excitement, sought for its own sake and gone as soon as it is over.
Adventure, as he uses the word, is a serious undertaking with a purpose beyond
itself, whose satisfaction lies in having done something that mattered. The word
"solid" is doing the work of the sentence: a thrill is thin and vanishes, while
the satisfaction of adventure has substance and lasts.
(c) He spent six weeks in Madrid during the siege of the Spanish Civil War, in
constant danger — and says that the only *thrill* he got there came from reading
Rimbaud's poetry. The joke is deliberate. The most dangerous weeks of his life
produced no excitement at all; the excitement came from a book.
(d) It shows that Haldane judges experiences by their content rather than by the
feelings they produce. This is the same standard he applies everywhere else in
the essay: happiness is "unimpeded activity", not a sum of pleasures; health is
worth having because it makes work possible; a good death is one with the work
finished. He is not an ascetic — he likes books, baths and motor-cars — but he
consistently ranks purposeful doing above sensation.

**2.** (a) He is criticizing the central arrangement of **capitalism**: that the
value produced by the labour of workers is taken as profit by the private owners
of the factory or the business, so that the person who does the work does not
receive its fruit. Because of this, the connection between effort and benefit —
which is precisely what makes work satisfying — is broken for most people.
(b) His remedy is socialism, and specifically **workers' control**: he wants the
workers to control their conditions of work as he controls his own to a
considerable extent, and to receive the product of their labour in their own and
their friends' well-being. He believes that most work is dull, unhealthy and
exhausting only because of how it is organised, and that "after a few generations
of democracy in industry" this would cease to be true. His formula for it is
"Freedom should begin in the workshop."
(c) He offers his own grievance as evidence from the other end of the social
scale. His main personal complaint, he says, is that his work is not applied: he
discovers new biological facts, but no use is made of them, because although the
community would benefit, no individual would make a profit from their
application. The example is telling because Haldane is not a poor man — he is
pointing out that a system organised around private profit wastes the labour even
of the fortunate, and wastes discoveries that would help everybody.
(d) It is the public form of his first two private requirements. He requires work
"of which I can see the fruits", and he requires freedom; this sentence asks for
exactly those two things on behalf of everyone else. The whole movement of the
essay is visible in miniature here: a personal observation about what makes his
own life good is turned outward into a demand about how society should be
arranged.

value produced by the labour of workers is taken as profit by the private owners
of the factory or the business, so that the person who does the work does not
receive its fruit. Because of this, the connection between effort and benefit —
which is precisely what makes work satisfying — is broken for most people.
(b) His remedy is socialism, and specifically **workers' control**: he wants the
workers to control their conditions of work as he controls his own to a
considerable extent, and to receive the product of their labour in their own and
their friends' well-being. He believes that most work is dull, unhealthy and
exhausting only because of how it is organised, and that "after a few generations
of democracy in industry" this would cease to be true. His formula for it is
"Freedom should begin in the workshop."
(c) He offers his own grievance as evidence from the other end of the social
scale. His main personal complaint, he says, is that his work is not applied: he
discovers new biological facts, but no use is made of them, because although the
community would benefit, no individual would make a profit from their
application. The example is telling because Haldane is not a poor man — he is
pointing out that a system organised around private profit wastes the labour even
of the fortunate, and wastes discoveries that would help everybody.
(d) It is the public form of his first two private requirements. He requires work
"of which I can see the fruits", and he requires freedom; this sentence asks for
exactly those two things on behalf of everyone else. The whole movement of the
essay is visible in miniature here: a personal observation about what makes his
own life good is turned outward into a demand about how society should be
arranged.

chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- About the author
- The context
- The essay, paragraph by paragraph
- The definition Parker arrives at
- Themes
- Style and technique
- Glossary
- The opening: "Listen to me"
- Poverty is a smell
- Poverty is being tired
- Poverty is dirt
- Poverty is danger
- Poverty is asking for help
- Poverty is remembering
- The figures
- Poverty is looking into a black future
- The three official answers
- The verdict, the dream and the demand

This is the most uncomfortable text in your course, and it is meant to be. It is
a definition essay whose writer refuses to define from the outside. Instead of
telling you what poverty *is*, she makes you smell it, hear it and stand in it —
and then, in her last line, she turns the whole essay round and asks a question
about you rather than about her.

chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** For Parker, poverty is not simply a shortage of money but a whole
condition of life. It is a smell that never leaves the house; it is being always
tired, with anaemia, worms and no money for medicine; it is dirt, because soap,
hot water and fuel all cost money; it is insects, torn screens and a fire that
must be watched all night; it is the shame of asking for help; and it is an acid
that wears away pride and a chisel that chips away honour. Above all it is a trap
from which every exit costs money she does not have.

**2.** Her three children suffer in body, in schooling and in prospects. They
have worms, infections and pink-eye all summer; they are not starving but they
are malnourished; they sleep on the floor or in her single bed; the baby's skin
came away with a dried nappy, another child played with broken glass and the
eldest was left alone at the edge of a lake. At school they have no extra books,
magazines, pencils, crayons or paper — and two of them, she says, will already be
damaged before they ever get there. Looking ahead she expects her sons to drift
into theft, alcohol or drugs, and for her daughter "at best, there is a life like
mine."

**3.** She goes to the welfare office. She circles the block four or five times
before she can make herself go in, and goes only because she thinks of her
children. Inside, everyone is busy; the person who eventually comes out is never
the person she needs; and after telling her whole story — "spilling the whole
shame of your poverty all over the desk" — she is told this is the wrong office
and must begin the process again somewhere else, where it is no easier. Finally
she is told to wait, and cannot take in the reason because of the shame and
despair. The problems are therefore not only bureaucratic delay but repeated
humiliation, and the payment at the end is seventy-eight dollars a month for four
people.

**4.** Because pity is useless to her — "I cannot use your pity." Pity lets the
listener feel kind while changing nothing, and it places the poor person below
the listener as an object of charity rather than beside them as a person with a
case. What Parker wants instead is first understanding ("Listen with
understanding… put yourself in my shoes") and finally anger — anger that will
make the reader act and speak on her behalf. The refusal of pity at the start and
the demand for anger at the end frame the whole essay.

**5.** It means that Parker can see her children's future and it is as hopeless as
her present. Respectable families will not let their children play with her sons,
so the boys will attach themselves to boys who steal, and she can already picture
them "behind the bars of their prison instead of behind the bars of my poverty";
or they will escape into alcohol or drugs and be enslaved by them. For her
daughter the best she can imagine is a repetition of her own life. The sentence
states the essay's bleakest theme — that poverty is inherited — and the word
"black" carries no hope of dawn.

**6.** She means that poor people do not complain, do not protest and are never
heard. Earlier she has explained why: "the poor are always polite. The poor always
listen" — they accept a doctor's advice they cannot afford without saying so,
because objecting is dangerous and useless, and because shame keeps them quiet.
Their silence is what allows comfortable people to believe whatever they like
about them. This is why the essay exists: it is one of the silent speaking. And
because the next sentence is "Can you be silent too?", the phrase also becomes a
challenge — she has broken her silence, and the reader no longer has an excuse
for keeping his.

**7.** Because working cost more than it earned and endangered her children. She
was making twenty-two dollars a week, while a good nursery school for three
children cost twenty dollars a week, so almost nothing remained. When she left the
children with "Granny" instead, she came home to find the baby covered with fly
specks in a nappy that had not been changed — so hardened that when it came off,
bits of the baby's flesh came with it — one child playing with a sharp piece of
broken glass and the eldest alone at the edge of a lake. The episode is her
central proof that poverty is a trap rather than laziness.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** Money, food and medicine are all things Parker could be given. Opinions
cannot be, and it is opinions that decide whether she is given anything at all.
That is why she calls them, in effect, her greatest obstacle.

The prejudices are named one by one in the essay. The first is that cleanliness
is a matter of will: "Anybody can be clean," says the reader in clean clothes,
coming from a clean house — and Parker has to spend a whole paragraph explaining
that soap, hot water and fuel are purchases, not decisions. The second is that
the poor are lazy. Her answer is arithmetic: she worked for twenty-two dollars a
week when childcare cost twenty, and the children were injured and neglected while
she did it. The third is that the poor are immoral and deserve what they get, and
this is the one she attacks hardest, through the only other character she draws in
the whole essay — the large man who spends his days at the gas station, the
barbershop and the corner store "complaining about the government spending money
on the immoral mothers of illegitimate children," and who is also the neighbour
who will drive her to the clinic but "expects to get paid, one way or another."
In two sentences she convicts the respectable of exactly the vice they denounce.

These opinions are obstacles in the most practical sense. They decide how much
welfare is voted and how the office treats her; they are why she must prove her
poverty over and over again, and why asking for help costs so much shame; they are
why her county decided a surplus commodities programme cost too much; they are why
respectable children will not play with her sons, which in turn decides the
company the boys will keep. The other hardships wear down her body; prejudice
wears down her pride and closes the exits. This is also why the essay's final
demand is for **anger** rather than money — anger is what changes an opinion, and
opinion is what has to change first.

**2.** Parker deals with the three standard answers in turn, and in each case her
method is the same: she agrees that the thing exists, and then shows that it
cannot reach her.

**Welfare.** She does not deny that help is available — she is receiving it. She
attacks it on two grounds. The first is the amount: seventy-eight dollars a month
for four people, of which twenty goes on rent and almost all the rest on grits,
cornmeal, rice, milk and beans, with electricity rationed because every unit used
is food not bought. That is why there is no soap, no aspirin, no worm medicine,
no shampoo, "none of these things forever and ever and ever." The second, and to
her the worse, is the cost in dignity: circling the block before going in, the
wrong person, the wrong office, the whole shame spilt across a desk, the waiting,
the proving of her poverty again and again. Her dream is not for a larger cheque
alone but for an office as decent as other government offices, with enough staff,
where you tell your story once.

**Education.** "But you say to me, there are schools. Yes, there are schools." The
concession is followed by the destruction. Her children have no extra books, no
magazines, no pencils, crayons or paper — and, most important of all, no health.
They have worms and infections and pink-eye; they sleep on the floor; they suffer
from malnutrition even though they are not hungry. A school lunch programme exists,
but two of her children will already be damaged by the time they reach school, and
there is no surplus commodities programme in her county because it was judged too
expensive. Her point is that schooling can only work on a child who arrives fed,
rested and well; poverty has already disabled the remedy before it is applied.
She adds, drily, that she does remember what she was taught about health at
school, and that it does not do much good.

**Health clinics.** Again the concession: yes, there are clinics — "and they are
in the towns." She lives eight miles out. She could walk sixteen miles there and
back; her small children cannot. The neighbour with the car will take her, but
expects payment "one way or another," and that neighbour is the respectable man
who denounces immoral mothers. So the clinic is real, free at the point of entry
perhaps, and completely inaccessible.

Taken together, the three refutations make one argument. Society's solutions are
designed for people who already have the minimum — transport, health, decency of
treatment, time. Poverty removes precisely those things, so that the poorer a
person is, the less able she is to use the help that exists. It is not that the
remedies are absent; it is that they are out of reach.

**3.** **The opening strategy.** Parker begins most of her paragraphs with the
same two words — "Poverty is". "Poverty is being tired." "Poverty is dirt."
"Poverty is asking for help." "Poverty is remembering." "Poverty is looking into a
black future." "Poverty is an acid…" This is **anaphora**, and there is a clear
recurring pattern: each paragraph is a fresh, complete definition of the same
word. The effect is threefold. It imposes order on an experience that is
otherwise shapeless; it keeps reminding the reader that the essay is answering the
question in its title; and the hammering repetition makes the accumulation itself
feel like an argument, as though the word had to be defined again and again
because no single definition could hold it. A second, connected strategy is the
frequent opening concession — "But you say to me, there are schools" — which
allows her to voice the reader's objection before demolishing it.

**Paragraph development.** Each paragraph is then built the same way: a short flat
topic sentence; a challenge or a question to the reader; a run of small, exact,
physical details; and a closing sentence that supplies the reason, which is
almost always that the thing costs money. "I could bury it, but where is the
shovel? Shovels cost money." What makes each paragraph memorable is the quality of
those details. They are specific enough to be checked — the refrigerator that has
not worked, the onions that are cheap, the two-cent rise in the price of
Vaseline after two months of saving, the dried nappy that took the baby's skin
with it, the twenty-two dollars against the twenty. They also work through the
senses, especially smell and touch, which are the senses a comfortable reader can
least easily ignore. And the tone is level throughout: she never raises her voice,
which makes the facts do all the work.

**The final paragraph.** The questions at the end change the reader's position
from spectator to participant. Throughout the essay Parker has used the second
person to place the reader in her shoes; now she uses it to place a demand on
them. She tells them she did not come from another place or another time, and that
"others like me are all around you" — so the problem is local and present, not
distant. She asks them to look at her "with an angry heart", defining the anger
precisely: "anger that will help you help me. Anger that will let you tell of me."
Then the closing pair: "The poor are always silent. Can you be silent too?" This
is a **rhetorical question**, and it is unanswerable in the reader's favour. To
say yes is to admit indifference; to say no is to accept a duty. Because the essay
has spent its whole length establishing that she has no voice and the reader has
one, the question also transfers the work: she has broken her silence at the cost
of describing her own degradation, and the only decent response is for the reader
to break his.

**4.** *(A model imitation. Notice the repeated opening, the second-person
address, the concrete detail and the flat closing reason.)*

**Growing up in Poverty**

You ask me what it is to grow up poor. I will tell you. Do not be sorry for me.
Look instead, and remember.

Growing up in poverty is a cold, dark, endless morning. It is waking on a thin
mat in a room shared with four others, in clothes you also slept in, because
there is only one set and it must last. It is walking an hour to school on an
empty stomach because the tea is finished and the flour is for the evening.

Growing up in poverty is being hungry in a room full of books. The teacher speaks,
and you hear him, but your head is light and the words slide off. You are not
stupid. You are hungry. Nobody in that room knows the difference.

Growing up in poverty is shame. It is the torn shoe you keep behind the other
foot. It is the fee you cannot pay, read out in front of the class. It is the
friend's house you never invite anyone back from. Shame is cheap; it is the one
thing poverty gives you in plenty.

Growing up in poverty is waiting. Waiting for the remittance that is late.
Waiting for the health post to have the medicine. Waiting for a father who went
to the Gulf when you were six and writes that he will come next year, and next
year.

Growing up in poverty is a narrow, fixed, inherited future. Your father dug; you
will dig. Your mother left school at twelve; your sister will leave at twelve. The
land is too small to divide again, so somebody must go, and it will be you.

Some of you say you would study anyway, and work anyway, and rise anyway. Perhaps
you would — for a term, or a year. But for year after year after year, on an
empty stomach, in a torn shoe, with nobody at home who can read your homework?

I am not asking for your sympathy. I am asking you to look at the boy at the back
of your own classroom, the one who is always tired, and to stop calling him lazy.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) Both sentences are **metaphors**. In the first, poverty is an **acid**
dripping on pride: acid does not strike, it falls drop by drop and eats away the
surface it lands on, silently and without a sound, until nothing is left. In the
second, poverty is a **chisel** chipping at honour: a chisel works by many small
blows, each of which removes a little, until the shape of the thing is gone. Both
images say the same thing in different materials — that poverty destroys a person
not by one great disaster but by continuous small erosion over years. Neither
image allows for resistance: you cannot argue with acid.
(b) They are built identically — the same grammar, the same rhythm, the same
closing phrase "until all/until … is worn away" — which is **parallelism**. The
repetition doubles the force, makes the pair easy to remember, and, most
importantly, enacts the very thing being described: the second sentence wears at
the reader exactly as the first one did, so the form imitates the content. The
pairing of *pride* with *honour* also widens the claim from how a person feels
about herself to how she stands in the eyes of others.
(c) She immediately turns on the reader: some of you say that you would do
something in my situation, and maybe you would — "for the first week or the first
month, but for year after year after year?" The challenge is aimed precisely at
the comfortable listener's confidence that character would save him. Her answer is
that character is exactly what is being dissolved, and that no one's survives
indefinitely.
(d) Because by this point she has earned them. For most of the essay she has
refused figurative language and given nothing but hard physical fact — sour milk,
fly specks, two cents, seventy-eight dollars. The reader therefore trusts her as a
witness, and the two metaphors arrive as a verdict on evidence already heard,
rather than as decoration. They also lift the argument from the physical to the
moral at exactly the moment she needs to: she is about to ask for anger rather
than charity, and anger is a moral response.

**2.** (a) These lines are the last paragraph of the essay. They follow the
modest dream — money for soap and hot water, for worm medicine and a shovel and
needles and thread, and for a welfare office where you tell your story once and
are not made to prove your poverty over and over again. The essay therefore ends
by moving out of description altogether and speaking directly to the reader.
(b) She means that she is not a historical example or a foreign case study, and
that the reader cannot file her away as somebody else's problem. "Others like me
are all around you": the poverty she has described is happening now, in the
reader's own country, within walking distance of the reader's own clean house.
The sentence blocks the last available escape route, which is distance.
(c) She asks for **anger** — but a very precisely defined anger: "anger that will
help you help me. Anger that will let you tell of me." It is not rage for its own
sake but the emotion that produces action and speech. This is the exact opposite
of what she forbade in her first paragraph, where she said "Listen without pity. I
cannot use your pity." Pity looks down and does nothing; anger stands level and
acts. The essay therefore begins by refusing one emotion and ends by demanding
another, and the whole body of the text is the evidence that justifies the swap.
(d) Ending on a **rhetorical question** does three things. It reverses the
direction of the essay: for eleven paragraphs the reader has been examining her
life, and in seven words she is examining his. It makes evasion impossible,
because both answers convict — to say yes is to confess indifference, to say no is
to accept a duty. And it exploits the parallel she has just drawn: the poor are
silent because they have no choice, while the reader would be silent by choice,
which is a far worse thing. Because the essay stops there, with no reassurance and
no conclusion, the question is left with the reader rather than with the writer —
which is precisely where she wants it.

in the towns." She lives eight miles out. She could walk sixteen miles there and
back; her small children cannot. The neighbour with the car will take her, but
expects payment "one way or another," and that neighbour is the respectable man
who denounces immoral mothers. So the clinic is real, free at the point of entry
perhaps, and completely inaccessible.

Taken together, the three refutations make one argument. Society's solutions are
designed for people who already have the minimum — transport, health, decency of
treatment, time. Poverty removes precisely those things, so that the poorer a
person is, the less able she is to use the help that exists. It is not that the
remedies are absent; it is that they are out of reach.

**3.** **The opening strategy.** Parker begins most of her paragraphs with the
same two words — "Poverty is". "Poverty is being tired." "Poverty is dirt."
"Poverty is asking for help." "Poverty is remembering." "Poverty is looking into a
black future." "Poverty is an acid…" This is **anaphora**, and there is a clear
recurring pattern: each paragraph is a fresh, complete definition of the same
word. The effect is threefold. It imposes order on an experience that is
otherwise shapeless; it keeps reminding the reader that the essay is answering the
question in its title; and the hammering repetition makes the accumulation itself
feel like an argument, as though the word had to be defined again and again
because no single definition could hold it. A second, connected strategy is the
frequent opening concession — "But you say to me, there are schools" — which
allows her to voice the reader's objection before demolishing it.

**Paragraph development.** Each paragraph is then built the same way: a short flat
topic sentence; a challenge or a question to the reader; a run of small, exact,
physical details; and a closing sentence that supplies the reason, which is
almost always that the thing costs money. "I could bury it, but where is the
shovel? Shovels cost money." What makes each paragraph memorable is the quality of
those details. They are specific enough to be checked — the refrigerator that has
not worked, the onions that are cheap, the two-cent rise in the price of
Vaseline after two months of saving, the dried nappy that took the baby's skin
with it, the twenty-two dollars against the twenty. They also work through the
senses, especially smell and touch, which are the senses a comfortable reader can
least easily ignore. And the tone is level throughout: she never raises her voice,
which makes the facts do all the work.

**The final paragraph.** The questions at the end change the reader's position
from spectator to participant. Throughout the essay Parker has used the second
person to place the reader in her shoes; now she uses it to place a demand on
them. She tells them she did not come from another place or another time, and that
"others like me are all around you" — so the problem is local and present, not
distant. She asks them to look at her "with an angry heart", defining the anger
precisely: "anger that will help you help me. Anger that will let you tell of me."
Then the closing pair: "The poor are always silent. Can you be silent too?" This
is a **rhetorical question**, and it is unanswerable in the reader's favour. To
say yes is to admit indifference; to say no is to accept a duty. Because the essay
has spent its whole length establishing that she has no voice and the reader has
one, the question also transfers the work: she has broken her silence at the cost
of describing her own degradation, and the only decent response is for the reader
to break his.

**4.** *(A model imitation. Notice the repeated opening, the second-person
address, the concrete detail and the flat closing reason.)*

**Growing up in Poverty**

You ask me what it is to grow up poor. I will tell you. Do not be sorry for me.
Look instead, and remember.

Growing up in poverty is a cold, dark, endless morning. It is waking on a thin
mat in a room shared with four others, in clothes you also slept in, because
there is only one set and it must last. It is walking an hour to school on an
empty stomach because the tea is finished and the flour is for the evening.

Growing up in poverty is being hungry in a room full of books. The teacher speaks,
and you hear him, but your head is light and the words slide off. You are not
stupid. You are hungry. Nobody in that room knows the difference.

Growing up in poverty is shame. It is the torn shoe you keep behind the other
foot. It is the fee you cannot pay, read out in front of the class. It is the
friend's house you never invite anyone back from. Shame is cheap; it is the one
thing poverty gives you in plenty.

Growing up in poverty is waiting. Waiting for the remittance that is late.
Waiting for the health post to have the medicine. Waiting for a father who went
to the Gulf when you were six and writes that he will come next year, and next
year.

Growing up in poverty is a narrow, fixed, inherited future. Your father dug; you
will dig. Your mother left school at twelve; your sister will leave at twelve. The
land is too small to divide again, so somebody must go, and it will be you.

Some of you say you would study anyway, and work anyway, and rise anyway. Perhaps
you would — for a term, or a year. But for year after year after year, on an
empty stomach, in a torn shoe, with nobody at home who can read your homework?

I am not asking for your sympathy. I am asking you to look at the boy at the back
of your own classroom, the one who is always tired, and to stop calling him lazy.

self_checks.question: Model answers — reference to the context
self_checks.answer:
**1.** (a) Both sentences are **metaphors**. In the first, poverty is an **acid**
dripping on pride: acid does not strike, it falls drop by drop and eats away the
surface it lands on, silently and without a sound, until nothing is left. In the
second, poverty is a **chisel** chipping at honour: a chisel works by many small
blows, each of which removes a little, until the shape of the thing is gone. Both
images say the same thing in different materials — that poverty destroys a person
not by one great disaster but by continuous small erosion over years. Neither
image allows for resistance: you cannot argue with acid.
(b) They are built identically — the same grammar, the same rhythm, the same
closing phrase "until all/until … is worn away" — which is **parallelism**. The
repetition doubles the force, makes the pair easy to remember, and, most
importantly, enacts the very thing being described: the second sentence wears at
the reader exactly as the first one did, so the form imitates the content. The
pairing of *pride* with *honour* also widens the claim from how a person feels
about herself to how she stands in the eyes of others.
(c) She immediately turns on the reader: some of you say that you would do
something in my situation, and maybe you would — "for the first week or the first
month, but for year after year after year?" The challenge is aimed precisely at
the comfortable listener's confidence that character would save him. Her answer is
that character is exactly what is being dissolved, and that no one's survives
indefinitely.
(d) Because by this point she has earned them. For most of the essay she has
refused figurative language and given nothing but hard physical fact — sour milk,
fly specks, two cents, seventy-eight dollars. The reader therefore trusts her as a
witness, and the two metaphors arrive as a verdict on evidence already heard,
rather than as decoration. They also lift the argument from the physical to the
moral at exactly the moment she needs to: she is about to ask for anger rather
than charity, and anger is a moral response.

**2.** (a) These lines are the last paragraph of the essay. They follow the
modest dream — money for soap and hot water, for worm medicine and a shovel and
needles and thread, and for a welfare office where you tell your story once and
are not made to prove your poverty over and over again. The essay therefore ends
by moving out of description altogether and speaking directly to the reader.
(b) She means that she is not a historical example or a foreign case study, and
that the reader cannot file her away as somebody else's problem. "Others like me
are all around you": the poverty she has described is happening now, in the
reader's own country, within walking distance of the reader's own clean house.
The sentence blocks the last available escape route, which is distance.
(c) She asks for **anger** — but a very precisely defined anger: "anger that will
help you help me. Anger that will let you tell of me." It is not rage for its own
sake but the emotion that produces action and speech. This is the exact opposite
of what she forbade in her first paragraph, where she said "Listen without pity. I
cannot use your pity." Pity looks down and does nothing; anger stands level and
acts. The essay therefore begins by refusing one emotion and ends by demanding
another, and the whole body of the text is the evidence that justifies the swap.
(d) Ending on a **rhetorical question** does three things. It reverses the
direction of the essay: for eleven paragraphs the reader has been examining her
life, and in seven words she is examining his. It makes evasion impossible,
because both answers convict — to say yes is to confess indifference, to say no is
to accept a duty. And it exploits the parallel she has just drawn: the poor are
silent because they have no choice, while the reader would be silent by choice,
which is a far worse thing. Because the essay stops there, with no reassurance and
no conclusion, the question is left with the reader rather than with the writer —
which is precisely where she wants it.
