## Model answers — long questions

**1.** The flashback in *A Sunny Morning* is unusual: nothing is staged, no scene
changes, and no character steps back in time. The past is delivered entirely
through dialogue, and — this is the crucial point — through a **disguise**. Gonzalo
speaks of "my cousin" and Laura of "my best friend", so that the two lovers narrate
their own history while pretending it belongs to other people. The effects are
several and all of them are dramatic rather than decorative.

**It supplies the whole background without stopping the play.** In three or four
minutes the audience learns of the villa Maricela, the window with the red roses,
the girl called "The Silver Maiden", the horseman who threw up a bouquet each
morning and caught one each afternoon, the merchant her parents preferred, the
insult beneath the window, and the duel at sunrise on the beach. All of it arrives
as conversation between two strangers on a bench, so exposition and action are the
same thing.

**It becomes the recognition scene.** Each detail one of them adds is also a clue
to the other. "You seem to know the story well." "And so do you." The flashback is
therefore not an interruption of the plot but the plot itself: the past is the
mechanism by which the present is discovered.

**It creates the play's central irony.** Because the audience works out the truth
before the characters admit it, every sentence of the flashback carries two
meanings. When Laura says of her friend, "She was very unfortunate and had a sad
love affair," and Gonzalo replies simply "Very sad," we are watching two people
discuss their own tragedy with perfect politeness, which is both funny and
painful.

**It measures the distance travelled.** Setting the black-eyed girl at the window
and the gallant horseman among the roses beside the white-haired lady with a
parasol and the gouty gentleman with a reading glass is what gives the comedy its
undertow of sadness, and what makes both of them decide to stay silent.

**And it sets up the ending.** Because the audience has been shown the bouquet
thrown up to the balcony, the final stage direction — they smile "as if she were
again at the window and he below in the rose garden" — can restore the whole past
in one image, and the violets Gonzalo stoops for are recognisably the same flowers
fifty years later.

**2.** The play is a comedy that keeps turning into a love scene, and the two
effects are produced by the same means.

**The humour of character.** Both old people are vain, quarrelsome and thoroughly
enjoying themselves. Gonzalo demands a bench "to himself" in a public park, wants
three priests "routed out", and then lectures Laura that "the benches here are
public property" — an inconsistency she pounces on at once. He boasts about killing
hares and partridges and about a wild boar's head in his study; she answers, "Yes,
kill time. That is all you kill," and trumps him with a tiger's skin in her
boudoir.

**The humour of physical comedy.** The "enormous pair of glasses" plus a reading
glass, which make Laura say "I thought you were taking out a telescope"; the two of
them sneezing three times each in alternation after the snuff; and the old man
dragging his feet so that "a carriage would not raise more dust."

**The humour of repartee.** "Do you use your handkerchief as a shoe brush?" / "Why
not?" / "Do you use a shoe brush as a handkerchief?" The dialogue works by
reversal, each speaker turning the other's own words round — which is also how we
learn that these two are perfectly matched.

**Verbal irony** is everywhere in the first half. Laura's "You are very polite" to a
man who has just refused to listen to her; her delight when he loses the other
bench too, "Serves him right for scaring the birds."

**Dramatic irony** governs the second half and gives the play its depth. The
audience knows who these people are long before they say so, so ordinary lines
acquire a double meaning: "The daughters of the mothers I once loved kiss me now as
they would a graven image", read out as a joke by a man beside the woman he loved;
"Very sad", said of his own ruined love affair; "Fate is curious. Here are you and
I, complete strangers…" said by a woman who knows they are nothing of the kind. The
two elaborate lies are the high point, because each character is simultaneously
deceiving, being deceived, and privately seeing through the deception — "She lies
worse than I do."

**Situational irony** frames the whole piece: a quarrel about scattered birds
becomes a reunion of lovers, and two people who have spent fifty years apart, when
finally given the chance to speak, agree to say nothing.

Finally, and most importantly, the humour is never cruel. The Quinteros laugh at
old age — the gout, the spectacles, the boasting, the melodrama — while giving
their two old people more dignity and more feeling than most young stage lovers
have. That combination of laughter and tenderness is the play's real achievement,
and it is why the ending can be funny and moving in the same breath.

**3.** The title is justified on at least four levels, and a good answer should
climb from the literal to the symbolic.

**Literally**, it names the setting. The opening stage direction reads, "A sunny
morning in a retired corner of a park in Madrid. Autumn." Dona Laura's first words
are "I am so glad to be here… What a beautiful morning!" and Petra replies that the
sun is hot. The entire action takes place on that one morning, in real time, in
sunshine.

**Structurally**, the sunshine causes the plot. It is the sunny morning that brings
both old people out of doors, fills the benches, leaves the three priests
comfortably settled on the one Gonzalo wants, and so forces him to sit beside the
only lady in the park. He says so himself: "The authorities should place more
benches here for these sunny mornings. Well, I suppose I must resign myself and sit
on the bench with the old lady." Without the sun there is no meeting.

**Symbolically**, the sun is the warmth that grows between them. The play begins
cold — a scattering of birds, insults, "senile old lady" — and ends in a glow of
affection. Set against **autumn**, the season of the play, the sunshine becomes an
exact image of what the Quinteros are describing: brightness late in the year,
beauty in the season of decline, a last warm day in two long lives.

**In the plot's final moments**, the phrase becomes the condition of their future.
"Good-bye until tomorrow." "Until tomorrow." "If it is sunny." "A sunny morning."
The words are repeated four times in nine lines, and by then they mean far more
than weather: a sunny morning is now the name of their appointment, their renewed
courtship, and their agreement to go on living in the present rather than in the
past.

A final point worth making: the title is deliberately *light*. The play could have
been called "The Silver Maiden" or "Twenty Years Pass", and either would have
promised a tragedy. "A Sunny Morning" promises a pleasant hour — which is exactly
the tone the brothers wanted, and exactly the disguise under which they smuggle in
a story about lost love.

**4.** **Was it wise?** There are two defensible answers, and the best response
weighs both.

The case that they were **right** to keep silent is the one the play itself
endorses. Each explains the decision in terms of the other's happiness: "Better
that she recall the gallant horseman"; "It is better he should remember me as the
black eyed girl tossing flowers." A confession would have forced two exposures at
once — the ruin that age has made of both of them, and the shabby truth about the
separation (a marriage two years later, a ballet dancer in Paris within three
months). Silence keeps the memory intact and lets a friendship begin without the
weight of an old grievance. It also preserves the play's delicacy: what they have
agreed to is more intimate than a confession, because each knows, each knows the
other knows, and neither needs to say it.

The case that they were **wrong** is also real. They are seventy, and they have
already lost fifty years to a set of intercepted letters and a misunderstanding.
An open confession would have allowed them the honest companionship of whatever
time remains, instead of a friendship built on two large lies. And lies are
inconvenient: if they meet daily, Gonzalo must keep a dead cousin dead and Laura
must keep a drowned friend drowned.

On balance, the decision looks wise *in the moment* and unsustainable *in the long
run* — which is precisely why the play ends where it does.

**What will happen tomorrow?** A reasonable prediction, grounded in the text:

He will come, and he will bring the crumbs he promised — his own version of the
bouquets he once threw to her balcony. They will sit on the same bench, and the
quarrelling will continue, but as a game. Neither will make a formal confession
straight away; instead the truth will keep leaking out in the same way it did on
the first morning — through a remembered name, a line of Campoamor, another slip.
Since each now knows that the other knows, the pretence will become a shared joke
rather than a defence, and the "cousin" and the "friend" may well go on being
discussed for weeks, with both of them enjoying it.

In the end I think the fiction will simply be allowed to fade rather than be
broken: they will become inseparable companions of the park bench, and the words
"Laura" and "Gonzalo" will be spoken aloud one day without any scene at all. What
the play makes certain is the important part — that the two of them have found
each other again, and that neither intends to be alone tomorrow.

**5.** **Summary.** On a sunny autumn morning in a quiet corner of a park in
Madrid, Dona Laura, a refined white-haired lady of about seventy, arrives on the
arm of her young maid Petra and settles on what she calls "my seat". She sends
Petra off to meet the park guard she is in love with, and amuses herself by
throwing bread crumbs to the pigeons, naming them as she feeds them.

Don Gonzalo, an impatient, gouty gentleman of the same age, enters with his servant
Juanito, grumbling about idlers and about three priests who have taken "his" bench.
Walking about in search of a seat, he scatters Laura's birds. She rebukes him
sharply, and the two exchange insults — he mutters that she is a "senile old lady"
who should be at home counting her beads, she remarks that he is "very polite" —
before he is forced to share her bench. He calls for his book and a huge pair of
glasses; she asks whether he is taking out a telescope. Then he offers her a pinch
of snuff, they sneeze three times each, and, as she notes in an aside, "the snuff
has made peace between us."

He reads aloud from the poet Campoamor, including the lines "Twenty years pass. He
returns. And each, beholding the other, exclaims — Can it be that this is he?
Heavens, is it she?" Laura recites them without spectacles, privately admitting, "I
know every word by heart." Conversation turns to Valencia, and then to a seaside
villa called Maricela, where, Gonzalo remembers, there once lived a beautiful girl
named Laura Llorente, known as "The Silver Maiden".

Both are startled; both realise who the other is; and both decide to say nothing.
Instead, under cover of speaking about "my cousin" and "my best friend", they
retell their own love story — the horseman who tossed flowers up to her window, the
merchant her parents wanted her to marry, the quarrel and the duel at sunrise on
the beach. To explain why the lovers never met again, each invents a splendid
death: Gonzalo says his cousin fell in a trench in Africa clutching the flag of
Spain, and Laura says her friend walked into the rising tide at sunset after
writing his name on the sand. Their asides tell the audience the truth — she
married two years later, and he ran off to Paris with a ballet dancer within three
months — and each privately recognises the other's lie.

The quarrel is long forgotten. He admits he was unreasonable; she asks sweetly
whether he will come again tomorrow; he promises to bring crumbs for the birds. Yet
each, with the other's back turned, resolves not to confess: "I am grotesque now",
"I am too sadly changed" — each preferring that the other keep the memory of their
youth. Petra returns with violets from her guard, and a few fall as Laura takes
them. As they part, Don Gonzalo stoops "trembling and with a great effort" to pick
up the fallen flowers, and Laura turns and catches him at it. "Yes, it is he!" "It
is she, and no mistake." Waving farewell, they quote the poem to each other — "Can
it be that this is he?" "Heavens, is it she?" — smile as though she were at her
window again and he below among the roses, and leave on the arms of their servants,
having agreed to meet tomorrow, if it is sunny.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (i) The speaker is **Dona Laura**, the white-haired lady of about seventy
who is the heroine of the play. She has just arrived at her favourite bench in a
park in Madrid, leaning on her maid's arm and using her parasol as a walking stick.
(ii) "You" refers to **Petra**, her young maid, who is about twenty years old.
Petra has just said, "The sun is hot," and Laura's reply — "Yes, you are only
twenty" — means that at twenty one feels the heat, while at seventy one is grateful
for it.
(iii) The "guard" is the young **park keeper** whom Petra is in love with and who
is waiting for her among the trees. Laura teases her about him a moment later —
"He belongs more to you than he does to the park" and "Your head is where your
heart is — with the guard." It is this same guard who later sends Laura the bunch
of violets that brings about the recognition at the end of the play.
(iv) Three things. First, Laura's **age and frailty**: "I feel more tired today
than usual," and she must be helped to her seat. Second, her **kindness and
humour**: she notices Petra's impatience, sends her off to her sweetheart without
being asked, and only stipulates ten minutes — she is an indulgent mistress who
enjoys young people's happiness. Third, her **loneliness**: once the maid has gone
she is left alone with a bag of bread crumbs and a flock of pigeons, to whom she
talks as if they were friends. The play needs all three facts in place before Don
Gonzalo arrives, and it establishes them in four lines.

**2.** (i) She is addressing **Don Gonzalo**, the impatient old gentleman who has
just entered with his servant Juanito, looking for a bench of his own and walking
about the park in irritation. At this moment they are complete strangers to each
other — or believe they are.
(ii) She was **feeding the pigeons**. Having sent Petra away, she had risen, walked
towards the trees and thrown three handfuls of bread crumbs, distributing them with
great enjoyment — "These are for the spryest, these for the gluttons, and these for
the little ones which are the most persistent" — and had gone back to her seat to
watch them eat.
(iii) **Don Gonzalo** scared them, by walking towards the birds with Juanito while
hunting for a free bench. No, they are **not pet birds**: they are the wild pigeons
of a public park, which Dona Laura feeds every day and has come to know
individually — "that big one is always first! I know him by his big head." That is
exactly what makes her claim on them so comic and so touching: she has no legal
right to the birds at all, yet they are plainly hers.
(iv) They are in a **park in Madrid**, the capital of Spain — in "a retired corner"
of it, beside a bench, on a sunny autumn morning. Dona Laura is seated on the bench
she regards as her own; Don Gonzalo is standing near the trees where the pigeons
were feeding.
(v) Because everything else grows out of it. Dramatically, it is the **inciting
incident**: it forces two strangers into conversation who would otherwise have sat
in silence, and it is Gonzalo's failure to find another seat that puts him on her
bench. Thematically, it establishes both characters in a few strokes — her
warmth and her fighting spirit, his selfishness and his absurd sense of ownership
(he complains that the priests have taken "his" bench, and is instantly caught out
when he claims that benches are "public property"). And it sets up the play's final
reversal: the bad-tempered old man who scattered her birds in the first minutes
promises, in the last, to bring crumbs for them himself — which is the play's quiet
way of saying that he is in love with her again.

**Situational irony** frames the whole piece: a quarrel about scattered birds
becomes a reunion of lovers, and two people who have spent fifty years apart, when
finally given the chance to speak, agree to say nothing.

Finally, and most importantly, the humour is never cruel. The Quinteros laugh at
old age — the gout, the spectacles, the boasting, the melodrama — while giving
their two old people more dignity and more feeling than most young stage lovers
have. That combination of laughter and tenderness is the play's real achievement,
and it is why the ending can be funny and moving in the same breath.

**3.** The title is justified on at least four levels, and a good answer should
climb from the literal to the symbolic.

**Literally**, it names the setting. The opening stage direction reads, "A sunny
morning in a retired corner of a park in Madrid. Autumn." Dona Laura's first words
are "I am so glad to be here… What a beautiful morning!" and Petra replies that the
sun is hot. The entire action takes place on that one morning, in real time, in
sunshine.

**Structurally**, the sunshine causes the plot. It is the sunny morning that brings
both old people out of doors, fills the benches, leaves the three priests
comfortably settled on the one Gonzalo wants, and so forces him to sit beside the
only lady in the park. He says so himself: "The authorities should place more
benches here for these sunny mornings. Well, I suppose I must resign myself and sit
on the bench with the old lady." Without the sun there is no meeting.

**Symbolically**, the sun is the warmth that grows between them. The play begins
cold — a scattering of birds, insults, "senile old lady" — and ends in a glow of
affection. Set against **autumn**, the season of the play, the sunshine becomes an
exact image of what the Quinteros are describing: brightness late in the year,
beauty in the season of decline, a last warm day in two long lives.

**In the plot's final moments**, the phrase becomes the condition of their future.
"Good-bye until tomorrow." "Until tomorrow." "If it is sunny." "A sunny morning."
The words are repeated four times in nine lines, and by then they mean far more
than weather: a sunny morning is now the name of their appointment, their renewed
courtship, and their agreement to go on living in the present rather than in the
past.

A final point worth making: the title is deliberately *light*. The play could have
been called "The Silver Maiden" or "Twenty Years Pass", and either would have
promised a tragedy. "A Sunny Morning" promises a pleasant hour — which is exactly
the tone the brothers wanted, and exactly the disguise under which they smuggle in
a story about lost love.

**4.** **Was it wise?** There are two defensible answers, and the best response
weighs both.

The case that they were **right** to keep silent is the one the play itself
endorses. Each explains the decision in terms of the other's happiness: "Better
that she recall the gallant horseman"; "It is better he should remember me as the
black eyed girl tossing flowers." A confession would have forced two exposures at
once — the ruin that age has made of both of them, and the shabby truth about the
separation (a marriage two years later, a ballet dancer in Paris within three
months). Silence keeps the memory intact and lets a friendship begin without the
weight of an old grievance. It also preserves the play's delicacy: what they have
agreed to is more intimate than a confession, because each knows, each knows the
other knows, and neither needs to say it.

The case that they were **wrong** is also real. They are seventy, and they have
already lost fifty years to a set of intercepted letters and a misunderstanding.
An open confession would have allowed them the honest companionship of whatever
time remains, instead of a friendship built on two large lies. And lies are
inconvenient: if they meet daily, Gonzalo must keep a dead cousin dead and Laura
must keep a drowned friend drowned.

On balance, the decision looks wise *in the moment* and unsustainable *in the long
run* — which is precisely why the play ends where it does.

**What will happen tomorrow?** A reasonable prediction, grounded in the text:

He will come, and he will bring the crumbs he promised — his own version of the
bouquets he once threw to her balcony. They will sit on the same bench, and the
quarrelling will continue, but as a game. Neither will make a formal confession
straight away; instead the truth will keep leaking out in the same way it did on
the first morning — through a remembered name, a line of Campoamor, another slip.
Since each now knows that the other knows, the pretence will become a shared joke
rather than a defence, and the "cousin" and the "friend" may well go on being
discussed for weeks, with both of them enjoying it.

In the end I think the fiction will simply be allowed to fade rather than be
broken: they will become inseparable companions of the park bench, and the words
"Laura" and "Gonzalo" will be spoken aloud one day without any scene at all. What
the play makes certain is the important part — that the two of them have found
each other again, and that neither intends to be alone tomorrow.

**5.** **Summary.** On a sunny autumn morning in a quiet corner of a park in
Madrid, Dona Laura, a refined white-haired lady of about seventy, arrives on the
arm of her young maid Petra and settles on what she calls "my seat". She sends
Petra off to meet the park guard she is in love with, and amuses herself by
throwing bread crumbs to the pigeons, naming them as she feeds them.

Don Gonzalo, an impatient, gouty gentleman of the same age, enters with his servant
Juanito, grumbling about idlers and about three priests who have taken "his" bench.
Walking about in search of a seat, he scatters Laura's birds. She rebukes him
sharply, and the two exchange insults — he mutters that she is a "senile old lady"
who should be at home counting her beads, she remarks that he is "very polite" —
before he is forced to share her bench. He calls for his book and a huge pair of
glasses; she asks whether he is taking out a telescope. Then he offers her a pinch
of snuff, they sneeze three times each, and, as she notes in an aside, "the snuff
has made peace between us."

He reads aloud from the poet Campoamor, including the lines "Twenty years pass. He
returns. And each, beholding the other, exclaims — Can it be that this is he?
Heavens, is it she?" Laura recites them without spectacles, privately admitting, "I
know every word by heart." Conversation turns to Valencia, and then to a seaside
villa called Maricela, where, Gonzalo remembers, there once lived a beautiful girl
named Laura Llorente, known as "The Silver Maiden".

Both are startled; both realise who the other is; and both decide to say nothing.
Instead, under cover of speaking about "my cousin" and "my best friend", they
retell their own love story — the horseman who tossed flowers up to her window, the
merchant her parents wanted her to marry, the quarrel and the duel at sunrise on
the beach. To explain why the lovers never met again, each invents a splendid
death: Gonzalo says his cousin fell in a trench in Africa clutching the flag of
Spain, and Laura says her friend walked into the rising tide at sunset after
writing his name on the sand. Their asides tell the audience the truth — she
married two years later, and he ran off to Paris with a ballet dancer within three
months — and each privately recognises the other's lie.

The quarrel is long forgotten. He admits he was unreasonable; she asks sweetly
whether he will come again tomorrow; he promises to bring crumbs for the birds. Yet
each, with the other's back turned, resolves not to confess: "I am grotesque now",
"I am too sadly changed" — each preferring that the other keep the memory of their
youth. Petra returns with violets from her guard, and a few fall as Laura takes
them. As they part, Don Gonzalo stoops "trembling and with a great effort" to pick
up the fallen flowers, and Laura turns and catches him at it. "Yes, it is he!" "It
is she, and no mistake." Waving farewell, they quote the poem to each other — "Can
it be that this is he?" "Heavens, is it she?" — smile as though she were at her
window again and he below among the roses, and leave on the arms of their servants,
having agreed to meet tomorrow, if it is sunny.

self_checks.question: Model answers — reference to the context
self_checks.answer:
**1.** (i) The speaker is **Dona Laura**, the white-haired lady of about seventy
who is the heroine of the play. She has just arrived at her favourite bench in a
park in Madrid, leaning on her maid's arm and using her parasol as a walking stick.
(ii) "You" refers to **Petra**, her young maid, who is about twenty years old.
Petra has just said, "The sun is hot," and Laura's reply — "Yes, you are only
twenty" — means that at twenty one feels the heat, while at seventy one is grateful
for it.
(iii) The "guard" is the young **park keeper** whom Petra is in love with and who
is waiting for her among the trees. Laura teases her about him a moment later —
"He belongs more to you than he does to the park" and "Your head is where your
heart is — with the guard." It is this same guard who later sends Laura the bunch
of violets that brings about the recognition at the end of the play.
(iv) Three things. First, Laura's **age and frailty**: "I feel more tired today
than usual," and she must be helped to her seat. Second, her **kindness and
humour**: she notices Petra's impatience, sends her off to her sweetheart without
being asked, and only stipulates ten minutes — she is an indulgent mistress who
enjoys young people's happiness. Third, her **loneliness**: once the maid has gone
she is left alone with a bag of bread crumbs and a flock of pigeons, to whom she
talks as if they were friends. The play needs all three facts in place before Don
Gonzalo arrives, and it establishes them in four lines.

**2.** (i) She is addressing **Don Gonzalo**, the impatient old gentleman who has
just entered with his servant Juanito, looking for a bench of his own and walking
about the park in irritation. At this moment they are complete strangers to each
other — or believe they are.
(ii) She was **feeding the pigeons**. Having sent Petra away, she had risen, walked
towards the trees and thrown three handfuls of bread crumbs, distributing them with
great enjoyment — "These are for the spryest, these for the gluttons, and these for
the little ones which are the most persistent" — and had gone back to her seat to
watch them eat.
(iii) **Don Gonzalo** scared them, by walking towards the birds with Juanito while
hunting for a free bench. No, they are **not pet birds**: they are the wild pigeons
of a public park, which Dona Laura feeds every day and has come to know
individually — "that big one is always first! I know him by his big head." That is
exactly what makes her claim on them so comic and so touching: she has no legal
right to the birds at all, yet they are plainly hers.
(iv) They are in a **park in Madrid**, the capital of Spain — in "a retired corner"
of it, beside a bench, on a sunny autumn morning. Dona Laura is seated on the bench
she regards as her own; Don Gonzalo is standing near the trees where the pigeons
were feeding.
(v) Because everything else grows out of it. Dramatically, it is the **inciting
incident**: it forces two strangers into conversation who would otherwise have sat
in silence, and it is Gonzalo's failure to find another seat that puts him on her
bench. Thematically, it establishes both characters in a few strokes — her
warmth and her fighting spirit, his selfishness and his absurd sense of ownership
(he complains that the priests have taken "his" bench, and is instantly caught out
when he claims that benches are "public property"). And it sets up the play's final
reversal: the bad-tempered old man who scattered her birds in the first minutes
promises, in the last, to bring crumbs for them himself — which is the play's quiet
way of saying that he is in love with her again.

chapters.summary:
- *Refund* (1938) is a one-act farce by the Hungarian satirist **Fritz (Frigyes)
  Karinthy (1887–1938)**, adapted for English-speaking audiences by **Percival
  Wilde**.
- **Wasserkopf**, a bearded man under forty, jobless and broke, returns to his old
  school after eighteen years and demands his tuition fees back, saying he learned
  nothing and is now good for nothing.
- The idea came from his old classmate **Leaderer**, who was making money
  speculating in foreign exchange and told Wasserkopf that if he did not understand
  how, he should go and get his fees back.
- Wasserkopf demands a **re-examination** to prove he knows nothing, and threatens
  the Ministry of Education.
- The Principal calls a staff conference. The **Mathematics Master** proposes the
  plan: "Whatever his answers, we agree beforehand that they are correct" —
  because "if he fails he succeeds", and one refund would bring a queue of others.
- Before any subject is examined, his rudeness earns **Manners: Excellent**, his
  refusal of a chair **Physical Culture: Excellent**, and his sitting down
  **Alertness: Very Good**, along with Perseverance, Logic and Ambition.
- **History**: the Thirty Years' War lasted "exactly seven meters", justified by
  Einstein and by deducting meals, siestas and social distractions — *Very Good*.
  **Physics**: "You're an ass!", justified by the ass's sad look and optical
  illusion — *Very Good*. **Geography**: the capital of Brunswick is "Same",
  justified by the Barbarossa legend — *Excellent*.
- **Mathematics**: the Master's absurd "easy" question is answered with 2,629
  litres, declared wrong by one litre, and Wasserkopf is marked *Failure* — but
  the "difficult" question is how much the refund should be, and when Wasserkopf
  calculates **6,450 crowns 50 heller** exactly, he is declared a mathematical
  genius and passed.
- The Principal announces that Wasserkopf has **passed with distinction in every
  subject**, congratulates the staff on having taught him so well, and orders:
  "get out before I have you thrown out!" The Servant throws him out.
- The closing line is the play's whole satire: "In the future it will be our
  proudest boast that in this school a pupil simply cannot fail!"
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- About the author
- The characters
- The play, step by step
- The double trap
- Themes
- Satire, humour and technique
- Glossary
- 1. The visitor with a beard
- 2. The demand
- 3. Where the idea came from
- 4. The conference
- 5. Marks for nothing
- 6. The four examinations
- 7. The double trick, and the end

A man walks into his old school eighteen years after leaving it and asks for his
tuition fees back, on the grounds that he was taught nothing. To prove it, he sets
out to fail an examination on purpose. The school, to protect its reputation,
sets out to make sure he passes. *Refund* is a farce built on that single absurd
collision — and it is one of the sharpest attacks on examinations ever put on a
stage.

chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** Because he believes the school took his money and gave him nothing in
return. He had studied there for six years, eighteen years ago, and holds a leaving
certificate saying he was educated; but he has just been dismissed from his job, he
is penniless, and he cannot do anything. As he puts it, "Because I didn't get my
money's worth, that's why! This certificate here says I got an education. Well, I
didn't. I didn't learn anything and I want my money back." The immediate push came
from his old classmate Leaderer, who was making money on foreign exchange and told
him that if he did not even understand how, he should go and get his tuition fees
back.

**2.** Because his life has proved it to him. He has been "fired from my last job",
he is "quite broke", and he says plainly, "If I get a job I can't keep it." His
meeting with Leaderer was humiliating: a schoolfellow was growing rich by
speculating on the fall of Hungarian money, and Wasserkopf could not even follow
the explanation. He blames the school for it — "You took my money and you taught me
nothing. Now I'm no good for anything, and I can't do the things that I should have
learned in school" — and says bitterly that his education "made nothing but an
incompetent ass out of me."

**3.** They decided to conspire to make him pass. The Mathematics Master saw the
danger at once: "The object is to prevent him from failing, because if he fails he
succeeds." So the staff agreed to stick together, ask easy questions, and — the key
sentence — "Whatever his answers, we agree beforehand that they are correct," with
the Mathematics Master as the judge of what counted as correct. His motive was not
educational but institutional: if Wasserkopf got his money, "tomorrow there will be
two more former pupils, and the next day a dozen", and the school would face a
"pedagogical scandal".

**4.** Wasserkopf gave ridiculous answers deliberately, in order to **fail on
purpose**, because failing was the only way to prove his claim that the school had
taught him nothing and so recover his fees. He announces the plan openly: "Ask me
questions, professors — I mean, long-eared asses! I'd like to see you get a single
correct answer out of me," and "two times two is five, and I make up my own
multiplication tables as I go along." The teachers accepted the answers because of
their prior agreement, and because each of them, once cornered, could invent a
learned justification — Einstein and relativity for "seven meters", optical illusion
and the sad donkey for "You're an ass!", and the Barbarossa legend for "Same". They
were protecting the school's reputation, not judging his knowledge.

**5.** He describes Wasserkopf, before the examination begins, as "a sly, crafty
individual, who will try to get the better of us — and his money back — by hook or
crook", a man who has "pursued advanced studies in the school of life" and must be
checkmated. After the examination he reverses the description completely and calls
him a **"mathematical genius"**, because Wasserkopf worked out the total of six
years of fees, to the last heller, entirely in his head. Both descriptions are
accurate, and together they make the play's point: the man is genuinely able, and
the school never noticed.

**6.** By using his own greed against him. The Mathematics Master first pretended
to do exactly what Wasserkopf wanted — he rejected the answer of 2,629 litres
because the correct figure was 2,628, and declared, "I refuse to pass the
candidate. Mark him 'Failure.'" He then agreed that the refund was now
Wasserkopf's right and asked, innocently, "How much do we owe you, Herr
Wasserkopf?" Wasserkopf, "greedily, forgetting everything else", rattled off the
entire account to the heller — 6,450 crowns 50 heller. The Master checked it,
shook his hand and said, "I congratulate you! That was my difficult question." By
answering it perfectly, Wasserkopf had passed mathematics, and with it the whole
examination.

**7.** His demand is rejected completely. The Principal announces that "Herr
Wasserkopf has passed with distinction in every subject, and has again shown that
he is entitled to the certificate we awarded him on his graduation," and the staff
accept "a large share" of the congratulations for having taught him so excellently.
Since he has proved that his education was sound, there is no ground for a refund.
The Principal then drops the courtesy entirely — "get out before I have you thrown
out!" — and the Servant seizes him by the collar and the seat of his trousers and
rushes him off the stage. He leaves without a single crown.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** The theme of *Refund* is the **failure of an education system that issues
certificates instead of giving knowledge, and then defends itself rather than admit
it**. Several strands run out of that centre.

**Education as a commodity that was never delivered.** Wasserkopf's case is the
case of a dissatisfied customer: he paid, in crowns and heller, for six years of
schooling, and got nothing usable. "Because I didn't get my money's worth, that's
why!" The play gives his grievance real weight — he has lost his job, he cannot
keep another, and a classmate is growing rich by something he cannot even
understand.

**The certificate as a lie.** The paper says he was educated; Wasserkopf says he
was not; and the school's response is not to teach him, or even to test him, but to
reissue the paper. The last thing the Principal does before throwing him out is to
certify that he "is entitled to the certificate we awarded him on his graduation."
Nothing has changed except the volume of praise.

**Institutional self-protection.** Every decision in the play is taken to protect
the school's reputation. The Principal fears the inspector and the newspapers; the
Mathematics Master fears a queue of claimants — "if he fails, tomorrow there will
be two more former pupils, and the next day a dozen"; and the sentence "This is a
good school. It is our duty to see that nothing ever injures its reputation" is
spoken while the staff are falsifying an examination.

**The emptiness of marks.** Before any subject is examined, rudeness has been
marked "Manners: Excellent", refusing a chair has earned "Physical Culture:
Excellent", and greed has become "Ambition: Boundless". Karinthy's point is that
grades record what the institution needs to say, not what the pupil can do.

**Learning versus cleverness.** The deepest irony is saved for the end. Wasserkopf
really does possess an outstanding ability — he calculates six years of fees in his
head, to the heller, faster than the mathematics teacher can verify them. He is, as
the Master finally says, a "mathematical genius" who has "pursued advanced studies
in the school of life". The school spent six years on him and never found it.

The play therefore has two targets, not one: a system that certifies without
teaching, and a system that cannot see ability when it is standing in front of it.

**2.** **Wasserkopf** is one of the great comic creations of the modern one-act
stage — not a hero, not quite a villain, and completely convincing.

**Appearance and manner.** The stage direction introduces him as a bearded man
"carelessly dressed, somewhat under forty", who is "energetic and decided". He
enters the conference room without waiting to be shown in, hat over one ear, hands
in his pockets, "most truculent", and stares insolently at the staff.

**Aggressive and insulting.** His first words to the bowing masters are, "Who the
hell are you? Sit down, you loafers!" — and the stage direction adds that he
"grins, waiting to be thrown out", so the rudeness is calculated. He calls the
teachers long-eared asses, numskull, cannibal, whiskered baboon, hypocrite, nitwit
and old stick-in-the-mud, and gleefully reminds the Physics Master that it was he
who tied the string across the aisle to trip him up.

**Bitter and self-pitying.** Underneath the aggression is real defeat. He has been
sacked, he is broke, and he believes his life was ruined by six wasted years. His
bitterest line is aimed at himself as much as at the school: the education he
received "made nothing but an incompetent ass out of me."

**Greedy and shameless.** He is frank about the fact that money, not justice, is
his object: "If I were a rich man I'd tell you to keep them… But I'm not a rich
man, and I need the money." He intends to buy Leaderer a present out of the
proceeds, and he threatens the Ministry of Education within minutes of arriving.

**Cunning — but not cunning enough.** He is quick, watchful and hard to trap. When
he realises that standing up has earned him marks he sits down instantly: "You
caught me once, didn't you? Well, you won't do it again. From now I'll have my ears
open." He even reports the Physics Master for prompting him. Yet it is precisely
his greed that defeats him: the moment money is mentioned he forgets his guard, and
the Mathematics Master takes him.

**Genuinely able.** This is the point most students miss, and it lifts the
character out of farce. His mental arithmetic is faultless, instantaneous and
verified on paper by a professional mathematician. He also has a sharp, inventive
wit — "Same" and "seven meters" are not stupid answers but clever ones.

**Verdict.** His very name, Wasserkopf, means "water-head", or blockhead, and the
joke of the play is that it is wrong. He is coarse, dishonest and greedy, and he
deserves to be thrown out; but he is also the sanest voice in the room, and the
uncomfortable question he asks — what exactly did six years and 6,450 crowns buy? —
is never answered by anyone.

**3.** *Refund* is set in a Hungarian school of the 1930s, but every Nepali student
recognises it, which is itself an argument that the satire still bites.

**Where the play fits our situation.** Karinthy attacks three things: teaching that
produces no usable ability, examinations that can be passed without knowledge, and
institutions that defend their reputation instead of their standards. All three are
familiar. A student may complete school with a good grade sheet and still be unable
to write a job application, keep accounts, read a contract, use a spreadsheet, wire
a plug, or explain how a bank loan works. Every year thousands of certificate
holders leave for foreign employment to do work for which their certificates are
irrelevant. Wasserkopf's complaint — "I can't do the things that I should have
learned in school" — is heard in Nepali households constantly.

**Where the criticism is fair.** Our syllabus is wide but shallow; much of it is
learned for one paper and forgotten within a month. Practical, project and
laboratory work is often reduced to a formality. Career guidance is rare. And
because schools are judged publicly by their pass percentages, there is a
temptation — exactly the Principal's temptation — to protect the result rather than
the learning.

**Where the criticism is unfair.** Three things must be said in the school's
defence. First, Wasserkopf is not a reliable witness: nothing in the play suggests
he ever worked, and a pupil who learns nothing is not always the victim of a
teacher who taught nothing. Second, education is not only vocational training. The
ability to read a paragraph carefully, to argue without shouting, to follow an
argument in another language, to handle proportion and percentage — these do
prepare a person for life, even though no employer asks for them by name. Third,
much of what Wasserkopf wanted, such as knowing how foreign exchange works, is
learned after school, by anybody willing to ask.

**My own view.** The education system prepares students for **examinations** well
and for **life** only partly, and the gap is caused less by bad teachers than by a
structure in which everything that is not examined is quietly abandoned. The remedy
is not to abolish examinations but to change what they reward — projects, spoken
work, practical problems, real writing — together with serious career counselling
and work experience. Until then, Karinthy's play will keep being funny, which is
the least comfortable thing about it.

**4.** **Does memorisation dominate, and is the knowledge impractical?** To a large
extent, yes. Most of our examinations can be passed by reproducing remembered
material, so that is what students rationally do. The result is knowledge that
exists only in the form in which it was memorised: a student can state a
definition of interest and not calculate the interest on a real loan; can recite
the parts of a flower and not identify one in the field; can list the causes of
soil erosion and not connect them with the hillside behind the house. Karinthy
dramatises this exactly — his masters can produce impressive learned language
(relativity, the quantum theory, the law of conservation of energy) that explains
nothing whatever, and that is what unapplied knowledge sounds like.

But the accusation must be kept in proportion. Memorisation is not the enemy of
thinking; it is its raw material. Nobody thinks creatively in a subject whose basic
facts they do not hold in their head — multiplication tables, vocabulary, formulae,
dates, the shape of a map. The real complaint is not that we memorise, but that we
**stop** at memorising.

**Who is to blame?** No single party, and it is worth naming them honestly.

*The examination system* carries the largest share. It is the tail that wags the
dog: what is tested is taught, and what is not tested is dropped. As long as papers
reward reproduction, teaching will train reproduction.

*Curriculum and textbook design* comes next — courses that are too long for the

*Teachers* share it, though often without choice: large classes, little training in

the questions we ask in examinations, shorten and deepen the syllabus, train and
support teachers, and stop treating the certificate as the purpose of the exercise.

**5.** **Will a certificate earned only for the examination help in a career?** Up
to a point, and that point comes early.

**What a certificate does do.** It is a passport. It is required to apply, to sit a
selection test, to enrol in the next course, to obtain a licence, to go abroad for

**What a certificate cannot do.** It cannot keep the job it helped to obtain. This
is precisely Wasserkopf's position: he holds a leaving certificate from a
well-regarded school and says, "If I get a job I can't keep it." The certificate

follows selection is work, and work tests the thing itself and not the record of

references. A certificate obtained by cramming survives none of these.

**The play's warning to both sides.** Karinthy's ending is the sharpest possible
statement of the case. Wasserkopf leaves the school "passed with distinction in
every subject", carrying a second endorsement of his certificate — and he is thrown
out by the collar, as poor, as jobless and as unemployable as when he came in. The
paper improved; the man did not. That is what learning only for the examination
buys.

**A practical conclusion for a student reading this book.** Get the certificate; it
is necessary. But treat it as evidence of learning, not as a substitute for it, and
add to it the things no paper records — a language you can actually speak, a skill
you can demonstrate, work you have really done, and the habit of asking how
something works. Wasserkopf, ironically, had such a gift all along: a head for
figures that astonished a professional mathematician. Had he ever thought to
develop it instead of demanding a refund for it, the play would have had a
different ending.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (i) The speaker is **Wasserkopf**, the bearded, carelessly dressed man of
under forty who has come back to his old school after eighteen years. He is
speaking to **the Principal**, who has just risen from his desk and asked what he
can do for him.
(ii) He says them because the Principal, when told the name "Wasserkopf", has shaken
his head and said flatly, "No" — he does not remember him at all. Wasserkopf offers
the passage of time as an explanation ("It's possible I've changed"), swears in
irritation, and then appeals to the one thing that cannot forget him: the school's
**class records**, which will show that he really was a pupil there and therefore
that he has a legitimate claim on the institution. The words are the opening move
of his case; a moment later he states the claim itself — a refund of the tuition
fees paid for his education eighteen years ago. There is also hurt behind the
sentence. He adds, "You were probably glad to forget me," which tells us he was not
a successful or popular pupil, and his grievance is partly the grievance of a man
who was written off.
(iii) He is **in the Principal's office in a high school**, standing in front of the
flat-topped desk at which the Principal was seated when the play opened. He has just
been shown in by the Servant, and he "remains standing" — a small detail that
matters, because later his refusal to sit down will be awarded "Physical Culture:
Excellent".

**2.** (i) "How do you do?" is a **formal greeting, not a real question**. The
correct response is to repeat the same words — "How do you do?" — or to give some
equivalent courtesy such as "Good morning, gentlemen" or "Pleased to meet you",
usually with a bow or a handshake. No account of one's health is expected or wanted.
(ii) **No.** It is as impolite as it is possible to be. The staff have risen and
bowed to him "heartily", which is more courtesy than a former pupil could expect,
and he answers a formal greeting with an obscenity and an order. The discourtesy is
also **deliberate** — the stage direction says he "grins, waiting to be thrown
out", which shows that the rudeness is a tactic. If the staff throw him out, he can
go to the Ministry of Education; if they lose their tempers during the examination,
so much the better for him.
(iii) He rebukes them by refusing to recognise them as persons worth greeting —
"Who the hell are you?" — and then by commanding them like servants: **"Sit down,
you loafers!"** A *loafer* is an idler, so he is accusing the entire teaching staff
of being lazy and useless, which is the substance of his complaint against the
school put into a single word. It is the first of a long series of insults; he goes
on to call them long-eared asses, and the individual masters numskull, cannibal,
whiskered baboon, hypocrite, nitwit and old stick-in-the-mud.
(iv) "How dare you —" is the beginning of an angry rebuke, broken off. The Principal
means: *How do you have the impudence to speak to respectable teachers in that
manner in my school?* He is about to order Wasserkopf out, which is exactly what
Wasserkopf wants; and that is why the **Mathematics Master interrupts him** with
"Please!" and turns the insult into a compliment, declaring that Wasserkopf has
tactfully shown his approval of the school's "patriarchal manners" and awarding him
"Manners: Excellent". The unfinished sentence is therefore a small but crucial
piece of plotting: it marks the exact moment when the staff's conspiracy takes over
the play.

**3.** The line is Wasserkopf's answer to the Principal's question, "Why do you want
it back?", and it is the **thesis of the whole play** compressed into eight words.

**Its literal sense.** Wasserkopf is treating his schooling as a purchase. Fees were
paid over six years; in exchange the school undertook to educate him; the goods
were defective; he wants his money returned. He goes on immediately to state the
evidence: "This certificate here says I got an education. Well, I didn't. I didn't
learn anything and I want my money back."

**Why he believes it.** The proof, for him, is his life. He has just been dismissed
from his job; he is "quite broke"; "If I get a job I can't keep it"; and he has just
been humiliated in the street by a classmate who is making money on foreign
exchange while Wasserkopf cannot even understand what foreign exchange is. His
summary of the transaction is blunt: "You took my money and you taught me nothing.
Now I'm no good for anything, and I can't do the things that I should have learned
in school."

**What Karinthy is doing with it.** Three things. First, it turns education into a
**commercial contract**, which is the joke of the play — and the satire lies in the
fact that the school cannot find an honest answer to it. Second, it puts the
**certificate on trial**: a document certifies that something was delivered, and
the man holding it says it was not. Third, it is the line that forces the school to
reveal itself, because instead of examining what Wasserkopf knows, the staff agree
in advance that whatever he says is right.

**The irony.** By the end of the play the sentence has been turned inside out. The
school "proves" that he did get his money's worth — he passes with distinction in
every subject — and he is thrown out by the collar without a crown, exactly as poor
and as unemployable as when he arrived. Nothing about him has improved except his
grade sheet, which is Karinthy's final comment on what a certificate is worth.

self_checks.question: Model answers — short questions
self_checks.answer:
**1.** Because he believes the school took his money and gave him nothing in
return. He had studied there for six years, eighteen years ago, and holds a leaving
certificate saying he was educated; but he has just been dismissed from his job, he
is penniless, and he cannot do anything. As he puts it, "Because I didn't get my
money's worth, that's why! This certificate here says I got an education. Well, I
didn't. I didn't learn anything and I want my money back." The immediate push came
from his old classmate Leaderer, who was making money on foreign exchange and told
him that if he did not even understand how, he should go and get his tuition fees
back.

**2.** Because his life has proved it to him. He has been "fired from my last job",
he is "quite broke", and he says plainly, "If I get a job I can't keep it." His
meeting with Leaderer was humiliating: a schoolfellow was growing rich by
speculating on the fall of Hungarian money, and Wasserkopf could not even follow
the explanation. He blames the school for it — "You took my money and you taught me
nothing. Now I'm no good for anything, and I can't do the things that I should have
learned in school" — and says bitterly that his education "made nothing but an
incompetent ass out of me."

**3.** They decided to conspire to make him pass. The Mathematics Master saw the
danger at once: "The object is to prevent him from failing, because if he fails he
succeeds." So the staff agreed to stick together, ask easy questions, and — the key
sentence — "Whatever his answers, we agree beforehand that they are correct," with
the Mathematics Master as the judge of what counted as correct. His motive was not
educational but institutional: if Wasserkopf got his money, "tomorrow there will be
two more former pupils, and the next day a dozen", and the school would face a
"pedagogical scandal".

**4.** Wasserkopf gave ridiculous answers deliberately, in order to **fail on
purpose**, because failing was the only way to prove his claim that the school had
taught him nothing and so recover his fees. He announces the plan openly: "Ask me
questions, professors — I mean, long-eared asses! I'd like to see you get a single
correct answer out of me," and "two times two is five, and I make up my own
multiplication tables as I go along." The teachers accepted the answers because of
their prior agreement, and because each of them, once cornered, could invent a
learned justification — Einstein and relativity for "seven meters", optical illusion
and the sad donkey for "You're an ass!", and the Barbarossa legend for "Same". They
were protecting the school's reputation, not judging his knowledge.

**5.** He describes Wasserkopf, before the examination begins, as "a sly, crafty
individual, who will try to get the better of us — and his money back — by hook or
crook", a man who has "pursued advanced studies in the school of life" and must be
checkmated. After the examination he reverses the description completely and calls
him a **"mathematical genius"**, because Wasserkopf worked out the total of six
years of fees, to the last heller, entirely in his head. Both descriptions are
accurate, and together they make the play's point: the man is genuinely able, and
the school never noticed.

**6.** By using his own greed against him. The Mathematics Master first pretended
to do exactly what Wasserkopf wanted — he rejected the answer of 2,629 litres
because the correct figure was 2,628, and declared, "I refuse to pass the
candidate. Mark him 'Failure.'" He then agreed that the refund was now
Wasserkopf's right and asked, innocently, "How much do we owe you, Herr
Wasserkopf?" Wasserkopf, "greedily, forgetting everything else", rattled off the
entire account to the heller — 6,450 crowns 50 heller. The Master checked it,
shook his hand and said, "I congratulate you! That was my difficult question." By
answering it perfectly, Wasserkopf had passed mathematics, and with it the whole
examination.

**7.** His demand is rejected completely. The Principal announces that "Herr
Wasserkopf has passed with distinction in every subject, and has again shown that
he is entitled to the certificate we awarded him on his graduation," and the staff
accept "a large share" of the congratulations for having taught him so excellently.
Since he has proved that his education was sound, there is no ground for a refund.
The Principal then drops the courtesy entirely — "get out before I have you thrown
out!" — and the Servant seizes him by the collar and the seat of his trousers and
rushes him off the stage. He leaves without a single crown.

self_checks.question: Model answers — long questions
self_checks.answer:
**1.** The theme of *Refund* is the **failure of an education system that issues
certificates instead of giving knowledge, and then defends itself rather than admit
it**. Several strands run out of that centre.

**Education as a commodity that was never delivered.** Wasserkopf's case is the
case of a dissatisfied customer: he paid, in crowns and heller, for six years of
schooling, and got nothing usable. "Because I didn't get my money's worth, that's
why!" The play gives his grievance real weight — he has lost his job, he cannot
keep another, and a classmate is growing rich by something he cannot even
understand.

**The certificate as a lie.** The paper says he was educated; Wasserkopf says he
was not; and the school's response is not to teach him, or even to test him, but to
reissue the paper. The last thing the Principal does before throwing him out is to
certify that he "is entitled to the certificate we awarded him on his graduation."
Nothing has changed except the volume of praise.

**Institutional self-protection.** Every decision in the play is taken to protect
the school's reputation. The Principal fears the inspector and the newspapers; the
Mathematics Master fears a queue of claimants — "if he fails, tomorrow there will
be two more former pupils, and the next day a dozen"; and the sentence "This is a
good school. It is our duty to see that nothing ever injures its reputation" is
spoken while the staff are falsifying an examination.

**The emptiness of marks.** Before any subject is examined, rudeness has been
marked "Manners: Excellent", refusing a chair has earned "Physical Culture:
Excellent", and greed has become "Ambition: Boundless". Karinthy's point is that
grades record what the institution needs to say, not what the pupil can do.

**Learning versus cleverness.** The deepest irony is saved for the end. Wasserkopf
really does possess an outstanding ability — he calculates six years of fees in his
head, to the heller, faster than the mathematics teacher can verify them. He is, as
the Master finally says, a "mathematical genius" who has "pursued advanced studies
in the school of life". The school spent six years on him and never found it.

The play therefore has two targets, not one: a system that certifies without
teaching, and a system that cannot see ability when it is standing in front of it.

**2.** **Wasserkopf** is one of the great comic creations of the modern one-act
stage — not a hero, not quite a villain, and completely convincing.

**Appearance and manner.** The stage direction introduces him as a bearded man
"carelessly dressed, somewhat under forty", who is "energetic and decided". He
enters the conference room without waiting to be shown in, hat over one ear, hands
in his pockets, "most truculent", and stares insolently at the staff.

**Aggressive and insulting.** His first words to the bowing masters are, "Who the
hell are you? Sit down, you loafers!" — and the stage direction adds that he
"grins, waiting to be thrown out", so the rudeness is calculated. He calls the
teachers long-eared asses, numskull, cannibal, whiskered baboon, hypocrite, nitwit
and old stick-in-the-mud, and gleefully reminds the Physics Master that it was he
who tied the string across the aisle to trip him up.

**Bitter and self-pitying.** Underneath the aggression is real defeat. He has been
sacked, he is broke, and he believes his life was ruined by six wasted years. His
bitterest line is aimed at himself as much as at the school: the education he
received "made nothing but an incompetent ass out of me."

**Greedy and shameless.** He is frank about the fact that money, not justice, is
his object: "If I were a rich man I'd tell you to keep them… But I'm not a rich
man, and I need the money." He intends to buy Leaderer a present out of the
proceeds, and he threatens the Ministry of Education within minutes of arriving.

**Cunning — but not cunning enough.** He is quick, watchful and hard to trap. When
he realises that standing up has earned him marks he sits down instantly: "You
caught me once, didn't you? Well, you won't do it again. From now I'll have my ears
open." He even reports the Physics Master for prompting him. Yet it is precisely
his greed that defeats him: the moment money is mentioned he forgets his guard, and
the Mathematics Master takes him.

**Genuinely able.** This is the point most students miss, and it lifts the
character out of farce. His mental arithmetic is faultless, instantaneous and
verified on paper by a professional mathematician. He also has a sharp, inventive
wit — "Same" and "seven meters" are not stupid answers but clever ones.

**Verdict.** His very name, Wasserkopf, means "water-head", or blockhead, and the
joke of the play is that it is wrong. He is coarse, dishonest and greedy, and he
deserves to be thrown out; but he is also the sanest voice in the room, and the
uncomfortable question he asks — what exactly did six years and 6,450 crowns buy? —
is never answered by anyone.

**3.** *Refund* is set in a Hungarian school of the 1930s, but every Nepali student
recognises it, which is itself an argument that the satire still bites.

**Where the play fits our situation.** Karinthy attacks three things: teaching that
produces no usable ability, examinations that can be passed without knowledge, and
institutions that defend their reputation instead of their standards. All three are
familiar. A student may complete school with a good grade sheet and still be unable
to write a job application, keep accounts, read a contract, use a spreadsheet, wire
a plug, or explain how a bank loan works. Every year thousands of certificate
holders leave for foreign employment to do work for which their certificates are
irrelevant. Wasserkopf's complaint — "I can't do the things that I should have
learned in school" — is heard in Nepali households constantly.

**Where the criticism is fair.** Our syllabus is wide but shallow; much of it is
learned for one paper and forgotten within a month. Practical, project and
laboratory work is often reduced to a formality. Career guidance is rare. And
because schools are judged publicly by their pass percentages, there is a
temptation — exactly the Principal's temptation — to protect the result rather than
the learning.

**Where the criticism is unfair.** Three things must be said in the school's
defence. First, Wasserkopf is not a reliable witness: nothing in the play suggests
he ever worked, and a pupil who learns nothing is not always the victim of a
teacher who taught nothing. Second, education is not only vocational training. The
ability to read a paragraph carefully, to argue without shouting, to follow an
argument in another language, to handle proportion and percentage — these do
prepare a person for life, even though no employer asks for them by name. Third,
much of what Wasserkopf wanted, such as knowing how foreign exchange works, is
learned after school, by anybody willing to ask.

**My own view.** The education system prepares students for **examinations** well
and for **life** only partly, and the gap is caused less by bad teachers than by a
structure in which everything that is not examined is quietly abandoned. The remedy
is not to abolish examinations but to change what they reward — projects, spoken
work, practical problems, real writing — together with serious career counselling
and work experience. Until then, Karinthy's play will keep being funny, which is
the least comfortable thing about it.

**4.** **Does memorisation dominate, and is the knowledge impractical?** To a large
extent, yes. Most of our examinations can be passed by reproducing remembered
material, so that is what students rationally do. The result is knowledge that
exists only in the form in which it was memorised: a student can state a
definition of interest and not calculate the interest on a real loan; can recite
the parts of a flower and not identify one in the field; can list the causes of
soil erosion and not connect them with the hillside behind the house. Karinthy
dramatises this exactly — his masters can produce impressive learned language
(relativity, the quantum theory, the law of conservation of energy) that explains
nothing whatever, and that is what unapplied knowledge sounds like.

But the accusation must be kept in proportion. Memorisation is not the enemy of
thinking; it is its raw material. Nobody thinks creatively in a subject whose basic
facts they do not hold in their head — multiplication tables, vocabulary, formulae,
dates, the shape of a map. The real complaint is not that we memorise, but that we
**stop** at memorising.

**Who is to blame?** No single party, and it is worth naming them honestly.

*The examination system* carries the largest share. It is the tail that wags the
dog: what is tested is taught, and what is not tested is dropped. As long as papers
reward reproduction, teaching will train reproduction.

*Curriculum and textbook design* comes next — courses that are too long for the
time given force teachers to cover rather than teach, and coverage is always
memorisation.

*Teachers* share it, though often without choice: large classes, little training in

*Schools and their managements* share it, and this is Karinthy's chief target —
institutions whose reputation depends on pass percentages have an interest in

*Parents and society* share it, for measuring children by grade sheets and by the

*And students share it too.* Wasserkopf, we should notice, never claims to have

The honest conclusion is that blame is distributed, and so is the remedy: change

**5.** **Will a certificate earned only for the examination help in a career?** Up

**What a certificate does do.** It is a passport. It is required to apply, to sit a
selection test, to enrol in the next course, to obtain a licence, to go abroad for

**What a certificate cannot do.** It cannot keep the job it helped to obtain. This

opened doors for eighteen years and closed them again each time, because what

**The play's warning to both sides.** Karinthy's ending is the sharpest possible
statement of the case. Wasserkopf leaves the school "passed with distinction in

out by the collar, as poor, as jobless and as unemployable as when he came in. The
paper improved; the man did not. That is what learning only for the examination
buys.

**A practical conclusion for a student reading this book.** Get the certificate; it
is necessary. But treat it as evidence of learning, not as a substitute for it, and
add to it the things no paper records — a language you can actually speak, a skill
you can demonstrate, work you have really done, and the habit of asking how
something works. Wasserkopf, ironically, had such a gift all along: a head for
figures that astonished a professional mathematician. Had he ever thought to
develop it instead of demanding a refund for it, the play would have had a
different ending.

chapters.name: Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dictionary Use
topics: Nouns: countable, uncountable and the forms Nepali learners mix up
Verbs: main, auxiliary and the five forms
chapters.summary:
- The eight classes are noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition,
  conjunction and determiner; class is decided by the job the word does in *that*
  sentence, not by its spelling.
- Uncountable nouns — *information, advice, furniture, luggage, equipment, news,
  work, traffic* — have no plural and take no *a/an*; count them with *a piece of*.
- Every verb has five forms: V1, -s, V2, V3, -ing. Learn irregulars as a row.
- Only transitive verbs have objects, and only transitive verbs can be made passive.
- Do not add prepositions English does not want: *discuss, return, reach, enter,
  marry, resemble, emphasise, comprise* take a direct object.
- Contractions replace missing letters with an apostrophe: *'s* = is/has,
  *'d* = had/would; *won't* and *shan't* are irregular; *its* ≠ *it's*.

chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- The eight word classes
- Nouns: countable, uncountable and the forms Nepali learners mix up
- Pronouns
- Verbs: main, auxiliary and the five forms
- Adjectives and adverbs
- Words that change class
- Contracted forms
- Using a dictionary

Every word in English belongs to a **word class** (also called a part of speech),
and the class decides where the word may stand in a sentence and what shape it may
take. Question 7 of the NEB paper is ten one-mark grammar items, and several of
them turn on class: you are asked to put the right *form* of a word in a blank
(`The ____ of the bridge took two years. (construct)`), to identify what a word is
doing, or to correct a sentence in which a noun has been used where an adjective
was needed. This chapter also covers contracted forms — tested in rewriting and in
dialogue-completion items — and how to pull grammar information out of a
dictionary, which is what the CDC syllabus means by "dictionary use".

## Chapter summary

- The eight classes are noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition,
  conjunction and determiner; class is decided by the job the word does in *that*
  sentence, not by its spelling.
- Uncountable nouns — *information, advice, furniture, luggage, equipment, news,
  work, traffic* — have no plural and take no *a/an*; count them with *a piece of*.
- Every verb has five forms: V1, -s, V2, V3, -ing. Learn irregulars as a row.
- Only transitive verbs have objects, and only transitive verbs can be made passive.
- Do not add prepositions English does not want: *discuss, return, reach, enter,
  marry, resemble, emphasise, comprise* take a direct object.
- Contractions replace missing letters with an apostrophe: *'s* = is/has,
  *'d* = had/would; *won't* and *shan't* are irregular; *its* ≠ *it's*.
- A dictionary entry gives class, countability [C]/[U], transitivity [T]/[I], verb
  pattern and register — all the grammar a Q7 item can test.

## Study route

Read the topics and identify unfamiliar terms.

Close the book and explain the key ideas in your own words.

Attempt a worked example before revealing its solution.

Complete the chapter practice, correct mistakes, then mark the chapter revised.
chapters.question_answers:
## Worked transformation 21.1 — choosing the right derived form

**Problem.** Fill in the blank: *The ____ of the Melamchi project changed
Kathmandu's water supply. (complete)*

**Solution — four steps.**

1. **Find the slot.** The blank comes after *The* and before *of*. A slot after a
   determiner is a **noun** slot.
2. **Confirm with the verb.** The sentence already has a finite verb, *changed*.
   So the blank is not the verb; it is the subject head noun.
3. **Build the noun from the cue.** *complete* → noun *completion*.
4. **Check number and article.** Singular, definite: *The completion*.

**Answer.** *The **completion** of the Melamchi project changed Kathmandu's water
supply.*

Writing *completed* would give a subject with no head noun; writing *completely*
would put an adverb after *the*, which is impossible.

## Worked transformation 21.2 — expanding contractions in formal rewriting

**Problem.** Rewrite formally: *They've told us they won't come, so we'd better
start without them.*

**Solution — step by step.**

1. **Mark every apostrophe:** *They've*, *won't*, *we'd*.
2. **Expand each, deciding the ambiguous ones from what follows.** *They've* + past
   participle *told* = *they have*. *won't* = *will not* (irregular). *we'd* +
   *better* = *we had* (the fixed phrase is *had better*).
3. **Rewrite, keeping everything else unchanged.**

**Answer.** *They **have** told us they **will not** come, so we **had** better
start without them.*

## Worked transformation 21.3 — labelling word class in a test sentence

**Problem.** State the word class of each underlined word: *Unfortunately, the
**bus** from Pokhara **arrived** very **late** **because** of the landslide.*

**Solution.**

| Word | Test applied | Class |
|---|---|---|
| bus | follows the determiner *the*; is the thing doing the arriving | **noun** |
| arrived | carries the tense; can become *arrives / will arrive* | **verb** |
| late | tells us *when* about the verb *arrived*; not describing a noun | **adverb** |
| because | joins the main clause to the reason that follows | **conjunction** |

Note that *late* would be an **adjective** in *the late bus*, where it describes
the noun. Always test the word in its own sentence.

## Topics to cover

- The twelve tenses at a glance
- The present tenses
- The past tenses
- The future tenses and other ways of talking about the future
- Signal words — the fastest way to spot the tense
- Worked transformations
- Simple present
- Present continuous
- Present perfect
- Present perfect continuous
- Simple past
- Past continuous
- Past perfect
- Past perfect continuous
- Simple future
- Future continuous
- Future perfect and future perfect continuous
- Three other future forms you must recognise

Tense is how an English verb shows **time**; aspect is how it shows whether the
action is finished, still going on, or both. Together they give twelve verb forms,
and almost every NEB Q7 paper contains two or three tense items — usually a blank
with the base verb in brackets (*She ____ in Biratnagar since 2015. (live)*) or a
sentence to correct. The whole area is learnable because each tense has one fixed
structure and a small set of signal words that give it away.

## Chapter summary

- Tense = time; aspect = simple / continuous / perfect / perfect continuous. Three
  times × four aspects = twelve forms.
- Structures: V1(+s) · am-is-are + V-ing · have/has + V3 · have/has been + V-ing ·
  V2 · was/were + V-ing · had + V3 · had been + V-ing · will + V1 · will be +
  V-ing · will have + V3 · will have been + V-ing.
- Third-person singular takes **-s** in the simple present, and loses it after
  *does/doesn't*.
- After *did / didn't / does / doesn't*, the main verb is always **V1**.
- A finished past time word (*yesterday, ago, last year*) forces the simple past;
  *since, for, just, already, yet* force the present perfect.
- Stative verbs (*have* = own, know, like, agree, understand, see, belong) take no
  continuous form.

  by the time* and in an *if*-clause of condition.
- Of two past actions, the earlier takes the **past perfect**.

chapters.question_answers:
## Worked transformation 22.1 — fill in with the correct tense

**Problem.** *My elder sister ____ in a hospital in Dharan since 2018. (work)*

**Solution — step by step.**

1. **Read the time marker.** *since 2018* means the period starts in the past and
   runs up to now. That rules out the simple past.
2. **Time = present, reaching back.** So the tense must be a **perfect** present
   form.
3. **Is it still going on?** Yes — she still works there. With *since* plus a
   continuing state, both present perfect and present perfect continuous are used;
   with a long-term job, the **present perfect** is the standard answer.
4. **Fit the subject.** *My elder sister* is third-person singular → *has*.

**Answer.** *My elder sister **has worked** (or **has been working**) in a hospital
in Dharan since 2018.*

## Worked transformation 22.2 — two past actions in the right order

**Problem.** Join into one sentence using the correct tenses:
*The doctor arrived. The patient died before that.*

**Solution — step by step.**

1. **List the two events and put them in real time order.** (i) the patient died —
   earlier; (ii) the doctor arrived — later.
2. **Rule:** the **earlier** past event takes the **past perfect**; the later one
   takes the **simple past**.
3. **Choose the joining word.** *before* goes after the later event, or *by the
   time* starts the later event.
4. **Write it.**

**Answer.** *The patient **had died** before the doctor **arrived**.*
(Equally: *By the time the doctor **arrived**, the patient **had died**.*)

A common wrong answer is *The patient died before the doctor had arrived*, which
reverses the order and says the arrival was earlier.

## Worked transformation 22.3 — correcting a tense error

**Problem.** Correct: *When I reached the bus park, the bus already left, so I am
waiting there for two hours.*

**Solution — step by step.**

1. **Check clause 1.** *When I reached* — a finished past time. Simple past is
   correct. Leave it.
2. **Check clause 2.** The bus left **before** I reached; two past events, the
   earlier one needs the **past perfect**: *had already left*.
3. **Check clause 3.** *for two hours*, and the waiting happened in the past, up to
   a past point — so past perfect continuous is wrong (the waiting came *after*),
   and the present *am waiting* is wrong because the whole sentence is past. The
   waiting was a past duration: **waited** (simple past) or **had to wait**.

**Answer.** *When I reached the bus park, the bus **had** already left, so I
**waited** there for two hours.*
