chapters.summary:
- A singular countable noun needs a determiner: *a/an*, *the*, a possessive or a
  demonstrative. A bare singular countable noun is almost always an error.
- *a/an* = first mention or one of a class; *the* = the listener knows which one.
- *an* goes before a vowel **sound** (*an hour, an MA*), *a* before a consonant
  **sound** (*a university, a one-rupee coin*).
- *the* with: second mention, unique things, superlatives, ordinals, rivers, seas,
  mountain ranges, plural country names, newspapers, nationalities, instruments.
- **No article** with: general plurals, general uncountables, names, languages,
  subjects, meals, games, festivals, *by* + transport, and places used for their
  purpose (*go to school, in hospital, in bed*).
- *many/few/a few* + plural countable; *much/little/a little* + uncountable;
  *some/any/a lot of/plenty of* with both.
- *a few* and *a little* are positive ("some"); *few* and *little* are negative
  ("hardly any").
- After *one of / each of / neither of*, the noun is plural and the verb singular.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- The noun phrase and the order of determiners
- The indefinite article: *a* and *an*
- The definite article: *the*
- The zero article — where students actually lose the mark
- Demonstratives and possessives
- Quantifiers
- many / much / a lot of
- few / a few / little / a little
- some / any
- each / every / all / both / either / neither

A **determiner** is the little word that opens a noun phrase and tells you how much
of the noun is meant and which one: *the, a, an, this, my, some, every, three, much*.
The three articles — *a*, *an* and **zero** (no article at all) — are the part
Nepali learners lose most marks on, because Nepali has no article system. NEB Q7
tests articles almost every year, usually as a fill-in-the-blank passage or as an
error-correction item where an article is missing or wrongly present.

## Chapter summary

- A singular countable noun needs a determiner: *a/an*, *the*, a possessive or a
  demonstrative. A bare singular countable noun is almost always an error.
- *a/an* = first mention or one of a class; *the* = the listener knows which one.
- *an* goes before a vowel **sound** (*an hour, an MA*), *a* before a consonant
  **sound** (*a university, a one-rupee coin*).
- *the* with: second mention, unique things, superlatives, ordinals, rivers, seas,
  mountain ranges, plural country names, newspapers, nationalities, instruments.
- **No article** with: general plurals, general uncountables, names, languages,
  subjects, meals, games, festivals, *by* + transport, and places used for their
  purpose (*go to school, in hospital, in bed*).
- *many/few/a few* + plural countable; *much/little/a little* + uncountable;
  *some/any/a lot of/plenty of* with both.
- *a few* and *a little* are positive ("some"); *few* and *little* are negative
  ("hardly any").
- After *one of / each of / neither of*, the noun is plural and the verb singular.

chapters.question_answers:
## Worked transformation 23.1 — filling a short article passage

**Problem.** *Yesterday I saw ____ old man near ____ Bagmati bridge. ____ man was
carrying ____ heavy sack of rice.*

**Solution — step by step.**

1. **Blank 1.** *old man* is singular countable, first mention. Article needed. The
   sound at the start of *old* is a vowel → **an**.
2. **Blank 2.** *Bagmati* is a river, and rivers take **the**.
3. **Blank 3.** The man has already been mentioned, so the listener knows which man
   → **The**.
4. **Blank 4.** *sack* is singular countable, first mention; *heavy* begins with a
   consonant sound → **a**.

**Answer.** *Yesterday I saw **an** old man near **the** Bagmati bridge. **The**
man was carrying **a** heavy sack of rice.*

## Worked transformation 23.2 — choosing between *few* and *a few*

**Problem.** Choose: *(Few / A few) people attended the meeting, so it was
cancelled.*

**Solution — step by step.**

1. **Check the noun.** *people* is plural countable → the pair is *few / a few*
   (not *little*).
2. **Read the result clause.** *so it was cancelled* tells us the number was
   **not enough** — a negative meaning.
3. **Match the meaning.** Negative, "hardly any" → **few**. *A few* would mean
   "some came", which does not explain a cancellation.

**Answer.** ***Few** people attended the meeting, so it was cancelled.*

## Worked transformation 23.3 — correcting an article error

**Problem.** Correct: *The honesty is the best policy, and the poor of our country
need an information about their rights.*

**Solution — step by step.**

1. ***The honesty***. *Honesty* is an abstract uncountable noun used in a general
   sense → **no article**.
2. ***the best policy***. A superlative takes **the**. Correct as it stands.
3. ***the poor***. An adjective used as a plural noun for a class takes **the**.
   Correct.
4. ***an information***. *Information* is uncountable, so it can take no *a/an* and
   no plural → **information**, or **a piece of information** if one item is meant.

**Answer.** ***Honesty** is the best policy, and the poor of our country need
**information** about their rights.*

chapters.name: Modal Verbs and Semi-modals
topics: Past forms of modals and what they criticise
chapters.summary:
- A modal takes the bare infinitive, never adds *-s*, needs no *do* for questions
  and negatives, and cannot be joined to another modal.
- Ability: *can* (now), *could* (past, general), *was/were able to* (one past
  success), *be able to* (all other forms).
- Permission rises in formality: *can → could → may → might*.
- Obligation: *must* (from the speaker), *have to* (from outside), *had to* (past),
  *should / ought to / had better* (advice).
- *mustn't* = forbidden; *needn't* and *don't have to* = not necessary. They are
  opposites, not synonyms.
- Certainty scale: *must* (sure it is) > *will* > *should* > *may* > *might/could*
  > *may not* > *can't* (sure it is not).
- For the past, add *have* + V3: *must have gone, might have gone, can't have gone*.
- *should have* + V3 criticises what was not done; *needn't have* + V3 says
  something done was unnecessary.
- Semi-modals — *be able to, have to, need to, used to, be going to, had better,
  would rather, be supposed to* — carry modal meanings but behave like ordinary
  verbs.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- The complete modal table
- Ability: *can*, *could*, *be able to*
- Permission, requests, offers and suggestions
- Obligation, necessity and their negatives
- Degrees of certainty — deduction
- Past forms of modals and what they criticise
- Semi-modals

A **modal verb** is a helping verb that does not describe an action but colours it:
it says whether the action is possible, permitted, necessary, advisable or likely.
The nine pure modals are *can, could, may, might, will, would, shall, should* and
*must*. NEB Q7 tests them in three ways — choose the right modal for a stated
function, rewrite a sentence with a modal of the same meaning (*It is necessary for
you to go* → *You must go*), or correct a sentence in which the modal is followed
by the wrong verb form.

## Chapter summary

- A modal takes the bare infinitive, never adds *-s*, needs no *do* for questions
  and negatives, and cannot be joined to another modal.
- Ability: *can* (now), *could* (past, general), *was/were able to* (one past
  success), *be able to* (all other forms).
- Permission rises in formality: *can → could → may → might*.
- Obligation: *must* (from the speaker), *have to* (from outside), *had to* (past),
  *should / ought to / had better* (advice).
- *mustn't* = forbidden; *needn't* and *don't have to* = not necessary. They are
  opposites, not synonyms.
- Certainty scale: *must* (sure it is) > *will* > *should* > *may* > *might/could*
  > *may not* > *can't* (sure it is not).
- For the past, add *have* + V3: *must have gone, might have gone, can't have gone*.
- *should have* + V3 criticises what was not done; *needn't have* + V3 says
  something done was unnecessary.
- Semi-modals — *be able to, have to, need to, used to, be going to, had better,
  would rather, be supposed to* — carry modal meanings but behave like ordinary
  verbs.

chapters.question_answers:
## Worked transformation 24.1 — a rewrite with the same meaning

**Problem.** Rewrite using a modal: *It is not necessary for you to attend the
Saturday class.*

**Solution — step by step.**

1. **Name the function.** "It is not necessary" = **absence of obligation**.
2. **Pick the modal for that function.** Absence of obligation is *needn't* or
   *don't have to*. It is **not** *mustn't*, which would mean the class is
   forbidden.
3. **Fit the subject and the bare infinitive.** *you* + *needn't* + *attend*.

**Answer.** *You **needn't attend** the Saturday class.*
(Also correct: *You **don't have to** attend the Saturday class.*)

## Worked transformation 24.2 — a deduction about the past

**Problem.** Express as a deduction: *I am sure Anita did not take the bus, because
her bicycle is missing.*

**Solution — step by step.**

1. **Is the statement positive or negative?** Negative — "did not take".
2. **How sure is the speaker?** Completely sure. On the certainty scale, "certain
   it is NOT true" is **can't**.
3. **Is the event past?** Yes, so add **have + V3** after the modal:
   *can't have taken*.
4. **Assemble.**

**Answer.** *Anita **can't have taken** the bus, because her bicycle is missing.*

Writing *mustn't have taken* is wrong: *mustn't* means prohibition, never negative
deduction.

## Worked transformation 24.3 — correcting a modal error

**Problem.** Correct: *When he was young he can run very fast, but now he will not
can run at all because he had better to rest his knee.*

**Solution — step by step.**

1. ***he can run* in a past sentence.** The time is past and the meaning is general
   ability → **could run**.
2. ***will not can run*.** Two modals cannot stand together. Replace the second with
   the semi-modal → **will not be able to run**.
3. ***had better to rest*.** *Had better* takes the bare infinitive → **had better
   rest**.

**Answer.** *When he was young he **could** run very fast, but now he **will not be
able to** run at all because he **had better rest** his knee.*

chapters.name: Passive Voice and Causatives
topics: The five steps of the transformation
Modals, infinitives and gerunds in the passive
Questions, imperatives and other special sentences
When and why the passive is used
chapters.summary:
- Passive = subject + correct form of **be** + **V3** (+ *by* + agent). Only
  transitive verbs have a passive.
- The tense never changes in a voice transformation; only the form of *be* does.
- Passive forms: is/are + V3 · is/are being + V3 · has/have been + V3 · was/were +
  V3 · was/were being + V3 · had been + V3 · will be + V3 · will have been + V3.
- The four **continuous-perfect** and **future continuous** tenses have no passive.
- Modals: modal + **be** + V3; past modals: modal + **have been** + V3.
- Verbs with two objects give two passives; the person-first one is more natural,
  and the thing-first one needs *to/for* before the person.
- Imperatives become *Let + object + be + V3*, or *You are requested to …*.
- *Who* → *By whom* in the passive question; pronouns after *by* take the object
  form.
- Causatives: *have/get + thing + V3* (a service), *make/let/have + person + V1*,
  *get + person + to + V1*. In the passive, *make* takes *to*.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- The five steps of the transformation
- The passive of every tense
- Modals, infinitives and gerunds in the passive
- Verbs with two objects
- Questions, imperatives and other special sentences
- When and why the passive is used
- Causative verbs

**Voice** tells you whether the subject of the sentence *does* the action or
*receives* it. In the active voice the doer is the subject (*The committee
approved the plan*); in the passive the receiver becomes the subject (*The plan was
approved by the committee*). NEB Q7 almost always contains one voice item, phrased
"Change into passive voice" or "Change into active voice". Causatives — *get the
house painted*, *have my hair cut* — are the passive's close relative and are
tested in the same question.

## Chapter summary

- Passive = subject + correct form of **be** + **V3** (+ *by* + agent). Only
  transitive verbs have a passive.
- The tense never changes in a voice transformation; only the form of *be* does.
- Passive forms: is/are + V3 · is/are being + V3 · has/have been + V3 · was/were +
  V3 · was/were being + V3 · had been + V3 · will be + V3 · will have been + V3.
- The four **continuous-perfect** and **future continuous** tenses have no passive.
- Modals: modal + **be** + V3; past modals: modal + **have been** + V3.
- Verbs with two objects give two passives; the person-first one is more natural,
  and the thing-first one needs *to/for* before the person.
- Imperatives become *Let + object + be + V3*, or *You are requested to …*.
- *Who* → *By whom* in the passive question; pronouns after *by* take the object
  form.
- Causatives: *have/get + thing + V3* (a service), *make/let/have + person + V1*,
  *get + person + to + V1*. In the passive, *make* takes *to*.

chapters.question_answers:
## Worked transformation 25.1 — active to passive, step by step

**Problem.** Change into the passive: *The municipality has cleared the garbage
from the riverbank.*

**Solution — the five steps.**

1. **Find the object.** *has cleared **what**?* → *the garbage from the riverbank*.
   The head of the object is *the garbage*.
2. **Move it to the front.** *The garbage from the riverbank …*
3. **Change the verb.** The active is **present perfect** (*has cleared*), so the
   passive is *have/has + been + V3*. The new subject *garbage* is singular →
   **has been cleared**.
4. **Attach the agent.** Old subject *the municipality* → *by the municipality*.
5. **Keep or drop the agent?** It is specific and informative, so keep it.

**Answer.** *The garbage **has been cleared** from the riverbank **by the
municipality**.*

## Worked transformation 25.2 — passive of a question

**Problem.** Change into the passive: *Who wrote this poem?*

**Solution — step by step.**

1. **Identify the parts.** Subject = *Who*; verb = *wrote* (simple past); object =
   *this poem*.
2. **The object becomes the subject.** *This poem …*
3. **Change the verb.** Simple past → *was/were* + V3. *Poem* is singular →
   **was written**.
4. **The subject *who* becomes the agent.** After *by*, *who* becomes *whom*:
   *by whom*.
5. **Keep it a question.** A wh- question begins with the wh- element, so *By whom*
   comes first and the auxiliary comes before the subject.

**Answer.** ***By whom was this poem written?***

(*Who was this poem written by?* is the informal version and is also accepted.)

## Worked transformation 25.3 — passive to active, and a causative

**Problem.** (a) Change into the active: *The injured were being carried to the
hospital by the volunteers.* (b) Rewrite using a causative: *A mechanic repaired my
scooter yesterday.*

**Solution.**

**(a)** 1. The agent *by the volunteers* becomes the subject → *The volunteers*.
2. The passive verb *were being carried* is **past continuous**, so the active is
*was/were* + V-ing → *were carrying*. 3. The passive subject *the injured* becomes
the object.
**Answer:** *The volunteers **were carrying** the injured to the hospital.*

**(b)** 1. The service was done for me by someone else, so use *have/get + object +
V3*. 2. The time is past, so *have* becomes *had*. 3. Order: *had* + *my scooter* +
*repaired*.
**Answer:** *I **had my scooter repaired** yesterday.* (Or *I **got** my scooter
**repaired** yesterday.*)

chapters.name: Reported Speech
topics: The reporting verb and the link word
Reporting commands, requests, advice and suggestions
chapters.summary:
- Four changes, in order: reporting verb and link → tense → pronouns → time and
  place words.
- *Tell* needs a person after it; *say* does not take one unless you add *to*.
- No backshift when the reporting verb is present or future, when the statement is a
  universal truth or still true, when a past time is stated, or in unreal
  conditionals and *wish* clauses.
- Backshift ladder: present → past; present perfect and simple past → past perfect;
  will → would; can → could; may → might; must → had to. Past perfect does not move.
- Statements take *that*; wh- questions keep the wh- word; yes/no questions take
  *if/whether*; commands and requests take *to* / *not to* + V1.
- Reported questions use **statement word order**, drop *do/does/did*, and lose the
  question mark.
- Exclamations are reported by naming the feeling: *exclaimed with joy / sorrow /
  wonder that …*.
- Pronouns follow SON: first person matches the **S**ubject of the reporting verb,
  second person matches the **O**bject, third person is **N**ot changed.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- The reporting verb and the link word
- The complete backshift table
- Pronoun changes
- Changes of time and place
- Reporting statements
- Reporting questions
- Reporting commands, requests, advice and suggestions
- Reporting exclamations and wishes

**Direct speech** repeats a speaker's exact words inside quotation marks; **reported
(indirect) speech** puts those words into your own sentence with no quotation marks.
NEB Q7 sets one or two items every year, worded "Change into indirect speech" or
"Report the following sentence". The change is completely mechanical: pick the right
reporting verb, backshift the tense, change the pronouns, and change the words for
time and place. Do those four things in that order and the item cannot go wrong.

## Chapter summary

- Four changes, in order: reporting verb and link → tense → pronouns → time and
  place words.
- *Tell* needs a person after it; *say* does not take one unless you add *to*.
- No backshift when the reporting verb is present or future, when the statement is a
  universal truth or still true, when a past time is stated, or in unreal
  conditionals and *wish* clauses.
- Backshift ladder: present → past; present perfect and simple past → past perfect;
  will → would; can → could; may → might; must → had to. Past perfect does not move.
- Statements take *that*; wh- questions keep the wh- word; yes/no questions take
  *if/whether*; commands and requests take *to* / *not to* + V1.
- Reported questions use **statement word order**, drop *do/does/did*, and lose the
  question mark.
- Exclamations are reported by naming the feeling: *exclaimed with joy / sorrow /
  wonder that …*.
- Pronouns follow SON: first person matches the **S**ubject of the reporting verb,
  second person matches the **O**bject, third person is **N**ot changed.

Close the book and explain the key ideas in your own words.

Complete the chapter practice, correct mistakes, then mark the chapter revised.
chapters.question_answers:
## Worked transformation 26.1 — a statement

**Problem.** Change into indirect speech: *Ram said to his sister, "I am going to
Kathmandu tomorrow to buy books for you."*

**Solution — the four changes.**

1. **Reporting verb and link.** It is a statement, and there is a listener, so
   *said to* → **told**, and the link is **that**.
2. **Tense.** *am going* is present continuous, and the reporting verb *said* is
   past → backshift to past continuous: **was going**.
3. **Pronouns.** *I* is the speaker Ram → **he**. *you* is the listener, his sister
   → **her**.
4. **Time words.** *tomorrow* → **the next day**.

**Answer.** *Ram **told** his sister **that he was going** to Kathmandu **the next
day** to buy books for **her**.*

## Worked transformation 26.2 — a yes/no question

**Problem.** Change into indirect speech: *The conductor said to me, "Did you buy a
ticket at the counter?"*

**Solution — step by step.**

1. **Sentence type.** The question mark and the auxiliary *Did* at the front make it
   a **yes/no question** → reporting verb **asked**, link **if / whether**.
2. **Word order.** Reported questions use statement order, so *you buy* becomes
   *I … buy* with no inversion.
3. **Drop the auxiliary.** *Did* disappears; its past tense goes onto the main verb,
   which then backshifts one further step: *buy* → *bought* → **had bought**.
4. **Pronouns.** *you* is the listener, who is *me* → **I**.
5. **Remove the question mark.**

**Answer.** *The conductor **asked me if (whether) I had bought** a ticket at the
counter.*

## Worked transformation 26.3 — a command and an exclamation together

**Problem.** Change into indirect speech: *"Don't waste water, children!" said the
teacher. "What a precious thing it is!"*

**Solution — step by step.**

1. **First sentence is a negative command.** Reporting verb **told** (or *ordered*);
   the imperative becomes **not to + V1**: *not to waste*.
2. **The addressee** *children* becomes the object of the reporting verb: *told the
   children*.
3. **Second sentence is an exclamation.** Reporting verb **exclaimed**, or better,
   *added, exclaiming*. Unpack *What a precious thing* into *a very precious thing*
   and add the link **that**.
4. **Backshift the exclamation clause.** *is* → **was**.

**Answer.** *The teacher **told the children not to waste** water and **exclaimed
that** it **was a very precious thing**.*

chapters.name: Conditional Sentences
topics: The shape of a conditional sentence
The five types in one table
Other ways of expressing a condition
chapters.summary:
- Type 0: *if* + present, present — always true.
- Type 1: *if* + present, **will** + V1 — a real future possibility.
- Type 2: *if* + past (*were* for all persons), **would** + V1 — unreal present.
- Type 3: *if* + had + V3, **would have** + V3 — unreal past, regret.
- Mixed: *if* + had + V3, **would** + V1 (past cause, present result); *if* + past,
  **would have** + V3 (present cause, past result).
- Never put *will* or *would* in the *if*-clause.
- A comma follows the *if*-clause only when it comes first.
- *Unless* = *if … not*, so do not add a second negative.
- *Were I…*, *Had I…*, *Should you…* are the inverted forms with *if* dropped.
- *Wish* + past = a present regret; *wish* + past perfect = a past regret;
  *wish* + *would* = annoyance.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- The shape of a conditional sentence
- The five types in one table
- Type 0 — the zero conditional
- Type 1 — the real future conditional
- Type 2 — the unreal present conditional
- Type 3 — the unreal past conditional
- Mixed conditionals
- Other ways of expressing a condition
- Leaving out *if* — inversion
- Unreal forms related to conditionals

A **conditional sentence** has two parts: an *if*-clause stating a condition and a
main clause stating the result. The whole system rests on one idea — how **real**
the speaker thinks the condition is. A real condition uses ordinary tenses; an
unreal one uses a tense one step further back than the time it refers to. NEB Q7
tests conditionals almost every year, usually as *Complete the sentence* or
*Rewrite using "if"*, and the marker is checking one thing: the correct pair of
verb forms across the two clauses.

## Chapter summary

- Type 0: *if* + present, present — always true.
- Type 1: *if* + present, **will** + V1 — a real future possibility.
- Type 2: *if* + past (*were* for all persons), **would** + V1 — unreal present.
- Type 3: *if* + had + V3, **would have** + V3 — unreal past, regret.
- Mixed: *if* + had + V3, **would** + V1 (past cause, present result); *if* + past,
  **would have** + V3 (present cause, past result).
- Never put *will* or *would* in the *if*-clause.
- A comma follows the *if*-clause only when it comes first.
- *Unless* = *if … not*, so do not add a second negative.
- *Were I…*, *Had I…*, *Should you…* are the inverted forms with *if* dropped.
- *Wish* + past = a present regret; *wish* + past perfect = a past regret;
  *wish* + *would* = annoyance.

## Study route

Read the topics and identify unfamiliar terms.

Close the book and explain the key ideas in your own words.

Attempt a worked example before revealing its solution.

Complete the chapter practice, correct mistakes, then mark the chapter revised.
chapters.question_answers:
## Worked transformation 27.1 — turning two facts into a conditional

**Problem.** Rewrite using *if*: *Sushma did not set an alarm, so she missed the
6 a.m. bus to Butwal.*

**Solution — step by step.**

1. **Find the two facts and their time.** Fact 1: she did not set an alarm (past).
   Fact 2: she missed the bus (past). Both are finished past facts.
2. **Choose the type.** We are imagining the opposite of a past fact → **type 3**.
3. **Flip the polarity of each fact.** "did not set" → *had set*; "missed" →
   *would not have missed*.
4. **Put them in the type-3 frame:** *if* + had + V3, would have + V3.

**Answer.** *If Sushma **had set** an alarm, she **would not have missed** the
6 a.m. bus to Butwal.*

## Worked transformation 27.2 — completing a type-2 sentence

**Problem.** Complete: *If I were the principal of this school, …*

**Solution — step by step.**

1. **Identify the type from the *if*-clause.** *were* is a simple past subjunctive →
   **type 2**, an unreal present.
2. **Recall the matching main clause.** Type 2 pairs with **would / could / might +
   V1** — never *will*, never *would have*.
3. **Write a sensible result in that form.**

**Answer.** *If I were the principal of this school, I **would build** a proper
library and **would start** a science club.*

Writing *I will build* would be a type-1 main clause and would lose the mark;
*I would have built* would be type 3 and refers to the past.

## Worked transformation 27.3 — *unless*, inversion and a mixed type

**Problem.** (a) Rewrite with *unless*: *If you do not submit the form today, your
application will be rejected.* (b) Rewrite without *if*: *If I had known about the
strike, I would have started earlier.* (c) Complete: *If Bishal had accepted the
job in Dubai, he … (be) here today.*

**Solution.**

**(a)** *Unless* already means "if … not", so remove the *do not* and keep the verb
positive.
**Answer:** ***Unless you submit** the form today, your application will be
rejected.*

**(b)** Type 3 inverts with *had*: drop *if*, move *had* to the front, keep the rest
unchanged.
**Answer:** ***Had I known** about the strike, I would have started earlier.*

**(c)** The *if*-clause is past perfect (a past condition) but *today* in the result
clause points to the present → a **mixed conditional**. The main clause therefore
takes *would* + V1, and the meaning is negative, because he is in fact here.
**Answer:** *… he **would not be** here today.*

2. **Choose the type.** We are imagining the opposite of a past fact → **type 3**.
3. **Flip the polarity of each fact.** "did not set" → *had set*; "missed" →

4. **Put them in the type-3 frame:** *if* + had + V3, would have + V3.

job in Dubai, he … (be) here today.*

**Solution.**

**(a)** *Unless* already means "if … not", so remove the *do not* and keep the verb
positive.
**Answer:** ***Unless you submit** the form today, your application will be
rejected.*

**(b)** Type 3 inverts with *had*: drop *if*, move *had* to the front, keep the rest
unchanged.
**Answer:** ***Had I known** about the strike, I would have started earlier.*

**(c)** The *if*-clause is past perfect (a past condition) but *today* in the result
clause points to the present → a **mixed conditional**. The main clause therefore
takes *would* + V1, and the meaning is negative, because he is in fact here.
**Answer:** *… he **would not be** here today.*

chapters.name: Relative Clauses and Connectives
topics: When the relative pronoun may be left out
chapters.summary:
- A relative clause goes immediately after the noun it describes.
- *who/whom* for people, *which* for things, *whose* for possession, *where/when/why*
  for place, time and reason.
- Defining clause: identifies the noun, no commas, *that* allowed, object pronoun may
  be dropped.
- Non-defining clause: extra information, commas both sides, *that* forbidden,
  pronoun never dropped.
- Do not repeat the noun or its pronoun inside the relative clause.
- A connective must match both the **relationship** and the **word class**:
  *although* + clause, *despite* + noun, *however* + new sentence.
- Never use two joiners for one relationship: *although … but*, *because … so* are
  wrong in English.
- *As well as* does not make a plural subject.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- Relative pronouns
- Defining relative clauses
- Non-defining relative clauses
- When the relative pronoun may be left out
- *Whose*, *where*, *when* and *why*
- Prepositions in relative clauses
- Reduced relative clauses
- Connectives by function

A **relative clause** is a clause that describes a noun, joined to it by a relative
pronoun such as *who, which* or *that*. A **connective** (or linking word) is a word
or phrase that joins ideas and shows the relationship between them — addition,
contrast, cause, result, purpose. Both belong to the same skill: turning short
sentences into longer, better-organised ones. NEB Q7 tests them as *Join the
sentences using a relative pronoun*, *Fill in the blank with a suitable
connective*, or *Choose the correct linker from the brackets*.

## Chapter summary

- A relative clause goes immediately after the noun it describes.
- *who/whom* for people, *which* for things, *whose* for possession, *where/when/why*
  for place, time and reason.
- Defining clause: identifies the noun, no commas, *that* allowed, object pronoun may
  be dropped.
- Non-defining clause: extra information, commas both sides, *that* forbidden,
  pronoun never dropped.
- Do not repeat the noun or its pronoun inside the relative clause.
- A connective must match both the **relationship** and the **word class**:
  *although* + clause, *despite* + noun, *however* + new sentence.
- Never use two joiners for one relationship: *although … but*, *because … so* are
  wrong in English.
- *As well as* does not make a plural subject.

chapters.question_answers:
## Worked transformation 28.1 — joining with a relative pronoun

**Problem.** Join into one sentence: *I bought a second-hand laptop. The laptop
stopped working after a week.*

**Solution — step by step.**

1. **Find the repeated noun.** *laptop* appears in both sentences.
2. **Decide which sentence carries the main idea.** The important news is that it
   stopped working, so that becomes the main clause and the first sentence becomes
   the relative clause.
3. **Choose the pronoun.** *laptop* is a thing and is the **object** of *bought*, so
   use *which* or *that*.
4. **Place the clause immediately after the noun.**

**Answer.** *The laptop **which I bought second-hand** stopped working after a week.*

Because the pronoun is the object, it may also be dropped: *The laptop I bought
second-hand stopped working after a week.*

## Worked transformation 28.2 — defining or non-defining?

**Problem.** Join, and punctuate correctly: *Lumbini attracts thousands of pilgrims
a year. Lumbini is the birthplace of the Buddha.*

**Solution — step by step.**

1. **Repeated noun:** *Lumbini*.
2. **Is the clause needed to identify it?** No — *Lumbini* is a proper noun and is
   already fully identified. The clause only adds information.
3. **Therefore it is non-defining:** commas on both sides, and *that* is forbidden.
4. **Choose the pronoun:** a place treated as a thing → *which*.

**Answer.** *Lumbini, **which is the birthplace of the Buddha**, attracts thousands
of pilgrims a year.*

If the pronoun replaced the *place* meaning rather than the noun itself, *where*
would be used: *Lumbini, **where the Buddha was born**, attracts thousands of
pilgrims a year.*

## Worked transformation 28.3 — rewriting with a different connective

**Problem.** Rewrite each sentence with the word in brackets, keeping the meaning.
(a) *Although it was raining heavily, the programme continued.* (**despite**)
(b) *He missed the bus because he got up late.* (**because of**)
(c) *The soup was very salty. Nobody could eat it.* (**so … that**)

**Solution.**

**(a)** *Despite* is a preposition, so the clause *it was raining heavily* must
become a noun phrase: *the heavy rain*.
**Answer:** ***Despite the heavy rain**, the programme continued.*

**(b)** *Because of* also needs a noun phrase: *he got up late* → *his getting up
late* or *his late rising*.
**Answer:** *He missed the bus **because of his getting up late**.*

**(c)** The *so … that* pattern is *so* + adjective + *that* + result clause. Put
the adjective *salty* after *so* and attach the second sentence with *that*.
**Answer:** *The soup was **so salty that** nobody could eat it.*

chapters.name: Question Tags, Questions and Subject-Verb Agreement
chapters.summary:
- Questions invert the auxiliary and the subject; without an auxiliary, insert
  *do / does / did* and use V1.
- A subject question (*Who came?*) takes no *do / does / did* and no inversion.
- An embedded question keeps statement word order and needs no question mark.
- A tag = auxiliary + (n't) + pronoun, with the polarity reversed.
- Memorise: *I am → aren't I*, *Let's → shall we*, imperative *→ will you*,
  *There is → is there*, *everyone → they*, *nothing → it*.
- *Never, hardly, seldom, rarely, few, little* are negatives and take a positive tag.
- The verb agrees with the real subject, not with the nearest noun.
- *Each, every, either, neither, one of* + singular verb; *a number of* + plural,
  *the number of* + singular.
- *As well as, along with, together with* do not make a subject plural.
- Amounts of money, time and distance take a singular verb.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- The four kinds of question
- Yes / no questions
- Wh- questions
- Indirect and embedded questions
- Question tags — the basic rule
- Special tags you must memorise
- Subject–verb agreement: the core rules

This unit covers three closely related things, all of which depend on the
**auxiliary verb**: how questions are formed, how question tags are added, and how
the verb agrees with its subject. NEB Q7 almost always carries at least one question
tag and one agreement item, usually as *Add a suitable question tag*, *Change into a
question*, or *Fill in the blank with the correct form of the verb*. Every one of
them is decided by a fixed rule, so these are the easiest marks in the paper.

## Chapter summary

- Questions invert the auxiliary and the subject; without an auxiliary, insert
  *do / does / did* and use V1.
- A subject question (*Who came?*) takes no *do / does / did* and no inversion.
- An embedded question keeps statement word order and needs no question mark.
- A tag = auxiliary + (n't) + pronoun, with the polarity reversed.
- Memorise: *I am → aren't I*, *Let's → shall we*, imperative *→ will you*,
  *There is → is there*, *everyone → they*, *nothing → it*.
- *Never, hardly, seldom, rarely, few, little* are negatives and take a positive tag.
- The verb agrees with the real subject, not with the nearest noun.
- *Each, every, either, neither, one of* + singular verb; *a number of* + plural,
  *the number of* + singular.
- *As well as, along with, together with* do not make a subject plural.
- Amounts of money, time and distance take a singular verb.

## Study route

Close the book and explain the key ideas in your own words.

Attempt a worked example before revealing its solution.

Complete the chapter practice, correct mistakes, then mark the chapter revised.

## Worked transformation 29.1 — a tag with a hidden negative

**Problem.** Add a question tag: *Hari hardly ever attends the morning class, ____ ?*

**Solution — step by step.**

1. **Find the auxiliary.** There is none; *attends* is a present simple verb with a
   third-person singular subject → the auxiliary is **does**.
2. **Check the polarity.** *Hardly ever* is a negative adverb, so although the
   sentence has no *not*, it counts as **negative**.
3. **Flip it.** A negative statement takes a **positive** tag → *does*.
4. **Pronoun.** *Hari* → *he*.

**Answer.** *Hari hardly ever attends the morning class, **does he**?*

Writing *doesn't he* would be the standard error, because the negative is hidden in
*hardly*.

## Worked transformation 29.2 — framing a question

**Problem.** Frame questions to get the underlined answers.
(a) *<u>Sabina</u> won the debate competition.*
(b) *They reached Pokhara <u>at six o'clock</u>.*

**Solution.**

**(a)** The underlined part is the **subject** of the sentence. A subject question
takes no *did* and no inversion: simply replace the subject with *who* and leave the
verb exactly as it is.
**Answer:** ***Who won** the debate competition?*

**(b)** The underlined part is an adverbial of time, so the question word is *when*
(or *what time*). The verb *reached* is past simple with no auxiliary, so insert
*did* and change the verb back to V1.
**Answer:** ***When did** they **reach** Pokhara?*

## Worked transformation 29.3 — choosing the verb form

**Problem.** Choose the correct verb. (a) *The list of candidates (has / have) been
published.* (b) *Neither the principal nor the teachers (was / were) willing to
speak.* (c) *One of the mobiles that (is / are) displayed here (is / are) mine.*

**Solution.**

**(a)** Cross out the phrase *of candidates*. The subject is *the list*, singular.
**Answer:** *has been published.*

**(b)** With *neither … nor*, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, which is
*teachers*, plural.
**Answer:** *were willing to speak.*

**(c)** Two verbs, two subjects. Inside the relative clause, *that* refers to
*mobiles* (plural) → *are displayed*. The main subject is *one*, singular → *is
mine*.
**Answer:** *One of the mobiles that **are** displayed here **is** mine.*

chapters.name: Prepositions, Adjectives and Adverbs
chapters.summary:
- Time: *at* a clock time, *on* a day or date, *in* a month, season or year;
  *since* + point, *for* + length, *by* = not later than, *until* = up to.
- Place: *at* a point, *on* a surface, *in* an area; *between* two, *among* more than
  two; *beside* = next to, *besides* = in addition.
- Many verbs, adjectives and nouns have a fixed preposition — learn the pair.
- *Discuss, enter, marry, reach, resemble, answer, request, attack* take no
  preposition; avoid *return back*, *cope up with*, *repeat again*.
- Adjective order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose.
- One syllable → *-er / -est*; two or more → *more / most*; never both.
- *Senior, junior, superior, inferior, prefer* take *to*, not *than*.
- Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb but after *be*.
- *Hard / hardly*, *late / lately*, *near / nearly* are different words.
- *Too* = more than is acceptable; *very* is only an intensifier.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- Prepositions of time
- Prepositions of place and direction
- Prepositions fixed to a word
- Adjectives: kinds and order
- Degrees of comparison
- Adverbs

Prepositions show the relationship of a noun to the rest of the sentence — in time,
in space, or in a fixed partnership with a particular verb or adjective. Adjectives
describe nouns; adverbs describe verbs, adjectives and other adverbs. Together these
three classes supply a large share of NEB Q7: *Fill in the blanks with suitable
prepositions*, *Use the correct form of the adjective in brackets*, and
*Choose the correct word*. Much of it is memory work, so the tables below are meant
to be learnt, not just read.

## Chapter summary

- Time: *at* a clock time, *on* a day or date, *in* a month, season or year;
  *since* + point, *for* + length, *by* = not later than, *until* = up to.
- Place: *at* a point, *on* a surface, *in* an area; *between* two, *among* more than
  two; *beside* = next to, *besides* = in addition.
- Many verbs, adjectives and nouns have a fixed preposition — learn the pair.
- *Discuss, enter, marry, reach, resemble, answer, request, attack* take no
  preposition; avoid *return back*, *cope up with*, *repeat again*.
- Adjective order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose.
- One syllable → *-er / -est*; two or more → *more / most*; never both.
- *Senior, junior, superior, inferior, prefer* take *to*, not *than*.
- Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb but after *be*.
- *Hard / hardly*, *late / lately*, *near / nearly* are different words.
- *Too* = more than is acceptable; *very* is only an intensifier.

chapters.question_answers:
## Worked transformation 30.1 — choosing the preposition

**Problem.** Fill in the blanks: *(a) She has been living in Dhangadhi ____ 2074.
(b) Our team is confident ____ winning. (c) Divide the prize money ____ the five
players.*

**Solution.**

**(a)** *2074* is a **point** in time, not a length, so the answer is *since*, not
*for*. **Answer:** *since 2074.*

**(b)** *Confident* is an adjective with a fixed partner. The pair is *confident
**of***, and after a preposition the verb takes *-ing*. **Answer:** *confident of
winning.*

**(c)** There are five players, that is more than two, so *among* — *between* is used
for two. **Answer:** *among the five players.*

## Worked transformation 30.2 — degrees of comparison

**Problem.** Rewrite without changing the meaning.
(a) *No other peak in Nepal is as high as Everest.* (use a superlative)
(b) *Sarita is the more intelligent of the two sisters.* (use *not as … as*)

**Solution.**

**(a)** *No other … as high as X* means X is higher than all the rest, so the
superlative form is required, with *the* and a following *in Nepal*.
**Answer:** *Everest is **the highest peak in Nepal**.*

**(b)** If Sarita is the more intelligent, then the other sister is the less
intelligent. Turn it round with *not as … as*, keeping the adjective in its base
form.
**Answer:** *The other sister is **not as intelligent as** Sarita.*

## Worked transformation 30.3 — correcting a sentence with several faults

**Problem.** Correct: *Although he entered into the hall lately, he discussed about
the problem more better than any student.*

**Solution — one fault at a time.**

1. *enter* takes no preposition → *entered the hall*.
2. *lately* means "recently"; the meaning here is "not on time" → *late*.
3. *discuss* takes no preposition → *discussed the problem*.
4. *more better* is a double comparative → *better*.
5. *than any student* would include himself; a comparative comparing one member with
   the rest needs *any other* → *than any other student*.

**Answer.** *Although he entered the hall **late**, he **discussed the problem
better than any other student**.*

topics: Turning an outline into a story
Reading a chart, a graph or a table
chapters.summary:
- Guided writing (Q4, 7 marks) supplies the material; you supply the sentences.
  Content 3, organisation 2, language 2. Write 150–200 words in about 15 minutes.
- A story from an outline: read all the notes first, invent a *who / where / when*,
  write in the **simple past** and **third person**, expand each note into two to four
  sentences, paragraph by stage, title and moral last.
- Direct speech: comma before the speech, capital letter inside, punctuation inside the
  closing marks, and a new line for each new speaker.
- Describing data: paraphrase the title, give an overview with the highest and lowest
  values, then the details with figures, then one closing sentence.
- Change verbs — *rose, climbed, doubled / fell, dropped, halved / remained steady,
  levelled off* — with *sharply, steadily, gradually, slightly*.
- It is *an increase **in** the number*, *a rise **of** 12 per cent*, *a fall **from**
  62 **to** 58*.
- Describe, never explain: no causes and no opinions unless the question asks.

## Topics to cover

- What the guided-writing question asks
- Turning an outline into a story
- The language of narrative
- Reading a chart, a graph or a table

- Checking your own answer

Question 4 carries seven marks for writing that is **guided** — the material is handed
to you and your job is to turn it into continuous English. Two kinds come up year after
year: outline notes to be expanded into a story, and a chart, graph or table to be
described. Neither asks you to invent facts. Both ask you to dress fixed information in
sentences a stranger could follow without seeing the original.

## Chapter summary

- Guided writing (Q4, 7 marks) supplies the material; you supply the sentences.
  Content 3, organisation 2, language 2. Write 150–200 words in about 15 minutes.
- A story from an outline: read all the notes first, invent a *who / where / when*,
  write in the **simple past** and **third person**, expand each note into two to four
  sentences, paragraph by stage, title and moral last.
- Direct speech: comma before the speech, capital letter inside, punctuation inside the
  closing marks, and a new line for each new speaker.
- Describing data: paraphrase the title, give an overview with the highest and lowest
  values, then the details with figures, then one closing sentence.
- Change verbs — *rose, climbed, doubled / fell, dropped, halved / remained steady,
  levelled off* — with *sharply, steadily, gradually, slightly*.
- It is *an increase **in** the number*, *a rise **of** 12 per cent*, *a fall **from**
  62 **to** 58*.

chapters.question_answers:
## Model answer 31.1 — a story from an outline

**Question.** Develop a readable story with the help of the outlines given below and
give it a suitable title. [7]
*A poor farmer of Dang — walks to the weekly market — finds a cloth bag on the path
— opens it, full of money — nobody around — takes it to the police post — a
schoolteacher claims it — offers a reward — the farmer refuses — the teacher pays
the school fees of the farmer's daughter — moral.*

**Model answer.**

**A Bag on the Path**

Khagendra Chaudhary was the poorest man in his village in Dang. He owned half a
bigha of land, two goats and a bicycle that had lost its bell. Every Thursday he
walked five kilometres to the weekly market with a basket of vegetables on his
head.

One Thursday morning, while he was crossing the dry stream near the school, his foot
struck something soft. It was a red cloth bag, tied at the neck. He untied it and sat
down heavily on a stone. The bag was full of thousand-rupee notes. He looked up and
down the empty path; there was nobody at all. For a long moment he thought of his
leaking roof and of his daughter's unpaid fees.

Then he tied the bag again and walked to the police post at the bazaar. The head
constable counted the notes twice and wrote the amount in a register.

By evening the owner had come — Mr Poudel, the mathematics teacher, who had been
carrying the salary of every teacher in the school. He held out five thousand rupees.

"Please keep this," he said. "You have saved my job."

"I only returned what was not mine," Khagendra answered. "A man cannot take payment
for that."

The next week the school register showed that the fees of Khagendra's daughter had
been paid for the whole year.

*An honest man may be poor, but he is never cheap.*

**Why it scores.** Every outline point appears, in order; the invented frame (a name,
Dang, a Thursday) contradicts nothing. The simple past runs throughout, there are
four paragraphs and two lines of direct speech, and the moral grows out of the last
event instead of being stuck on.

## Model answer 31.2 — describing a bar chart

**Question.** Study the bar chart given above and describe it in about 150 words.
[7]

**Model answer.**

The bar chart compares the percentage of students who passed Grade 11 English at one
secondary school in each of the five academic years from 2077 to 2081 BS.

Taken as a whole, the pass rate improved a great deal over the period, climbing from
62 per cent to 86 per cent — a rise of 24 percentage points. The best year was the
last one, 2081, and the weakest was 2078.

The only fall came at the start. Between 2077 and 2078 the figure dropped four
points, from 62 to 58 per cent, the lowest point on the chart. After that the trend
was upward every year. The sharpest rise came in 2079, when the pass rate jumped
thirteen points to 71 per cent; growth then slowed, with nine more points in 2080 and
six in 2081. In short, after one poor year the school recovered steadily, and by 2081
more than four students in five were passing.

**Why it scores.** Sentence 1 paraphrases the title; sentence 2 gives the overview
with the highest and lowest values. Every figure is quoted with its unit, and
*dropped, jumped, gained* replace a fourfold repetition of *increased*. The last
sentence restates the pattern and invents no reason.

## Model answer 31.3 — describing a pie chart

**Question.** The pie chart above shows the means of transport used by 200 students
of a college in Kathmandu. Write a description of it. [7]

**Model answer.**

The pie chart shows how two hundred students of a Kathmandu college travel to their
campus each day, with the share taken by each means of transport given as a
percentage.

Walking is by far the commonest choice. Two students in five, that is 40 per cent or
eighty students, come on foot, and this slice is larger than any other. The public
bus comes second at 30 per cent, or sixty students. Together these two cheap options
account for 70 per cent of the whole college.

The remaining three groups are much smaller. Fifteen per cent, or thirty students,
cycle, and ten per cent, twenty students, ride a motorbike — half as many as those
who cycle. Only 5 per cent, ten students in all, use some other means such as a car
or a taxi, the smallest slice of the chart. Overall, seven students out of ten either
walk or take a bus.

**Why it scores.** It turns every percentage into a number of students, which shows
that the whole of 200 has been understood; it groups the three small slices instead
of listing them flatly; and it uses *half as many as* and *by far the commonest*
rather than repeating *more* and *less*.

self_checks.question: Model answer 31.1 — a story from an outline
self_checks.answer:
**Question.** Develop a readable story with the help of the outlines given below and
give it a suitable title. [7]
*A poor farmer of Dang — walks to the weekly market — finds a cloth bag on the path
— opens it, full of money — nobody around — takes it to the police post — a
schoolteacher claims it — offers a reward — the farmer refuses — the teacher pays
the school fees of the farmer's daughter — moral.*

**Model answer.**

**A Bag on the Path**

Khagendra Chaudhary was the poorest man in his village in Dang. He owned half a
bigha of land, two goats and a bicycle that had lost its bell. Every Thursday he
walked five kilometres to the weekly market with a basket of vegetables on his
head.

One Thursday morning, while he was crossing the dry stream near the school, his foot
struck something soft. It was a red cloth bag, tied at the neck. He untied it and sat
down heavily on a stone. The bag was full of thousand-rupee notes. He looked up and
down the empty path; there was nobody at all. For a long moment he thought of his
leaking roof and of his daughter's unpaid fees.

Then he tied the bag again and walked to the police post at the bazaar. The head
constable counted the notes twice and wrote the amount in a register.

By evening the owner had come — Mr Poudel, the mathematics teacher, who had been
carrying the salary of every teacher in the school. He held out five thousand rupees.

"Please keep this," he said. "You have saved my job."

"I only returned what was not mine," Khagendra answered. "A man cannot take payment
for that."

The next week the school register showed that the fees of Khagendra's daughter had
been paid for the whole year.

*An honest man may be poor, but he is never cheap.*

**Why it scores.** Every outline point appears, in order; the invented frame (a name,
Dang, a Thursday) contradicts nothing. The simple past runs throughout, there are
four paragraphs and two lines of direct speech, and the moral grows out of the last
event instead of being stuck on.

chapters.summary:
- Q5, functional writing, 8 marks: roughly half for format, half for language and
  register. Fix the skeleton before you write.
- Formal letter, block style, in order: sender's address · date · receiver's address ·
  subject · salutation · three body paragraphs · close · signature, name, post.
- *Dear Sir / Madam* → **Yours faithfully**; *Dear Mr Rai* → **Yours sincerely**.
  Only the first word of the close is capitalised.
- Formal register: *I should be grateful if you would…*, *I regret any inconvenience
  caused*, *I look forward to hearing from you*. No contractions.
- Avoid *Myself Ram*, *kindly do the needful*, *reply back*, *Your's faithfully*,
  *request for leave*.
- An email needs a specific subject line, a greeting, short paragraphs and a signed
  sign-off; no SMS spelling, no capitals throughout.
- A job application names the advertisement and its date, then qualification,
  experience, skill, enclosures and a request for an interview.
- A CV for a student is one page: personal details, objective, qualifications,
  experience, skills, activities, referees.
- A notice is impersonal, boxed, fifty words or fewer, and carries the issuing body,
  the word NOTICE, the date, a heading and a signature with a post.

## Topics to cover

- The forms, and how formal each one is
- The formal letter: the parts and where they go

- Applications, and the curriculum vitae

Question 5 of the NEB paper carries eight marks for **functional writing** — the
everyday written forms an adult actually has to produce: a letter to an office, an
email, an application for a job or for leave, a notice on a board. Unlike an essay,
each of these has a **fixed shape**. Half the marks are for putting the right parts
in the right places; the other half are for hitting the right level of politeness.
Learn the shapes and this becomes the easiest question on the paper.

## Chapter summary

- Q5, functional writing, 8 marks: roughly half for format, half for language and
  register. Fix the skeleton before you write.
- Formal letter, block style, in order: sender's address · date · receiver's address ·
  subject · salutation · three body paragraphs · close · signature, name, post.
- *Dear Sir / Madam* → **Yours faithfully**; *Dear Mr Rai* → **Yours sincerely**.
  Only the first word of the close is capitalised.
- Formal register: *I should be grateful if you would…*, *I regret any inconvenience
  caused*, *I look forward to hearing from you*. No contractions.
- Avoid *Myself Ram*, *kindly do the needful*, *reply back*, *Your's faithfully*,

- An email needs a specific subject line, a greeting, short paragraphs and a signed
  sign-off; no SMS spelling, no capitals throughout.
- A job application names the advertisement and its date, then qualification,

## Model answer 32.1 — a letter to the editor

**Question.** Write a letter to the editor of a national daily drawing the attention
of the authorities to the dust and the broken road in your locality.
[8]

**Model answer.**

Ramesh Thapa
Ward No. 4, Lekhnath
Pokhara

14 Bhadra 2082

The Editor
The Himalayan Times
Kathmandu

Subject: Dust and broken road in Lekhnath

Dear Sir or Madam,

Through the columns of your respected daily I wish to draw the attention of the
Pokhara Metropolitan City office to the condition of the road that runs from Lekhnath
chowk to the campus gate.

The road was dug up for a water pipeline eight months ago and has not been resurfaced
since. In the dry season the dust is so thick that shopkeepers must close their
shutters by midday, and three of the four schools on this stretch report a rise in
chest complaints among their pupils. In the monsoon the same stretch becomes a line
of pits in which two motorcyclists have already been injured.

I therefore request the city office to resurface the road before the festival season
and, until that is done, to water it twice a day. A reply through your newspaper
would reassure several thousand residents.

Yours faithfully,

Ramesh Thapa
Student, Grade 11

**Why it scores.** All eight parts of the skeleton are present and in block style;
*Dear Sir or Madam* is correctly paired with *Yours faithfully*; the three paragraphs
do three separate jobs — why, what, what next; and the complaint is supported by
facts rather than by anger.

## Model answer 32.2 — an application for a job

**Question.** An advertisement in *The Kathmandu Post* of 5 Asoj invites applications
for the post of Office Assistant at Everest Trading Pvt. Ltd., Naxal. Write an
application for the post. [8]

**Model answer.**

Sabina Rai
Ward No. 9, Dhankuta

8 Asoj 2082

The Manager
Everest Trading Pvt. Ltd.
Naxal, Kathmandu

Subject: Application for the post of Office Assistant

Dear Sir or Madam,

With reference to your advertisement in *The Kathmandu Post* of 5 Asoj 2082, I wish
to apply for the post of Office Assistant in your organisation.

I passed the Secondary Education Examination in 2080 with a GPA of 3.4 and am at
present studying in Grade 11 at Dhankuta Multiple Campus. For the past eight months I
have kept the sales register and answered the telephone at a stationery shop in
Dhankuta, so I am used to dealing with customers. I can type in both Nepali and
English and can work in Word and Excel.

I am enclosing my curriculum vitae, copies of my certificates and a copy of my
citizenship certificate. I should be grateful for the opportunity of an interview at
any time convenient to you.

Thank you for considering my application.

Yours faithfully,

Sabina Rai

**Why it scores.** It names the advertisement and its date in the first line, so the
reader knows at once which post is meant; qualification, experience and skill come in
that order; the enclosures are listed; and the request for an interview is polite
without being humble.

## Model answer 32.3 — a notice

**Question.** You are the secretary of the school's eco club. Write a notice in not
more than fifty words informing the students about a tree-plantation programme.
[8]

**Model answer.**

**SHREE JANATA SECONDARY SCHOOL, BIRATNAGAR**

**N O T I C E**

22 Asoj 2082

**Tree-plantation Programme**

All students of Grades 9 to 12 are informed that the Eco Club will plant three
hundred saplings on the school ground on Saturday, 28 Asoj, from 7 a.m. Students
should bring a spade and a water bottle. Names may be given to the class teacher by
26 Asoj.

Sd/-
Nirmala Gurung
Secretary, Eco Club

**Why it scores.** The body is 46 words. It is impersonal — *students are informed*,
not *I inform you* — and it answers what, who, where, when and what to bring. The
date, the heading and the signature block are all in their proper places.

chapters.summary:
- Question 6 is worth **10 marks**: about 4 for content, 3 for organisation, 3 for
  language. Plan five minutes, write twenty, check five.
- A **paragraph** is one idea: topic sentence, supports in a chosen order, closing
  sentence. Unity and coherence are what the organisation mark measures.
- An **essay** is a funnel: general opening, a one-sentence **thesis**, body paragraphs
  that defend it, a conclusion that widens out and adds nothing new.
- The four kinds — narrative, descriptive, expository, argumentative — are distinguished
  by their **order**. Take the kind from the wording of the question.
- A **memoir** is one remembered slice of time in the first person, built on concrete
  detail, turning on a single moment, and ending with reflection on what it meant.
- **Critical writing** is judgement plus evidence. Summarise in three sentences at most;
  quote briefly; after every quotation, say what it shows.
- Link paragraphs with cohesive devices, hedge large claims, vary sentence length, and
  avoid the stock openings and closings every examiner has read a thousand times.

## Topics to cover

- What Question 6 asks
- The paragraph: the unit an essay is built from
- The shape of a whole essay
- Four kinds of essay, and how each is organised
- The memoir
- Critical writing
- Language that lifts a free-writing answer

Question 6 gives you ten marks and, for the first time in the paper, no format to
copy. You are handed a topic and asked to think. That freedom is why the question is
worth the most marks in the writing section, and why it is the one most often thrown
away. Free writing is not writing whatever comes; it is writing to a shape you chose
before you began. This chapter teaches three of those shapes — the essay, the memoir
and the critical response — and the paragraph that all three are built from.

## Chapter summary

  language. Plan five minutes, write twenty, check five.
- A **paragraph** is one idea: topic sentence, supports in a chosen order, closing
  sentence. Unity and coherence are what the organisation mark measures.
- An **essay** is a funnel: general opening, a one-sentence **thesis**, body paragraphs
  that defend it, a conclusion that widens out and adds nothing new.

  by their **order**. Take the kind from the wording of the question.

- **Critical writing** is judgement plus evidence. Summarise in three sentences at most;

## Model answer 33.1 — an argumentative essay (10 marks)

**Question:** *Should mobile phones be allowed in schools? Write an essay of about 250
words giving your opinion.*

**Mobile Phones in School**

Ten years ago a mobile phone in a school bag was unusual; today it is almost the rule.
Teachers confiscate them, parents insist their children carry them, and the same
argument comes round every year. In my view schools should allow phones on the
premises but forbid their use inside the classroom, because a total ban answers a real
problem in the wrong way.

The first reason is safety. Many students in our hills travel an hour or more to
school, on roads that close after heavy rain and during strikes. A parent who cannot
reach a child on such a day is helpless. A phone switched off in a bag costs the
school nothing and gives a family a great deal.

The second reason is that a phone is a library. A student who cannot afford a
dictionary can carry one; past papers, recorded lectures and news in English are all
within reach. Used for twenty minutes with a purpose, the device teaches more than it
distracts.

Against this it is argued, fairly, that phones invite cheating, distraction and
bullying. These are genuine harms. But a ban does not remove them; it moves them to
the corridor and the toilet, where no teacher is watching. A clear rule — phones off
and out of sight from the first bell to the last, with the penalty known in advance —
protects lessons without wasting what the device can do.

Schools exist to prepare students for a world in which these machines are everywhere.
Teaching students when not to use a phone is a better lesson than pretending the phone
does not exist.

*(288 words)*

## Model answer 33.2 — a memoir (10 marks)

**Question:** *Write a memoir of about 250 words about an experience that changed the
way you think.*

**My Grandmother's Radio**

The radio in my grandmother's room was the size of a brick and the colour of weak tea.
It had one dial, and the dial had a crack in it shaped like a river. Every evening at
seven she turned it on, and every evening at seven the room went quiet, even the
cousins, even me.

I was nine and I thought the ritual was silly. There was a television downstairs with
colour in it. I told her so one evening, standing in the doorway with my arms folded,
and I remember being rather pleased with the sentence.

She did not argue. She moved along the bed and patted the space beside her, and I sat
because I was nine and it was easier to sit than to keep standing. The news came on.
There had been a landslide above Sindhupalchok. The reader said the name of a village,
and my grandmother's hand went still on the blanket, and she said, very quietly, *your
grandfather walked through there in 2018*.

I did not understand what I was being told. I understood only that the little brown
box was not entertainment; it was how she kept the map of her life in one piece.

I have a phone now that can play a thousand stations, and I use it for almost nothing.
What that evening taught me is that a thing is worth what it carries, not what it
costs — and that the quickest way to miss what somebody loves is to compare it with
something newer.

*(263 words)*

## Model answer 33.3 — a critical response (10 marks)

**Question:** *Write a critical appreciation of Oscar Wilde's "The Selfish Giant".*

Oscar Wilde's "The Selfish Giant" is a short fairy tale that uses the simplest
machinery of the form — a garden, a wall, a child — to make a serious claim about
selfishness and its cure. It is a slight story that carries a surprising weight.

The Giant returns after seven years, finds children playing in his garden, and walls
them out with the notice "TRESPASSERS WILL BE PROSECUTED". Spring never comes to the
garden again until the children creep back through a gap, and the Giant, watching a
small boy who cannot reach the branches, knocks the wall down himself.

Wilde's chief device is the personification of the seasons. Snow, Frost, the North
Wind and the Hail move into the garden like tenants, and the reader understands
without being told that the winter is the Giant's own. The wall is equally plain in
its meaning, and the plainness is deliberate: this is a fable, and a fable wants its
symbol visible.

The weakness of the story is its ending. The boy's return, with "the wounds of Love"
on his hands and feet, converts a moral tale into a religious one very abruptly, and
some readers find the shift sentimental. Yet the form protects Wilde. A fairy tale is
allowed a miracle, and the earlier writing has earned this one.

"The Selfish Giant" is therefore best read not as a children's story with a moral
attached, but as a moral argument that has chosen the shape of a children's story
because that shape can say hard things gently.

*(268 words)*

self_checks.question: Model answer 33.3 — a critical response (10 marks)
self_checks.answer:
**Question:** *Write a critical appreciation of Oscar Wilde's "The Selfish Giant".*

Oscar Wilde's "The Selfish Giant" is a short fairy tale that uses the simplest
machinery of the form — a garden, a wall, a child — to make a serious claim about
selfishness and its cure. It is a slight story that carries a surprising weight.

The Giant returns after seven years, finds children playing in his garden, and walls
them out with the notice "TRESPASSERS WILL BE PROSECUTED". Spring never comes to the
garden again until the children creep back through a gap, and the Giant, watching a
small boy who cannot reach the branches, knocks the wall down himself.

Wilde's chief device is the personification of the seasons. Snow, Frost, the North
Wind and the Hail move into the garden like tenants, and the reader understands
without being told that the winter is the Giant's own. The wall is equally plain in
its meaning, and the plainness is deliberate: this is a fable, and a fable wants its
symbol visible.

The weakness of the story is its ending. The boy's return, with "the wounds of Love"
on his hands and feet, converts a moral tale into a religious one very abruptly, and
some readers find the shift sentimental. Yet the form protects Wilde. A fairy tale is
allowed a miracle, and the earlier writing has earned this one.

"The Selfish Giant" is therefore best read not as a children's story with a moral
attached, but as a moral argument that has chosen the shape of a children's story
because that shape can say hard things gently.

## Worked example 34.1 — reference words

A reference question is free marks if you test your answer by substitution.

> *Farmers in the middle hills have grown maize on terraces for centuries. **It** is a
> crop that tolerates thin soil, and for that reason it has outlasted every attempt to
> replace it.*

**Question:** What does *it* refer to?

A careless answer is *the middle hills*, because that phrase is nearest. Substitute and
test: *The middle hills is a crop that tolerates thin soil* — nonsense. Test the next
candidate: *Maize is a crop that tolerates thin soil* — correct. The answer is **maize**.

Substitution beats proximity. The nearest noun is often not the referent, and the test
takes four seconds.

## Worked passage A — with answers (8 marks)

**Read the passage and answer the questions.**

> Teenagers are often accused of laziness for sleeping late, but the accusation
> misreads the biology. At about the age of thirteen the body clock shifts. The
> hormone that signals the brain to sleep begins to be released roughly two hours
> later than it does in a child or in an adult, so a fifteen-year-old who is wide awake
> at eleven at night is not being difficult; she is being fifteen.
>
> The consequences are not trivial. Sleep is not an interruption of learning but a part
> of it. During the night the brain replays the day's new material and files it, and
> experiments consistently show that a student who sleeps after studying remembers more
> than one who studies for the same length of time and stays awake. Cutting sleep,
> then, does not buy extra study; it spends the study already done.
>
> Most adolescents need between eight and ten hours. Few get them, and the reasons are
> familiar: homework, coaching classes, and a screen that is bright, absorbing and
> within arm's reach. Light in the evening tells the clock that the day is not over,
> and a phone held close to the face is a small, insistent sun.
>
> Some school systems have responded by starting the day later, and where they have,
> attendance has improved and accidents on the way to school have fallen. Such changes
> are expensive and unpopular with parents and bus operators. But the alternative is a
> classroom in which the first period is taught to bodies that, biologically speaking,
> are still asleep.

**Questions**

1. At what age does the body clock begin to shift? [1]
2. Why does the writer say a fifteen-year-old awake at eleven is "not being difficult"?
   [1]
3. What does *it* refer to in *"Sleep is not an interruption of learning but a part of
   it"*? [1]
4. Find a word in the third paragraph that means "holding the attention completely".
   [1]
5. State whether each is True, False or Not Given.
   (a) Students who sleep after studying remember more than students who stay awake.
   (b) Most adolescents in Nepal sleep fewer than eight hours.
   [2]
6. Explain the phrase *"a small, insistent sun"*. [1]
7. Suggest a suitable title for the passage. [1]

**Answers**

1. At about the age of thirteen.
2. Because at that age the sleep hormone is released about two hours later than in a
   child or an adult, so staying awake is biological, not wilful.
3. *It* refers to **learning**. (Substitute: *Sleep is a part of learning* — sense.
   *A part of sleep* — nonsense.)
4. **Absorbing.** (One word, copied in the form used.)
5. (a) **True** — the passage says experiments consistently show it.
   (b) **Not Given** — the passage says *most adolescents* and *few get them*, but it
   never mentions Nepal. Knowing the answer from your own life is exactly the trap.
6. The phone's screen acts like a small sun held near the face: its light keeps telling
   the body clock that daylight has not ended, so sleep is delayed. *Insistent* shows
   the light will not be ignored.
7. *Why Teenagers Sleep Late* or *Sleep, Screens and the School Day.* Three to six
   words; covers the whole passage; not a sentence.

## Worked passage B — with answers (7 marks)

**Read the passage and answer the questions.**

> The porter who carried our kit to Ghorepani was called Dhan Bahadur, and he was, he
> told us on the first morning, fifty-one. He said it the way a man states a price,
> without complaint and without invitation to admire him, and then he picked up a load
> I could not have lifted to my knee and walked up the hill at a speed that made
> conversation impossible for the rest of us.
>
> At the first tea shop he did not sit with the guides. He drank his tea standing,
> looking back down the valley at the way we had come, and when I asked him what he was
> looking at he said, *my village is behind that ridge; I have not been home since
> Dashain.* Then he put down the glass and lifted the load again before anyone had
> suggested moving.
>
> I have been told since that the trekking season is short and that a porter who rests
> is a porter who is not paid. I did not know it then. What I knew then was only that I
> had been carrying a small day-pack and complaining about it, and that I had asked
> him, that morning, whether the work was hard, and that he had smiled and said it was
> all right.

**Questions**

1. How old was Dhan Bahadur? [1]
2. What does the comparison "the way a man states a price" tell us about how he spoke?
   [1]
3. Why did Dhan Bahadur drink his tea standing, do you think? [2]
4. Find a word in the passage that means "the long ridge of high ground". [1]
5. What is the writer's feeling in the last paragraph? Support your answer.
   [2]

**Answers**

1. Fifty-one.
2. It tells us he spoke flatly and factually, as a matter of information — neither
   complaining about his age nor asking to be praised for working at it.
3. Two acceptable lines, each needing evidence. Either: he did not regard the stop as
   his rest, because *a porter who rests is a porter who is not paid* — he stood so as
   to be ready to move, and indeed *lifted the load again before anyone had suggested
   moving*. Or: he did not sit with the guides because he did not see himself as one of
   them; the sentence *he did not sit with the guides* is placed first for that reason.
4. **Ridge.**
5. Shame, or self-reproach — not pity. The evidence is the contrast he draws between
   Dhan Bahadur's load and his own *small day-pack* which he had been *complaining
   about*, and the remembered question *whether the work was hard*, which he now sees
   was a thoughtless thing to ask. The writer never states the feeling; the reader is
   left to draw it, which is why the answer must quote.

chapters.summary:
- Question 8 is five one-mark items on vocabulary. Word class and spelling must both be
  right; there are no part marks.
- **Silent letters** often reappear when a suffix is added (*sign → signature*), which
  is a clue to word families.
- **Stress** matters: two-syllable noun/verb pairs stress the first syllable as a noun
  and the second as a verb; the endings *-ion, -ity, -ic, -ical, -graphy* pull the
  stress onto the syllable before them.
- A **prefix** changes meaning; a **suffix** changes word class. The negative prefix is
  *im-* before *b, m, p*; *il-* before *l*; *ir-* before *r*; *in-* elsewhere.
- Four spelling rules cover adding suffixes: drop silent *e* before a vowel suffix,
  *y → i* after a consonant, double the final consonant when the stress is at the end,
  and *-ful* has one *l*.
- **Synonyms are rarely exact** — they differ in formality and in feeling. Some antonyms
  are made with a prefix, others are separate words.
- **Idioms and phrasal verbs** are fixed. A pronoun object must split a separable
  phrasal verb (*call it off*) but never an inseparable one (*look after her*).
- An unknown word can be reasoned out from its **parts, class, signal words and
  direction**.

chapters.question_answers:
## Worked example 35.1 — hearing the difference

Read each pair aloud, putting the loudness where the bold mark shows.

1. *The rebels planned to re**bel** against the king.* — noun first, verb second.
2. *The government will not **per**mit … you need a per**mit**.* Careful: here the
   **noun** is *permit* (a document) and the **verb** is *permit* (to allow), so the
   order in the sentence above is verb, then noun — *per**mit*** then ***per**mit*.
3. *Their **con**duct was poor, though the teacher con**duc**ted the class well.*

The test: if the word is doing something in the sentence, stress the second syllable;
if it is a thing you can put *the* or *a* in front of, stress the first.

## Worked example 35.2 — one root, eight words

Root: **act** — "to do".

| Word | Class | Built from | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| act | verb / noun | root | to do; a deed |
| action | noun | act + -ion | the doing of something |
| active | adjective | act + -ive | doing things, busy |
| activity | noun | active + -ity | something done |
| inactive | adjective | in- + active | not doing anything |
| react | verb | re- + act | to act in response |

Now the exam item *"Fill the gap: after the operation he remained ______ for a month
(act)"* answers itself. The gap follows *remained*, which needs an adjective; the sense
is negative; so the answer is **inactive** — not *inaction*, which is a noun.

## Worked example 35.3 — reasoning to a meaning

> *The road was **impassable** after the landslide, and lorries queued for three days
> at Krishnabhir.*

**Parts:** *im-* (not, before *p*) + *pass* + *-able* (able to be) — "not able to be
passed".
**Class:** it follows *was*, so it is an adjective describing *the road*.
**Direction:** lorries queued for three days, so the sense must be negative.
All three agree. The answer is **not able to be travelled along; blocked**.

Now the same reasoning on a harder word:

> *Her account of the accident was **corroborated** by two witnesses who had been
> standing at the junction.*

**Parts:** nothing familiar. **Class:** *was ____ by* — a passive verb. **Signal:** the
agents are *two witnesses*. **Direction:** witnesses standing at the junction make her
account more believable, not less. So *corroborated* must mean something like
**confirmed, supported by evidence** — which is exactly right. You reached a correct
answer from a word you had never seen.
