chapters.name: Neighbours - Tim Winton
topics: Setting, structure and point of view
chapters.summary:
- "Neighbours" is a very short story by the Australian writer Tim Winton (b.
  1960), collected in *Scission* (1985); the Nepali textbook's attribution to
  *Migrants of Australia* could not be verified.
- A young, newly married Australian couple move into an inner-city street of
  European migrants and at first feel "like sojourners in a foreign land".
- The neighbours are a loud Macedonian family on one side and a solitary Polish
  widower on the other; the couple find their noise, habits and watchfulness
  offensive, and the neighbours in turn disapprove of a household where the wife
  earns and the husband stays at home.
- The barrier begins to fall over a vegetable garden in autumn, and falls
  completely when the Polish widower rebuilds their collapsed henhouse although
  "they could not understand a word he said".
- The story is organised by the seasons: garden in autumn, gifts in winter,
  duck-killing and the pregnancy in spring, the neighbourhood's celebration in
  summer, and the birth at the close.
- Nobody in the story is given a name, which makes the characters representative
  and reflects the fact that names cannot be exchanged across a language barrier.
- It is told in third person limited point of view through the young man, in free
  indirect style, so that the reader's prejudices are corrected at the same pace
  as his.
- The central themes are community across language, the slow correction of mild
  prejudice, the inadequacy of book learning before lived experience, and birth as
  a shared, physical event.
- The climax is wordless: twelve faces at the fences, a cheer at dawn, and a man
  weeping at his back door because "the twentieth century novel had not prepared
  him for this."
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- About the author
- The story
- Characters
- Themes
- Setting, structure and point of view
- Style and literary devices
- Glossary
- Textbook exercises

"Neighbours" is a very short story by the Australian writer Tim Winton. A young,
newly married couple move into an inner-city street full of European migrants,
find everything about it strange, and then — over the course of one year and one
pregnancy — stop being strangers themselves. Almost nothing dramatic happens: a
vegetable patch is dug, a henhouse falls down, ducks are killed, a baby is born.
The whole story is about the distance between people and how it quietly closes,
and it opens the Grade 12 course because it teaches you to read a text in which
the meaning is carried by small actions rather than by speeches.

  offensive, and the neighbours in turn disapprove of a household where the wife
  earns and the husband stays at home.
- The barrier begins to fall over a vegetable garden in autumn, and falls
  completely when the Polish widower rebuilds their collapsed henhouse although
  "they could not understand a word he said".
- The story is organised by the seasons: garden in autumn, gifts in winter,
  duck-killing and the pregnancy in spring, the neighbourhood's celebration in
  summer, and the birth at the close.
- Nobody in the story is given a name, which makes the characters representative
  and reflects the fact that names cannot be exchanged across a language barrier.

  indirect style, so that the reader's prejudices are corrected at the same pace
  as his.

  prejudice, the inadequacy of book learning before lived experience, and birth as
  a shared, physical event.

  weeping at his back door because "the twentieth century novel had not prepared

## Model answers — short questions

**1.** Because the street was full of European migrants whose language, habits and
noise were completely unfamiliar to them. They had grown up in the "expansive
outer suburbs where good neighbours were seldom seen and never heard", so the
daybreak watering, the spitting and the shouting of the Macedonian family made
them feel that they, and not the migrants, were the outsiders.

**2.** For most of the story he did nothing with it: he hammered nails into wood
only to pull them out again, and added to the stack of salvaged timber in his yard
without ever building with it. In the late spring he finally began to sink posts
and pour cement, and by late summer he had almost completed a two-car garage —
although he owned no car.

**3.** The parents visited and "cast shocked glances across the fence" at the
migrant neighbours. The couple, who had themselves been wary only months before,
felt "superior and proud" — which shows both how far they had moved and that their
tolerance was at that stage still a way of feeling better than somebody else.

**4.** They taught them to slaughter, pluck and dress the muscovy ducks the couple
had kept through the winter. Everyone sat on blocks and upturned buckets, the men
butchering and the women plucking, telling "barely understood stories"; the couple
felt intoxicated in the haze of down and steam, and "found themselves shouting" —
behaving at last exactly like the neighbours whose noise had once appalled them.

**5.** Because the boy behaved in ways the young man found crude and could not
interpret — he urinated in the street and sprayed the cat from the back step — and
because of the way he watched. He would stand at the fence with "only his cobalt
eyes showing", so that the young man was observed by a child he could neither see
properly nor speak to.

**6.** In the last light of the day he saw faces at each fence, watching the house
— he counted twelve of them. The Macedonian family waved and called out what
sounded like their best wishes. It was the first sign that the whole street was
keeping watch with him through the night.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** Winton builds the friendship in stages, and every stage is an action rather
than a conversation. It begins in mutual suspicion: the couple are "wary", the
street feels like "a foreign land", and it takes six months for them to realise
that the Macedonians are talking and not murdering each other. The first contact
is made over work — the couple dig and manure their backyard under "the open and
measured gaze" of the neighbours, who come to the fence with advice about spacing,
hilling and mulching, and the young man, while resenting the interference, "took
careful note of what was said". The first physical contact follows: the young wife
strokes the little boy's stubble and is given a bagful of garlic cloves. The
decisive moment is the henhouse. It falls down, the Polish widower slides through
the fence uninvited and rebuilds it, and Winton lets the silence speak: "They could
not understand a word he said." After that the exchange becomes routine — cabbages
out, grappa and firewood in — and reaches its high point when the couple join the
duck-killing, sitting on upturned buckets in "fractured dialogue" and ending by
shouting themselves. The pregnancy makes the street a single household, and the
birth completes the process with a cheer from people who cannot say what they
mean. Winton's argument is that community is not made of shared opinions, shared
language or even shared culture; it is made of shared work, shared food and shared
waiting. Understanding follows intimacy rather than producing it.

**2.** The story has scarcely any plot, and the seasons supply the shape that plot
would otherwise give. The couple arrive and endure a period of unmarked, unhappy
months; then autumn arrives with the digging and planting of the vegetable patch,
which is the first occasion for contact. Winter, with its "vermilion sunsets" and
the smell of wood smoke, is the season of exchange — cabbages for grappa and
firewood — and the season in which the ducks are kept. Spring brings the killing
of the ducks, the full entry of the couple into the life of the street, and the
beginning of the pregnancy; the Polish widower's hoarded lumber also finally
begins to be used. Summer is the season of the neighbourhood's public celebration
of the coming child, and the year ends with the birth. The seasonal frame does
three jobs. It makes the story's slowness meaningful, since the change in these
people is organic and cannot be hurried any more than a crop can. It produces a
sustained parallel between the vegetable garden and the human one, so that things
planted in autumn and a child conceived in autumn come to fruition together. And
it lends the ending a sense of natural completion: a full turn of the year has
been made, and the arrival of new life is presented as the season's own work
rather than as a plot twist.

**3.** The fence is the story's governing image. It is a literal wooden boundary
between three backyards, but everything that matters in the story is defined by
its relation to that boundary. At first the fence is where misunderstanding is
manufactured: it is where the shaven-headed boy stands with "only his cobalt eyes
showing", where eyebrows are raised at the newcomers' habits, and where the young
man watches his neighbours as if they were specimens. Then it becomes a counter
over which goods pass — advice, garlic cloves, cabbages, grappa, firewood, a
barrowful of scraps. The Polish widower's great act is precisely a violation of
it: he "slid through the fence uninvited". And at the close the fence is lined
with twelve faces, and then with a cheering queue, so that the barrier has become
the place where the community gathers. Winton exposes the young man's prejudice by
telling the story through his eyes in free indirect style, letting us hear his
assumptions in the narrator's own voice: the boy's head "was shaved regularly, he
assumed, in order to make his hair grow thick". That small phrase "he assumed"
lets us catch him inventing explanations for people he has never spoken to. The
same technique records his disgust, his resentment and his suspicion that the
widower is antagonising him on purpose — and then, by giving us no commentary at
all in the final paragraph, it drops him into an experience he cannot analyse. He
simply weeps. The correction is complete because the instrument of judgement has
been taken away from him.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) The "newcomers" are the young, newly married Australian couple who have
just moved into the street; the "neighbours" are the Macedonian family living
immediately on their left. (b) The Macedonians conducted ordinary family
conversation at a volume the couple had never encountered: they "shouted, ranted,
screamed". Having grown up in quiet outer suburbs "where good neighbours were
seldom seen and never heard", the couple could only interpret such noise as
violence. (c) Six months is a long time to be wrong about something so simple, and
Winton chooses the figure deliberately. It measures the depth of the couple's
isolation — in half a year they had not asked a single question or crossed the
fence once — and it shows that prejudice is not corrected by proximity alone but
only by contact. It also makes the reader's own first judgement suspect. (d) The
change is complete and is deliberately marked in the same terms. At the duck
killing in spring, in "the haze of down and steam and fractured dialogue", the
couple "found themselves shouting" — they have joined the noise instead of
decoding it. At the end, the noise that wakes the young man is the neighbours
cheering his son, and it makes him weep.

**2.** (a) "Him" is the young man, the husband and new father; "this" is
everything he has just lived through — his wife's labour and the birth of his son,
and then the discovery that his migrant neighbours have waited all night at the
fence and are cheering at dawn. (b) He is a postgraduate student who has spent the
whole story writing a thesis on the development of the twentieth century novel; it
is mentioned at every stage, and it is what he abandons "for the telephone" when
labour begins. (c) The irony is double. First, a man whose profession is the study
of modern human experience is completely unprepared for the most ordinary human
experience there is. Second, the education he thought made him superior to his
neighbours — he and his wife had felt "superior and proud" — turns out to be
exactly what left him unequipped, while the "uneducated" migrants knew without
being told how to garden, how to build, how to deliver kindness and how to welcome
a child. (d) It states the story's theme in a single line. Winton is contrasting a
private, ironic, verbal, intellectual way of meeting the world with a communal,
physical, wordless one, and declaring the second the more real. It also completes
the young man's character arc: having spent the story interpreting people from
behind a window, he ends it unable to interpret anything and simply weeping, which
in this story is a sign not of failure but of arrival.

chapters.summary:
- "A Respectable Woman" is a short story by the American writer Kate Chopin
  (1850–1904), first published in *Vogue* on 15 February 1894 and collected in
  *A Night in Acadie* (1897).
- Mrs. Baroda is annoyed that her husband Gaston has invited his old college
  friend Gouvernail, a journalist, to stay on their Louisiana sugar plantation,
  and has already decided to dislike a man she has never met.
- The real Gouvernail is quiet, undemanding and entirely uninterested in
  impressing her, which first puzzles her, then leaves her "piqued".
- The climax comes at night on a bench beneath a live oak: Gouvernail sits beside
  her, quotes Whitman to the darkness and talks about his lost ambitions, and she
  finds that "her physical being was for the moment predominant" and longs to
  touch him.
- She resists — "the stronger the impulse grew... the further, in fact, did she
  draw away" — tells nobody, and leaves for the city on the early train.
- She does not confess to her husband because "there are some battles in life
  which a human being must fight alone".
- A year later she herself proposes that Gouvernail visit again, and tells Gaston,
  "I have overcome everything! ... This time I shall be very nice to him" — a line
  that can mean either that she has conquered the attraction or that she has
  conquered her resistance to it.
- The themes are desire against respectability, the reality of the inner life,
  self-knowledge, and the limits of even a loving marriage.
- The technique is third person limited point of view with free indirect style, a
  classical plot shape applied to an entirely internal action, and a deliberately
  open ending.

"A Respectable Woman" is a very short story by the American writer Kate Chopin.
A wife on a Louisiana sugar plantation is annoyed to hear that her husband has
invited an old college friend to stay; she then finds the quiet, unimpressive
guest disturbing in a way she had not expected, and spends one night on a garden
bench discovering something about herself. Nothing is confessed and nothing is
done. Everything in the story happens inside Mrs. Baroda's mind, and the last
three sentences leave the reader with a question that has been argued over for a
hundred and thirty years.

chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** She had "unconsciously formed an image of him in her mind", picturing him
tall, slim and cynical, wearing eyeglasses and carrying his hands in his pockets —
and on that basis she decided that she did not like him. The picture was almost
entirely wrong: he was slim, but not very tall and not at all cynical, and he wore
no eyeglasses and did not keep his hands in his pockets.

**2.** Because he asked nothing of her. She could not understand him, and when she
deliberately left him alone with her husband he "took no manner of exception" to
it. A hostess whose importance depends on being needed found herself unnecessary,
and the injury to her vanity turned her puzzlement into irritation.

**3.** She could see nothing in the dark but "the approaching red point of a
lighted cigar", and she knew from that alone that it must be Gouvernail, "for her
husband did not smoke". Her own white gown then revealed her to him.

**4.** He spoke of his college days with Gaston and of "the days of keen and blind
ambitions and large intentions", and said that all that was left to him now was "a
philosophic acquiescence to the existing order — only a desire to be permitted to
exist, with now and then a little whiff of genuine life, such as he was breathing
now."

**5.** That she was sensible as well as respectable, and "she knew there are some
battles in life which a human being must fight alone." Telling Gaston would have
relieved her own feelings at the cost of his peace and his oldest friendship.

**6.** It is Gaston who invites Gouvernail in the first place, and it is Gaston who
sends Gouvernail out into the dark garden with his wife's white scarf. The husband
thus arranges, in perfect innocence and out of simple kindness, the one encounter
that threatens his marriage.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** The story sets a natural impulse against an acquired identity and shows the
identity winning — at a price. Chopin prepares the ground carefully. Mrs. Baroda's
interest in Gouvernail is not presented as love; it grows out of vanity, because
he does not court her good opinion, and then out of curiosity, as she tries "to
penetrate the reserve in which he had unconsciously enveloped himself". On the
bench, in darkness, with a voice speaking Whitman's lines about the night, the
feeling becomes unmistakably physical: "Her physical being was for the moment
predominant," and she wants to touch his face and lips and to whisper against his
cheek — she "did not care what". Chopin then names the restraint precisely: she
would have done it "if she had not been a respectable woman". This is a social
category, not a moral one, and that is the story's quiet daring. The conflict is
then compressed into a single antithesis: "The stronger the impulse grew to bring
herself near him, the further, in fact, did she draw away from him." The cost of
the victory is measured in the next paragraph. Because respectable women may not
even name such feelings, she cannot tell the husband "who was also her friend",
and must fight "one of those battles in life which a human being must fight
alone". Chopin neither condemns the desire nor celebrates the restraint. She shows
a woman locked out of her own marriage by a word — and then, with the last line,
declines to tell us whether the lock held.

**2.** Chopin tells the story in the third person but stays entirely inside Mrs.
Baroda, and much of it is written in free indirect style, so that the character's
judgements reach us as if they were the narrator's: "she did not like him", "he
tires me frightfully". This has three consequences. First, we adopt her prejudice
before we examine it, and are therefore surprised along with her when Gouvernail
turns out to be likeable — the reader is caught out in exactly the way she is.
Second, it makes the crisis visible. Nothing happens on the bench that an observer
would notice; the whole event is a movement of feeling, and only an interior
viewpoint could record it. Third, and most cunningly, it controls what we are
allowed to know. We know what Gouvernail cannot know and what Gaston never learns,
which gives the final scene its dramatic irony — a delighted husband misreading
his wife in front of a reader who has more information than he does. But the same
device creates the famous ambiguity of the ending. Because the narration reports
Mrs. Baroda's speech without entering her mind at that moment, "I have overcome
everything! ... This time I shall be very nice to him" can mean that she has
conquered the attraction or that she has conquered her resistance to it. Chopin
had spent the whole story telling us what her heroine felt; by withholding it at
the last moment she forces the reader to supply the verdict, and whichever verdict
we supply tells us more about our own assumptions than about Mrs. Baroda. In a
magazine world that expected virtue to be rewarded visibly, that refusal was itself
a bold act.

**3.** Gouvernail's passivity is the mechanism of the entire story. He does not
flirt, does not flatter and does not pursue; Chopin states flatly that he "made no
direct appeal to her approval or even esteem". He will not fish or shoot, he is
happy to sit on the portico with a cigar listening to somebody else, and when his
hostess withdraws he "took no manner of exception". Had he made the smallest
advance, the story would have become a conventional tale of a predatory guest, and
Mrs. Baroda's struggle would have been merely a struggle against him. Because he
does nothing, everything that happens must come from inside her, and the story
becomes what Chopin wanted: a study of a woman discovering herself. His
indifference is also the precise cause of the trouble, since it is his
self-sufficiency that wounds her vanity and sets her pursuing him along the
batture. His innocence is maintained to the end — he sits down beside her "without
a suspicion that she might object", quotes Whitman "half to himself" in an
apostrophe that "was not addressed to her", and lights a fresh cigar as she
escapes. He never learns that anything occurred. At the same time Chopin makes him
more than a device: the disappointed man who asks only "to be permitted to exist,
with now and then a little whiff of genuine life" is a real and rather touching
figure, and it is his weariness, not any charm, that moves her. He is the still
centre of the story, and all its motion is measured against him.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) "She" is Mrs. Baroda, mistress of the plantation; "him" is Gouvernail,
her husband's old college friend, who is staying with them as a guest. (b) It
happens at night in the garden, on a bench beneath a live oak at the edge of the
gravel walk, where she had gone to sit alone with her confused thoughts and where
Gouvernail has joined her, bringing a scarf sent by her husband. (c) The impulse
is physical desire: she has stopped listening to his words and is "drinking in the
tones of his voice", and she wants to reach out in the darkness and touch his face
or lips with her fingertips and to whisper against his cheek. What restrains her is
stated in the previous sentence — she would have done it "if she had not been a
respectable woman", that is, her social identity rather than her conscience.
(d) The sentence is built on **antithesis** and balanced comparatives — "the
stronger... the further" — so that the two opposing forces are measured against
each other inside a single clause, and the interpolated "in fact" gives it the
tone of a discovery rather than a judgement. It matters because it states the
story's whole conflict in one line and explains all her subsequent behaviour: her
flight to the city, her year of "strenuous opposition", and the impossibility of
telling even her husband. It also prepares the ending, since a woman who retreats
hardest when she is most tempted may still be retreating when she says she has
"overcome everything".

**2.** (a) Mrs. Baroda speaks them to her husband Gaston, laughing and after
pressing "a long, tender kiss" upon his lips, about a year after Gouvernail's
visit, on the occasion of her own unexpected proposal that he should be invited
again. (b) Gaston had just said that he was glad she had "finally overcome your
dislike for him", adding that "truly he did not deserve it" — assuming, as he has
throughout, that her objection was a groundless prejudice. (c) "Everything" may
mean (i) the attraction itself, so that she is announcing that she has mastered her
feelings and is now safe enough to receive him as an ordinary guest; or (ii) her
own resistance — the scruples, the respectability and the year of opposition — so
that the invitation is issued with a very different intention, and "I shall be very
nice to him" becomes a promise rather than a courtesy. Notice that she corrects
her husband's word "dislike" with the much larger word "everything", which is what
makes the second reading possible. (d) Chopin ends here because the story's subject
is the reader's judgement as much as Mrs. Baroda's conduct. To continue would be to
settle the question, and settling it would turn a study of a woman's inner life

assumption the title raises.

self_checks.question: Model answers — short questions
self_checks.answer:
**1.** She had "unconsciously formed an image of him in her mind", picturing him
tall, slim and cynical, wearing eyeglasses and carrying his hands in his pockets —
and on that basis she decided that she did not like him. The picture was almost
entirely wrong: he was slim, but not very tall and not at all cynical, and he wore
no eyeglasses and did not keep his hands in his pockets.

**2.** Because he asked nothing of her. She could not understand him, and when she
deliberately left him alone with her husband he "took no manner of exception" to
it. A hostess whose importance depends on being needed found herself unnecessary,
and the injury to her vanity turned her puzzlement into irritation.

**3.** She could see nothing in the dark but "the approaching red point of a
lighted cigar", and she knew from that alone that it must be Gouvernail, "for her
husband did not smoke". Her own white gown then revealed her to him.

**4.** He spoke of his college days with Gaston and of "the days of keen and blind
ambitions and large intentions", and said that all that was left to him now was "a
philosophic acquiescence to the existing order — only a desire to be permitted to
exist, with now and then a little whiff of genuine life, such as he was breathing
now."

**5.** That she was sensible as well as respectable, and "she knew there are some
battles in life which a human being must fight alone." Telling Gaston would have
relieved her own feelings at the cost of his peace and his oldest friendship.

**6.** It is Gaston who invites Gouvernail in the first place, and it is Gaston who
sends Gouvernail out into the dark garden with his wife's white scarf. The husband
thus arranges, in perfect innocence and out of simple kindness, the one encounter
that threatens his marriage.

self_checks.question: Model answers — long questions
self_checks.answer:
**1.** The story sets a natural impulse against an acquired identity and shows the
identity winning — at a price. Chopin prepares the ground carefully. Mrs. Baroda's
interest in Gouvernail is not presented as love; it grows out of vanity, because
he does not court her good opinion, and then out of curiosity, as she tries "to
penetrate the reserve in which he had unconsciously enveloped himself". On the
bench, in darkness, with a voice speaking Whitman's lines about the night, the
feeling becomes unmistakably physical: "Her physical being was for the moment
predominant," and she wants to touch his face and lips and to whisper against his
cheek — she "did not care what". Chopin then names the restraint precisely: she
would have done it "if she had not been a respectable woman". This is a social
category, not a moral one, and that is the story's quiet daring. The conflict is
then compressed into a single antithesis: "The stronger the impulse grew to bring
herself near him, the further, in fact, did she draw away from him." The cost of
the victory is measured in the next paragraph. Because respectable women may not
even name such feelings, she cannot tell the husband "who was also her friend",
and must fight "one of those battles in life which a human being must fight
alone". Chopin neither condemns the desire nor celebrates the restraint. She shows
a woman locked out of her own marriage by a word — and then, with the last line,
declines to tell us whether the lock held.

**2.** Chopin tells the story in the third person but stays entirely inside Mrs.
Baroda, and much of it is written in free indirect style, so that the character's
judgements reach us as if they were the narrator's: "she did not like him", "he
tires me frightfully". This has three consequences. First, we adopt her prejudice
before we examine it, and are therefore surprised along with her when Gouvernail
turns out to be likeable — the reader is caught out in exactly the way she is.
Second, it makes the crisis visible. Nothing happens on the bench that an observer
would notice; the whole event is a movement of feeling, and only an interior
viewpoint could record it. Third, and most cunningly, it controls what we are
allowed to know. We know what Gouvernail cannot know and what Gaston never learns,
which gives the final scene its dramatic irony — a delighted husband misreading
his wife in front of a reader who has more information than he does. But the same
device creates the famous ambiguity of the ending. Because the narration reports
Mrs. Baroda's speech without entering her mind at that moment, "I have overcome
everything! ... This time I shall be very nice to him" can mean that she has
conquered the attraction or that she has conquered her resistance to it. Chopin
had spent the whole story telling us what her heroine felt; by withholding it at
the last moment she forces the reader to supply the verdict, and whichever verdict
we supply tells us more about our own assumptions than about Mrs. Baroda. In a
magazine world that expected virtue to be rewarded visibly, that refusal was itself
a bold act.

**3.** Gouvernail's passivity is the mechanism of the entire story. He does not
flirt, does not flatter and does not pursue; Chopin states flatly that he "made no
direct appeal to her approval or even esteem". He will not fish or shoot, he is
happy to sit on the portico with a cigar listening to somebody else, and when his
hostess withdraws he "took no manner of exception". Had he made the smallest
advance, the story would have become a conventional tale of a predatory guest, and
Mrs. Baroda's struggle would have been merely a struggle against him. Because he
does nothing, everything that happens must come from inside her, and the story
becomes what Chopin wanted: a study of a woman discovering herself. His
indifference is also the precise cause of the trouble, since it is his
self-sufficiency that wounds her vanity and sets her pursuing him along the
batture. His innocence is maintained to the end — he sits down beside her "without
a suspicion that she might object", quotes Whitman "half to himself" in an
apostrophe that "was not addressed to her", and lights a fresh cigar as she
escapes. He never learns that anything occurred. At the same time Chopin makes him
more than a device: the disappointed man who asks only "to be permitted to exist,
with now and then a little whiff of genuine life" is a real and rather touching
figure, and it is his weariness, not any charm, that moves her. He is the still
centre of the story, and all its motion is measured against him.

self_checks.answer:
**1.** (a) "She" is Mrs. Baroda, mistress of the plantation; "him" is Gouvernail,

chapters.summary:
- "A Devoted Son" is a short story by the Indian writer Anita Desai (born 1937), from
  her collection *Games at Twilight and Other Stories* (1978).
- Rakesh, the son of a poor, illiterate man who worked forty years at a kerosene
  depot, stands first in the country in his medical examination, wins a scholarship
  to the USA, returns, marries the girl his mother chooses (Veena), becomes hospital
  director and then the richest doctor in town.
- After his wife's death and his retirement, old Varma "went to pieces". Rakesh
  nurses him tenderly but takes over his diet: halwa, fried and sweet food are banned,
  meals are weighed, and pills and tonics "became his diet".
- Varma resists in small ways — the jalebi plot, complaints to old Bhatia — and
  cries, "Let me die"; the family hears only "an incoherent croak".
- In the last scene Rakesh reaches out to press his father's feet and Varma tucks
  them away; Varma sweeps the tonic bottle out of his son's hand and prays, "God is
  calling me — now let me go."
- The title is ironic: Rakesh is devoted to Varma's health but deaf to his wishes.
  Themes: duty and its limits, care versus control, appearance and reality, class
  ambition, old age and loneliness.
- Techniques: irony (verbal, situational, dramatic), satire, hyperbole, simile,
  contrast and the shifting point of view; motifs of feet, food and medicine; the
  signboard and the tonic bottle as symbols.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- About the author
- The story
- Characters
- Themes
- Setting, structure and point of view
- Style and literary devices
- Glossary

Anita Desai's "A Devoted Son" begins with a boy touching his father's feet and
ends with a father tucking his feet away from his son's hands. Between those two
gestures lie forty years of Indian family life: a poor clerk's son who becomes the
most successful doctor in town, and a father who lives to see every wish of his
old age overruled by that son's medical judgement. The story is short, funny in
the first half and bitter in the second, and it never quite tells you whether
Rakesh is a saint or a tyrant. That refusal is what your examiner is testing.

chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** He bowed down and touched his father's feet. Varma repeated it because it proved
that his son, for all his new glory, was still respectful — the kind of "exemplary
filial behaviour" that made the parents proud, and of which the neighbours said, "One
does not often see such behaviour in sons any more."

**2.** Because "the USA" sounded grander and more familiar, "with a grand familiarity",
than "America", which was what the "ignorant neighbours" said. It shows Varma's pride
in his son's success and his wish to rise above the neighbours; Desai smiles at his
small snobbery.

**3.** She chose a plump, uneducated girl from her own village, the daughter of a
childhood friend: "so old-fashioned, so placid, so complaisant". That Rakesh accepted
her "almost without argument" shows his obedience to his mother and his lack of
interest in a foreign or educated wife.

**4.** One day Varma, ill, had ordered soojie halwa and eaten it with a saucerful of
cream. Rakesh walked in "with the confident and rather contemptuous stride of the
famous doctor" and announced "No more halwa for you, papa." After that everything
fried, then everything sweet, and finally everything the old man enjoyed was crossed
off his diet.

**5.** Bhatia was shocked. He asked in disbelief whether "even in this evil age" a son
could refuse his own father food, and murmured "Never" and "Your own son?" He is the
voice of common sense, and his amazement tells the reader that Rakesh's care has gone
too far.

**6.** Varma refused it: "Keep your tonic — I want none." With a sudden, "grand" wave
of his hand he swept the bottle out of Rakesh's grasp, so that it smashed and the
brown syrup stained his son's white trousers.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** The title names Rakesh a "devoted son", and Desai spends the first half of the
story proving it. He touches his father's feet on the day of the results and again on
his return from the USA; he comes home when he could have stayed abroad; he marries the
girl his mother chose; he nurses his mother "at the last moment"; he brings his
father's tea in his favourite tumbler, reads him the news, arranges his pillows and
carries him out to the lawn on summer nights. Even the "most rancorous" neighbours admit
his goodness.

In the second half Desai shows the other side. Rakesh bans halwa and then every fried,
sweet and enjoyable food; he weighs his father's cereal; he replaces meals with pills; he
laughs outside the door at the old man's complaints; and he ignores the plain plea, "Let
me die." The narrator says it outright: "his masterly efficiency was nothing but cold
heartlessness, his authority was only tyranny in disguise." At the end, when Rakesh
comes with a new tonic, Varma tucks away his feet and smashes the bottle.

So Rakesh is devoted to Varma's *health*, duty and public image, but not to Varma's
*wishes*. The title is therefore ironic: he is a devoted son in every outward sense, yet
the old man's dignity is lost in that devotion.

**2.** Irony — the gap between appearance and reality — is the method of the story.
(a) The **title** means one thing in the first half and another in the second.
(b) **Verbal irony**: "such a son as few women had borne", "that pearl amongst pearls",
and the "radiant heights of fame and fortune" echo the community's exaggerated praise
with a gentle smile. (c) **Situational irony**: the son who does everything right makes
his father miserable; the medicine meant to prolong life prolongs a life the old man
wants to end; and the mother's death is greeted with "a sigh that sounded positively
happy". (d) **Dramatic irony**: the reader believes Varma when he says "I'm dying",
while the family, used to his fake deaths, laughs. (e) The **shift** in the narrator's
stance after "talent and skill... cease to dazzle" turns the same acts of care
into tyranny. (f) The **ending** reverses the opening gesture: the feet Rakesh touched
in respect are now tucked away in refusal. Desai never explains the irony; she lets
the reader feel it, which is why the story is disturbing rather than merely sad.

**3.** Rakesh's care is medically sound. Varma's diet is cut, his pills taken and his
hospital visits made because a doctor believes that a long life is the greatest gift.
But Varma wants something else: to eat what he loves, to be heard, and, at the last, to
be allowed to go: "I do not want to live only to eat your medicines." The story sets
care and freedom against each other.

Desai gives the reader the details of what care costs: the scales, the boiled
lentils, the propped-up pillows, the stomach pump, and the servants thumping the bed
down on the veranda. She shows that the old man's dignity is lost step by step, and that
the family cannot tell a fair complaint from "a peevish whim". His final act — sweeping
the bottle from his son's hand — is the only free act left to him, and it is "suddenly
grand, suddenly effective". The story does not say that care is wrong; it says that care
without listening becomes control, and that even loving control can be a kind of
cruelty.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) Old Varma speaks them to his son Rakesh on the veranda of their house one
summer evening. (b) Rakesh had just arrived from the clinic in his sky-blue Ambassador,
sat on the edge of the bed, reached out to press his father's feet and offered him a new
tonic ("Promise me you will take it regularly, papa"). (c) Varma sweeps the bottle out of
Rakesh's hand "with a wave of his own, suddenly grand, suddenly effective": it shows that
the old man, weak and unheard for years, has found one moment of power and dignity, and
that he refuses the medical regime that has replaced his life. (d) The story opened
with Rakesh bowing to touch his father's feet in respect; it ends with Rakesh reaching for
those feet and Varma tucking them away, then rejecting the son's gift. The ritual of
respect has become an act of refusal, and the "devoted son" of the title is shown to be
devoted to the wrong thing.

**2.** (a) The talent and skill are Rakesh's — his brilliance in examinations, his
scholarship, his surgery and his success as director and clinic owner. (b) The very next
lines describe Varma, who, "having retired from work and having lost his wife", "very
quickly went to pieces", growing complaining, ill and theatrical. (c) Until now the
narrator echoed the community's praise; from here the story turns from admiring the
son to watching the father, and the same qualities begin to look different: the
narrator will soon say that "efficiency" was "cold heartlessness". (d) The sentence is the
hinge of the story. It says that public glory fades with habit, that a whole town has
stopped looking at the doctor, and that only the father, who lives with him, is left to
judge. It also introduces the story's real subject, which is not success but what success
does to those closest to it.

chapters.name: The Treasure in the Forest - H. G. Wells
topics: Setting, structure and point of view
chapters.summary:
- "The Treasure in the Forest" is a short story by the English writer H. G. Wells (1866–1946),
  first published in *Pall Mall Budget* on 23 August 1894 and collected in *The Stolen Bacillus
  and Other Incidents* (1895).
- Two British adventurers, Evans and Hooker, approach a tropical island by canoe with a stolen
  Chinese map, guided by a dotted line from a gap in the coral reef to a clump of palms; the star
  marks the treasure where the line cuts a river.
- In a dream Evans recalls how they overheard three Chinese men talk of a Spanish galleon's treasure
  that Chang-hi had found and reburied "very safe" — and how they took the map from him by force;
  Chang-hi's last grin haunts the dream.
- They drink at the river, cross the cool, silent forest and find a dead Chinese man beside a dug hole
  with gold ingots half uncovered; Hooker thinks he was killed by a snake.
- Evans is pricked by a "little thorn" twice while loading the gold; he becomes irritable and ill and
  dies in convulsions. Hooker is pricked in the thumb and understands that the map's "little dashes"
  were poisoned thorns and Chang-hi's "safety" a trap. He waits, dying, beside the gold.
- Themes: greed and punishment, appearance against reality, nature as silent judge, prejudice that
  blinds; techniques: foreshadowing, suspense, dramatic irony, symbolism, pathetic fallacy and a
  close third-person viewpoint.
- The story is a moral tale in the form of a thriller; the dead man, not Chang-hi, is the body in the
  forest; the killing of Chang-hi is only implied.

"The Treasure in the Forest" is one of H. G. Wells's earliest short stories and one
of his most compact. Two men paddle a canoe towards a tropical island with a
stolen map. In the first pages they are thirsty and eager; by the last page they are
dying in a silent forest beside a heap of gold. Nothing in the story is wasted:
every small detail — the map's "little dashes", a "little prick" on the thumb, the
grin on a dead man's face — turns out to be a clue. It is a story about greed, but
it is also a lesson in how a storyteller plants a secret in plain sight and then
lets the reader discover it a moment before the characters do.

## Chapter summary

- "The Treasure in the Forest" is a short story by the English writer H. G. Wells (1866–1946),
  first published in *Pall Mall Budget* on 23 August 1894 and collected in *The Stolen Bacillus
  and Other Incidents* (1895).
- Two British adventurers, Evans and Hooker, approach a tropical island by canoe with a stolen
  Chinese map, guided by a dotted line from a gap in the coral reef to a clump of palms; the star
  marks the treasure where the line cuts a river.
- In a dream Evans recalls how they overheard three Chinese men talk of a Spanish galleon's treasure
  that Chang-hi had found and reburied "very safe" — and how they took the map from him by force;
  Chang-hi's last grin haunts the dream.
- They drink at the river, cross the cool, silent forest and find a dead Chinese man beside a dug hole
  with gold ingots half uncovered; Hooker thinks he was killed by a snake.
- Evans is pricked by a "little thorn" twice while loading the gold; he becomes irritable and ill and
  dies in convulsions. Hooker is pricked in the thumb and understands that the map's "little dashes"
  were poisoned thorns and Chang-hi's "safety" a trap. He waits, dying, beside the gold.
- Themes: greed and punishment, appearance against reality, nature as silent judge, prejudice that
  blinds; techniques: foreshadowing, suspense, dramatic irony, symbolism, pathetic fallacy and a
  close third-person viewpoint.
- The story is a moral tale in the form of a thriller; the dead man, not Chang-hi, is the body in the
  forest; the killing of Chang-hi is only implied.

## Model answers — short questions

**1.** They knew that a Spanish galleon from the Philippines had been wrecked and its ingots
buried, and that Chang-hi had found and reburied them "very safe". They learned it by overhearing
three Chinese men talk in pidgin English round a fire one moonlit night; later they took Chang-hi's
map from him.

**2.** The "little marks" looked like the plan of a house, and the "little dashes, pointing this way
and that" in the corner could not be explained by either man. In fact the dashes showed where poisoned
thorns had been set around the gold.

**3.** They had made a long night voyage in an unprovisioned canoe under a blazing sun and were
almost mad with thirst — Evans said he would "have to drink sea water" and finally sucked up the water
with his lips. Their physical need was stronger than their greed, for a moment.

**4.** He supposed "some poisonous snake" had killed him: "He stole a march on his friends. He came
here alone, and some poisonous snake has killed him." The neck was "puffed and purple" and the hands
and ankles swollen, which matches a snakebite, and this wrong guess kept the danger hidden.

**5.** He felt a little prick on the ball of his thumb and found a slender thorn two inches long.
Seeing Evans twitching and the blue body among the trees, he "thought of the little dashes in the
corner of the plan, and in a moment he understood": the thorns were like those the Dyaks poison for
their blowpipes.

**6.** It shows that Chang-hi knew something the thieves did not: that his treasure was guarded by
poisoned thorns, so that anyone who took the map would be killed. It is a moment of silent triumph, and
when Hooker "understood that grin now" it becomes the key to the story.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** Every stage of the story shows greed leading to destruction. Evans and Hooker are "stranded
British wastrels" who have seized a map by force from Chang-hi; they cross the sea without water;
and on the island Evans's only reaction to the dead body is fury that "somebody has been here
before". When the gold is found they think only of carrying it away. Even after Evans is pricked twice
they keep on lifting ingots, and Evans refuses Hooker's wish to bury the corpse: "Let that mass of
corruption bide." Each small act of greed takes them closer to the thorns.

The punishment fits the crime. They have stolen a treasure from a man who had guarded it by
poison; he is avenged without being present. The forest's silence and the falling petals suggest that
nature itself has passed judgement. Wells states no moral; the men's deaths do it for him.

**2.** **Foreshadowing** is planted in every scene: the map's "little dashes"; Chang-hi's "great stress
on the safety"; his "incomprehensible and startling grin"; Evans's dream of devils feeding him with
burning coals and of a furnace in his mouth; the corpse's swollen neck, hands and ankles; Hooker's unease,
"It scares me somehow"; Evans's two pricks; his sudden "unreasonable anger". Each looks
like a small piece of description and later proves to be a clue.

**Suspense** comes from delay and partial knowledge. The story withholds the cause of the danger until
the last page, allows a false explanation (a snake), hides the real symptoms behind Evans's bad temper
and tiredness, and keeps the reader watching a man reach for more gold while the clues pile up. The
structure (calm beach, cool silent forest, dead man, gold, collapse) raises the tension by stages;
the final lines, in which Hooker sits silent by the ingots, leave the reader in the stillness.

**3.** Evans is the more impulsive, loud and greedy. He drinks so greedily that he leans out of the canoe to suck up the water, shouts and stamps at the discovery of the corpse, is exultant at the gold, insults his
partner, and dismisses a dead man as "that mass of corruption". His anger, which hides his poisoning,
is his most characteristic feature.

Hooker is quieter and more observant. He tastes the water, sees "something blue", notices the swollen
neck, suggests burying the body, and keeps staring "searchingly among the grey depths between the trees".
He wants the gold too and helped to seize the map, so he is not innocent; but he has a conscience and an
imagination, and these make him the one who finally understands.

The two are opposite in temperament but equal in guilt, and the story ends by treating them alike: both
are killed by the same thorns, in the same way, for the same reason.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) Evans says it, in the forest beside the dug hole, to Hooker. (b) The gold ingots have
been found in the hole, "dull yellow bars", beside the body of a dead Chinese man. (c) He
overlooks the danger: the dead man, the swollen neck, the "little thorn" that has already pricked
his hand, and the fact that "somebody has been here before". He also overlooks Hooker's unease. (d) It
shows that Evans is practical, calculating and completely absorbed in the gold. He thinks
at once of the next step — hiding and selling — and has no room for doubt, pity or caution. It is also
dramatic irony, for the reader senses that neither man will ever reach the mainland.

**2.** (a) "He" is Hooker; the grin belongs to Chang-hi, the Chinese man who found and buried the
treasure and drew the map. (b) It appeared in Evans's dream at the moment when Evans held Chang-hi by
the pigtail and Chang-hi "grinned, a most incomprehensible and startling grin". (c) Hooker has just
understood that the thorns that pricked him and Evans are poisoned like the Dyaks' blowpipe darts, that
the little dashes on the map marked them, and that Chang-hi's "assurance of the safety" of his treasure
was literally true: the grin meant he knew the thieves would be killed. (d) It is the climax of the
story and the answer to the mystery. It turns every earlier clue into meaning, reveals Chang-hi's
cunning, and completes the irony: the victim has won. It also happens at the moment when it is too
late for the characters to profit from the knowledge.

A man travels for days in the depth of winter to sell his family's old house and to
take his mother and nephew away to a new place. On the way he remembers a boyhood
friend, a boy with a silver necklet who once stabbed at a badger-like animal under a
golden moon. Then the friend arrives — old before his time, shivering, and calling him
"Master". Lu Xun's "My Old Home" is a short, quiet and moving story that turns a
family's leaving into a picture of a whole country: the cruelty of class, the
poverty of the peasant, and the faint, stubborn hope that the next generation may
live differently. Its last paragraph, about hope and a road, is one of the most quoted
in modern Chinese literature.

## Chapter summary

chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** He has come "with the sole object of saying goodbye". The old house, in which his clan had lived
for many years, has been sold and must be handed over before New Year's Day; he has come to take his
mother and nephew to the place where he now works.

**2.** He sees "a golden moon suspended in a deep blue sky", a seashore planted with jade-green
watermelons, and in the middle a boy of eleven or twelve in a silver necklet thrusting a steel pitchfork
at a *zha*, which dodges the blow and escapes between his legs. The boy is the young Runtu.

**3.** Mrs Yang is a neighbour of about fifty who used to sit in the beancurd shop across the road and
was then called the "Beancurd Beauty". She is called "the Compass" because she stands with her
hands on her hips and her trousered legs apart, "just like the compass in a box of geometrical
instruments".

**4.** The round, crimson-faced boy of memory has become a sallow, deeply wrinkled man twice his former size,
with swollen, red-rimmed eyes, a shabby felt cap, a single thin padded jacket and hands "like the bark of a
pine tree". He is shivering, almost speechless and addresses the narrator respectfully as "Master".

**5.** He takes two long tables, four chairs, an incense burner and candlesticks, and a balance, and asks for all
the ashes from the stove, which are used as fertiliser for the sandy soil.

**6.** Hongr asks, "Uncle, when shall we go back?" because Shuisheng has invited him to his home. It
matters because the children, unlike the adults, show no class barrier between them; the question
brings the narrator hope that the next generation will not be divided.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** The heart of the story is the difference between the two meetings of the same two people. In childhood,
the narrator, a rich man's "spoilt" son, and Runtu, a labourer's son, become "fast friends" in a few hours.
They share stories of birds and watermelons and cry at parting. Thirty years later, Runtu stands in the
doorway with swollen eyes and calls his friend "Master". The narrator feels "a shiver" and knows "what a
lamentably thick wall had grown up between us". The narrator cannot speak; Runtu refuses the familiar name
that the narrator's mother offers: "What bad manners that would be. I was a child then and didn't understand."

The wall is made by class. Runtu has been crushed by poverty, taxes and the habit of deference, and the narrator
has been raised above him by money and education. Neither is at fault; the society they live in is. The story ends
with the narrator feeling "an invisible high wall, cutting me off from my fellows". Lu Xun shows the wall as
something made by people, and therefore something that can be taken down; the children Hongr and Shuisheng,
who play together without hesitation, prove it.

**2.** Hope is the last theme of the story and is treated honestly. As the boat leaves, the narrator sees Hongr and
Shuisheng as friends and hopes that "they will not allow a barrier to grow up between them"; he wants them to
have "a new life, a life we have never experienced". But immediately he is "afraid": when Runtu asked for the incense
burner and candlesticks, he had laughed up his sleeve at his idol-worship, yet now he sees that "what I now called hope
was no more than an idol I had created myself", only more remote.

The closing sentences turn that doubt into a positive idea: "hope cannot be said to exist, nor can it be said not to
exist", like roads across the earth: there were none to begin with, but "when many men pass one way, a road is made". Hope is not a fact or a promise but a direction; it becomes real only when many people
walk the same way. The story's last image, the golden moon and the green seashore, returns to the picture of childhood
and recasts it as a picture of the future.

**3.** Runtu is the story's portrait of the Chinese peasant. As a boy he is bright, brave and knowledgeable
about nature; as a man he is "sallow", wrinkled, shivering in one thin jacket, with a hand "like the bark of a pine tree".
His own words give the causes: many children, bad harvests, and taxes that mean that when he sells he loses money and when
he does not sell his produce rots. The narrator adds "famines, taxes, soldiers, bandits, officials and landed gentry", all
of which had "squeezed him as dry as a mummy".

Runtu has lost his voice as well as his health: his lips move without sound, he cannot express his bitterness, and his
face is "just as if he were a stone statue". He is polite, dignified and religious, choosing the incense burner and
candlesticks, which shows his need of consolation. Through him Lu Xun shows a people exhausted by poverty and
oppression, yet still human — and still worth hoping for.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) "I" is the narrator of the story, a man who has come back to sell the family home; "us" means himself and
Runtu. (b) Runtu has just come into the room after thirty years and, instead of greeting him by name, has said
respectfully "Master!". (c) The "wall" is the invisible barrier of class and habit — rich and poor, master and servant —
that has grown between two boyhood friends. It is not built of stone but of deference, poverty, and the way society has
taught each man to treat the other. (d) It is the moment of recognition: until now the narrator had hoped to find his
friend unchanged; with one word he understands that the boyhood of the golden moon is gone and that the wall
cannot be crossed by goodwill alone. The rest of the story — Runtu's complaints, the furniture, Mrs Yang's suspicion,
the narrator's sense of being cut off — follows from it.

**2.** (a) He is lying in the cabin of the boat that is carrying him and his family away from the old home at night,
listening to the water under the boat and half asleep. (b) He has thought of his nephew Hongr and of Shuisheng, who
already wish to meet again, and wondered whether the wall between their fathers will be repeated in their lives; then he
has realised that his hope may be no more than an idol. (c) A road does not exist until people walk on the same ground
again and again; in the same way, hope is not a fact but something made by the collective action of many people. (d) The
sentence says that the future is not given but has to be made; it is neither naive optimism nor despair. The
story's whole movement — from winter gloom and the wall between two men, to children who play without one — leads to
this sentence: change is possible, but only if people walk together.

respectfully "Master!". (c) The "wall" is the invisible barrier of class and habit — rich and poor, master and servant —
that has grown between two boyhood friends. It is not built of stone but of deference, poverty, and the way society has
taught each man to treat the other. (d) It is the moment of recognition: until now the narrator had hoped to find his
friend unchanged; with one word he understands that the boyhood of the golden moon is gone and that the wall
cannot be crossed by goodwill alone. The rest of the story — Runtu's complaints, the furniture, Mrs Yang's suspicion,
the narrator's sense of being cut off — follows from it.

**2.** (a) He is lying in the cabin of the boat that is carrying him and his family away from the old home at night,
listening to the water under the boat and half asleep. (b) He has thought of his nephew Hongr and of Shuisheng, who
already wish to meet again, and wondered whether the wall between their fathers will be repeated in their lives; then he
has realised that his hope may be no more than an idol. (c) A road does not exist until people walk on the same ground
again and again; in the same way, hope is not a fact but something made by the collective action of many people. (d) The
sentence says that the future is not given but has to be made; it is neither naive optimism nor despair. The
story's whole movement — from winter gloom and the wall between two men, to children who play without one — leads to
this sentence: change is possible, but only if people walk together.

## Topics to cover

- About the author
- The story
- Characters
- Themes
- Setting, structure and point of view
- Style and literary devices
- Glossary
- Textbook exercises
- Part One: the tourist's speech
- Part Two: the guide's speech

Most stories tell you what happened. This one lets two men talk. A foreign tourist,
warmed by whisky in a Kathmandu guest-house, tells his guide how wonderful Nepal is — its
peace, its gods, its carved windows, its momos, its smiles. The next day the guide takes the
tourist up a hill to a farmer's house and shows him what the tourist's words have left out.
Shankar Lamichhane's story has almost no action: it is two speeches, each addressed to a silent
listener, and a pair of eyes. Yet by the last sentence it has asked a question that every Nepali
reader knows: *what do visitors see when they look at us, and what do they not see?*

chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** He means that the East has given the West religion, the Puranas, brass images, ivory ornaments, palm-leaf
manuscripts, copperplate inscriptions, civilisation and wisdom, and has done so "innocent of the notion of ownership",
while the West has taken. It is an admiring speech, but it treats the East as a giver and not as an equal.

**2.** It is the gaze of perception "pure and without contamination; sight that perceives everything in its true
form". The tourist attributes it to the shaven-headed monks and nuns; *samyak* is Sanskrit for "right" or "complete",
as in the Buddhist "right view".

**3.** The tourist has already seen and "understood" such sights and even "preached" them; the temple, with its Shiva
shrine, Buddha images and prayer wheels, is an example of tolerance he already admires. The guide wants to show him the
reality that is not on the tourist's map: a poor farmer's house.

**4.** He tells them that the tourist is a doctor, so that they welcome him with hope and a smile that the tourist
had praised the day before. The guide lies in order to show the tourist what a smile based on hope alone is worth, since
it will be "extinguished" when the visitor goes.

**5.** The child, says the guide, "can neither give nor take anything at all". He says it in answer to the tourist's
claim that Easterners "always" give to the West: here is an Easterner who cannot give, and his "endurance" is not a
virtue but the silence of a helpless body.

**6.** The guide says that the child's eyes are "eyes surrounded by mountains", eyes that "welcome you" and "build", and that
"in these eyes hides the end of life". He ends: "They are just as beautiful as the setting sun's reflection in the
eyes of the Buddha!" — uniting the boy's eyes with the image from the title.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** Eyes are the story's central image and its unifying thread. In Part One the tourist sees Nepal as "a land of
eyes": the half-closed eyes of the Buddha, the eyes of the carved windows and the painted door panels, the eyes on
the stupas, the eyes of the people, and the Himalaya "peeping" through the hills. He admires the "samyak gaze" of
the monks and asks to be shown "beautiful, full eyes". The eyes stand for calm, wisdom, welcome and spiritual
sight.

In Part Two the guide shows a different pair: the eyes of a paralysed child, "the only living parts of his body",
unmoved and expressionless, though they light up with longing when he sees his sister. They too are "the eyes you
wanted", he tells the tourist. By answering the tourist's romantic eyes with a suffering child's, the story asks
what it really means to *see*: the samyak gaze, he hints, is not a visitor's rapture but a look at the whole truth.

The image also joins the two halves, and the last line unites them: the boy's eyes are "just as beautiful as the
setting sun's reflection in the eyes of the Buddha". Beauty, the story says, and the end of life are in the same
eyes.

**2.** The **tourist** sees Nepal as a beautiful, peaceful, spiritual country: a green valley with earthen houses, a
place of carved temples and eternal calm, inhabited by smiling, generous people who have always "given" to the
West. He is happy, romantic, and a little drunk; he knows it from books; and he praises the country for qualities (innocence, endurance,
harmony) that are comforting to a visitor. He wants the "eyes without equal" that will make his journey unforgettable.

The **guide** knows the same places but sees "the pulse of our reality". He does not deny the harmony of Adinath, but
he refuses to show it. He shows instead a poor farmer's family, taxed by a city landlord, who cook no momos and tell no
stories; a child paralysed by polio and without help; and parents whose smile depends on a lie. His tone is ironic,
controlled and angry. He tests the tourist's praise — "this can surely only be found in an Easterner!" — by
showing what "endurance" means in a helpless body.

The two views are not wholly opposed. Both love the country and both speak of harmony. The difference is that the
tourist sees the surface and the guide sees what is under it; one looks at a picture, the other at a person.

**3.** Your textbook describes the story's technique as **stream of consciousness**. Instead of a narrator telling
what happened, the story consists of two long speeches, each a flow of thought, image and memory addressed to a silent
listener. The tourist moves by association from the aeroplane view to history, art, food, smiles and eyes, and his
speech is broken by drinks; the guide moves from a hill to a temple, a house, a child and the child's imagined words.
There is very little plot; what matters is the contrast between two ways of seeing.

The technique has several effects. It lets us know each speaker from within: the tourist's sentimentality and the
guide's irony and discomfort. It shows how a mind moves from one picture to another, in the way of a drunk man's rapture and
a sober man's anger. It makes the reader the silent listener and therefore a participant. And it gives the story a
pattern of speech and answer, joined by the image of eyes. The form is unconventional, but the pattern is exact: the
tourist asks for eyes and the guide shows them.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) The guide speaks to the tourist in the farmer's house on the hill near Chobhar, looking at the paralysed
child. (b) The day before, the tourist had said that "we Eastern peoples were always making contributions to the West";
he had praised Easterners as givers who know nothing of taking. (c) The guide is pointing out that the tourist's compliment
is empty: here is an Easterner who can give nothing and take nothing, who is helpless, and whose "endurance" is
merely survival. He asks the tourist to imagine how it feels to be unable to move a finger or speak. (d) The tone is
quiet, controlled and bitterly ironic, with an undercurrent of anger; the guide is polite ("Shall I give you some
water?") but every word is an answer to the tourist's romantic phrases.

**2.** (a) The guide says it to the tourist, at the farmer's house, before bringing him to the child. (b) He wants the tourist
to see what a smile of welcome can mean: the tourist had praised the Nepali smile as "a smile from the soul", and the
guide wants to show that in the village it is a smile of hope that a stranger can cure a child; he also wants the
tourist to see the parents' faith with his own eyes. (c) The parents welcome the visitor "as if your coming here were
preordained", like an eldest son who has brought a remedy across seven seas; they smile with gratitude. The guide knows the smile
will last only while the tourist is there and then they will "sink back into the same old darkness". (d) It shows that the
guide is angry and disillusioned, able to use deceit to make a point, and uneasy about it: he is not simply a spokesman but a man
who has done something ambiguous, and the story does not excuse him.

chapters.name: A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings - Gabriel Garcia Marquez
topics: Setting, structure and point of view
chapters.summary:
- "A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings" (Spanish: *Un señor muy viejo con unas alas enormes*) is a short story by the
  Colombian writer **Gabriel García Márquez** (1927–2014; Nobel Prize 1982), written in 1968, subtitled *A Tale for
  Children*, and translated into English by Gregory Rabassa.
- After three days of rain, Pelayo finds a very old, filthy man with huge buzzard's wings in his muddy courtyard. His wife
  Elisenda and he first think him a castaway; a neighbour woman calls him an angel; Father Gonzaga, who greets him in
  Latin, doubts it and writes to Rome.
- They lock the old man in the chicken coop, and Elisenda charges five cents to see him. Crowds come, torment and exploit him;
  the family grows rich. The angel's only supernatural virtue is patience; his "miracles" are comic.
- A travelling show with a woman changed into a spider for disobeying her parents takes the crowd away. The couple build a
  mansion with iron bars on the windows.
- The angel grows ill and old in the yard and shed, survives a winter, grows new feathers and flies away; Elisenda watches him
  become "an imaginary dot on the horizon of the sea", no longer an annoyance.
- Themes: the way people turn a wonder into a spectacle, greed and commercialism, cruelty to the weak, the limits of
  religious and scientific knowledge, old age and dignity. Techniques: magical realism, irony, satire, deadpan humour,
  hyperbole, symbol and a calm third-person narrator.
- The old man is never proved an angel; the story's interest is in how people treat him.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- About the author
- The story
- Characters
- Themes
- Setting, structure and point of view
- Style and literary devices
- Glossary
- Textbook exercises

After three days of rain, a man throwing dead crabs into the sea comes back to find a filthy,
toothless old man lying in the mud of his courtyard — with the enormous, dirty wings of a
buzzard. A neighbour says he is an angel; a priest says he is an impostor; a doctor says he is
a wonder of nature; and a village that has never seen anything like him first gapes, then pays
five cents to stare at him, and then drifts off to a show about a woman changed into a spider. Gabriel
García Márquez's story is funny, sad and strange, and it is built on a simple trick: the most
extraordinary event in the world is told in the tone of a village rumour. It is the standard example
of **magical realism** in your course.

## Chapter summary

chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** After three days of rain the house was full of dead crabs, and the newborn child had a fever that the family blamed on the smell.
Pelayo crossed the flooded courtyard to throw the crabs into the sea, and on his way back found the old man.

**2.** The neighbour woman, who "knew everything about life and death", said the old man was an angel who had probably come for
the sick child but had been knocked down by the rain because he was so old. She also advised killing him.

**3.** He went into the chicken coop and greeted the old man in Latin. The old man did not understand, which made the priest suspect an
impostor, since an angel should know "the language of God". He also noticed that the old man smelled, was full of parasites and was
"much too human".

**4.** Elisenda fenced in the courtyard and charged five cents admission to see the angel. Pilgrims and curious visitors came from far away, and in less than a
week the couple had "crammed their rooms with money"; they later built a two-storey mansion.

**5.** The spider woman's show cost less, she answered questions, and her story of disobeying her parents was a clear moral lesson "full of so much human
truth". The angel, by contrast, was silent and aloof, and his "miracles" (three new teeth for a blind man, sunflowers for a leper) were absurd.

**6.** After a hard winter, the old man grows new feathers and, one morning, flies away clumsily but successfully. Elisenda, cutting onions, feels relief
"for herself and for him" as she watches him become "an imaginary dot on the horizon of the sea".

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** Magical realism tells extraordinary events in the plain, matter-of-fact voice of everyday life. García Márquez's story opens with real, unpleasant
details — three days of rain, dead crabs, a feverish baby — and in the middle of them puts an impossible event, a very old man with buzzard's wings lying in the mud. The
narrator does not gasp. Pelayo and Elisenda "found him familiar" and skip "the inconvenience of the wings". The neighbour identifies him as an angel in one practical sentence,
and the priest's first worry is that he cannot speak Latin.

Other marvels are treated in the same tone: the "consolation miracles" (teeth for a blind man, sunflowers for a leper), the woman changed into a spider who lives on meatballs, the woman who counts her heartbeats
and runs out of numbers, sea and sky as "a single ash-gray thing", and the angel's flight seen by a woman chopping onions. Magic and reality are mixed in every paragraph, and the effect is both funny
and moving. The technique lets Márquez show that people react to wonders as they react to anything else: with curiosity, business sense and boredom.

**2.** The people treat the old man badly in many ways. The neighbours toss him food as if he were a circus animal; the crowd lets the hens peck his wings, pulls out his feathers, throws stones and burns him with
a branding iron. Pelayo and Elisenda lock him in a chicken coop, sell tickets, neglect him and later chase him out of the bedroom with a broom, shouting that it is "hell full of angels". Father Gonzaga treats him as a
theological question and leaves him in the coop while waiting for Rome. Only the child and the doctor come close to treating him as a living being.

This shows human nature in several lights: **curiosity** without kindness, **greed** that turns a wonder into a business, **cruelty** towards anyone weak or different, **fickleness** (the crowd leaves for a cheaper show), and
**self-interest** disguised as faith. Yet the couple are not monsters: they are kind enough not to club him and they feel relief at the end, so Márquez shows ordinary people, not villains, as the source of cruelty.

**3.** The angel is a symbol with many possible readings, and Márquez fixes none. He may stand for **the helpless stranger or the refugee**, caged and exploited; for **the aged and unwanted**, who are a burden
when they are no longer useful; for **the artist or the divine**, whom society admires as a spectacle but does not understand; or for **faith itself** in a world of commerce and bureaucracy. He is both holy
and human: verminous, feverish, deaf to Latin, but patient and dignified.

The ending is ambiguous too. His flight is a release, for him and for the family. Elisenda's sigh of relief "for herself and for him" shows that she is free of a nuisance and feels, perhaps without knowing it, something like
gladness that he is free. The "imaginary dot on the horizon" suggests that a marvel that has been treated as an annoyance has left the world unchanged, and the house with its iron bars remains closed to angels.

## Model answers — reference to the context

**1.** (a) The old man with enormous wings, whom the neighbour woman calls an angel. (b) The hens pecked at him, cripples pulled out his feathers to touch their sores, the merciful threw stones to make him stand, and
the crowd burned his side with a branding iron to see whether he was dead. Others tried to make him eat mothballs and papal lunches and heated him with lamps and candles. (c) Because, apart from
his wings, nothing about him was supernatural: he smelled, he had parasites, he was ill and old. The only thing that set him apart from ordinary men was the endless calm with which he endured cruelty. (d) The tone is dry, deadpan and
ironic: the narrator speaks of the marvellous as if it were a minor fact and uses the word "virtue" lightly, yet the sentence carries a real pity.

**2.** (a) "He" is the old man, the angel; "her" is Elisenda, Pelayo's wife. (b) After a difficult winter the old man has grown new feathers and, while Elisenda is cutting onions in the kitchen, has flown away from the shed.
She has watched him until he vanished over the sea. (c) Elisenda feels relief: she is rid of the annoyance he had become; but her sigh is "for herself and for him", so there is also a trace of sympathy, perhaps
gladness that he has escaped. (d) The ending is fitting because it is quiet and unsentimental: the most marvellous thing in the story ends with a household chore, a sigh and a tiny dot in the distance. It returns the
story to the ordinary life from which it began, and it leaves the reader to decide what has been lost.
