self_checks.answer:
**1.** After three days of rain the house was full of dead crabs, and the newborn child had a fever that the family blamed on the smell.
Pelayo crossed the flooded courtyard to throw the crabs into the sea, and on his way back found the old man.

**2.** The neighbour woman, who "knew everything about life and death", said the old man was an angel who had probably come for
the sick child but had been knocked down by the rain because he was so old. She also advised killing him.

**3.** He went into the chicken coop and greeted the old man in Latin. The old man did not understand, which made the priest suspect an
impostor, since an angel should know "the language of God". He also noticed that the old man smelled, was full of parasites and was
"much too human".

**4.** Elisenda fenced in the courtyard and charged five cents admission to see the angel. Pilgrims and curious visitors came from far away, and in less than a
week the couple had "crammed their rooms with money"; they later built a two-storey mansion.

**5.** The spider woman's show cost less, she answered questions, and her story of disobeying her parents was a clear moral lesson "full of so much human
truth". The angel, by contrast, was silent and aloof, and his "miracles" (three new teeth for a blind man, sunflowers for a leper) were absurd.

**6.** After a hard winter, the old man grows new feathers and, one morning, flies away clumsily but successfully. Elisenda, cutting onions, feels relief
"for herself and for him" as she watches him become "an imaginary dot on the horizon of the sea".

self_checks.question: Model answers — long questions
self_checks.answer:
**1.** Magical realism tells extraordinary events in the plain, matter-of-fact voice of everyday life. García Márquez's story opens with real, unpleasant
details — three days of rain, dead crabs, a feverish baby — and in the middle of them puts an impossible event, a very old man with buzzard's wings lying in the mud. The
narrator does not gasp. Pelayo and Elisenda "found him familiar" and skip "the inconvenience of the wings". The neighbour identifies him as an angel in one practical sentence,
and the priest's first worry is that he cannot speak Latin.

Other marvels are treated in the same tone: the "consolation miracles" (teeth for a blind man, sunflowers for a leper), the woman changed into a spider who lives on meatballs, the woman who counts her heartbeats
and runs out of numbers, sea and sky as "a single ash-gray thing", and the angel's flight seen by a woman chopping onions. Magic and reality are mixed in every paragraph, and the effect is both funny
and moving. The technique lets Márquez show that people react to wonders as they react to anything else: with curiosity, business sense and boredom.

**2.** The people treat the old man badly in many ways. The neighbours toss him food as if he were a circus animal; the crowd lets the hens peck his wings, pulls out his feathers, throws stones and burns him with
a branding iron. Pelayo and Elisenda lock him in a chicken coop, sell tickets, neglect him and later chase him out of the bedroom with a broom, shouting that it is "hell full of angels". Father Gonzaga treats him as a
theological question and leaves him in the coop while waiting for Rome. Only the child and the doctor come close to treating him as a living being.

This shows human nature in several lights: **curiosity** without kindness, **greed** that turns a wonder into a business, **cruelty** towards anyone weak or different, **fickleness** (the crowd leaves for a cheaper show), and
**self-interest** disguised as faith. Yet the couple are not monsters: they are kind enough not to club him and they feel relief at the end, so Márquez shows ordinary people, not villains, as the source of cruelty.

**3.** The angel is a symbol with many possible readings, and Márquez fixes none. He may stand for **the helpless stranger or the refugee**, caged and exploited; for **the aged and unwanted**, who are a burden
when they are no longer useful; for **the artist or the divine**, whom society admires as a spectacle but does not understand; or for **faith itself** in a world of commerce and bureaucracy. He is both holy
and human: verminous, feverish, deaf to Latin, but patient and dignified.

The ending is ambiguous too. His flight is a release, for him and for the family. Elisenda's sigh of relief "for herself and for him" shows that she is free of a nuisance and feels, perhaps without knowing it, something like
gladness that he is free. The "imaginary dot on the horizon" suggests that a marvel that has been treated as an annoyance has left the world unchanged, and the house with its iron bars remains closed to angels.

self_checks.question: Model answers — reference to the context
self_checks.answer:
**1.** (a) The old man with enormous wings, whom the neighbour woman calls an angel. (b) The hens pecked at him, cripples pulled out his feathers to touch their sores, the merciful threw stones to make him stand, and
the crowd burned his side with a branding iron to see whether he was dead. Others tried to make him eat mothballs and papal lunches and heated him with lamps and candles. (c) Because, apart from
his wings, nothing about him was supernatural: he smelled, he had parasites, he was ill and old. The only thing that set him apart from ordinary men was the endless calm with which he endured cruelty. (d) The tone is dry, deadpan and
ironic: the narrator speaks of the marvellous as if it were a minor fact and uses the word "virtue" lightly, yet the sentence carries a real pity.

**2.** (a) "He" is the old man, the angel; "her" is Elisenda, Pelayo's wife. (b) After a difficult winter the old man has grown new feathers and, while Elisenda is cutting onions in the kitchen, has flown away from the shed.
She has watched him until he vanished over the sea. (c) Elisenda feels relief: she is rid of the annoyance he had become; but her sigh is "for herself and for him", so there is also a trace of sympathy, perhaps
gladness that he has escaped. (d) The ending is fitting because it is quiet and unsentimental: the most marvellous thing in the story ends with a household chore, a sigh and a tiny dot in the distance. It returns the
story to the ordinary life from which it began, and it leaves the reader to decide what has been lost.

chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- About the poet
- The poem: text, title and date
- The poem, stanza by stanza
- Paraphrase in plain English
- Central idea and themes
- Form, metre, rhyme and structure
- Imagery, figures of speech and sound devices
- Tone
- Critical appreciation
- Glossary
- Stanza 1 — the sunrise, in four pictures
- Stanza 2 — the hills, the birds, and a child's conclusion
- Stanza 3 — the turn
- Stanza 4 — the dominie
- Understanding the text
- Reference to the context
- Reference beyond the text

A child comes running in with news. *I'll tell you how the sun rose* — and out it
comes, in a rush, in pictures, in the wrong grammar, with a shout at the end.
Then the child stops. *But how he set, I know not.* The second half of the poem
is spoken more slowly, in a lowered voice, and by the last line something has
happened that the speaker does not quite have words for. Emily Dickinson's "A
Day" is sixteen short lines long, uses almost no word of more than two
syllables, and is one of the most quietly frightening poems in your course. Read
it once for the colours. Read it again for what happens to the voice.

chapters.question_answers:
## a. How does the poet describe the morning sun in the first stanza?

She never describes the sun itself — only its effects. The light arrives "a
ribbon at a time", in narrow bands unrolled slowly one after another. It strikes
the church spires first, so that "the steeples swam in amethyst", floating in a
violet glow. Then it spreads down over the town quickly and unevenly, "like
squirrels", as though the news of morning were running from house to house.

## b. What does the line 'The news like squirrels ran' mean?

The "news" is the news of daybreak — the light itself, and with it the knowledge
that morning has come. The simile compares its spread to squirrels running:
quick, darting, in short bursts with pauses, scattering in several directions at
once rather than advancing in a straight line. It captures exactly the way
sunlight jumps unevenly from roof to roof and tree to tree, and it fills the
stanza with small animal life.

## c. What do you understand by the line 'The hills untied their bonnets'?

A bonnet is a hat tied with strings under the chin. Before sunrise the hilltops
are wrapped in mist as though wearing bonnets; as the sun warms the ground the
mist loosens and lifts away. Dickinson personifies the hills as women untying
and taking off their hats — a homely, domestic gesture that makes the landscape
seem to relax and become sociable now that the day has begun.

## d. Is the speaker watching the morning sun? Why? Why not?

Not directly. Every image in stanzas 1 and 2 is of something the sun is doing to
*other* things — steeples, hills, birds, the town. The speaker's own conclusion,
"That must have been the sun!", is a **deduction** made afterwards, not a
report of something seen: the word *must* proves she inferred the cause from the
effects. She is watching the sunrise, not the sun. (This is also physically
true: one cannot look at the rising sun, and it is a child's habit to watch the
lit world instead.)

## e. How does the sun set?

The speaker admits at once that she does not know — "But how he set, I know
not." What she offers instead is a guess in the form of a picture. There
*seemed* to be a purple stile at the horizon, and little yellow boys and girls —
the last golden rays, or the small lit evening clouds — were climbing over it
all the while. When they had all reached the other side, a grey figure like a
schoolmaster or pastor gently put up the evening bars, closing the gap in the
fence, and led them away like a shepherd with his flock. So the sunset is
described not as an event in nature but as children being taken home at the end
of school, and beneath that, as a gentle death.

## a. What, according to the speaker, is a day?

For this speaker a day is not a measure of time but a small complete story with
two unequal halves, and the shape of that story is the shape of a human life.

The first half is public, noisy and knowable. Dawn is something she can narrate
to somebody else — "I'll tell you how the sun rose" — and she narrates it in
four images drawn from a working town: a ribbon unrolled, steeples swimming in
amethyst, news running like squirrels, hills untying their bonnets. Everything
is busy, coloured and slightly comic, and it ends in the exclamation of a child
who has just worked out what caused the show.

The second half is private, hushed and unknowable. "But how he set, I know not."
A day, then, is something that begins in certainty and ends in mystery. The
evening is not described but imagined: a purple stile at the edge of the world,
little yellow children climbing over it, a dominie in grey who shuts the gate
behind them and leads the flock away.

Put the two halves together and the day becomes an allegory of a lifetime.
Morning is birth and childhood — loud, colourful, easy to tell. Evening is age
and death — quiet, uncertain, and managed by someone else. The stile is the
boundary between this world and whatever is on "the other side"; the flock and
the shepherd are the oldest Christian image of the dead in God's keeping. A day,
for Dickinson, is a life in miniature, and the most important thing she can say
about it is that we can report its beginning and can only guess at its end.

## b. What purpose does the hyphen in the first line serve in the poem?

First, a point of accuracy that will improve the answer: the mark Dickinson
wrote there is not a hyphen but a **dash** (a hyphen joins parts of a word; a
dash holds a sentence open). Your textbook prints it as a long rule after the
comma. Dickinson used dashes constantly, and modern editors preserve them
because they do work that no other punctuation mark can do.

In this line — "I'll tell you how the sun rose, ___" — the dash does four
things.

It creates a **pause and an intake of breath** exactly where a storyteller would
pause: the promise has been made, and now the listener must wait half a second
for the goods. The line becomes speech rather than writing.

It works as a **colon without the finality of a colon**. It announces that what
follows is the content of the telling, but it refuses to close the sentence off;
the poem seems to spill forward into stanza 1 rather than to start it.

It establishes the **presence of a listener**. A dash at that point is a turn of
the head towards somebody. Without it the line is an announcement; with it, it
is the opening of a conversation, which matters in a poem whose whole first half
is a performance for someone else.

Finally, it sets up the poem's **structural silence**. The dash is a place where
language stops and the reader supplies something. That is precisely what happens
on a larger scale at "I know not" — the poem hands the unsayable part over to
us. The little silence in line 1 rehearses the big one in line 9.

## c. What makes this poem lyrical and sonorous? Discuss.

A **lyric** is a short poem in the voice of a single speaker expressing personal
feeling, and originally a poem meant to be sung; **sonorous** means full and
pleasing in sound. "A Day" earns both words.

*It is built on a song form.* The four abcb quatrains are in **common metre**,
the 8-6-8-6 pattern of the English hymn book that Dickinson heard every Sunday
in Amherst. Any stanza of this poem can be sung to the tune of "Amazing Grace".
The alternation of a long line and a short line gives the poem a rocking,
predictable pulse, and the short fourth line lets each stanza come to rest.

*The rhyme is light but sure.* Only lines 2 and 4 rhyme — *begun / sun*, *stile
/ while*, *gray / away* — so the poem chimes without jingling. The one slant
rhyme, *time / ran*, keeps the opening from sounding too neat.

*The consonants are soft.* Listen to the sibilants running through the sunrise:
"the **s**un ro**s**e", "the **s**teeples **s**wam", "like **s**quirrels",
"I **s**aid **s**oftly". Almost nothing in the poem is harsh; there are no
clusters that stop the mouth. The vowels chime too — *how / sun / must*;
*little / climbing / while*.

*The diction is plain and mostly monosyllabic.* Out of about a hundred words,
only *ribbon, amethyst, steeples, bobolinks, bonnets, softly, purple, yellow,
little, dominie, gently, evening* have more than one syllable. Short words move
quickly and sound clean.

*And there is a single feeling behind it.* Lyric poems are unified by emotion
rather than argument, and the emotion here — delight turning into awe — is
carried right through without a break. The music is the emotion: loud and quick
in the morning stanzas, slow and low in the evening ones.

## d. Who are the target audience of the speaker? Why?

The poem is addressed, on its surface, to **children**, and there is plenty of
evidence for it.

The opening is the opening of a story told to a child: "I'll tell you how the
sun rose" is how an adult begins, or how one child begins to another. The
vocabulary is deliberately simple and concrete — ribbon, squirrels, bonnets,
boys and girls, bars, flock. The grammar is a child's grammar: "The bobolinks
begun". The conclusion of stanza 2, "That must have been the sun!", is the
delighted over-obviousness of a young listener working something out. And the
figures of the second half are drawn from a child's world — a stile to climb, a
schoolmaster, being taken home at the end of the day.

But it is worth saying in an answer that the poem is not *only* for children,
and the best answers say so. The allegory of stanzas 3–4 is transparent to any
adult: the stile is the edge of life, the yellow children are the dying light,
the dominie in grey is death or God, "the other side" is the next world. Children
will enjoy the pictures; adults will see what the pictures are of. Dickinson has
written a poem that can be read aloud to a child at bedtime and leave the adult
doing the reading quietly shaken.

There is a third audience: **the speaker herself**. "Then I said softly to
myself" reminds us that half of this poem is a person thinking aloud. That is
usually true of Dickinson, who wrote for a drawer rather than a public.

**e. The poem seems to describe a day for children. How would the adult people
respond to this poem? Discuss this poem with your parents or guardians and write
the answer based on their responses.**
[5]

*This question asks you to talk to somebody and report what they said, so your
answer must contain your own family's words. The model below shows the shape and
the depth expected; replace the reported opinions with real ones.*

I read "A Day" aloud to my mother and my grandfather one evening and asked what
they made of it.

My mother's first response was to the pictures. She said the line about the
hills untying their bonnets was exactly what the ridge above our town looks like
when the mist comes off it in Asar, and that she had never thought of the mist
as a hat before. For her the pleasure of the poem was recognition — a child's
way of seeing a morning she has seen ten thousand times.

My grandfather responded to the second half, and he did not think it was a
children's poem at all. He said that once you are old you know what "the other
side" is, and that the poem is about dying. What struck him was the word
*gently*. He said most people are afraid of death because they imagine it as
violent, and that this poem imagines it as a teacher closing a gate at the end
of the school day — nobody is hurt, nobody is left behind, and the children go
home together. He also noticed that the poet will not say she believes it: "she
says *there seemed*," he said, "not *there was*."

That is the difference an adult reader makes. A child reads a bright morning and
a slightly sad evening. An adult reads innocence and experience — the confident
telling of what we have lived through, and the silence about what is still to
come. The poem does not change; the reader brings the second meaning with them.
That is why it belongs in a Grade 12 textbook and not only in a picture book.

## b. Write a personal essay on "A Day in the School".

*A personal essay is written in the first person, about your own experience, in
a voice that sounds like you. It needs a shape, not just a timetable. The
outline below follows Dickinson's own structure — a bright, knowable morning and
an evening that closes gently — and you should fill it with your own school.*

respond to this poem? Discuss this poem with your parents or guardians and write
the answer based on their responses.**

answer must contain your own family's words. The model below shows the shape and
the depth expected; replace the reported opinions with real ones.*

I read "A Day" aloud to my mother and my grandfather one evening and asked what
they made of it.

My mother's first response was to the pictures. She said the line about the
hills untying their bonnets was exactly what the ridge above our town looks like
when the mist comes off it in Asar, and that she had never thought of the mist
as a hat before. For her the pleasure of the poem was recognition — a child's
way of seeing a morning she has seen ten thousand times.

My grandfather responded to the second half, and he did not think it was a
children's poem at all. He said that once you are old you know what "the other
side" is, and that the poem is about dying. What struck him was the word
*gently*. He said most people are afraid of death because they imagine it as
violent, and that this poem imagines it as a teacher closing a gate at the end

says *there seemed*," he said, "not *there was*."

That is the difference an adult reader makes. A child reads a bright morning and
a slightly sad evening. An adult reads innocence and experience — the confident
telling of what we have lived through, and the silence about what is still to
come. The poem does not change; the reader brings the second meaning with them.

self_checks.answer:
*A personal essay is written in the first person, about your own experience, in
a voice that sounds like you. It needs a shape, not just a timetable. The
outline below follows Dickinson's own structure — a bright, knowable morning and
an evening that closes gently — and you should fill it with your own school.*

chapters.summary:
"Every Morning I Wake" is the sunset poem of the Reverend Eli Jenkins in Dylan
Thomas's radio play *Under Milk Wood*, a play for voices covering one spring day
in the invented Welsh village of Llareggub, first read publicly in New York in
May 1953 and first broadcast by the BBC in January 1954, after Thomas's death at
thirty-nine. Its sixteen lines are four quatrains made of eight perfect rhyming
couplets — aabb ccdd eeff gghh — in loose iambic tetrameter. Stanza by stanza it
moves through a day: a morning prayer that God should keep a loving eye on "all
poor creatures born to die"; an evening blessing on the town, with the frank
admission that survival is "touch-and-go"; a plea to be judged fairly, since "We
are not wholly bad or good / Who live our lives under Milk Wood"; and a final
request for "another day", ending with the whole community bowing to the setting
sun and saying "good-bye – but just for now!" The poem asks for mercy rather
than miracles, speaks for a community rather than a self, faces death without
fear, and lets its unbroken couplets supply the reassurance its words are too
honest to promise.

A village minister stands at his door at the end of the day and says a short
prayer out loud. He does not ask for money, or for rain, or for his enemies to
be punished. He asks God to keep an eye on "all poor creatures born to die", to
notice that the people of his town are "not wholly bad or good", and to let them
all have one more day. Then he says good night to the sun — "but just for now".
Sixteen lines, eight rhyming couplets, hardly a word above two syllables. It is
the gentlest poem in your course, and its gentleness is an argument.

chapters.question_answers:
## d. What does Milk Wood sound like? A type of wood or a place? Why?

It sounds like both, and Thomas intends the ambiguity. Because it is capitalised
and preceded by "under", it works as a **place name** — the wood on the hill
above the village, and by extension the little world the villagers live in ("who
live our lives under Milk Wood" means, in effect, "who live here"). But the
words themselves, *milk* and *wood*, are the names of a substance and a
material, so on first hearing it also sounds like a **kind of timber**, soft,
pale and gentle. The milkiness colours the whole poem: it suggests mildness,
nourishment, and something childlike about the people being prayed for.

**e. Why do the inhabitants of Milk Wood bow to the setting sun 'but just for
now'?** [2]

Because the parting is temporary. They bow as a mark of respect and farewell at
sun-down, but they know the sun will rise again in the morning, so the goodbye
is only "for now" rather than forever. The phrase also carries a second,
unstated meaning: since the poem has just prayed for "poor creatures born to
die", saying that a nightly goodbye is only temporary quietly suggests that
death, too, may be a parting rather than an ending. The speaker never claims
this outright; he lets a cheerful everyday phrase imply it.

## a. Discuss "Every Morning When I Wake" as a prayer to the God.

The poem is a prayer in the strict formal sense and in a very unusual spirit.

## c. How does the poet highlight the magnificence of the God?

Not by describing Him. There is no throne in this poem, no light, no angels, no
thunder and no judgement seat. Thomas's method is the opposite of the usual one:
he makes God magnificent by making Him **generous, attentive and near**.

*By scale of attention.* "All poor creatures born to die" is the largest phrase
in the poem — it takes in every living thing that has ever existed — and it is
governed by a single organ, "Thy loving eye". One glance covers the whole of
mortal creation. The magnificence lies in the ratio between the enormous object
and the effortless means.

*By moral generosity.* "Thou … wilt be the first / To see our best side, not our
worst." God is great because He is the most charitable reader of human beings in
existence — better than neighbours, better than the villagers are to each other,
better than they are to themselves. Notice that this is the only statement in
the poem the speaker introduces with "I know". Of everything in heaven and
earth, God's kindness is the one thing he is sure of.

*By the reverence of the language.* The archaic *Thy*, *Thou*, *wilt* and the
capitalised pronoun place God in the register of the Bible; "O please" and "Dear
Lord" place Him within speaking distance. Holding both at once is itself a way
of saying that He is both above us and beside us.

*By what is left for Him to do.* Every other authority in the poem is absent.
There is no mention of church, doctrine, sin or hell — only a man at a door, a
town, a night and the sun. Into that emptiness God is invited simply to *look
kindly*, and that turns out to be the largest thing anyone in the poem can
imagine.

*By contrast with human smallness.* "A little prayer", "poor creatures", "we are
not wholly bad or good", "just for now" — everything on the human side of the
poem is diminutive and provisional. Against that steady smallness, a being who
can hold the whole of it in one loving eye is made to seem immense without a
single grand adjective being used.

## d. How does the rhyme scheme of the poem reinforce its message?

The poem is written in **rhyming couplets** — aabb ccdd eeff gghh — arranged in
four quatrains, and every one of the eight rhymes is perfect: *wake / make*,
*eye / die*, *sun-down / town*, *no / touch-and-go*, *good / Wood*, *first /
worst*, *day / pray*, *bow / now*. Four features of that scheme do real work.

chapters.name: I Was My Own Route - Julia de Burgos
topics: Stanza 1 (nine lines) — the confession and the refusal
Stanza 6 (eight lines) — the same beginning, a different end
chapters.summary:
Julia de Burgos (1914–1953), born in Carolina, Puerto Rico, teacher,
nationalist, journalist for *Pueblos Hispanos* in New York, and precursor of the
Nuyorican poets, published "Yo misma fui mi ruta" in her first collection
*Poema en veinte surcos* (1938); the English text you study is Jack Agüeros's
translation. Its thirty-seven lines fall into six free-verse stanzas of 9, 3, 10,
6, 1 and 8 lines. The speaker confesses that she once tried to be what men wanted
— "an attempt at life", "a game of hide and seek with my being" — then declares
herself "made of nows" and walks forward, mocking the ashes, towards "the kiss of
new paths". The old guard tear her back with desperate flapping wings; every
whiplash only separates her look further from the distant, familiar horizons.
Unpinned forever, her face expands from within into "a feeling of intimate
liberation", and she claims all the soils of the earth, soils without history,
without a future and without edges. A single line — "And I was all in me as was
life in me" — is the summit. The last stanza repeats the opening word for word
and ends differently: when the heralds announce her at the regal parade of the
old guard, her desire to follow men warps, and the homage is left waiting. The
poem's argument is that identity lives in the present and inside the self, and
that the final act of freedom is to decline the honour the old order offers.

## Topics to cover

The poem begins with a confession and ends with an empty chair. In between, a
woman walks. She starts by admitting that she once tried to be what men wanted —
"an attempt at life", she calls it, a rough draft of a person — and she finishes
by simply not turning up to the ceremony where the old order had planned to
honour her. Nothing in the poem is smashed. Nobody is shouted at. The rebellion
consists entirely of walking forward and declining an invitation, and that is
what makes it frightening to the people it is aimed at.

chapters.question_answers:
## a. Why did the speaker try to be the way men wanted her to be?

The poem does not give a reason in so many words, and the honest answer says so
before supplying the implied one. She tried because that was the only shape
available to a woman in her society: she had been brought up looking at
"distant familiar horizons" — ambitions inherited rather than chosen — and
behind them stood "the old guard", with its heralds, its parade and its power to
grant or withhold honour. Conforming was the route to acceptance and reward. The
poem's judgement on that choice is severe: it produced not a life but "an
attempt at life", and a permanent "game of hide and seek" with her own self.

## b. What do you understand by her feet 'would not accept walking backwards'?

Walking backwards means returning to the past — to tradition, to the role men
had assigned her, to the "ashes" of what was already finished. Her feet, planted
"level on the promissory earth", refuse it and go "forward, forward" instead.
The refusal is put in the feet rather than the mind on purpose: it is not a
decision she argues her way to but something her body will not do. It has
become instinct.

## c. Who are the old guards? Why did they grow desperate?

The "old guard" are the defenders of the established order — the patriarchal
society, its customs and its authorities, the people who benefit from things
staying as they are. In the poem they appear as birds with "desperate flapping
wings" that rip her back, and later as the organisers of a "regal parade". They
grow desperate because she is walking away and they cannot stop her. Their
violence is a sign of weakness, not of strength: an order that is secure does
not need to claw at the back of one woman who is leaving.

## d. How did the speaker have 'a feeling of intimate liberation'?

It came from inside her, not from any change in her circumstances. Once "the
branch was unpinned forever" her gaze moved further from the inherited horizons
with every fresh whiplash, and her face "took the expansion that came from
within" — the growth showed outwardly. The poem says precisely where the feeling
came from: it "surged / from the balance between my life / and the truth of the
kiss of the new paths" — that is, from her life and her direction finally
matching each other. It is called *intimate* because it is private and personal;
nobody granted it and nobody witnessed it.

## e. Why did the speaker's desire to follow men warp in her?

Because by the time the reward arrived, she no longer wanted it. At the moment
the heralds announced her at "the regal parade of the old guard" — the point at
which the establishment finally offered her a place of honour — the wish to fall
in behind men "warped", that is, twisted out of shape and became unusable, like
wood that has buckled. She had become "made of nows", and a woman who lives in
the present has no use for an honour conferred by the past. So the homage was
left waiting for someone who never came.

## c. What, according to the speaker, did it feel like to be free?

The poem describes freedom four times, and each description adds something.

## d. Why does the speaker prefer the present to the past?

Because in this poem the past is not merely earlier — it is the instrument by
which she was controlled, and the present is the only material she is actually
made of.

Look at what belongs to the past in the poem. "Like men wanted me to be" is an
expectation formed before she was born. The "ashes" are what is burnt out and
finished. The "old guard" are, by definition, the guardians of what already
exists. The "distant / familiar horizons" are goals inherited rather than
chosen. The "regal parade" is ceremony, which is the past performing itself. Every
oppressive thing in the poem is old.

Now look at the present. She is "made of nows" — the coined plural is the
poem's central claim, and it says that her substance is a series of present
moments, not a lineage. Her course is "now set in the present". Her feet stand
on "the promissory earth", ground that promises rather than remembers. And what
she walks towards is "new paths", twice given a kiss.

The preference is therefore **logical, not merely temperamental**. A person made
of present moments cannot be governed by decisions taken in the past, because
there is nothing in her for those decisions to grip. This is why she "would not
accept walking backwards": going back is not difficult for her, it is
impossible, the way it is impossible to return to yesterday.

Stanza 4 extends the argument to its limit. She claims soils "without history"
and even soils "without a future" — refusing not only the past that ruled her
but the destiny that might replace it. What is left is the present with no edges
at all.

Finally, the preference is **strategic**. The past is the old guard's only real
weapon: their authority is entirely inherited. A woman who lives in the present
is the one opponent they cannot reach, which is precisely what happens at the
end. They assemble their parade, their heralds, their homage — all of it
ceremony, all of it history — and she is not there.

**e. John Donne, in his poem "No Man is an Island", says, "No man is an island
entire of itself." Would Burgos agree with Donne? Do you agree with Donne or
Burgos?** [5]

*A point of accuracy first, which will impress an examiner: the famous passage
is not strictly a poem. It comes from Donne's prose work* Devotions upon
Emergent Occasions *(1624), Meditation XVII, and has been set out in verse lines
by later editors. Donne's argument is that every human being is a piece of the
continent, that any man's death diminishes him "because I am involved in
mankind", and therefore "never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for
thee".*

chapters.name: The Awakening Age - Ben Okri
topics: Imagery, figures of speech and sound devices
chapters.summary:
Sir Ben Okri (born 1959 in Minna, Nigeria; the textbook's "1949" is a misprint)
spent his early childhood in London, returned to Nigeria during the civil war,
and won the Booker Prize in 1991 for *The Famished Road*. "The Awakening Age" was
written in 1999 for Oxfam's "On The Line" project, which linked communities along

Fourteen lines, seven pairs, one line drawn round the earth. Ben Okri's poem is
the shortest text in your literature course and in some ways the easiest to
misread, because everything in it is pleasant — hope, vision, light, harvest —

lack, and that this description is itself part of what keeps them poor. Change

chapters.question_answers:
## a. Who are the people 'who travel the meridian line'?

Literally, they are the people who live along and move across the Greenwich
Meridian — the line of zero longitude that runs from Britain down through France
and Spain into Algeria, Mali, Burkina Faso, Togo and Ghana. The poem was written
in 1999 for Oxfam's "On The Line" project, which linked communities along exactly
that route. More widely, they are all human beings, since the meridian encircles
the whole earth: travellers, migrants, and anyone connected to distant others by
the line that joins north to south, rich to poor.

## d. What can we gain after our perceptions are changed?

"There's much to gain": the poem names it as "a flowering of truth instead of
pain." Once people stop seeing the poor as nothing but poor, the truth about them
opens out naturally, like a flower, and the suffering caused by that false
description ends. Practically, what is gained is the recognition of a people's
work, wisdom and creativity, and the possibility of ascending together "to a new
height".

## a. What does the poet mean by 'the awakening age'?

The phrase names the historical moment the poem hopes for, and it does so with a
word chosen very carefully.

## b. Why, in your view, have these people 'lived with poverty's rage'?

First, notice the exact phrase. It is not "lived in poverty" but "lived **with**
poverty's rage" — as one lives *with* an illness or a violent relative:
continuously, at close quarters, without the option of leaving. And poverty is
given a temper of its own. It is not a quiet absence; it is furious.

## And the poem adds a cause that most accounts leave out: perception itself.

Couplet 6 is a correction — "There's more to a people than their poverty" — and
you only correct somebody who has been saying something false. A people
continuously described as nothing but hungry is denied credit, investment,
respect and self-belief, and that description becomes one of the mechanisms that
keeps them poor. In this sense they have lived with poverty's rage partly because
the world decided that poverty was all they were.

## c. Why does the poet appeal for solidarity among the people?

Because, in this poem, solidarity is not a kindness but a **fact** — and the
appeal is only to act on something that is already true.

## d. Does the poet present migration in a positive light? Why? Why not?

*A careful answer begins by being honest about the question.* The poem was
written in 1999 for Oxfam's "On The Line" project about communities along the
Greenwich Meridian, and its subject is the connection between rich and poor
nations rather than migration as such. There is no migrant in it, no departure,
no arrival and no border. What the poem gives us is people who "**travel the
meridian line**" — which may mean movement, and certainly means contact across
distance. With that said, the poem can be read as presenting movement between
peoples very positively, and here is why.

## Write an essay on 'The Impacts of Migration on Nepali Society'.

the level. Aim for about 450 words and use real figures where you are sure of
them; if you are not sure, write "roughly" rather than inventing a number.*

chapters.summary:
Abhi Subedi (born 1945 in Sabla, Terhathum; for about forty years a teacher in
the Central Department of English at Tribhuvan University) writes in both Nepali
and English; his collections include *Manas*, *Chasing Dreams: Kathmandu Odyssey*
and *Shabdara Chot*, and his plays *Dreams of Peach Blossoms* and *Fire in the
Monastery*. "Soft Storm" runs to **nine free-verse stanzas and 106 lines** (21,
11, 10, 7, 11, 6, 19, 15, 6). Its structural engine is anaphora: the line **"I
became soft" appears exactly eight times**, with three variations, and stops after
stanza 6. Stanzas 1–6 record the occasions of the softening — the tumult and the
eerie stillness, homeless children crying with hunger in **Thamel** under the
bat-bearing trees of **Kesharmahal**, a forlorn child with a transistor radio
round his neck hunting for his mother "in the corridors of violent history", a
man beaten "by nobody for no reason / in no sensible times", and a blood-stained
shirt "speaking in the earth's ears / with bruised human lips". Stanzas 7–8 turn
from witnessing to reflection: crocuses have come up through the stone, but the
speaker's soft storm "rages and rages / over silent pages, / silent stones, /
silent forlorn shirts carrying war memories", and the mad time winds up
deforested land, a warming earth and rhododendron blooming in winter. The final
stanza contracts the whole poem to one person: "in these hard times" the speaker
wants to melt his soft storm like a rainbow into "your minuscule sky", where it
"dances in ripples / of your uneasy lake." The poem's governing figure is the
**oxymoron** of its title, and its argument is that in a senseless time the
strongest available response is a compassion large enough to be a storm.

A storm that is soft is not a storm at all — and that contradiction, sitting in
the title and repeated more than a dozen times inside the poem, is the whole
argument. Abhi Subedi watches a city in a violent decade: hungry children under
the trees at Kesharmahal, a child running with a transistor radio looking for his
mother, a man beaten for no reason in front of his family, a blood-stained shirt
lying in a far corner. He does not become angry. He becomes **soft**. The poem
is about what a decent person turns into when the times are indecent and there is
nothing to be done except see clearly and write it down.

chapters.question_answers:
## a. When does the speaker grow soft? Enlist the occasions when he grows soft.

He grows soft whenever he witnesses suffering or senselessness. The occasions, in
order, are: (i) after hearing the tumult and crashing on the eerie stillness that
followed it, on the night the moon skidded down the walls and the city spoke "the
language / of posters and politics"; (ii) when homeless children in Thamel cried
with hunger under the bat-bearing trees of Kesharmahal; (iii) when he returned
from the melee where ceremony "dances with mad steps / on the unwedded gardens of
history"; (iv) when he turned alone to "you", leaving "deep dents of words" on
white sheets; (v) when he saw a forlorn child with a transistor radio round his
neck running about wailing for his mother; (vi) when he saw a man beaten
mercilessly before his family "by nobody for no reason"; (vii) when he saw a
blood-stained shirt speaking in the earth's ears; and (viii) because "you" gave
words but did not listen to them, and gave storms but did not wait to see their
Leela.

## c. Describe the poor children portrayed in the poem.

Two children appear. The first are the **homeless children in Thamel**, who
"cried with hunger under the bat-bearing / trees of Kesharmahal" — nameless,
faceless, given nothing but hunger and a location, starving in the richest and
brightest street of the capital, beside a Rana palace. The second is the

## d. What do you understand by 'the unwedded gardens of history'?

*Unwedded* means unmarried, never joined. The phrase describes a national past
that has never been properly married to the country's present life — a history
that is celebrated in ceremonies but not actually connected to how people live.
Public ceremony "dances with mad steps" on these gardens, performing on ground
that has never accepted it, where instead of flowers there are "protruded rocks".
It suggests a history that remains barren and unfruitful because nothing has ever
been joined to it.

## g. Why does the speaker call our time 'mad time'?

Because the age has lost its reasons. A man is beaten "for no reason … by nobody
for no reason / in no sensible times"; children starve in the wealthiest street;
ceremony dances "with mad steps"; and the natural order is deranged as well —
"deforested land", the "warming earth", "birds singing of bizarre journeys" and
"rhododendron blooming in winter". The time "spools", winding everything onto its
reel mechanically, without sense or choice. It is mad because cause and effect no
longer connect.

## h. What does the speaker want to do in "hard times"?

He wants to give his feeling away, gently, to one person: "in these hard times /
I want to melt like a rainbow / my soft storm in your minuscule sky." He does not
want to fight, punish or protest. He wants his soft storm to dissolve like a
rainbow into someone's small private sky, where it "dances in ripples / of your
uneasy lake" — that is, to turn an enormous public grief into something small
enough to be shared with one human being.

## b. What is the speaker's attitude towards the time he describes in the poem?

His attitude has four layers, and a good answer separates them.

## c. What is the speaker like? Is he a rebel? Why? Why not?

[5]

## Close on the image you opened with.

> I want to live in a country where that boy is inside the hotel — not selling
> eggs, and not being discussed. Not as a subject on a programme, but as a guest.
> Let us be the generation that was too soft to hate and too stubborn to look
> away. Thank you.

chapters.summary:
- "On Libraries" is a personal essay by the neurologist and writer **Oliver Sacks**
  (1933–2015); it praises libraries as places of **intellectual freedom, community and
  serendipitous discovery**, and was published in *The Threepenny Review* and, as
  "Libraries", in *Everything in Its Place* (2019).
- Childhood: the **oak-panelled home library** (father's Hebrew scholarship, Ibsen, war
  poets, brothers' adventure books, *The Jungle Book*; mother's Dickens, Trollope,
  Thackeray, Shaw, Kipling, Shakespeare, Milton); he read at **three or four** and was
  found in the library when late for meals.
- **Willesden Public Library** was his "Ur-library" and his "real education". He disliked
  school but was "not a good pupil, but … a good learner": in libraries he was **free**
  to choose and "become myself".
- Science: the **Walker Library** at St Paul's lacked chemistry, so a testimonial got him
  into the **Science Museum library** (Mellor's *Treatise*, Gmelin's *Handbook*).
- Oxford: the **Radcliffe Science Library** and the **Bodleian** (traced to 1602; Theodore
  Hook, over 500 improvised operas; British Museum Library); above all the **Queen's
  College library** (Wren; catacombs; incunabula, Gesner 1551, Agassiz, Darwin, Browne,
  Swift, Johnson, Hume, Pope, Dryden) — "a sense of history, and of my own language".
- New York, 1965: *Migraine* begun on top of a refrigerator; the **Albert Einstein
  College of Medicine** library gave space, lucky finds and friendships (*Brain* from
  1890).
- The turn: by the **1990s** students ignored the shelves, books were disposed of; Sacks
  was **horrified** ("a murder, a crime"), was told everything "of worth" had been
  digitised, and answered that a physical book has "its look, its smell, its heft".
- Devices: first-person memoir, catalogues, contrast, metaphors of maze and quest, hyperbole
  ("murder"), the symbol of the physical book.

Most people meet a library as a place where you must be quiet. Oliver Sacks met it as
the place where he became himself. His essay "On Libraries" is a short memoir of the
rooms in which he read — the oak-panelled library at home, the public library five
minutes from his door, the school and museum libraries where he hunted for chemistry,
the vaults under an Oxford college — and it ends, unexpectedly, in grief: the shelves
he loved are being emptied because students now find everything on a screen. It is one
of the easiest essays in your book to read and one of the hardest to answer badly,
because every paragraph is a memory and every memory carries a small argument.

chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** *Ur-* is a German prefix meaning "original". Willesden, the public library a
five-minute walk from his home, was the first great library of his life and the standard
for every library after it: there, he says, he "received my real education".

**2.** The Walker Library at his school, St Paul's, had few science books, so a
schoolmaster wrote him a special **testimonial**. With that recommendation he obtained a
ticket to the Science Museum library and read the huge chemistry works of Mellor and
Gmelin.

**3.** He appreciates it for its **magnificent building** (designed by Wren), its
underground "maze of heating pipes and shelves", and above all its holdings: ancient
books, Gesner's *Historiae Animalium*, Agassiz, Darwin's works in original editions, Browne,
Swift, and the seventeenth- and eighteenth-century writers. The books were freely available

look, and few visited the stacks at all.

library his favourite place — the beginning of a lifelong habit of learning in libraries.

large table where he could read and write and shelves and stacks where he could wander and

to friendships, and it gave him a sense of **community, even intimacy**.

already been **digitised**, so nothing valuable was lost.

**9.** He values what only a **physical book** can offer — "its look, its smell, its
heft" — and the freedom of browsing among shelves. He does not use a computer himself, and
he feels a digital copy cannot replace the book, the shelf and the reader's community.

**10.** As he grew older his interest turned to **astronomy and chemistry**. The essay says
his reading became "increasingly biased towards the sciences", and his hunger for chemistry

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** Sacks describes the **traditional library** in loving detail: oak-panelled rooms, open
shelves and stacks, quiet tables, whispered talk that turns to friendship, old books
in original editions — and, at the end, a **digital library** in which books are scanned and
the paper copies thrown away. I find the traditional library more impressive, and Sacks
gives me the reasons. First, it gives **freedom to browse**: he "roamed the shelves" and
found "unexpected treasures, lucky finds", such as Hook in the Bodleian and Liveing's
*Megrim* in the stacks. A search returns only what you ask for; a shelf shows you
what you did not know to ask. Second, it builds **community**: readers looking for the same
volume of *Brain* became friends, and handling books and seeing earlier borrowers' names
created "camaraderie". Third, the physical book has a **sensory and historical value** —
"its look, its smell, its heft" — which a scan cannot carry. That said, a digital library
has real advantages: it reaches distant readers, it saves space and it can protect fragile
texts. The wisest answer is that we should **add** the digital library to the traditional
one, not use it to destroy the shelves; Sacks's grief is at the destruction, not at the
technology itself.

**2.** The headnote's three phrases each name a strand of the essay. **Intellectual
freedom** is the freedom to choose what to read, which he found at Willesden, where he was
"free to look at the thousands, tens of thousands, of books" and "to become myself", in
contrast with school where he was passive. **Community** is the intimacy of strangers
in a quiet room: two readers whispering over the same old book, sharing volumes and seeing
each other's names on the library slips. **Serendipity** is the joy of lucky finds —
discovering Hook, or Sir Thomas Browne in the stacks, or the 1873 book that inspired
his first book. All three depend on **physical shelves and open access**, which is why the
essay ends in sorrow when students ignore them and colleges dispose of the books.
The praise of libraries is therefore also a defence of a certain kind of education:
self-directed, sociable and full of surprise.

**3.** *Home library:* books and reading became his first memories; he read at three or four
and found fantasy in *The Jungle Book*. *Willesden:* his "real education"; freedom to choose;
independence from the school that bored him. *Walker Library and Science Museum library:*
his first serious training in chemistry, when his school could not supply the books.
*Oxford:* the Bodleian gave him a subject in Theodore Hook and a quiet place to write; the
Queen's College library gave him "a sense of history, and of my own language" through
original editions of Darwin, Browne, Swift and others. *New York:* the Einstein College
library gave him space to read and write after his cramped flat, lucky finds and
friendships. *The 1990s:* the library as he had known it began to disappear, and he was
left grieving. The relationship therefore grows from **shelter** to **freedom** to
**training** to **scholarship** to **community**, and ends as a **loss** he cannot
prevent.

**4.** I agree with Sacks that it is a great loss, though not one to be blamed on
technology alone. His argument is that digitisation saves the *text* but destroys the
*book*: its "look, its smell, its heft", its neighbours on the shelf and the names of
earlier readers. It also destroys **serendipity**: he found Hook and *Megrim* only by
wandering among real shelves. And a library that disposes of its old books cannot
rediscover them later; once a book is thrown out and the scan is lost or unreadable,
knowledge vanishes. In my own experience, a book on a school shelf beside the one I
wanted has often taught me something I did not plan to learn. On the other hand, I know
that digital libraries help students in remote parts of Nepal who have no shelves at
all. So the loss is real but avoidable: keep the books and add the screens.

- Part 5 — normative marriage and its six dimensions

Ask a class why people marry and the answers will be about love, family and happiness.
Steven Nock, an American sociologist, asks a different question: *what is a marriage?*
His answer, in this passage from his book *Marriage in Men's Lives*, is that a marriage is
never just two people. It is a relationship that comes with **rules, expectations and
helpers already attached** — laws, religion, custom, relatives — which existed before the
couple met and will exist after they are gone. Those rules limit the couple, but they also
protect and guide them. Nock's essay is the most academic in your book, but it has a clear
line of argument and a very small number of ideas, and the ideas are easy to remember once
you have seen them laid out.

chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** Marriage is an institution because it is **culturally patterned** and **integrated into the
other basic institutions** of society — education, the economy and politics. Its rules come
from outside the couple and are supported by law, religion and custom, so the marriage of
any one couple follows a pattern that everyone understands.

**2.** Yes. Friendship and other personal ties have few rules, but marriage is **defined by legal,
moral and conventional assumptions** that originate outside the couple and mark it off from all
other relationships. Married people know what they owe each other, their children and their
relatives, and others expect the same of them.

**3.** Following Durkheim, marriage matters to men because it **gives structure to their lives
and organises their ambitions**. By restraining uncontrollable desires and tying a man to one
partner and one set of duties, it gives him a "moral equilibrium" and a sense of purpose.

**4.** Yes, marriage is a social institution. It is culturally patterned, joined to education,
the economy and politics, governed by rules that come from society rather than the couple, and
backed by law, religion and custom. Unlike cohabitation, it gives the couple a template and
creates binding obligations to kin and children.

**5.** "Soft boundaries" are the rules, originating outside a particular couple, that set the
**commonly understood limits of behaviour** which distinguish marriage from all other
relationships. They are "soft" because they are enforced by custom, opinion and law together
rather than by force, and they allow variation within them.

**6.** Durkheim held that, once basic needs are met, human desire for comfort, luxury and
prestige is **limitless**. Marriage, "an organ of society", restrains it: it binds a man to one
partner "forever", "assigns a strictly definite object to the need for love, and closes the
horizon". He restricts his wants to what is permitted and so finds moral balance.

**7.** Because it shows that such a relationship is **not governed by convention**. Married
people can say "my wife" or "my husband" and everyone knows what is meant; there is no
common word for an unmarried partner because society has not agreed on the rules. To Nock this
suggests that cohabitation "is not an institution".

**8.** Social capital is a network of people linked by trust and obligation. Through marriage,
husbands and wives gain **new kin** and friends of kin, bound by obligations that last; in
need, they can call on relatives for help. This asset exists only in relationships and is
therefore "an individual asset" that is intangible but valuable.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** Nock writes that marriage is defined by "soft boundaries", and in the last paragraph he
restates the **six dimensions** that define normative marriage in America. First, marriage is
**voluntary**: two people enter it by choice. Second, it is entered by **mature adults**, not
by children. Third, it is **heterosexual**, between a man and a woman. Fourth, husbands are
expected to be the **principal earners**. Fifth, both partners are expected to be **sexually
faithful**. Sixth, married people are expected to **become parents**. Nock adds that many
marriages depart from these ideals, but they remain "the core of normative marriage as it is
expressed in law, religion, and custom". Normative marriage is a form of **social control**:
it channels behaviour and aspirations and is "a force greater than the individuals involved"
because it expresses the collective sentiments of others. The six dimensions are therefore the
definition with which Nock proceeds in the rest of his book.

**2.** Nock's first claim is that marriage is "much more than the sum of two spouses". It is a
relationship defined by **legal, moral and conventional assumptions**, and it is an **institution**:
culturally patterned and integrated into education, the economy and politics. Its rules
originate outside any particular couple and set **soft boundaries** that distinguish it from
all other relationships. Married couples are "heirs to a vast system of understood principles".
A husband and wife pledge faithfulness, commitment to children and responsibility to relatives,
and these pledges are "enforceable", supported by laws, religion and customs. Marriage also
generates **social capital**: bonds of trust and obligation with new kin. By contrast, an
unmarried couple has no template and not even a word for a partner, so its relationship "is not
an institution". Marriage is thus a social institution, not only a private arrangement.

**3.** *Cohabitation* offers **freedom**: there are no widely accepted boundaries, so each couple
decides how to treat each other's parents, whether to share holidays, how to handle money.
But it also offers **no guidance**: the partners, their parents and friends must invent the
relationship, with no established expectations, no agreed word to introduce a partner, and no
enforceable obligations. *Marriage* offers a **template** — "a pattern to follow" for domestic
life — with pledges of faithfulness and commitment that law, religion and custom support. It
also supplies kin networks and social capital. Nock concludes that marriage gives its partners
more: it structures their lives, organises their ambitions and connects them to a wider
community, while cohabitation gives only the freedom to start from nothing. The price is that
marriage limits freedom, but Durkheim's argument is that such limits are good for people.

**4.** Durkheim argued, about a century before Nock, that once basic needs are met, human
desires turn to comfort, luxury and prestige, and these have no natural limit; once one
appetite is satisfied another appears. Modern society therefore needs institutions to set
"legitimate boundaries" on desire, and marriage does so for men. By binding a man to one
partner for life, marriage "assigns a strictly definite object to the need for love, and closes
the horizon"; he cannot seek other satisfactions without "transgressing his duty", so he limits
his wants and finds "moral equilibrium". The argument is persuasive in part: people do find
peace in clear commitments, and unlimited choice can make them restless. But it treats
marriage as benefiting men mainly by restraint, and it does not say what marriage does for
women or for unhappy couples, so a modern reader may want to qualify it.

chapters.summary:
- **Bertrand Russell** (1872–1970), British philosopher, logician and social critic, Nobel
  Prize for Literature 1950, wrote "Knowledge and Wisdom" in **1954**.
- Central idea: our age far surpasses earlier ages in knowledge without a matching increase in
  wisdom; **knowledge may become harmful unless combined with wisdom**.
- Textbook headnote: knowledge = acquiring data and information; wisdom = practical application
  of knowledge to create value. Russell's own account: wisdom is **comprehensive vision**.
- Factors of wisdom: **sense of proportion** (medicine and atom examples); **awareness of the
  ends of human life** (Hegel); **feeling as well as intellect**; **freedom from personal
  prejudice** (philosopher's stone; Mr A and Mr B).
- **Essence of wisdom**: emancipation from "the tyranny of the here and now" — moving towards
  impartiality by knowing the remote in time and space.
- Wisdom **can be taught**, by a larger intellectual element in moral instruction; hatred of
  evil is itself "a kind of bondage to evil"; understanding, not force. Elizabeth I, Henry IV
  and Lincoln show that wisdom is not weakness.
- Education should produce good **citizens of the world**; "with every increase of knowledge and
  skill, wisdom becomes more necessary".
- Style: argument and example, hypothetical dialogue, antithesis, aphorism, irony, allusion,
  calm tone.

A student can know the date of every treaty in a history book and still quarrel with a
classmate for a year over a borrowed pen. A scientist can understand the atom perfectly and
still build something that frightens the world. Bertrand Russell's short essay asks why
**more knowledge has not made us wiser** — and what wisdom actually is. He was one of the
great thinkers of the twentieth century, and he wrote this piece in 1954, nine years after the
bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and in the year the United States tested a hydrogen bomb at
Bikini Atoll. It is a calm, clear, argued essay, and it rewards close reading, because each
paragraph adds one idea to the last.

## Chapter summary

- **Bertrand Russell** (1872–1970), British philosopher, logician and social critic, Nobel
  Prize for Literature 1950, wrote "Knowledge and Wisdom" in **1954**.
- Central idea: our age far surpasses earlier ages in knowledge without a matching increase in
  wisdom; **knowledge may become harmful unless combined with wisdom**.
- Textbook headnote: knowledge = acquiring data and information; wisdom = practical application
  of knowledge to create value. Russell's own account: wisdom is **comprehensive vision**.
- Factors of wisdom: **sense of proportion** (medicine and atom examples); **awareness of the
  ends of human life** (Hegel); **feeling as well as intellect**; **freedom from personal
  prejudice** (philosopher's stone; Mr A and Mr B).
- **Essence of wisdom**: emancipation from "the tyranny of the here and now" — moving towards
  impartiality by knowing the remote in time and space.
- Wisdom **can be taught**, by a larger intellectual element in moral instruction; hatred of
  evil is itself "a kind of bondage to evil"; understanding, not force. Elizabeth I, Henry IV
  and Lincoln show that wisdom is not weakness.
- Education should produce good **citizens of the world**; "with every increase of knowledge and
  skill, wisdom becomes more necessary".

  calm tone.

## Model answers — short questions

**1.** According to the textbook's summary, knowledge is the acquisition of data and information,
while wisdom is the practical application of that knowledge to create value. In Russell's own
account, knowledge is what a specialist knows; wisdom is a **comprehensive vision** — a sense of
proportion, awareness of the ends of life, freedom from prejudice and from the "tyranny of the
here and now". Knowledge can be harmful without wisdom.

**2.** Because "with every increase of knowledge and skill, wisdom becomes more necessary".
More knowledge gives people greater power to achieve their purposes, and so greater power for
**evil** if their purposes are unwise. Since knowledge will go on increasing, the world will need
wisdom even more in the future than now.

**3.** Yes, I agree. Knowledge tells us what we *can* do; wisdom tells us what we *should* do.
Without wisdom, knowledge can be harmful, as nuclear weapons and misused medicine show. A
person with wisdom can continue to learn and will use what he knows for good, but a person
with knowledge alone may harm others.

**4.** The central idea is that knowledge and wisdom are different, that our age has gained
enormously in knowledge without a corresponding increase in wisdom, and that **knowledge may
become harmful unless it is combined with wisdom**, which can and should be taught.

**5.** Russell says it can be taught "in some degree", by giving moral teaching a **larger
intellectual element**: in the course of teaching facts, teachers can point out the disastrous
results of hatred and narrow-mindedness. For example, when teaching atomic physics they can
show how the atom has been used for destruction; by applying the Samaritan parable to today's
enemies, teachers can show that hatred harms the hater.

**6.** Hegel's philosophy of history was comprehensive in time, but its chief lesson was that from
400 AD Germany had been the most important nation and the standard-bearer of progress. His
**national pride distorted** the facts, so he lacked the awareness of the ends of human life and
the freedom from prejudice that wisdom needs.

**7.** Two men who hate each other and are ruined by their hatred each give an equally
one-sided list of the other's vices, partly true and partly false. By showing each that the
other says the same, a wise person can make both see that the other has "only the normal share
of human wickedness" and that their **enmity harms both**. That is a "fragment of wisdom":
seeing a quarrel from outside oneself.

**8.** It means the natural **self-centredness** of our senses and feelings, which tie us to our
own bodies, needs and moment. An infant knows only its own hunger. Wisdom is freedom from this
as far as possible, by understanding and caring about things remote in time and space.

**9.** Because hatred makes the hater **as harmful as the enemy** and is unlikely to persuade
anyone to give up evil ways. "Hatred of evil is itself a kind of bondage to evil." The way out is
**understanding**, though he does not advocate non-resistance: resistance should use the
smallest force compatible with preserving what is good.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** Russell begins from the fact that our age far surpasses earlier ages in knowledge, without
a corresponding increase in wisdom. He defines wisdom through its factors. The first is a
**sense of proportion**, the capacity to take account of all the important factors in a problem
and give each its due weight; specialists often lack this, as the medical researcher and the
atomic physicist show. The second is **awareness of the ends of human life**: Hegel's
comprehensive history failed because national pride bent it. The third is **feeling** as well as
intellect, since people with wide knowledge but narrow feelings are not wise. The fourth is
**freedom from personal prejudice**, in private life as well as public, as the stories of the
alchemists and of Mr A and Mr B show. The essence of all these is **emancipation from the
tyranny of the here and now** — a continual approach towards impartiality, by knowing things
remote in time and space and giving them their due weight in our feelings. For Russell, wisdom
is therefore a comprehensive vision of mind and heart, and a rare one.

**2.** Russell proves the statement with examples. A medical researcher lowers the infant
death-rate; but because no one weighs the wider results, the food supply becomes inadequate and
living standards fall in crowded regions. A physicist studies the atom from pure curiosity, and
the result is that "powerful lunatics" can destroy the human race. In each case knowledge itself
is good, but without **comprehensive vision** it leads to harm. The same is true in history: Hegel
knew a great deal, but national pride produced a false lesson. And in the final paragraph Russell
explains why this will get worse: each increase of knowledge and skill increases our capacity to
realise our purposes, "and therefore augments our capacity for evil, if our purposes are
unwise". The statement is therefore true: the answer is not less knowledge but more wisdom,
taught alongside it.

**3.** Russell answers yes, "in some degree". The need is great, because people are taught on
Sundays to love their neighbours and on other days to hate them; the Good Samaritan's lesson
would be understood today only if we put "Communist or anti-Communist" in his place. He holds
that hatred of evil is "a kind of bondage to evil": hate makes us as harmful as those we hate
and rarely persuades them; the way out is understanding, combined with resistance using the
smallest force necessary. Examples from history (Elizabeth I, Henry IV, Lincoln) show that such
wisdom is not weakness. In education, moral instruction should have a larger **intellectual
element**: while teaching knowledge, teachers should show the disastrous results of hatred and
narrow-mindedness; skills should be put in the context of human life by wider surveys; and
technicians should be good **citizens of the world**. Knowledge and morals should not be
separated.

**4.** According to Russell, wisdom is more necessary than ever because the power of knowledge
has grown enormously. "With every increase of knowledge and skill, wisdom becomes more
necessary", since greater power to realise our purposes is also greater power to do evil if the
purposes are unwise. Nuclear weapons, unknown to earlier ages, show what this means: for the
first time humans can destroy themselves. Modern specialisation also narrows the vision of
experts, who therefore cannot see the wider effects of their work. And if knowledge continues
to grow, "the world will need wisdom in the future even more than it does now". I agree. Modern
examples such as climate change and the misuse of the internet show that cleverness without
responsibility is dangerous, and that schools and colleges should teach the question "What is
this knowledge for?" as well as the answer.

- **Yuval Noah Harari** (born 1976) is a historian at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and
  the author of *Sapiens*, *Homo Deus* and *21 Lessons for the 21st Century*; "Humility" is an
  extract from chapter 12 of the last.

## Topics to cover

- About the author
- The essay: shape and argument
- The essay, part by part
- Ideas and themes
- Style and devices
- Glossary
- Textbook exercises
- Part 1 — "You are not the centre of the world"
- Part 2 — "All these claims are false"
- Part 3 — "my own people" and the yoga story
- Part 4 — the escalation, and the method

Every group of people likes to believe that its story is the most important story ever told.
Greeks say history began in Athens, Chinese nationalists say it began with the Yellow Emperor,
some Hindu nationalists say aeroplanes were flying in the age of the sages, pious Muslims see
all earlier history as irrelevant, and the Aztecs thought the sun would not rise without their
sacrifices. Yuval Noah Harari collects these claims in one breezy, funny and unsettling
essay, and then does something unusual: he turns the same lens on **his own people**. "Humility"
is an essay about the most dangerous form of pride — the belief that *my* nation, *my* culture,
*my* religion is the centre of the world. It is shorter than the other essays in this unit and
very easy to read, but examiners like it because the claims are concrete and the question
"Why is history a contested issue?" invites a good, thoughtful answer.

chapters.question_answers:
## Model answers — short questions

**1.** According to Harari, the universal human abilities are **morality, art, spirituality and
creativity**. They are "embedded in our DNA", he says, and they began in Stone Age Africa, long
before any present-day nation or religion.

**2.** They "dismiss these Chinese boasts" by claiming something larger: that even **airplanes and
nuclear bombs** were invented by ancient sages in the Indian subcontinent long before Confucius
or Plato, not to mention Einstein and the Wright brothers — for instance, that Bhardwaj invented
rockets and aeroplanes and Kanad was the father of atomic theory.

**3.** Harari means that every group inflates its own importance — "hot-air balloons" are full of
air and nothing else — and that only the members of each group can best puncture their own pride.
By criticising his own people first, he hopes to make readers honest about their own nation,
culture or religion, so that they see how ridiculous exaggerated claims are.

**4.** Because no nation, culture or religion was the source of human history. Modern
civilisation developed from abilities that all humans share and that arose in Stone Age Africa,
long before any present-day nation; every group makes the same claim of centrality, so all the
claims cancel out. Thinking otherwise is "crass egotism".

**5.** He says these abilities existed **before any of today's nations or religions**, when humans
colonised the world, domesticated plants and animals, built the first cities and invented writing
and money, so they cannot belong to any one of them; they are common to all human groups and
have their genesis in Stone Age Africa. In my opinion the conclusion is convincing: people of
every culture paint, pray, tell stories and distinguish right from wrong, which suggests a
common, very ancient inheritance.

**6.** Yes, I agree. History is debated because it gives **pride, identity and power**. Each group
wants to be seen as the oldest or the most creative, and tells the past in ways that flatter it.
Disputes about textbooks, monuments and ancient achievements show this, and since each version
contradicts the next, history becomes contested.

**7.** The Aztecs believed that without the human sacrifices they offered every year, **the sun
would not rise** and the whole universe would fall apart. Harari uses this as an extreme case of a
people imagining that their rituals were part of the laws of nature — an example of crass
egotism.

**8.** Because, he says, "it is more polite to criticise one's own people than to criticise
foreigners". He also knows the Jews best, and starting with them shows that he is not singling
out anyone else. The yoga story and the belief that the cosmos exists for the rabbis' study show
how ludicrous self-important narratives are, and he leaves readers to treat their own tribes the
same way.

## Model answers — long questions

**1.** In his catalogue of national claims, Harari first reports that **Chinese nationalists**
say history began with the Yellow Emperor and the Xia and Shang dynasties and that whatever
Westerners, Muslims or Indians achieved is a pale copy of Chinese breakthroughs. Then he reports
the answer of **Hindu nativists**: they "dismiss these Chinese boasts" and argue that even
**airplanes and nuclear bombs** were invented by ancient sages in the Indian subcontinent long
before Confucius or Plato, not to mention Einstein and the Wright brothers. They give examples:
Maharishi Bhardwaj is said to have invented rockets and aeroplanes; Vishwamitra invented and used
missiles; Acharya Kanad was the father of atomic theory; and the Mahabharata is said to describe
nuclear weapons accurately. So the Hindu nativists do not refute the Chinese claim by evidence;
they answer it with a bigger claim of their own. Harari quotes all this in a mocking tone
("Did you know …?") to show that such claims rest on pride and not on proof, and he later says
that all such claims "are false".

**2.** Harari supports the thesis in four steps. First, he shows by a **long catalogue** that every
group believes it is at the centre: Greeks, Chinese nationalists, Hindu nativists, pious Muslims,
Turkish, Iranian and Egyptian nationalists, British, French, Germans and others, and even the
Aztecs, who thought the sun needed their sacrifices. Since all claim the centre, none can be
right. Second, he gives a **verdict and reasons**: "All these claims are false"; none of today's
nations or religions existed when humans colonised the world, domesticated plants and animals,
built the first cities and invented writing and money. Third, he states the **truth**: morality,
art, spirituality and creativity are universal human abilities embedded in our DNA and born in
Stone Age Africa, so placing them in China, Greece or Arabia is "crass egotism". Fourth, he gives
a **personal example**: the Jews, his own people, who claim to have invented yoga and believe that
the cosmos exists for the rabbis' study. By criticising his own people first, he gains authority
and invites every reader to puncture their own tribe's "hot-air balloons".

**3.** History is a contested issue first because it gives a **group its identity and pride**.
Harari's catalogue shows that every group wants to be the origin of civilisation, because
being first seems to give a right to respect and leadership. Second, history is used as a
**political tool**: governments use the past to justify their authority, borders and policies, and
to unite people against "others". Third, the **memory of injury** — conquest, colonialism, war —
leaves different communities with different versions of the same events. Fourth, in the age of
social media, flattering stories spread faster than careful research. Finally, because there is
seldom a single complete record, many claims cannot be disproved easily, and emotion fills the
gap. The result, as the essay shows, is that groups with contradictory claims each think they are
the centre. The answer is the humility Harari recommends: test claims against evidence, admit our
debt to others, and treat the human past as a common inheritance.

**4.** The title "Humility" is well chosen. Humility means not thinking oneself more important
than one is, and the whole essay is about its opposite, **pride in one's group**, which Harari
calls "crass egotism". The catalogue shows proud claims from many nations; the verdict shows
that they are false; the positive message is that the great human abilities belong to everyone,
so no group has reason for superiority; and the method of criticising his own people first is
itself an act of humility. The title is also ironic: the essay never mentions humility in its
text, but it teaches the virtue by showing the absurdity of its absence. The textbook's note,
which says Harari "exemplifies the virtue of humility", supports the title.
