chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- principal, rate, time and simple interest
- amount and the interest formula
- finding rate or time when the others are known
- simple interest in daily life: saving and borrowing
- The simple interest formula
- Finding principal, rate or time
- Simple interest in daily life
- Reading the interest formula four ways

When you keep money in a bank, the bank pays you for the use of it; when you
borrow money, you pay the lender. That payment is **interest**, and the amount
borrowed or deposited is the **principal**. At this level the interest is
simple: it is a fixed percentage of the original sum for each year, so it grows
in a straight line and never earns interest on itself. This chapter works the
formula in every direction and ends with the practical arithmetic of saving and
borrowing.

## Chapter summary

- $I=\frac{PTR}{100}$ and $A=P+I$, with $T$ always in years.
- Rearranged: $P=\frac{100I}{TR}$, $R=\frac{100I}{PT}$, $T=\frac{100I}{PR}$.
- When the amount is given, use
  $A=P\left(1+\frac{TR}{100}\right)$ and solve for $P$.
- Simple interest is the same every year, so it grows in a straight line.
- Comparing two offers means comparing $P\times T\times R$, not the rate alone.

## Study route

Read the topics and identify unfamiliar terms.

Close the book and explain the key ideas in your own words.

Attempt a worked example before revealing its solution.

Complete the chapter practice, correct mistakes, then mark the chapter revised.
chapters.question_answers:
## Finding the interest and the amount

**Problem.** Find the simple interest and the amount on Rs 5,000 for 3 years at
10 % per annum.

**Solution.** $P=5000$, $T=3$, $R=10$.

$$I=\frac{PTR}{100}=\frac{5000\times3\times10}{100}=\text{Rs }1500$$

$$A=P+I=5000+1500=\text{Rs }6500$$

**Answer.** Interest Rs 1,500; amount Rs 6,500.

**Check.** 10 % of 5000 is 500 a year, and 3 years gives
$3\times500=1500$ ✓ — simple interest is the same every year.

## A time in months

**Problem.** Find the simple interest on Rs 8,400 for 9 months at 8 % per annum.

**Solution.** Convert the time: $T=\frac{9}{12}=0.75$ years.

$$I=\frac{8400\times0.75\times8}{100}=\text{Rs }504$$

**Answer.** Rs 504.

**Check.** One year's interest would be $0.08\times8400=\text{Rs }672$;
nine months is $\frac34$ of a year, so $672\times0.75=504$ ✓.

## Finding the rate

**Problem.** A sum of Rs 6,000 earns Rs 1,080 as simple interest in 3 years.
Find the rate percent per annum.

**Solution.**

$$R=\frac{100I}{PT}=\frac{100\times1080}{6000\times3}=\frac{108000}{18000}=6\%$$

**Answer.** 6 % per annum.

**Check.** 6 % of 6000 is 360 a year, and $3\times360=1080$ ✓.

## Finding the principal

**Problem.** What sum will earn Rs 900 as simple interest in 2 years at
7.5 % per annum?

**Solution.**

$$P=\frac{100I}{TR}=\frac{100\times900}{2\times7.5}=\frac{90\,000}{15}
=\text{Rs }6000$$

**Answer.** Rs 6,000.

**Check.** 7.5 % of 6000 is 450 a year, and two years give 900 ✓.

## Finding the time

**Problem.** In how many years will Rs 12,000 earn Rs 2,160 as simple interest
at 9 % per annum?

**Solution.**

$$T=\frac{100I}{PR}=\frac{100\times2160}{12\,000\times9}
=\frac{216\,000}{108\,000}=2\text{ years}$$

**Answer.** 2 years.

**Check.** 9 % of 12,000 is 1,080 a year, and $2\times1080=2160$ ✓.

## Working from the amount

**Problem.** A sum becomes Rs 7,200 in 4 years at 5 % simple interest per
annum. Find the principal.

**Solution.** The amount is $A=P+I$, and
$I=\frac{PTR}{100}=\frac{P\times4\times5}{100}=0.2P$. So

$$A=P+0.2P=1.2P\;\Longrightarrow\;P=\frac{7200}{1.2}=\text{Rs }6000$$

**Answer.** Rs 6,000.

**Check.** $I=0.2\times6000=\text{Rs }1200$, and $6000+1200=7200$ ✓.

## Finding the rate, then the time

**Question.** A sum of Rs 16,000 amounts to Rs 20,800 in 4 years at simple
interest. (i) Find the rate. (ii) In how many years would the same sum earn
Rs 9,600 at that rate?

**Answer.**
(i) $I = 20800 - 16000 = 4800$. $R = \frac{100 \times 4800}{16000 \times 4} =
\frac{480000}{64000} = \textbf{7.5 \%}$ per annum.
(ii) $T = \frac{100 \times 9600}{16000 \times 7.5} = \frac{960000}{120000} =
\textbf{8 years}$.

## Two sums, one comparison

**Question.** Ram puts Rs 20,000 in a bank at 6 % and Sita puts Rs 15,000 in a
cooperative at 9 %, both for 3 years. Who earns more, and by how much?

**Answer.** Ram: $I = \frac{20000 \times 3 \times 6}{100} = $ Rs 3,600.
Sita: $I = \frac{15000 \times 3 \times 9}{100} = $ Rs 4,050.
**Sita earns Rs 450 more**, although she deposited Rs 5,000 less — the rate
mattered more than the principal here.

**Problem.** Find the simple interest and the amount on Rs 5,000 for 3 years at
10 % per annum.

**Solution.** $P=5000$, $T=3$, $R=10$.

$$I=\frac{PTR}{100}=\frac{5000\times3\times10}{100}=\text{Rs }1500$$

$$A=P+I=5000+1500=\text{Rs }6500$$

**Answer.** Interest Rs 1,500; amount Rs 6,500.

**Check.** 10 % of 5000 is 500 a year, and 3 years gives
$3\times500=1500$ ✓ — simple interest is the same every year.

**Solution.** Convert the time: $T=\frac{9}{12}=0.75$ years.

**Answer.** Rs 504.

**Check.** One year's interest would be $0.08\times8400=\text{Rs }672$;
nine months is $\frac34$ of a year, so $672\times0.75=504$ ✓.

## Topics to cover

- area of triangles
- area of quadrilaterals (parallelogram, rhombus, trapezium)
- area of a circle and its parts
- surface area and volume of a cylinder
- area and volume problems of the SEE type
- Area of triangles
- Area of quadrilaterals
- Area and circumference of a circle
- Surface area and volume of a cylinder
- Choosing the right formula

Mensuration is arithmetic done with a ruler. A farmer measures a field in
*bigha*, a mason orders sand by the cubic metre, and a painter buys tin by the
square metre — all three are using the formulas in this chapter. The work is to
know which formula fits the shape, to keep the units consistent, and to remember
that an area is measured in square units and a volume in cubic units.

## Chapter summary

- Triangle: $\frac12 bh$, or Heron's formula with $s=\frac{a+b+c}{2}$.
- Rectangle $lb$; square $a^2$; parallelogram $bh$; rhombus and kite
  $\frac12 d_1d_2$; trapezium $\frac12(a+b)h$.
- Circle: circumference $2\pi r$, area $\pi r^2$; sector area
  $\frac{\theta}{360°}\pi r^2$; arc length $\frac{\theta}{360°}2\pi r$.
- Cylinder: curved surface $2\pi rh$, total surface $2\pi r(r+h)$, volume
  $\pi r^2h$.
- A ring or path is the difference of two circles, not a circumference times a
  width.
- Areas are in square units and volumes in cubic units, and all lengths must be
  in the same unit.

chapters.question_answers:
## Area of a triangle, two ways

**Problem.** A triangle has sides 6 m, 8 m and 10 m. Find its area by Heron's
formula, and check the answer using base and height.

**Solution.** At this level the syllabus uses base and height, so take the
longest side 10 m as the base first, and note that $6^2+8^2=100=10^2$, so the
triangle is right-angled with the 6 m and 8 m sides perpendicular.

$$\text{Area}=\frac12\times6\times8=24\ \text{m}^2$$

By Heron: $s=\frac{6+8+10}{2}=12$, so

$$\text{Area}=\sqrt{12(12-6)(12-8)(12-10)}
=\sqrt{12\times6\times4\times2}=\sqrt{576}=24\ \text{m}^2$$

**Answer.** 24 m², by both methods.

**Check.** The two methods agree, as they must; the height on the 10 m base is
$\frac{2\times24}{10}=4.8$ m, and $\frac12\times10\times4.8=24$ ✓.

## A trapezium and a rhombus

**Problem.** (a) A trapezium has parallel sides 12 m and 8 m and a distance of
5 m between them. Find its area. (b) A rhombus has diagonals 16 cm and 12 cm.
Find its area and the length of one side.

**Solution.** (a)

$$\text{Area}=\frac12(a+b)h=\frac12(12+8)\times5
=\frac12\times20\times5=50\ \text{m}^2$$

(b)

$$\text{Area}=\frac12 d_1d_2=\frac12\times16\times12=96\ \text{cm}^2$$

The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles, so each side is
the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 8 cm and 6 cm:

$$\text{side}=\sqrt{8^2+6^2}=\sqrt{100}=10\ \text{cm}$$

**Answer.** (a) 50 m². (b) area 96 cm², side 10 cm.

**Check.** (b) The four sides are equal at 10 cm, so the perimeter is 40 cm; and
$\frac12\times16\times12=96$ ✓.

## A circle and a sector

**Problem.** A circle has radius 7 cm. Find its circumference and area. Then
find the area of a sector of the same circle that subtends 90° at the centre.

**Solution.** Circumference $=2\times\frac{22}{7}\times7=44$ cm.

$$\text{Area}=\frac{22}{7}\times7^2=154\ \text{cm}^2$$

Sector:

$$\text{Area}=\frac{90}{360}\times154=\frac14\times154=38.5\ \text{cm}^2$$

**Answer.** 44 cm; 154 cm²; the quarter sector is 38.5 cm².

**Check.** The sector is a quarter of the circle, and
$\frac{154}{4}=38.5$ ✓.

## A circular path

**Problem.** A circular garden of radius 14 m has a path 1 m wide all round it,
outside the garden. Find the area of the path.

**Solution.** The path is the ring between two circles: the inner radius is
14 m and the outer radius is $14+1=15$ m.

$$\text{Area}=\pi(15^2-14^2)=\frac{22}{7}(225-196)=\frac{22}{7}\times29
\approx91.14\ \text{m}^2$$

**Answer.** About 91.14 m².

**Check.** The whole outer circle is $\frac{22}{7}\times225=707.14$ m² and the
garden is $\frac{22}{7}\times196=616$ m²; the difference is 91.14 m² ✓. Always
subtract the two circles rather than multiplying the circumference by the width,
which would overestimate.

## A water tank

**Problem.** A cylindrical water tank has a radius of 70 cm and a height of
1.5 m. Find its volume in litres and the area of sheet metal needed to make it
(with a closed top).

**Solution.** Keep the units consistent: $r=70$ cm $=0.7$ m, $h=1.5$ m.

$$\text{Volume}=\pi r^2h=\frac{22}{7}\times0.7^2\times1.5
=\frac{22}{7}\times0.49\times1.5=2.31\ \text{m}^3$$

Since 1 m³ $=1000$ litres, the volume is **2,310 litres**.

$$\text{Total surface area}=2\pi r(r+h)=\frac{44}{7}\times0.7\times(0.7+1.5)
=4.4\times2.2=9.68\ \text{m}^2$$

**Answer.** 2,310 litres; about 9.68 m² of sheet.

**Check.** The base area is $1.54$ m² and the height is 1.5 m, so
$1.54\times1.5=2.31$ m³ ✓.

## Walls, floor and cost in one question

**Question.** A hall is 12 m long, 9 m wide and 4 m high. It has two doors of
2 m × 1.2 m and four windows of 1.5 m × 1 m. Find (i) the area of the four
walls to be painted (ii) the cost of painting at Rs 95 per m².

**Answer.**
(i) Four walls $= 2h(l+b) = 2 \times 4 \times (12+9) = 168$ m².
Openings $= 2(2 \times 1.2) + 4(1.5 \times 1) = 4.8 + 6 = 10.8$ m².
Area to paint $= 168 - 10.8 = \textbf{157.2 m}^2$.
(ii) Cost $= 157.2 \times 95 = \textbf{Rs 14,934}$.

## From volume to litres

**Question.** A cylindrical tank of diameter 1.4 m and height 1.5 m is filled
to three-quarters of its height. How many litres does it hold? Take
$\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.

**Answer.** $r = 0.7$ m; filled height $= \frac{3}{4} \times 1.5 = 1.125$ m.
$V = \pi r^2 h = \frac{22}{7} \times 0.49 \times 1.125 = 1.7325$ m³.
$1$ m³ $= 1000$ litres, so the tank holds **1,732.5 litres**.

chapters.name: Indices
topics: The laws of indices in one place
chapters.summary:
- $a^m\times a^n=a^{m+n}$; $a^m\div a^n=a^{m-n}$; $(a^m)^n=a^{mn}$;
  $(ab)^n=a^nb^n$; $\left(\frac ab\right)^n=\frac{a^n}{b^n}$.
- $a^0=1$ for every non-zero $a$, and $a^{-n}=\frac{1}{a^n}$.
- Simplify inside brackets first, then apply powers, then multiply or divide
  like bases by adding or subtracting indices.
- An exponential equation is solved by writing both sides as powers of the same
  base and equating the indices.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- laws of indices
- simplification using the laws
- negative and zero indices
- exponential equations
- The laws of indices
- Simplifying expressions with several laws
- Exponential equations
- The laws of indices in one place

An index is shorthand for repeated multiplication: $2^5$ means
$2\times2\times2\times2\times2$. The shorthand is not just a saving of ink — it
turns multiplication into addition of indices, division into subtraction, and
powers of powers into multiplication, which is why indices appear in every later
chapter of algebra, in scientific notation, and in the arithmetic of growth.
This chapter sets out the laws, shows how to simplify expressions with them, and
shows how to solve the small exponential equations the syllabus asks for.

## Chapter summary

- $a^m\times a^n=a^{m+n}$; $a^m\div a^n=a^{m-n}$; $(a^m)^n=a^{mn}$;
  $(ab)^n=a^nb^n$; $\left(\frac ab\right)^n=\frac{a^n}{b^n}$.
- $a^0=1$ for every non-zero $a$, and $a^{-n}=\frac{1}{a^n}$.
- Simplify inside brackets first, then apply powers, then multiply or divide
  like bases by adding or subtracting indices.
- An exponential equation is solved by writing both sides as powers of the same
  base and equating the indices.

## Study route

Read the topics and identify unfamiliar terms.

Close the book and explain the key ideas in your own words.

Attempt a worked example before revealing its solution.

Complete the chapter practice, correct mistakes, then mark the chapter revised.
chapters.question_answers:
## Using the product and quotient laws

**Problem.** Simplify $\frac{3^5\times3^2}{3^4}$.

**Solution.** Add the indices in the numerator first:

$$3^5\times3^2=3^{5+2}=3^7$$

Then subtract: $3^7\div3^4=3^{7-4}=3^3=27$.

**Answer.** 27.

**Check.** $3^5=243$ and $3^2=9$, so the numerator is $2187$; and
$2187\div81=27$ ✓.

## An algebraic simplification

**Problem.** Simplify $\frac{12x^5y^3}{4x^2y}$.

**Solution.** Divide the numbers, then use the quotient law on each letter:

$$\frac{12}{4}=3,\qquad \frac{x^5}{x^2}=x^{5-2}=x^3,\qquad
\frac{y^3}{y}=y^{3-1}=y^2$$

$$\frac{12x^5y^3}{4x^2y}=3x^3y^2$$

**Answer.** $3x^3y^2$.

**Check.** Put $x=2$, $y=3$: the left side is
$\frac{12\times32\times27}{4\times4\times3}=\frac{10368}{48}=216$, and the right
side is $3\times8\times9=216$ ✓.

## Zero and negative indices

**Problem.** Evaluate $5^0+2^{-3}$ and simplify $\left(\frac{2x}{y}\right)^{-2}$.

**Solution.** $5^0=1$ and $2^{-3}=\frac{1}{2^3}=\frac18$, so

$$5^0+2^{-3}=1+\frac18=1\frac18=\frac98$$

For the second, a negative index on a fraction turns it upside down:

$$\left(\frac{2x}{y}\right)^{-2}=\left(\frac{y}{2x}\right)^{2}
=\frac{y^2}{4x^2}$$

**Answer.** $1\frac18$ and $\frac{y^2}{4x^2}$.

**Check.** For the second, put $x=1$ and $y=2$. The left side is
$\left(\frac{2}{2}\right)^{-2}=1^{-2}=1$, and the right side is
$\frac{4}{4\times1}=1$. They agree ✓. Using $x=2$, $y=1$ instead: the left side
is $4^{-2}=\frac{1}{16}$, and the right side is $\frac{1}{4\times4}=\frac{1}{16}$ ✓.

## A three-step simplification

**Problem.** Simplify $\left(\frac{2a^3b^{-2}}{4ab}\right)^2$.

**Solution.** **Step 1 — simplify inside the bracket.** Divide the numbers:
$\frac{2}{4}=\frac12$. For $a$: $a^{3-1}=a^2$. For $b$:
$b^{-2-1}=b^{-3}$. So inside we have $\frac{a^2b^{-3}}{2}$, that is
$\frac{a^2}{2b^3}$.

**Step 2 — square everything.**

$$\left(\frac{a^2}{2b^3}\right)^2=\frac{a^{4}}{4b^{6}}$$

**Answer.** $\frac{a^4}{4b^6}$.

**Check.** Put $a=1$, $b=1$: the original is
$\left(\frac{2}{4}\right)^2=\frac14$, and the answer is $\frac14$ ✓.

## Powers of a product

**Problem.** Simplify $(2x^2y)^3\times(3xy^2)^2$.

**Solution.** Apply the power to each factor:

$$(2x^2y)^3=2^3x^6y^3=8x^6y^3,\qquad
(3xy^2)^2=9x^2y^4$$

Now multiply, adding indices of like bases:

$$8x^6y^3\times9x^2y^4=72x^{6+2}y^{3+4}=72x^8y^7$$

**Answer.** $72x^8y^7$.

**Check.** Put $x=y=1$: the original is $2^3\times3^2=8\times9=72$, and the
answer gives $72$ ✓.

## Solving by making the bases equal

**Problem.** Solve $3^x=81$.

**Solution.** Write 81 as a power of 3: $81=3^4$. So

$$3^x=3^4\;\Longrightarrow\;x=4$$

**Answer.** $x=4$.

**Check.** $3^4=81$ ✓.

## An equation with a second term

**Problem.** Solve $2^{x+1}=64$.

**Solution.** $64=2^6$, so $2^{x+1}=2^6$ and therefore $x+1=6$, giving $x=5$.

**Answer.** $x=5$.

**Check.** $2^{5+1}=2^6=64$ ✓.

## An equation with a power on both sides

**Problem.** Solve $9^{x}=27^{2}$.

**Solution.** Write both numbers as powers of 3: $9=3^2$ and $27=3^3$. So

$$(3^2)^x=(3^3)^2\;\Longrightarrow\;3^{2x}=3^{6}$$

Equating indices: $2x=6$, so $x=3$.

**Answer.** $x=3$.

**Check.** $9^3=729$ and $27^2=729$ ✓.

## Working with mixed indices

**Question.** Simplify $\dfrac{(2^3)^2 \times 2^{-4}}{2^{-1}}$.

**Answer.** Numerator: $(2^3)^2 = 2^6$, so $2^6 \times 2^{-4} = 2^{2}$.
Dividing: $\frac{2^2}{2^{-1}} = 2^{2-(-1)} = 2^3 = \textbf{8}$.

## Solving for an index

**Question.** Solve $3^{2x-1} = 81$.

**Answer.** Write both sides with the same base: $81 = 3^4$.
So $2x - 1 = 4 \Rightarrow 2x = 5 \Rightarrow x = \frac{5}{2} = \textbf{2.5}$.

self_checks.question: Using the product and quotient laws
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** Simplify $\frac{3^5\times3^2}{3^4}$.

**Solution.** Add the indices in the numerator first:

$$3^5\times3^2=3^{5+2}=3^7$$

Then subtract: $3^7\div3^4=3^{7-4}=3^3=27$.

**Answer.** 27.

**Check.** $3^5=243$ and $3^2=9$, so the numerator is $2187$; and
$2187\div81=27$ ✓.

self_checks.question: An algebraic simplification
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** Simplify $\frac{12x^5y^3}{4x^2y}$.

**Solution.** Divide the numbers, then use the quotient law on each letter:

$$\frac{12}{4}=3,\qquad \frac{x^5}{x^2}=x^{5-2}=x^3,\qquad
\frac{y^3}{y}=y^{3-1}=y^2$$

$$\frac{12x^5y^3}{4x^2y}=3x^3y^2$$

**Answer.** $3x^3y^2$.

**Check.** Put $x=2$, $y=3$: the left side is
$\frac{12\times32\times27}{4\times4\times3}=\frac{10368}{48}=216$, and the right
side is $3\times8\times9=216$ ✓.

self_checks.question: Zero and negative indices
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** Evaluate $5^0+2^{-3}$ and simplify $\left(\frac{2x}{y}\right)^{-2}$.

**Solution.** $5^0=1$ and $2^{-3}=\frac{1}{2^3}=\frac18$, so

$$5^0+2^{-3}=1+\frac18=1\frac18=\frac98$$

For the second, a negative index on a fraction turns it upside down:

$$\left(\frac{2x}{y}\right)^{-2}=\left(\frac{y}{2x}\right)^{2}
=\frac{y^2}{4x^2}$$

**Answer.** $1\frac18$ and $\frac{y^2}{4x^2}$.

**Check.** For the second, put $x=1$ and $y=2$. The left side is
$\left(\frac{2}{2}\right)^{-2}=1^{-2}=1$, and the right side is
$\frac{4}{4\times1}=1$. They agree ✓. Using $x=2$, $y=1$ instead: the left side
is $4^{-2}=\frac{1}{16}$, and the right side is $\frac{1}{4\times4}=\frac{1}{16}$ ✓.

self_checks.question: A three-step simplification
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** Simplify $\left(\frac{2a^3b^{-2}}{4ab}\right)^2$.

**Solution.** **Step 1 — simplify inside the bracket.** Divide the numbers:
$\frac{2}{4}=\frac12$. For $a$: $a^{3-1}=a^2$. For $b$:
$b^{-2-1}=b^{-3}$. So inside we have $\frac{a^2b^{-3}}{2}$, that is
$\frac{a^2}{2b^3}$.

**Step 2 — square everything.**

$$\left(\frac{a^2}{2b^3}\right)^2=\frac{a^{4}}{4b^{6}}$$

**Answer.** $\frac{a^4}{4b^6}$.

**Check.** Put $a=1$, $b=1$: the original is
$\left(\frac{2}{4}\right)^2=\frac14$, and the answer is $\frac14$ ✓.

self_checks.question: Powers of a product
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** Simplify $(2x^2y)^3\times(3xy^2)^2$.

**Solution.** Apply the power to each factor:

$$(2x^2y)^3=2^3x^6y^3=8x^6y^3,\qquad
(3xy^2)^2=9x^2y^4$$

Now multiply, adding indices of like bases:

$$8x^6y^3\times9x^2y^4=72x^{6+2}y^{3+4}=72x^8y^7$$

**Answer.** $72x^8y^7$.

**Check.** Put $x=y=1$: the original is $2^3\times3^2=8\times9=72$, and the
answer gives $72$ ✓.

self_checks.question: Solving by making the bases equal
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** Solve $3^x=81$.

**Solution.** Write 81 as a power of 3: $81=3^4$. So

$$3^x=3^4\;\Longrightarrow\;x=4$$

**Answer.** $x=4$.

**Check.** $3^4=81$ ✓.

self_checks.question: An equation with a second term
An equation with a power on both sides
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** Solve $9^{x}=27^{2}$.

**Solution.** Write both numbers as powers of 3: $9=3^2$ and $27=3^3$. So

$$(3^2)^x=(3^3)^2\;\Longrightarrow\;3^{2x}=3^{6}$$

Equating indices: $2x=6$, so $x=3$.

**Answer.** $x=3$.

**Check.** $9^3=729$ and $27^2=729$ ✓.

self_checks.answer:
**Question.** Solve $3^{2x-1} = 81$.

**Answer.** Write both sides with the same base: $81 = 3^4$.
So $2x - 1 = 4 \Rightarrow 2x = 5 \Rightarrow x = \frac{5}{2} = \textbf{2.5}$.

chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- review of factorisation
- highest common factor of algebraic expressions
- lowest common multiple
- factorisation by grouping and by using identities
- Terms, coefficients and like terms
- Highest common factor of expressions
- Lowest common multiple of expressions
- Factorisation by taking out a common factor
- Factorisation by grouping
- The standard identities
- The three identities as areas

An algebraic expression is arithmetic with letters in it, and factorising is the
art of writing it as a product instead of a sum. That single change is what
makes it possible to cancel, to solve and to see structure. This chapter
reviews the vocabulary, then works through the highest common factor and the
lowest common multiple of expressions, factorisation by taking out a common
factor and by grouping, and the three standard identities that every later
chapter depends on.

## Chapter summary

- Terms, coefficient, constant and degree describe the parts of an expression;
  only like terms can be combined.
- $\text{HCF}$: every factor common to all the expressions, to its **lowest**
  power.
- $\text{LCM}$: every factor appearing in any expression, to its **highest**
  power.
- For two expressions, $\text{HCF}\times\text{LCM}=$ product of the expressions.
- $ab+ac=a(b+c)$; group four terms in pairs when no single factor is common to
  all of them.
- The standard identities in both directions: $(a\pm b)^2=a^2\pm2ab+b^2$ and
  $(a+b)(a-b)=a^2-b^2$.
- Factorise completely: take out the common factor first, then look for an
  identity, then check by expanding.

## Study route

Read the topics and identify unfamiliar terms.

Close the book and explain the key ideas in your own words.

Attempt a worked example before revealing its solution.

Complete the chapter practice, correct mistakes, then mark the chapter revised.
chapters.question_answers:
## HCF of two expressions

**Problem.** Find the HCF of $12x^3y^2$ and $18x^2y^4$.

**Solution.** Factorise each:

$$12x^3y^2=2^2\times3\times x^3y^2,\qquad
18x^2y^4=2\times3^2\times x^2y^4$$

Common to both: one 2, one 3, $x^2$ and $y^2$.

$$\text{HCF}=2\times3\times x^2\times y^2=6x^2y^2$$

**Check.** $\frac{12x^3y^2}{6x^2y^2}=2x$ ✓ and
$\frac{18x^2y^4}{6x^2y^2}=3y^2$ ✓ — both quotients are whole expressions, as
they must be for a common factor.

## HCF of three expressions

**Problem.** Find the HCF of $8a^2b$, $12ab^2$ and $20a^2b^2$.

**Solution.** Numbers: HCF of 8, 12 and 20 is 4. For $a$: the smallest power is
$a^1$. For $b$: the smallest power is $b^1$.

$$\text{HCF}=4ab$$

**Check.** Dividing each by $4ab$ gives $2a$, $3b$ and $5ab$ ✓, none of which
has a further common factor.

## LCM of two expressions

**Problem.** Find the LCM of $6x^2y$ and $9xy^3$.

**Solution.** Numbers: LCM of 6 and 9 is 18. For $x$: highest power $x^2$. For
$y$: highest power $y^3$.

$$\text{LCM}=18x^2y^3$$

**Check.** Using the product rule (here the product is
$6x^2y\times9xy^3=54x^3y^4$):
$\text{LCM}=\frac{54x^3y^4}{3xy}=18x^2y^3$ ✓, agreeing with the direct answer.

## HCF and LCM together

**Problem.** For $4a^3b^2$ and $10a^2b^3$, find both the HCF and the LCM, and
verify that $\text{HCF}\times\text{LCM}$ equals the product of the two
expressions.

**Solution.** HCF: numbers 2, $a^2$, $b^2$, so $\text{HCF}=2a^2b^2$.

LCM: numbers 20, $a^3$, $b^3$, so $\text{LCM}=20a^3b^3$.

$$\text{HCF}\times\text{LCM}=2a^2b^2\times20a^3b^3=40a^5b^5$$

Product of the expressions:
$4a^3b^2\times10a^2b^3=40a^5b^5$. They agree ✓.

## Factorising a binomial

**Problem.** Factorise $4x^3-8x^2$.

**Solution.** The HCF of the two terms is $4x^2$, so

$$4x^3-8x^2=4x^2(x-2)$$

**Check.** Expanding: $4x^2\times x-4x^2\times2=4x^3-8x^2$ ✓. Always expand your
answer back — it takes ten seconds and it is the only complete check in
factorising.

## A common binomial factor

**Problem.** Factorise $3a(x+y)+5b(x+y)$.

**Solution.** The whole bracket $(x+y)$ is common:

$$3a(x+y)+5b(x+y)=(x+y)(3a+5b)$$

**Answer.** $(x+y)(3a+5b)$.

## Factorising four terms by grouping

**Problem.** Factorise $6x^2+9x+4x+6$.

**Solution.** Group the first two and the last two:

$$6x^2+9x+4x+6=3x(2x+3)+2(2x+3)$$

Now $(2x+3)$ is common:

$$=(2x+3)(3x+2)$$

**Answer.** $(2x+3)(3x+2)$.

**Check.** Expanding: $6x^2+4x+9x+6=6x^2+13x+6$ ✓, which is the original.

## Grouping with a sign change

**Problem.** Factorise $a^2-ab+ac-bc$.

**Solution.** Group as $(a^2-ab)+(ac-bc)$:

$$=a(a-b)+c(a-b)=(a-b)(a+c)$$

**Answer.** $(a-b)(a+c)$.

**Check.** Expanding: $a^2+ac-ab-bc$ ✓.

**Note.** If the second group had been written as $(ac-bc)=c(a-b)$, the brackets
matched. If they come out matching with opposite signs, take the minus sign out
of the whole group, which reverses both terms inside it.

## The difference of two squares

**Problem.** Factorise $9x^2-16y^2$.

**Solution.** Both terms are perfect squares: $9x^2=(3x)^2$ and
$16y^2=(4y)^2$. Using $a^2-b^2=(a+b)(a-b)$,

$$9x^2-16y^2=(3x+4y)(3x-4y)$$

**Answer.** $(3x+4y)(3x-4y)$.

**Check.** Expanding: $9x^2-12xy+12xy-16y^2=9x^2-16y^2$ ✓.

## Squaring a binomial

**Problem.** Expand $(2x+5)^2$.

**Solution.** With $a=2x$ and $b=5$:

$$(2x+5)^2=(2x)^2+2(2x)(5)+5^2=4x^2+20x+25$$

**Answer.** $4x^2+20x+25$.

**Check.** Put $x=1$: the original is $7^2=49$, and the answer is
$4+20+25=49$ ✓.

## Using an identity to evaluate a number

**Problem.** Evaluate $103\times97$ and $102^2$ without a calculator.

**Solution.** Write each as an identity.

$$103\times97=(100+3)(100-3)=100^2-3^2=10\,000-9=9991$$

$$102^2=(100+2)^2=10\,000+400+4=10\,404$$

**Check.** $103\times97=9991$ ✓ and $102\times102=10\,404$ ✓.

## Factorising with a common factor first

**Problem.** Factorise $2x^3-8x$ completely.

**Solution.** Take out the common factor 2 first, then recognise a difference of
two squares:

$$2x^3-8x=2x(x^2-4)=2x(x+2)(x-2)$$

**Answer.** $2x(x+2)(x-2)$.

**Check.** Expanding: $2x(x^2-4)=2x^3-8x$ ✓. Notice that "completely" is not
satisfied by $2x(x^2-4)$; the bracket still factorises.

## Identities as a shortcut

**Question.** Evaluate without a calculator: (i) $103^2$ (ii) $97^2$
(iii) $56 \times 44$.

**Answer.**
(i) $(100+3)^2 = 10000 + 600 + 9 = \textbf{10609}$.
(ii) $(100-3)^2 = 10000 - 600 + 9 = \textbf{9409}$.
(iii) $(50+6)(50-6) = 2500 - 36 = \textbf{2464}$.

## Factorising in two steps

**Question.** Factorise $2x^2 - 18$.

**Answer.** Take out the common factor first: $2(x^2 - 9)$.
Now use the difference of two squares: $2(x+3)(x-3)$.
**Note:** always look for the common factor before reaching for an identity.

chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- simplification of algebraic fractions
- addition and subtraction of algebraic fractions
- multiplication and division of algebraic fractions
- equations involving algebraic fractions
- Reducing a fraction to its lowest terms
- Adding and subtracting algebraic fractions
- Multiplying and dividing
- Equations containing fractions
- Why factorising comes first

An algebraic fraction is a fraction whose top, bottom or both contain letters.
Everything you already do with number fractions — cancelling, taking a common
denominator, multiplying and dividing — works in exactly the same way, with one
extra step in front: **factorise first**. Nothing can be cancelled until the top
and bottom are written as products, because cancelling is division and division
only removes whole factors.

## Chapter summary

- Factorise the top and bottom before cancelling anything; only factors cancel.
- The LCM of the denominators is the common denominator; multiply top and bottom
  by whatever each fraction is missing.
- When subtracting, put the second numerator in brackets and distribute the
  minus sign.
- Multiply fractions straight across; divide by inverting the second fraction.
- Solve a fractional equation by multiplying every term by the LCM, and state
  the values the variable may not take.
- Check every answer numerically in the original expression.

Read the topics and identify unfamiliar terms.

Close the book and explain the key ideas in your own words.

Attempt a worked example before revealing its solution.

chapters.question_answers:
## Reducing with monomials

**Problem.** Simplify $\frac{12x^3y^2}{18x^2y^4}$.

**Solution.** Divide the numbers by their HCF 6, and subtract indices on the
letters:

$$\frac{12}{18}=\frac23,\qquad \frac{x^3}{x^2}=x,\qquad
\frac{y^2}{y^4}=\frac{1}{y^2}$$

$$\frac{12x^3y^2}{18x^2y^4}=\frac{2x}{3y^2}$$

**Answer.** $\frac{2x}{3y^2}$.

**Check.** Put $x=2$, $y=1$: the original is
$\frac{12\times8}{18\times4}=\frac{96}{72}=\frac43$, and the answer is
$\frac{2\times2}{3}=\frac43$ ✓.

## Reducing after factorising

**Problem.** Simplify $\frac{x^2-9}{x^2+6x+9}$.

**Solution.** Factorise both parts:

$$x^2-9=(x+3)(x-3),\qquad x^2+6x+9=(x+3)^2$$

$$\frac{x^2-9}{x^2+6x+9}=\frac{(x+3)(x-3)}{(x+3)(x+3)}=\frac{x-3}{x+3}$$

**Answer.** $\frac{x-3}{x+3}$, with $x\ne-3$.

**Check.** Put $x=0$: the original is $\frac{-9}{9}=-1$, and the answer is
$\frac{-3}{3}=-1$ ✓.

## Adding with unlike denominators

**Problem.** Simplify $\frac{3}{x}+\frac{5}{y}$.

**Solution.** The LCM of $x$ and $y$ is $xy$.

$$\frac{3}{x}=\frac{3y}{xy},\qquad \frac{5}{y}=\frac{5x}{xy}$$

$$\frac{3}{x}+\frac{5}{y}=\frac{3y+5x}{xy}$$

**Answer.** $\frac{3y+5x}{xy}$.

**Check.** Put $x=1$, $y=1$: the original is $3+5=8$, and the answer is
$\frac{3+5}{1}=8$ ✓.

## Subtracting with an algebraic LCM

**Problem.** Simplify $\frac{2}{x-1}-\frac{1}{x+1}$.

**Solution.** The LCM of $(x-1)$ and $(x+1)$ is their product, $(x-1)(x+1)$.

$$\frac{2}{x-1}=\frac{2(x+1)}{(x-1)(x+1)},\qquad
\frac{1}{x+1}=\frac{x-1}{(x-1)(x+1)}$$

Subtracting the numerators:

$$\frac{2(x+1)-(x-1)}{(x-1)(x+1)}=\frac{2x+2-x+1}{(x-1)(x+1)}
=\frac{x+3}{x^2-1}$$

**Answer.** $\frac{x+3}{x^2-1}$.

**Check.** Put $x=2$: the original is $\frac21-\frac13=\frac53$, and the answer
is $\frac{5}{4-1}=\frac53$ ✓.

## Three denominators

**Problem.** Simplify $\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{2x}+\frac{1}{3x}$.

**Solution.** The LCM of $x$, $2x$ and $3x$ is $6x$. Rewrite each:

$$\frac{6}{6x}+\frac{3}{6x}+\frac{2}{6x}=\frac{11}{6x}$$

**Answer.** $\frac{11}{6x}$.

**Check.** Put $x=1$: $1+\frac12+\frac13=\frac{11}{6}$ ✓.

## With a factorisable denominator

**Problem.** Simplify $\frac{1}{x^2-4}+\frac{1}{x+2}$.

**Solution.** Factorise the first denominator:
$x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)$. The LCM is $(x-2)(x+2)$.

$$\frac{1}{(x-2)(x+2)}+\frac{x-2}{(x-2)(x+2)}
=\frac{1+x-2}{(x-2)(x+2)}=\frac{x-1}{x^2-4}$$

**Answer.** $\frac{x-1}{x^2-4}$.

**Check.** Put $x=3$: the original is $\frac15+\frac15=\frac25$, and the answer
is $\frac{2}{9-4}=\frac25$ ✓.

## Multiplication

**Problem.** Simplify $\frac{x^2-4}{x+3}\times\frac{x+3}{x-2}$.

**Solution.** Factorise the difference of squares:
$x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)$. Then

$$\frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x+3}\times\frac{x+3}{x-2}=\frac{(x+2)}{1}=x+2$$

after cancelling $(x-2)$ and $(x+3)$.

**Answer.** $x+2$.

**Check.** Put $x=4$: the original is $\frac{12}{7}\times\frac{7}{2}=6$, and the
answer is $6$ ✓.

## Division

**Problem.** Simplify $\frac{a^2-b^2}{a+b}\div\frac{a-b}{a}$.

**Solution.** Invert and multiply, having factorised
$a^2-b^2=(a+b)(a-b)$:

$$\frac{(a+b)(a-b)}{a+b}\times\frac{a}{a-b}
=\frac{(a-b)}{1}\times\frac{a}{(a-b)}=a$$

**Answer.** $a$.

**Check.** Put $a=3$, $b=1$: the original is $\frac{8}{4}\div\frac{2}{3}
=2\times\frac32=3$, and the answer is $a=3$ ✓.

## Solving a fractional equation

**Problem.** Solve $\frac{x}{2}+\frac{x}{3}=5$.

**Solution.** The LCM of 2 and 3 is 6. Multiply every term by 6:

$$6\times\frac{x}{2}+6\times\frac{x}{3}=6\times5$$

$$3x+2x=30\;\Longrightarrow\;5x=30\;\Longrightarrow\;x=6$$

**Answer.** $x=6$.

**Check.** $\frac62+\frac63=3+2=5$ ✓.

## An equation with the unknown in a denominator

**Problem.** Solve $\frac{3}{x}=\frac{5}{x+2}$.

**Solution.** Cross-multiplying removes both denominators:

$$3(x+2)=5x\;\Longrightarrow\;3x+6=5x\;\Longrightarrow\;6=2x
\;\Longrightarrow\;x=3$$

**Answer.** $x=3$.

**Check.** $\frac33=1$ and $\frac{5}{5}=1$ ✓.

**Note.** Always state the values the variable may not take:
here $x\ne0$ and $x\ne-2$, and $x=3$ is allowed.

## Simplify and state the excluded values

**Question.** Simplify $\dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x^2 + 5x + 6}$ and state the values of
$x$ for which it is undefined.

**Answer.** Numerator $= (x+2)(x-2)$. Denominator $= (x+2)(x+3)$.
Cancelling $(x+2)$: $\dfrac{x-2}{x+3}$.
The original denominator is zero at $x = -2$ and $x = -3$, so the expression is
**undefined at $x = -2$ and $x = -3$**.

## Adding two algebraic fractions

**Question.** Simplify $\dfrac{2}{x-1} + \dfrac{3}{x+2}$.

**Answer.** LCM of the denominators is $(x-1)(x+2)$.
$$\frac{2(x+2) + 3(x-1)}{(x-1)(x+2)} = \frac{2x + 4 + 3x - 3}{(x-1)(x+2)}
= \frac{5x + 1}{(x-1)(x+2)}$$

self_checks.question: Reducing with monomials
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** Simplify $\frac{12x^3y^2}{18x^2y^4}$.

**Solution.** Divide the numbers by their HCF 6, and subtract indices on the
letters:

$$\frac{12}{18}=\frac23,\qquad \frac{x^3}{x^2}=x,\qquad
\frac{y^2}{y^4}=\frac{1}{y^2}$$

$$\frac{12x^3y^2}{18x^2y^4}=\frac{2x}{3y^2}$$

**Answer.** $\frac{2x}{3y^2}$.

**Check.** Put $x=2$, $y=1$: the original is
$\frac{12\times8}{18\times4}=\frac{96}{72}=\frac43$, and the answer is
$\frac{2\times2}{3}=\frac43$ ✓.

self_checks.question: Reducing after factorising
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** Simplify $\frac{x^2-9}{x^2+6x+9}$.

**Solution.** Factorise both parts:

$$x^2-9=(x+3)(x-3),\qquad x^2+6x+9=(x+3)^2$$

$$\frac{x^2-9}{x^2+6x+9}=\frac{(x+3)(x-3)}{(x+3)(x+3)}=\frac{x-3}{x+3}$$

**Answer.** $\frac{x-3}{x+3}$, with $x\ne-3$.

**Check.** Put $x=0$: the original is $\frac{-9}{9}=-1$, and the answer is
$\frac{-3}{3}=-1$ ✓.

self_checks.question: Adding with unlike denominators
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** Simplify $\frac{3}{x}+\frac{5}{y}$.

**Solution.** The LCM of $x$ and $y$ is $xy$.

$$\frac{3}{x}=\frac{3y}{xy},\qquad \frac{5}{y}=\frac{5x}{xy}$$

$$\frac{3}{x}+\frac{5}{y}=\frac{3y+5x}{xy}$$

**Answer.** $\frac{3y+5x}{xy}$.

**Check.** Put $x=1$, $y=1$: the original is $3+5=8$, and the answer is
$\frac{3+5}{1}=8$ ✓.

self_checks.question: Subtracting with an algebraic LCM
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** Simplify $\frac{2}{x-1}-\frac{1}{x+1}$.

**Solution.** The LCM of $(x-1)$ and $(x+1)$ is their product, $(x-1)(x+1)$.

$$\frac{2}{x-1}=\frac{2(x+1)}{(x-1)(x+1)},\qquad
\frac{1}{x+1}=\frac{x-1}{(x-1)(x+1)}$$

Subtracting the numerators:

$$\frac{2(x+1)-(x-1)}{(x-1)(x+1)}=\frac{2x+2-x+1}{(x-1)(x+1)}
=\frac{x+3}{x^2-1}$$

**Answer.** $\frac{x+3}{x^2-1}$.

**Check.** Put $x=2$: the original is $\frac21-\frac13=\frac53$, and the answer
is $\frac{5}{4-1}=\frac53$ ✓.

**Solution.** The LCM of $x$, $2x$ and $3x$ is $6x$. Rewrite each:

**Answer.** $\frac{11}{6x}$.

**Check.** Put $x=1$: $1+\frac12+\frac13=\frac{11}{6}$ ✓.

**Answer.** $\frac{x-1}{x^2-4}$.

**Check.** Put $x=3$: the original is $\frac15+\frac15=\frac25$, and the answer
is $\frac{2}{9-4}=\frac25$ ✓.

The graph of a linear equation

  then add or subtract) or substitution (make one variable the subject).

chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- linear equations in one variable
- simultaneous linear equations
- inequality and its graph on the number line
- graph of a linear equation
- Linear equations in one variable
- Simultaneous linear equations
- The graph of a linear equation
- Inequality and its graph
- 12.2.1 The elimination method
- 12.2.2 The substitution method

An equation is a balance: whatever you do to one side you must do to the other.
A graph is a picture of every pair of values that keeps the balance. Putting the
two together turns algebra into something you can see — the point where two
lines cross *is* the solution of the two equations, and an inequality is simply
a region of the graph rather than a line.

## Chapter summary

- A linear equation is solved by clearing fractions, expanding brackets,
  collecting like terms and dividing by the coefficient.
- Simultaneous equations are solved by elimination (make one coefficient match,
  then add or subtract) or substitution (make one variable the subject).
- A linear equation has infinitely many solutions, and its graph is a straight
  line; two points fix the line and a third checks it.
- The solution of two simultaneous equations is the coordinates of the point
  where their graphs cross.
- An inequality is solved like an equation, but multiplying or dividing by a
  negative number reverses the sign.
- On a number line, an open circle means the value is excluded and a filled
  circle means it is included.

## Study route

Read the topics and identify unfamiliar terms.

Close the book and explain the key ideas in your own words.

Attempt a worked example before revealing its solution.

Complete the chapter practice, correct mistakes, then mark the chapter revised.
chapters.question_answers:
## With brackets

**Problem.** Solve $3(x-2)+5=2x+4$.

**Solution.** Expand the bracket:

$$3x-6+5=2x+4\;\Longrightarrow\;3x-1=2x+4$$

Subtract $2x$ from both sides and add 1:

$$x=5$$

**Answer.** $x=5$.

**Check.** Left side: $3(5-2)+5=9+5=14$. Right side: $2(5)+4=14$ ✓.

## With fractions

**Problem.** Solve $\frac{2x-1}{3}=\frac{x+2}{2}$.

**Solution.** Multiply both sides by the LCM 6:

$$2(2x-1)=3(x+2)\;\Longrightarrow\;4x-2=3x+6\;\Longrightarrow\;x=8$$

**Answer.** $x=8$.

**Check.** Left: $\frac{16-1}{3}=5$. Right: $\frac{10}{2}=5$ ✓.

## Elimination by adding

**Problem.** Solve $x+y=10$ and $x-y=4$.

**Solution.** The coefficients of $y$ are $+1$ and $-1$, so adding eliminates
$y$:

$$2x=14\;\Longrightarrow\;x=7$$

Substituting into $x+y=10$ gives $7+y=10$, so $y=3$.

**Answer.** $x=7$, $y=3$.

**Check.** $7+3=10$ ✓ and $7-3=4$ ✓.

## Elimination by scaling

**Problem.** Solve $2x+3y=13$ and $3x-2y=0$.

**Solution.** **Step 1 — make the $x$ coefficients equal.** Multiply the first
equation by 3 and the second by 2:

$$6x+9y=39,\qquad 6x-4y=0$$

**Step 2 — subtract.**

$$(6x+9y)-(6x-4y)=39-0\;\Longrightarrow\;13y=39\;\Longrightarrow\;y=3$$

**Step 3 — substitute.** From $3x-2y=0$: $3x=6$, so $x=2$.

**Answer.** $x=2$, $y=3$.

**Check.** $2(2)+3(3)=4+9=13$ ✓ and $3(2)-2(3)=0$ ✓.

## Substitution

**Problem.** Solve $y=2x+1$ and $3x+y=11$.

**Solution.** $y$ is already the subject, so substitute:

$$3x+(2x+1)=11\;\Longrightarrow\;5x=10\;\Longrightarrow\;x=2$$

Then $y=2(2)+1=5$.

**Answer.** $x=2$, $y=5$.

**Check.** $5=2(2)+1$ ✓ and $3(2)+5=11$ ✓.

## A word problem

**Problem.** The sum of two numbers is 25 and their difference is 7. Find the
numbers.

**Solution.** Let the numbers be $x$ and $y$, with $x>y$. Then

$$x+y=25,\qquad x-y=7$$

Adding: $2x=32$, so $x=16$; then $y=25-16=9$.

**Answer.** 16 and 9.

**Check.** $16+9=25$ ✓ and $16-9=7$ ✓.

## Solving simultaneous equations graphically

**Problem.** Draw the graphs of $x+y=6$ and $y=x-2$ on the same axes and read
off the solution.

**Solution.** **Table for $x+y=6$, that is $y=6-x$:** when $x=0$, $y=6$; when
$x=2$, $y=4$; when $x=6$, $y=0$. **Table for $y=x-2$:** when $x=0$, $y=-2$;
when $x=2$, $y=0$; when $x=6$, $y=4$.

Plot both lines. They cross at $(4,2)$.

**Answer.** $x=4$, $y=2$.

**Check.** $4+2=6$ ✓ and $2=4-2$ ✓. At the crossing point both equations hold,
which is exactly what the solution means.

## Solving and graphing an inequality

**Problem.** Solve $3x-5\le7$ and show the solution on a number line.

**Solution.** Add 5 to both sides: $3x\le12$. Divide by 3 (positive, so the
sign does not change): $x\le4$.

On the number line, put a **filled** circle at 4 and shade everything to the
left, including 4.

**Check.** Try $x=4$: $3(4)-5=7\le7$ ✓ (allowed, because of the $\le$ sign).
Try $x=5$: $15-5=10>7$ ✗, correctly outside the shaded region.

## An inequality with a negative coefficient

**Problem.** Solve $5-2x<11$ and graph the solution.

**Solution.** Subtract 5: $-2x<6$. Divide by $-2$, reversing the sign:
$x>-3$.

On the number line, put an open circle at $-3$ and shade to the right.

**Check.** Try $x=0$: $5-0=5<11$ ✓, and 0 is inside the region.
Try $x=-4$: $5+8=13<11$ is false ✗, correctly excluded.

chapters.name: Lines and Angles
topics: pairs of angles: complementary, supplementary, adjacent, vertically opposite
chapters.summary:
- Complementary angles add to 90°; supplementary angles add to 180°; angles
  round a point add to 360°.
- Vertically opposite angles are equal; angles in a linear pair are
  supplementary.
- When a transversal cuts two **parallel** lines: corresponding angles are equal,
  alternate angles are equal, and co-interior angles add to 180°.

- Remember the shapes: F for corresponding, Z for alternate, C for co-interior.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- straight lines, rays and angles
- pairs of angles: complementary, supplementary, adjacent, vertically opposite
- parallel lines and a transversal
- corresponding, alternate and co-interior angles
- Points, lines and angles
- Pairs of angles
- Parallel lines and a transversal
- Reasons are the marks

Two straight lines that never meet, a transversal that cuts them, and the eight
angles that appear: that picture contains almost every angle fact you will need
in geometry. The whole chapter is really one idea — when a transversal crosses
parallel lines, four angles come out equal in one way and four in another, and
recognising which is which settles a question in one line.

## Chapter summary

- Complementary angles add to 90°; supplementary angles add to 180°; angles
  round a point add to 360°.
- Vertically opposite angles are equal; angles in a linear pair are
  supplementary.
- When a transversal cuts two **parallel** lines: corresponding angles are equal,
  alternate angles are equal, and co-interior angles add to 180°.
- Two lines are parallel if any one of those three conditions holds.
- Remember the shapes: F for corresponding, Z for alternate, C for co-interior.

## Study route

Read the topics and identify unfamiliar terms.

Close the book and explain the key ideas in your own words.

Attempt a worked example before revealing its solution.

Complete the chapter practice, correct mistakes, then mark the chapter revised.
chapters.question_answers:
## Complementary and supplementary angles

**Problem.** Two angles are supplementary. One of them is 40° more than the
other. Find both.

**Solution.** Let the smaller be $x$; then the larger is $x+40$. Because they are
supplementary,

$$x+(x+40)=180\;\Longrightarrow\;2x=140\;\Longrightarrow\;x=70$$

**Answer.** 70° and 110°.

**Check.** $70+110=180$ ✓ and $110-70=40$ ✓.

## Vertically opposite angles

**Problem.** Two straight lines cross. One of the four angles is 65°. Find the
other three, giving a reason for each.

**Solution.** The angle vertically opposite 65° is also **65°** (vertically
opposite angles are equal). Each of the other two is supplementary to 65°, so
each is $180-65=115°$; and they are equal to each other because they are
vertically opposite.

**Answer.** 65°, 115°, 115°.

**Check.** $65+115+65+115=360$ ✓, which is the angle sum round a point.

## Finding angles with a transversal

**Problem.** In the figure above, angle 1 is 120°. Find angles 2, 3, 4, a, b, c
and d, giving a reason for each.

**Solution.**

| Angle | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 60° | angles 1 and 2 form a linear pair on a straight line |
| 3 | 120° | vertically opposite to angle 1 |
| 4 | 60° | vertically opposite to angle 2 |
| a | 120° | corresponding to angle 1 |
| b | 60° | corresponding to angle 2 (or vertically opposite to $a$) |
| c | 120° | alternate to angle 1 |
| d | 60° | corresponding to angle 4 |

**Check.** Angle 2 and angle $a$ are co-interior: $60+120=180$ ✓. All the acute
angles are 60° and all the obtuse ones 120°, which is exactly what parallel
lines force.

## Two unknowns

**Problem.** Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. A pair of co-interior
angles are $3x$ and $2x+20$. Find $x$ and the size of each angle.

**Solution.** Co-interior angles are supplementary:

$$3x+(2x+20)=180\;\Longrightarrow\;5x=160\;\Longrightarrow\;x=32$$

The angles are $3(32)=96°$ and $2(32)+20=84°$.

**Answer.** $x=32$; the angles are 96° and 84°.

**Check.** $96+84=180$ ✓, as co-interior angles must.

## Testing for parallel lines

**Problem.** A transversal cuts two lines. A pair of alternate angles are 75°
and 78°. Are the two lines parallel? Give a reason.

**Solution.** Alternate angles are equal only when the lines are parallel. Here
$75°\ne78°$, so the alternate angles are not equal.

**Answer.** The lines are **not** parallel; they meet on the side where the
angles open out. The test for parallel lines is exactly the equality of such a
pair.

## A four-mark angle chase, written for marks

**Question.** Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is
$116°$. Find the other seven, with reasons.

**Answer.**
Vertically opposite to $116°$: $\textbf{116°}$ — *vertically opposite angles*.
On the straight line with it: $180° - 116° = \textbf{64°}$ — *linear pair*;
and its vertically opposite is $\textbf{64°}$.
On the second parallel line, the corresponding angle is $\textbf{116°}$ —
*corresponding angles*; its vertically opposite is $\textbf{116°}$.
The remaining two are $\textbf{64°}$ each — *co-interior with $116°$*
($116° + 64° = 180°$) and *vertically opposite*.

self_checks.question: Complementary and supplementary angles
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** Two angles are supplementary. One of them is 40° more than the
other. Find both.

**Solution.** Let the smaller be $x$; then the larger is $x+40$. Because they are
supplementary,

$$x+(x+40)=180\;\Longrightarrow\;2x=140\;\Longrightarrow\;x=70$$

**Answer.** 70° and 110°.

**Check.** $70+110=180$ ✓ and $110-70=40$ ✓.

self_checks.question: Vertically opposite angles
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** Two straight lines cross. One of the four angles is 65°. Find the
other three, giving a reason for each.

**Solution.** The angle vertically opposite 65° is also **65°** (vertically
opposite angles are equal). Each of the other two is supplementary to 65°, so
each is $180-65=115°$; and they are equal to each other because they are
vertically opposite.

**Answer.** 65°, 115°, 115°.

**Check.** $65+115+65+115=360$ ✓, which is the angle sum round a point.

self_checks.question: Finding angles with a transversal
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** In the figure above, angle 1 is 120°. Find angles 2, 3, 4, a, b, c
and d, giving a reason for each.

**Solution.**

| Angle | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 60° | angles 1 and 2 form a linear pair on a straight line |
| 3 | 120° | vertically opposite to angle 1 |
| 4 | 60° | vertically opposite to angle 2 |
| a | 120° | corresponding to angle 1 |
| b | 60° | corresponding to angle 2 (or vertically opposite to $a$) |
| c | 120° | alternate to angle 1 |
| d | 60° | corresponding to angle 4 |

**Check.** Angle 2 and angle $a$ are co-interior: $60+120=180$ ✓. All the acute
angles are 60° and all the obtuse ones 120°, which is exactly what parallel
lines force.

self_checks.question: Two unknowns
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. A pair of co-interior
angles are $3x$ and $2x+20$. Find $x$ and the size of each angle.

**Solution.** Co-interior angles are supplementary:

$$3x+(2x+20)=180\;\Longrightarrow\;5x=160\;\Longrightarrow\;x=32$$

The angles are $3(32)=96°$ and $2(32)+20=84°$.

**Answer.** $x=32$; the angles are 96° and 84°.

**Check.** $96+84=180$ ✓, as co-interior angles must.

self_checks.question: Testing for parallel lines
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** A transversal cuts two lines. A pair of alternate angles are 75°
and 78°. Are the two lines parallel? Give a reason.

**Solution.** Alternate angles are equal only when the lines are parallel. Here
$75°\ne78°$, so the alternate angles are not equal.

**Answer.** The lines are **not** parallel; they meet on the side where the
angles open out. The test for parallel lines is exactly the equality of such a
pair.

self_checks.question: A four-mark angle chase, written for marks
self_checks.answer:
**Question.** Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is
$116°$. Find the other seven, with reasons.

**Answer.**
Vertically opposite to $116°$: $\textbf{116°}$ — *vertically opposite angles*.
On the straight line with it: $180° - 116° = \textbf{64°}$ — *linear pair*;
and its vertically opposite is $\textbf{64°}$.
On the second parallel line, the corresponding angle is $\textbf{116°}$ —
*corresponding angles*; its vertically opposite is $\textbf{116°}$.
The remaining two are $\textbf{64°}$ each — *co-interior with $116°$*
($116° + 64° = 180°$) and *vertically opposite*.

## Topics to cover

- triangles: classification and properties
- quadrilaterals and their properties
- construction of triangles and quadrilaterals
- polygons: interior and exterior angles
- the circle: radius, chord, arc, sector
- Triangles
- Quadrilaterals
- Polygons
- Construction
- The circle

A plane figure is a flat shape: a triangle, a quadrilateral, a polygon, a
circle. Geometry at this level is mostly bookkeeping with two facts — the angles
of a triangle add to 180°, and the angles of a polygon follow from splitting it
into triangles. Everything else is a consequence, and the figures are what make
those consequences visible.

## Chapter summary

- The angles of a triangle add to 180°; an exterior angle equals the sum of the
  two interior opposite angles.
- Equilateral, isosceles and scalene are classified by sides; acute, right and
  obtuse by angles.
- The angles of a quadrilateral add to 360°; a parallelogram has equal opposite
  angles and supplementary adjacent angles, and its diagonals bisect each other.
- For a polygon of $n$ sides: interior angles sum to $(n-2)\times180°$; exterior
  angles always sum to 360°.
- The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord; the angle in a
  semicircle is 90°.
- Constructions are done with ruler and compasses, with every arc left in place.

chapters.question_answers:
## Angles of a triangle

**Problem.** In a triangle the angles are in the ratio $2:3:4$. Find each angle
and classify the triangle.

**Solution.** Let the angles be $2x$, $3x$ and $4x$. Their sum is 180°:

$$2x+3x+4x=180\;\Longrightarrow\;9x=180\;\Longrightarrow\;x=20$$

The angles are $40°$, $60°$ and $80°$. All three are less than 90°, so the
triangle is **acute-angled**.

**Check.** $40+60+80=180$ ✓, and the ratios $40:60:80=2:3:4$ ✓.

## Isosceles triangle

**Problem.** In an isosceles triangle the vertex angle is 40°. Find the base
angles.

**Solution.** The two base angles are equal; let each be $x$. Then

$$40+x+x=180\;\Longrightarrow\;2x=140\;\Longrightarrow\;x=70$$

**Answer.** Each base angle is 70°.

**Check.** $40+70+70=180$ ✓. The vertex angle is the odd one out, and the two
angles opposite the equal sides are equal.

## Angles of a quadrilateral

**Problem.** Three angles of a quadrilateral are 85°, 95° and 110°. Find the
fourth.

**Solution.** The four angles add to 360°, so the fourth is

$$360-(85+95+110)=360-290=70°$$

**Answer.** 70°.

**Check.** $85+95+110+70=360$ ✓.

## Properties of a parallelogram

**Problem.** In a parallelogram, one angle is 65°. Find the other three and
state the property you used each time.

**Solution.** The opposite angle is **65°** (opposite angles of a parallelogram
are equal). Each of the other two is the supplement: $180-65=115°$ (adjacent
angles of a parallelogram are supplementary), and they are equal to each other
by the opposite-angle property.

**Answer.** 65°, 115°, 115°.

**Check.** $65+115+65+115=360$ ✓.

## Interior and exterior angles

**Problem.** Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 24°. Find the number of
sides, the sum of the interior angles, and each interior angle.

**Solution.** The exterior angles add to 360°, so

$$n=\frac{360}{24}=15$$

Sum of interior angles:
$(15-2)\times180=13\times180=2340°$.

Each interior angle: $\frac{2340}{15}=156°$, or equivalently
$180-24=156°$.

**Answer.** 15 sides; 2340°; 156°.

**Check.** $156+24=180$ ✓ — an interior and its exterior angle form a linear
pair.

## Finding the number of sides

**Problem.** The sum of the interior angles of a polygon is 1260°. Find the
number of sides.

**Solution.** $(n-2)\times180=1260$, so $n-2=7$ and $n=9$.

**Answer.** A nonagon, with 9 sides.

**Check.** $(9-2)\times180=1260$ ✓.

## A chord and the centre

**Problem.** A chord of length 16 cm is drawn in a circle of radius 10 cm. Find
the distance of the chord from the centre.

**Solution.** The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so half the
chord is 8 cm. That, the radius and the distance $d$ form a right triangle with
the radius as the hypotenuse:

$$d=\sqrt{10^2-8^2}=\sqrt{100-64}=\sqrt{36}=6\ \text{cm}$$

**Answer.** 6 cm from the centre.

**Check.** $\sqrt{6^2+8^2}=\sqrt{36+64}=10$ ✓, which is the radius.

chapters.summary:
- Congruent figures have the same shape **and** size; similar figures have the
  same shape at different sizes.
- The four tests of congruence are **SSS, SAS, ASA and RHS**; there is no SSA
  test.
- The order of the letters in $\triangle ABC\cong\triangle PQR$ gives the
  correspondence, and corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal.
- Two triangles are similar if two angles match (AA), or if the three pairs of
  sides are in the same ratio (SSS similarity), or if two pairs of sides are in
  the same ratio with equal included angles (SAS similarity).
- In similar triangles, corresponding sides are in the same ratio $k$ and areas
  are in the ratio $k^2$.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- congruent figures and congruent triangles
- tests of congruence (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS)
- similar figures and similar triangles
- ratio of areas of similar triangles
- Congruent figures
- The four tests of congruence
- Similar figures

Two figures are **congruent** when they are exactly the same shape and the same
size, so that one can be placed on the other and fit perfectly. They are
**similar** when they are the same shape but not necessarily the same size, so
that one is an enlargement of the other. Both ideas are tests: given a few
measurements, they let you say that two triangles must match without measuring
everything.

## Chapter summary

- Congruent figures have the same shape **and** size; similar figures have the
  same shape at different sizes.
- The four tests of congruence are **SSS, SAS, ASA and RHS**; there is no SSA
  test.
- The order of the letters in $\triangle ABC\cong\triangle PQR$ gives the
  correspondence, and corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal.
- Two triangles are similar if two angles match (AA), or if the three pairs of
  sides are in the same ratio (SSS similarity), or if two pairs of sides are in
  the same ratio with equal included angles (SAS similarity).
- In similar triangles, corresponding sides are in the same ratio $k$ and areas
  are in the ratio $k^2$.

## Study route

Read the topics and identify unfamiliar terms.

Close the book and explain the key ideas in your own words.

Attempt a worked example before revealing its solution.

Complete the chapter practice, correct mistakes, then mark the chapter revised.
chapters.question_answers:
## A congruence proof

**Problem.** In the figure, $AB=AC$ and $D$ is the midpoint of $BC$. Prove that
$\triangle ABD\cong\triangle ACD$, and hence that $AD$ is perpendicular to
$BC$.

**Solution.**

**Given.** $AB=AC$ and $BD=DC$ ($D$ is the midpoint).

**To prove.** $\triangle ABD\cong\triangle ACD$ and $\angle ADB=90°$.

**Proof.**

| Statement | Reason |
|---|---|
| $AB=AC$ | given |
| $BD=DC$ | $D$ is the midpoint of $BC$ |
| $AD=AD$ | common side |
| $\triangle ABD\cong\triangle ACD$ | SSS |
| $\angle ADB=\angle ADC$ | corresponding parts of congruent triangles |

Now $\angle ADB+\angle ADC=180°$, because $BDC$ is a straight line. Equal
angles adding to 180° are each 90°, so $\angle ADB=90°$ and therefore $AD\perp
BC$. ∎

**What it shows.** In an isosceles triangle the line from the apex to the
midpoint of the base is perpendicular to the base — and it also bisects the apex
angle, since it makes the two triangles congruent.

## A proof using ASA

**Problem.** Two triangles have $\angle B=\angle Q$, $\angle C=\angle R$ and
$BC=QR$. Prove the triangles congruent.

**Solution.**

**Proof.** In a triangle the angles add to 180°, so

$$\angle A=180°-(\angle B+\angle C),\qquad
\angle P=180°-(\angle Q+\angle R)$$

Since $\angle B=\angle Q$ and $\angle C=\angle R$, it follows that
$\angle A=\angle P$. We now have $\angle B=\angle Q$, $BC=QR$ (the side between
them) and $\angle C=\angle R$. Therefore

$$\triangle ABC\cong\triangle QRP\quad\text{(ASA)}$$

**Note.** We never measured $\angle A$; it was forced by the angle sum. This is
why ASA works with only two angles.

**Check.** The equal side must be the one lying **between** the two equal
angles. Here $BC$ lies between angles $B$ and $C$ ✓.

## Similar triangles and a missing side

**Problem.** Triangles $ABC$ and $PQR$ are similar, with $AB=6$ cm, $BC=9$ cm
and $PQ=4$ cm. Find $QR$.

**Solution.** Corresponding sides are in the same ratio:

$$\frac{AB}{PQ}=\frac{BC}{QR}\;\Longrightarrow\;\frac64=\frac{9}{QR}$$

Cross-multiplying: $6\times QR=36$, so $QR=6$ cm.

**Answer.** 6 cm.

**Check.** The scale factor is $\frac{6}{4}=1.5$, and
$9\div1.5=6$ ✓ — the same answer from the other direction.

## The area ratio

**Problem.** Two similar triangles have corresponding sides in the ratio
$2:5$. Find the ratio of their areas.

**Solution.** For similar figures, the ratio of areas is the **square** of the
ratio of corresponding sides:

$$\frac{\text{area}_1}{\text{area}_2}=\left(\frac25\right)^2=\frac{4}{25}$$

**Answer.** $4:25$.

**Note.** The enlarged triangle has sides 2.5 times as long but an area 6.25
times as large. This is why a map of twice the scale needs four times the paper,
and why a model house has far less surface than the house it copies.

## Using the angle sum to prove similarity

**Problem.** In triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$, $\angle A=50°$, $\angle B=70°$,
$\angle D=50°$ and $\angle E=70°$. Prove the triangles similar and write the
ratio of corresponding sides.

**Solution.** Two angles of the first equal two angles of the second:
$\angle A=\angle D$ and $\angle B=\angle E$. So

$$\triangle ABC\sim\triangle DEF\quad\text{(AA)}$$

The third angles are equal too:
$\angle C=\angle F=180-120=60°$. The ratio of corresponding sides is

$$\frac{AB}{DE}=\frac{BC}{EF}=\frac{CA}{FD}$$

**Check.** The matched order is A with D, B with E, C with F — because those are
the equal angles. Writing the correspondence in the wrong order gives wrong
ratios.

topics: prisms and pyramids: faces, edges and vertices
surface area of prisms and pyramids
Volume of a prism and a pyramid
chapters.summary:
- A prism has two identical parallel ends and rectangular sides; a pyramid has
  one base and triangular sides meeting at an apex.
- $F+V-E=2$ for every such solid.
- A net is a flat pattern that folds into the solid; a cube has eleven nets.
- Cube surface area $6a^2$, volume $a^3$; cuboid surface area
  $2(lb+bh+hl)$, volume $lbh$.
- Volume of a prism $=$ base area $\times$ length; volume of a pyramid
  $=\frac13\times$ base area $\times$ height.
- Surface area is in square units, volume in cubic units, and the two are never
  interchangeable.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- prisms and pyramids: faces, edges and vertices
- nets of solids
- surface area of prisms and pyramids
- volume of prisms and pyramids
- Prisms and pyramids
- Nets
- Surface area
- Volume of a prism and a pyramid

A box, a milk carton, a pyramid-shaped temple roof: all are solids with flat
faces, and every one of them can be cut out of a sheet of paper using a **net**.
This chapter counts faces, edges and vertices, unfolds the solids into nets, and
then does the arithmetic that matters in a workshop — how much material is
needed to make the box, and how much it holds.

## Chapter summary

- A prism has two identical parallel ends and rectangular sides; a pyramid has
  one base and triangular sides meeting at an apex.
- $F+V-E=2$ for every such solid.
- A net is a flat pattern that folds into the solid; a cube has eleven nets.
- Cube surface area $6a^2$, volume $a^3$; cuboid surface area
  $2(lb+bh+hl)$, volume $lbh$.
- Volume of a prism $=$ base area $\times$ length; volume of a pyramid
  $=\frac13\times$ base area $\times$ height.
- Surface area is in square units, volume in cubic units, and the two are never
  interchangeable.

Close the book and explain the key ideas in your own words.

Attempt a worked example before revealing its solution.

Complete the chapter practice, correct mistakes, then mark the chapter revised.
chapters.question_answers:
## Counting on a prism

**Problem.** A prism has a base that is a regular octagon. How many faces, edges
and vertices does it have? Check with Euler's relation.

**Solution.** The two ends are octagons, and there is one rectangular face for
each of the eight sides. So

$$F=2+8=10$$

Each of the 8 base edges appears at each end, so there are 16 base edges, plus
the 8 side edges:

$$E=16+8=24$$

There are 8 vertices at each end:

$$V=16$$

**Check.** $F+V-E=10+16-24=2$ ✓.

## A cuboid box

**Problem.** A closed box measures 20 cm by 15 cm by 10 cm. Find its total
surface area and its volume.

**Solution.** Take $l=20$, $b=15$ and $h=10$ cm.

$$S=2(lb+bh+hl)=2(300+150+200)=2\times650=1300\ \text{cm}^2$$

$$V=lbh=20\times15\times10=3000\ \text{cm}^3$$

**Answer.** 1300 cm² of card; volume 3000 cm³.

**Check.** The six faces are two of 300 cm², two of 150 cm² and two of 200 cm²,
giving $600+300+400=1300$ ✓. The volume is the base area $300\times$ the height
$10=3000$ ✓.

## A cube painted on the outside

**Problem.** A cube of side 12 cm is painted all over. Find the area painted, and
the volume.

**Solution.** $S=6a^2=6\times144=864$ cm².

$$V=a^3=12^3=1728\ \text{cm}^3$$

**Answer.** 864 cm²; 1728 cm³.

**Check.** Each face is $12\times12=144$ cm², and six of them give 864 ✓.

## A triangular prism

**Problem.** A triangular prism has a base that is a right-angled triangle with
legs 6 cm and 8 cm, and a length of 15 cm. Find its volume and its total surface
area.

**Solution.** **Volume.** Area of the triangular base
$=\frac12\times6\times8=24$ cm², so

$$V=24\times15=360\ \text{cm}^3$$

**Surface area.** Two triangular ends: $2\times24=48$ cm². The hypotenuse is
$\sqrt{6^2+8^2}=10$ cm, so the perimeter of the base is $6+8+10=24$ cm and the
three rectangular faces total $24\times15=360$ cm².

$$S=48+360=408\ \text{cm}^2$$

**Answer.** Volume 360 cm³; surface area 408 cm².

**Check.** The two triangular ends are 48 of the 408; the three rectangles are
$6\times15=90$, $8\times15=120$ and $10\times15=150$, which add to 360 ✓.

## A pyramid

**Problem.** A square pyramid has a base of side 10 m and a height of 12 m. Find
its volume.

**Solution.**

$$V=\frac13\times a^2\times h=\frac13\times100\times12=400\ \text{m}^3$$

**Answer.** 400 m³.

**Check.** The enclosing prism would have volume $100\times12=1200$ m³, and a
third of it is 400 ✓.

self_checks.question: Counting on a prism
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** A prism has a base that is a regular octagon. How many faces, edges
and vertices does it have? Check with Euler's relation.

**Solution.** The two ends are octagons, and there is one rectangular face for
each of the eight sides. So

$$F=2+8=10$$

Each of the 8 base edges appears at each end, so there are 16 base edges, plus
the 8 side edges:

$$E=16+8=24$$

There are 8 vertices at each end:

$$V=16$$

**Check.** $F+V-E=10+16-24=2$ ✓.

self_checks.question: A cuboid box
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** A closed box measures 20 cm by 15 cm by 10 cm. Find its total
surface area and its volume.

**Solution.** Take $l=20$, $b=15$ and $h=10$ cm.

$$S=2(lb+bh+hl)=2(300+150+200)=2\times650=1300\ \text{cm}^2$$

$$V=lbh=20\times15\times10=3000\ \text{cm}^3$$

**Answer.** 1300 cm² of card; volume 3000 cm³.

**Check.** The six faces are two of 300 cm², two of 150 cm² and two of 200 cm²,
giving $600+300+400=1300$ ✓. The volume is the base area $300\times$ the height
$10=3000$ ✓.

self_checks.question: A cube painted on the outside
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** A cube of side 12 cm is painted all over. Find the area painted, and
the volume.

**Solution.** $S=6a^2=6\times144=864$ cm².

$$V=a^3=12^3=1728\ \text{cm}^3$$

**Answer.** 864 cm²; 1728 cm³.

**Check.** Each face is $12\times12=144$ cm², and six of them give 864 ✓.

self_checks.question: A triangular prism
self_checks.answer:
**Problem.** A triangular prism has a base that is a right-angled triangle with
legs 6 cm and 8 cm, and a length of 15 cm. Find its volume and its total surface
area.

**Solution.** **Volume.** Area of the triangular base
$=\frac12\times6\times8=24$ cm², so

$$V=24\times15=360\ \text{cm}^3$$

**Surface area.** Two triangular ends: $2\times24=48$ cm². The hypotenuse is
$\sqrt{6^2+8^2}=10$ cm, so the perimeter of the base is $6+8+10=24$ cm and the
three rectangular faces total $24\times15=360$ cm².

$$S=48+360=408\ \text{cm}^2$$

**Answer.** Volume 360 cm³; surface area 408 cm².

**Check.** The two triangular ends are 48 of the 408; the three rectangles are
$6\times15=90$, $8\times15=120$ and $10\times15=150$, which add to 360 ✓.

## Topics to cover

- the coordinate plane and plotting points
- distance between two points on the axes and in the plane
- simple shapes drawn from coordinates
- The coordinate plane
- Distance between two points
- Shapes from coordinates
- Reading a point in four quadrants
- 17.2.1 Points on the same horizontal or vertical line
- 17.2.2 Any two points: the distance formula

A coordinate is a pair of numbers that says exactly where a point is: how far
across and how far up. With that one idea, geometry becomes arithmetic — a shape
is a list of points, a distance is a subtraction and a square root, and a
straight line is an equation. This chapter fixes the vocabulary, shows how to
plot and read points, and shows how to find the distance between two of them.

## Chapter summary

- A point is written $(x,y)$, $x$ first; the axes divide the plane into four
  quadrants, and the signs of the coordinates decide which.
- On a horizontal line the distance is the difference of the $x$-coordinates; on
  a vertical line it is the difference of the $y$-coordinates.
- For any two points,
  $d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}$, which is Pythagoras' theorem.
- Joining points and comparing the side lengths and the angles identifies the
  shape; equal sides alone give a rhombus, not a square.
- A triangle is right-angled exactly when the squares of two sides add to the
  square of the third.

chapters.question_answers:
## Horizontal and vertical distances

**Problem.** Find the distance between (a) $A(2,3)$ and $B(7,3)$, and
(b) $C(2,3)$ and $D(2,-4)$.

**Solution.** (a) The $y$-coordinates are equal, so
$AB=7-2=5$ units.

(b) The $x$-coordinates are equal, so $CD=3-(-4)=7$ units.

**Check.** In (a) both points lie on the line $y=3$; in (b) both lie on
$x=2$ ✓. For (b), the subtraction $3-(-4)=7$ shows why the sign must be handled
carefully — the points are on opposite sides of the $x$-axis.

## Using the distance formula

**Problem.** Find the distance between $A(1,1)$ and $B(6,5)$.

**Solution.**

$$d=\sqrt{(6-1)^2+(5-1)^2}=\sqrt{25+16}=\sqrt{41}\approx6.4\ \text{units}$$

**Answer.** About 6.4 units.

**Check.** The horizontal difference is 5 and the vertical is 4, so the distance
must be between 5 and 7 (it is the hypotenuse of a 5-4-right triangle), and 6.4
lies in that interval ✓.

## Finding a missing coordinate

**Problem.** The distance between $A(2,3)$ and $B(7,y)$ is 13 units. Find the
possible values of $y$.

**Solution.**

$$13=\sqrt{(7-2)^2+(y-3)^2}=\sqrt{25+(y-3)^2}$$

Squaring both sides: $169=25+(y-3)^2$, so $(y-3)^2=144$ and $y-3=\pm12$.

$$y=15\quad\text{or}\quad y=-9$$

**Answer.** $y=15$ or $y=-9$.

**Check.** $y=15$: $d=\sqrt{25+144}=\sqrt{169}=13$ ✓. $y=-9$:
$d=\sqrt{25+(-12)^2}=\sqrt{169}=13$ ✓. Two answers, one above $A$ and one
below — and both are correct, because a circle of radius 13 about $A$ meets the
line $x=7$ twice.

## Identifying a quadrilateral

**Problem.** The points $A(0,0)$, $B(4,0)$, $C(4,3)$ and $D(0,3)$ are joined in
order. What shape is $ABCD$? Find its perimeter and area.

**Solution.** The four sides are

$$AB=4,\quad BC=3,\quad CD=4,\quad DA=3$$

Opposite sides are equal, and $AB$ is horizontal while $BC$ is vertical, so the
angle at $B$ is a right angle. The figure is a **rectangle**.

Perimeter $=4+3+4+3=14$ units, and
area $=4\times3=12$ square units.

**Check.** The diagonal $AC=\sqrt{(4-0)^2+(3-0)^2}=\sqrt{25}=5$, and the
diagonals of a rectangle are equal, so $BD$ must also be 5: from $B(4,0)$ to
$D(0,3)$, $BD=\sqrt{16+9}=5$ ✓.

## A right-angled triangle from coordinates

**Problem.** Show that the triangle with vertices $P(1,1)$, $Q(5,1)$ and
$R(1,4)$ is right-angled, and find its area.

**Solution.** Compute the three sides:

$$PQ=\sqrt{(5-1)^2+0}=4,\qquad PR=\sqrt{0+(4-1)^2}=3$$

$$QR=\sqrt{(5-1)^2+(1-4)^2}=\sqrt{16+9}=5$$

Now test: $3^2+4^2=9+16=25=5^2$. Since the squares of the two shorter sides add
to the square of the longest, the angle between $PQ$ and $PR$ is a right angle,
so the triangle is **right-angled at $P$**.

$$\text{Area}=\frac12\times4\times3=6\ \text{square units}$$

**Check.** $PQ$ is horizontal and $PR$ is vertical, so they are perpendicular by
inspection as well as by Pythagoras ✓.

## Distance and midpoint together

**Question.** For $P(2, 3)$ and $Q(8, 11)$, find (i) the distance $PQ$
(ii) the midpoint of $PQ$.

**Answer.**
(i) $PQ = \sqrt{(8-2)^2 + (11-3)^2} = \sqrt{36 + 64} = \sqrt{100} =
\textbf{10 units}$.
(ii) Midpoint $= \left(\frac{2+8}{2}, \frac{3+11}{2}\right) = \textbf{(5, 7)}$.

## Area of a triangle from coordinates

**Question.** Find the area of the triangle with vertices $A(1,1)$, $B(5,1)$
and $C(1,6)$.

**Answer.** $AB$ is horizontal with length $5 - 1 = 4$; $AC$ is vertical with
length $6 - 1 = 5$; the angle at $A$ is a right angle.
Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 5 = \textbf{10 square units}$.

chapters.name: Tessellation
topics: tessellation and its use in design
chapters.summary:
- A tessellation covers a plane with no gaps and no overlaps; at every vertex the
  angles add to exactly 360°.
- Exactly three regular polygons tessellate alone: the equilateral triangle
  ($6\times60°$), the square ($4\times90°$) and the regular hexagon
  ($3\times120°$).
- A polygon tessellates alone only if its interior angle divides 360° exactly.
- Regular pentagons and octagons cannot tessellate alone; an octagon can be used
  with a square ($135+135+90=360$).
- In semi-regular tessellations the same arrangement of two or more regular
  polygons occurs at every vertex, written as a list such as 4.8.8.
- Tilings use translation, reflection, rotation and glide reflection, and a
  periodic tiling repeats by translation.
chapters.text_content:
## Topics to cover

- tessellation and its use in design
- regular tessellation
- semi-regular tessellation
- symmetry in tessellation
- Tessellation
- Which regular polygons tessellate?
- Semi-regular tessellations
- Symmetry in tessellation

Tessellation is the covering of a surface with shapes, without gaps and without
overlaps. It is the mathematics behind tiled floors, brick walls, honeycomb and
much of the decoration on Nepali temples and *dhunge dhara* spouts. The
surprising result of the chapter is that only three regular polygons can do the
job on their own, and the reason is a single angle sum.

## Chapter summary

- A tessellation covers a plane with no gaps and no overlaps; at every vertex the
  angles add to exactly 360°.
- Exactly three regular polygons tessellate alone: the equilateral triangle
  ($6\times60°$), the square ($4\times90°$) and the regular hexagon
  ($3\times120°$).
- A polygon tessellates alone only if its interior angle divides 360° exactly.
- Regular pentagons and octagons cannot tessellate alone; an octagon can be used
  with a square ($135+135+90=360$).
- In semi-regular tessellations the same arrangement of two or more regular
  polygons occurs at every vertex, written as a list such as 4.8.8.
- Tilings use translation, reflection, rotation and glide reflection, and a
  periodic tiling repeats by translation.

## Study route

Read the topics and identify unfamiliar terms.

Close the book and explain the key ideas in your own words.

Attempt a worked example before revealing its solution.

Complete the chapter practice, correct mistakes, then mark the chapter revised.
chapters.question_answers:
## Does a regular octagon tessellate?

**Problem.** A regular octagon has an interior angle of 135°. Show that it
cannot tessellate on its own.

**Solution.** At a vertex we should need $k$ octagons with

$$k\times135°=360°\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad k=\frac{360}{135}=2\frac23$$

But $k$ must be a whole number, because a whole number of tiles must meet at the
vertex. $2\frac23$ is impossible.

Checking the nearest whole numbers: $2\times135=270°$ leaves a gap of 90°, and
$3\times135=405°$ overlaps by 45°.

**Answer.** A regular octagon cannot tessellate alone. It **can** be used in a
semi-regular tessellation together with a square: $135+135+90=360°$, so two
octagons and one square meet at every vertex.

**Check.** $135+135+90=360$ ✓, which is exactly the condition.

## Testing three polygons together

**Problem.** Can one regular triangle, one regular hexagon and one square meet
at a vertex without a gap?

**Solution.** The angles are 60°, 120° and 90°. Their sum is

$$60+120+90=270°$$

which is less than 360°, so there is a gap of 90° at the vertex. If another
square is added, the total becomes $270+90=360°$ ✓.

**Answer.** Three tiles alone leave a gap; a triangle, a hexagon and two squares
($60+120+90+90$) fit exactly.

**Check.** $60+120+90+90=360$ ✓.
